definition: Sung without instrumental accompaniment.
example: They sang an a cappella Mass.

definition: A tablet placed horizontally on top of the capital of a column as an aid in supporting the architrave.
example: I’ve heard merchants still use an abacus for adding things up in China.
etymology: From Late Middle English abacus, abagus, agabus (“abacus; art of counting with an abacus”), from Latin abacus, abax (“sideboard or table with a slab at the top; slab at the top of a column; counting board, sand table;

definition: Any of various large edible marine gastropods of the genus Haliotis having an ear-shaped shell with pearly interior.
etymology: From American Spanish abulón, from an indigenous language of the Monterey Bay area such as Rumsen/Southern Ohlone aūlun (“red abalone”)

definition: Make less active or intense.
example: To abate a writ.
etymology: From Middle English abaten, from Anglo-Norman abatre, from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere.

definition: An interruption in the intensity or amount of something.
example: The abatement of a nuisance is the suppression thereof.
etymology: From Middle English abatement, from Anglo-Norman abatre (“to abate”) (from Old French abatre), + -ment; equivalent to abate + -ment.

definition: A building where animals are butchered.
example: Once the cows reach maturity, they're sent to the abattoir.
etymology: Borrowed from French abattoir, from abattre (“to slaughter”) (cognate to abate) + -oir (“-ory”).

definition: The superior of a group of nuns.
example: The abbess was always after the nuns to keep the convent immaculately clean.
etymology: From Middle English abbesse, from Old French abeesse (French abbesse), from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbatissa, feminine of Latin abbas, abbatis (“abbot”).

definition: Give up, such as power, as of monarchs and emperors, or duties and obligations.
example: The King abdicated when he married a divorcee.
etymology: Compare typologically abandon, Russian отказа́ться (otkazátʹsja), отре́чься (otréčʹsja).

definition: Take away to an undisclosed location against their will and usually in order to extract a ransom.
example: To abduct children.
etymology: * (physiology): Back-formation from abduction.

definition: Especially of muscles; drawing away from the midline of the body or from an adjacent part.
Markedly different from an accepted norm.
example: Aberrant behavior.
etymology: From Latin aberrāns, present active participle of aberrō (“go astray; err”), from ab (“from”) + errō (“to wander”). See aberr.

definition: Find repugnant.
example: She abhors cats.
etymology: First attested in 1449, from Middle English abhorren, borrowed from Middle French abhorrer, from Latin abhorreō (“shrink away from in horror”), from ab- (“from”) + horreō (“stand aghast, bristle with fear”).

definition: With competence; in a competent capable manner.
example: Ably done, handled, planned, said.
etymology: From Middle English abeliche, abelyche, abilliche, abliche; equivalent to able + -ly.

definition: A large hairy humanoid creature said to live in the Himalayas.
etymology: First attested in 1921. Calque of Tibetan མི་སྡུག་གངས་མི (mi sdug gangs mi), from མི་སྡུག (mi sdug, “repulsive, unlovely, ugly, hideous”) and གངས་མི (gangs mi, “snowman”).

definition: Failing to accomplish an intended result.
example: An abortive revolt.
etymology: First attested in 1382, with the meaning "causing stillbirth or miscarriage".

definition: Habitual absence from work.
etymology: From absentee + -ism.

definition: Aromatic herb of temperate Eurasia and North Africa having a bitter taste used in making the liqueur absinthe.
etymology: * (wormwood; figuratively bitterness, sorrow): From Middle English absinthe. * (liquor): From Modern French absinthe.

definition: A dark bitter oil obtained from wormwood leaves; flavors absinthe liqueurs.
A rotary encoder that maintains position information when power is removed from the system.
example: The output of absolute encoders indicates the current position of the shaft, making them angle transducers.

definition: Freed from any question of guilt.
example: Is absolved from all blame.

definition: (physics) material in a nuclear reactor that absorbs radiation.
etymology: From absorb + -er.

definition: The trait of abstaining (especially from alcohol).
example: Abstention from alcohol.
etymology: First attested in 1521. Borrowed from French abstention, from Late Latin abstēntiō from Latin abstinēō (“withhold, to abstain”)

definition: Lie adjacent to another or share a boundary.
example: It was a time when Germany still abutted upon Russia.
etymology: From Middle English abutten, from Medieval Latin abuttare and Old French abuter, aboter, abouter (“to touch at one end, to come to an end, aim, reach”), from Old French but (“end, aim, purpose”);

definition: Yield to another's wish or opinion.
example: To accede to a request.
etymology: First attested in the early 15th century. From Middle English acceden, from Latin accēdō (“approach, accede”), formed from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”) (English cede). Compare French accéder.

definition: An instrument for measuring the acceleration of aircraft or rockets.
etymology: From accelerate + -o- + -meter.

definition: Satisfactoriness by virtue of conforming to approved standards.
etymology: From Latin acceptābilitās. By surface analysis, accept + -ability.

definition: The act of accumulating.
A method of accounting in which each item is entered as it is earned or incurred regardless of when actual payments are received or made.
A person who is employed to collect payments (as for rent or taxes).
example: He is a great accumulator of bad jokes.
etymology: From Latin accumulātor, agent noun of accumulō (“pile up”), accumulate + -or.

definition: (computer science) a register that has a built-in adder that adds an input number to the contents of the register.
Under a curse.
etymology: From Middle English acursed, from acursen (“to curse”), from Old English ācursian, from ā- + cursian, from curs (“curse”). First attested in the 13th century.

definition: Containing or expressing accusation.
example: An accusative forefinger.
etymology: First attested in the mid 15th century. From Middle English accusative, from Anglo-Norman accusatif or Middle French acusatif or from Latin accūsātīvus (“having been blamed”), from accūsō (“to blame”).

definition: The case of nouns serving as the direct object of a verb.
An analgesic for mild pain but not for inflammation; also used as an antipyretic; (Datril, Tylenol, Panadol, Phenaphen, Tempra, and Anacin III are trademarks of brands of acetaminophen tablets).
etymology: A shortening of the chemical name para-acetylaminophenol. By surface analysis, acet- + amino- + -phen.

definition: Relating to or containing acetic acid.
etymology: From French acétique, from Latin acētum (“vinegar”), from acēre (“to be sour”). By surface analysis, acet- + -ic.

definition: A colorless pungent liquid widely used in manufacturing plastics and pharmaceuticals.
The organic group of acetic acid (CH3CO-).
etymology: aceto- + -yl. From Latin acētum (“vinegar”) + Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “substance”).

definition: Colorless liquid acyl chloride (CH3COCl) that has a pungent odor.
The organic group of acetic acid (CH3CO-).
The organic group of acetic acid (CH3CO-).
A neurotransmitter that is a derivative of choline; released at the ends of nerve fibers in the somatic and parasympathetic nervous systems.
A person with a record of successes.
example: His son would never be the achiever that his father was.
etymology: From achieve + -er.

definition: Organic compounds containing the group -COX where X is a halogen atom.
The process of becoming acid or being converted into an acid.
etymology: Borrowed from French acidification, equivalent to acid + -ification.

definition: Artillery designed to shoot upward at airplanes.
example: The army fired upon us with ack-ack.
etymology: From ack (“A”) + ack (“A”), RAF WWI signalese for AA (“anti-aircraft”). (In modern signalese it would be called alpha-alpha.)

definition: The most common form of acne; usually affects people from puberty to young adulthood.
An impairment in understanding spoken language that is not attributable to hearing loss.
An antique record player; the sound of the vibrating needle is amplified acoustically.
An acoustic waveguide is a physical structure for guiding sound waves.
Of or relating to the science of acoustics.
example: Acoustic properties of a hall.
etymology: From acoustic + -al.

definition: Cause to come to know personally.
example: Permit me to acquaint you with my son.
etymology: From Middle English aqueynten, acointen, from Old French acointier, from Early Medieval Latin accognitāre, from Late Latin accognitus, past participle of accognoscō, from Latin cognoscō, from nōscō. See also quaint, know.

definition: Pronounce not guilty of criminal charges.
example: The jury acquitted the prisoner of the charge.
etymology: From Middle English aquī̆ten (“to give in return; to pay, repay; to redeem (a pledge, security), to make good (a promise); to make amends; to relieve of an obligation; to acquit, clear of a charge; to free; to deprive of;

definition: Marked by strong resentment or cynicism.
example: An acrimonious dispute.

definition: An athlete who performs acts requiring skill and agility and coordination.
The citadel in ancient Greek towns.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀκρόπολις (akrópolis, “acropolis; high part of a city”), from ᾰ̓́κρος (ắkros, “at the edge; extreme, outermost”) + πόλῐς (pólĭs, “city; the Athenian citadel”).

definition: Someone versed in the collection and interpretation of numerical data (especially someone who uses statistics to calculate insurance premiums).
Moved to action.
example: A man actuated by unworthy desires.

definition: (music) a composition played in adagio tempo (slowly and gracefully).
example: They played the adagio too quickly.
etymology: Proto-Indo-European *(H)yéh₁kt ~ *(H)ih₁kéntder.

definition: Inflexibly; unshakably.
example: Adamantly opposed to the marriage.
etymology: From adamant + -ly.

definition: The process of adapting to something (such as environmental conditions).
Device that enables something to be used in a way different from that for which it was intended or makes different pieces of apparatus compatible.
etymology: From adapt + -or.

definition: A person who adds numbers.
example: They sought out cost adders with an eye toward eliminating them.
etymology: From add + -er.

definition: (of eggs) no longer edible.
example: An addled egg.
etymology: From Middle English addled, adyld, equivalent to addle (“urine, liquid filth”) + -ed.

definition: (biochemistry) a nucleoside that is a structural component of nucleic acids; it is present in all living cells in a combined form as a constituent of DNA and RNA and ADP and ATP and AMP.
etymology: From German Adenosin, corresponding to aden(ine) + (rib)os(e) + -ine.

definition: Sticking fast.
etymology: From Middle English adherent, from Old French adherent, from Latin adhaerēns, present participle of adhaereō (“to stick to, cling”).

definition: A farewell remark.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish adiós; see there for more. Doublet of adieu.

definition: A tumor consisting of fatty tissue.
Close at the end of a session.
example: The court adjourned.
etymology: From Middle English ajournen, from Old French ajorner (French ajourner), from the phrase a jor (nomé) ("to an (appointed) day").

definition: The termination of a meeting.
example: At midnight we made a motion for adjournment and everyone went home tired.
etymology: From Middle English ajournement, from Old French ajornement, from ajourner (“to postpone”) + -ment. Equivalent to adjourn + -ment. Doublet of aggiornamento.

definition: Can be changed to different settings.
One who investigates insurance claims or claims for damages and recommends an effective settlement.
example: A bar adjuster in kiteboarding.
etymology: From adjust + -er.

definition: Large Indian stork with a military gait.
Furnishing added support.
example: An adjuvant discipline to forms of mysticism.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin adiuvant-, adjuvant- + English -ant (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘exhibiting a condition or process’; and forming agent nouns).

definition: By or for an administrator.
example: This decision was made administratively.
etymology: From administrative + -ly.

definition: Cautionary advice about something imminent (especially imminent danger or other unpleasantness).
example: A letter of admonition about the dangers of immorality.
etymology: From Middle English amonicioun, from Old French amonicion, from Latin admonitio, stem of admonere. The -d- was restored in English in the 17th century.

definition: A person who adopts a child of other parents as his or her own child.
etymology: From adopt + -er.

definition: Servile flattery; exaggerated and hypocritical praise.
example: He was uncomfortable with the adulation from his fans.
etymology: From French adulation, from Latin adulātio (“flattery”).

definition: Characterized by adultery.
example: An adulterous relationship.

definition: The word class that qualifies verbs or clauses.
example: Manner adverb.
etymology: Borrowed from French adverbe, from Latin adverbium, from ad- (“to”) + verb(um) (“word, verb”) + -ium, so called because it is used to supplement other words (not specifically verbs). By surface analysis, ad- + verb.

definition: (Gnosticism) a divine power or nature emanating from the Supreme Being and playing various roles in the operation of the universe.
etymology: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

definition: An airfield equipped with control tower and hangars as well as accommodations for passengers and cargo.
A medium that was once supposed to fill all space and to support the propagation of electromagnetic waves.
Diffusing warmth and friendliness.
example: An affable smile.
etymology: Borrowed from French affable, from Latin affābilis, from affor (“to address”), from ad + for (“to speak, to talk”). See fable. By surface analysis, af- + fable.

definition: Stick or fasten to.
example: Affix the seal here.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin affixus, perfect passive participle of affigere (from ad- + figere). By surface analysis, af- + fix.

definition: Abundant wealth.
example: His affluence was surpassed by no man.
etymology: From Old French affluence, from Latin affluentia. Only relation to antonym indigence is common Latinate suffix;

definition: A fan of bull fighting.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish aficionado (“fan, amateur”), past participle of aficionar (“to inspire fondness in someone, to get someone interested in something”). Doublet of affectionate.

definition: Being the one previously mentioned or spoken of.
example: Works of all the aforementioned authors.
etymology: From Middle English aforesaid(e), aforeseid(e), past participle of aforesayen, aforeseyen, aforeseien, aforeseggen; formed with the prefix afore- and the several forms of seien (“to say”). Equivalent to afore- + said.

definition: Especially of a ship's lines etc.
example: With its sails afoul.
etymology: From a- + foul.

definition: Care and treatment of a convalescent patient.
etymology: From after- + care.

definition: A glow sometimes seen in the sky after sunset.
A tremor (or one of a series of tremors) occurring after the main shock of an earthquake.
etymology: From after- + shock.

definition: An afterimage of a taste.
example: Many people think certain artificial sweeteners have an unpleasant aftertaste.
etymology: From after- + taste.

definition: (Christian theology) the love of God or Christ for mankind.
etymology: From a- + gape. First known use by John Milton in Paradise Lost (1667).

definition: A colloidal extract of algae; used especially in culture media and as a gelling agent in foods.
etymology: Borrowed from Malay agar-agar (“jelly”).

definition: Tropical American plants with basal rosettes of fibrous sword-shaped leaves and flowers in tall spikes; some cultivated for ornament or for fiber.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀγαυή (Agauḗ, “Agave”), from ἀγαυός (agauós, “noble, illustrious”).

definition: Chiefly tropical and xerophytic plants: includes Dracenaceae (Dracaenaceae); comprises plants that in some classifications are divided between the Amaryllidaceae and the Liliaceae.
Continuing forever or indefinitely.
example: The ageless themes of love and revenge.
etymology: From age + -less.

definition: A jumbled collection or mass.
Struck with fear, dread, or consternation.
example: I was aghast when the incident unfolded in front of me.

definition: Try to stir up public opinion.
example: He was greatly agitated by the news.

definition: Causing or tending to cause anger or resentment.
One who agitates; a political troublemaker.
etymology: From agitate + -or.

definition: The marketplace in ancient Greece.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá).

definition: Largest known toad species; native to Central America; valuable destroyer of insect pests.
A Japanese martial art employing principles similar to judo.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 合(あい)気(き)道(どう) (aikidō, “aikido”, literally “way of adapting the spirit”), from 合(あい) (ai, “together, unify”) + 気(き) (ki, “spirit; breath”) + 道(どう) (dō, “way”). Doublet of hapkido.

definition: Aimlessly drifting.
example: An aimless life.
etymology: From aim + -less.

definition: A military attache who is a commissioned or warrant officer in an air force.
An atomizer to spray paint by means of compressed air.
etymology: From air + brush.

definition: The crew of an aircraft.
example: The aircrew ran to the bomber.
etymology: From air + crew.

definition: A member of an aircrew.
Delivery of supplies or equipment or personnel by dropping them by parachute from an aircraft.
example: Until then, front line troops will be supplied by airdrop.
etymology: From air + drop.

definition: The framework and covering of an airplane or rocket (excluding the engines).
example: This airframe has 2600 flight hours on it; the powerplant has just over 800.
etymology: From air + frame.

definition: A chamber that provides access to space where air is under pressure.
etymology: From air + lock.

definition: Letters and packages that are transported by aircraft.
example: To send a letter by airmail.
etymology: From air + mail.

definition: A letter sent by air mail.
The speed of an aircraft relative to the air in which it is flying.
etymology: From air + speed.

definition: Slightly open.
example: The door was ajar.
etymology: From Middle English ajar, on char (“on [the] turn”), from on (“on”) + char (“turn, occasion”), from Old English ċierr, cyrr (“turn”), from ċierran (“to turn, convert”), equivalent to a- + char.

definition: A compact fine-textured, usually white gypsum used for carving.
A crystalline amino acid that occurs in many proteins.
example: Potatoes can be a good source of alanine.

definition: In an alarming manner.
example: It grew alarmingly fast.
etymology: From alarming + -ly.

definition: A person who alarms others needlessly.
example: I don't mean to be an alarmist, but I do think you should prepare yourself for the worst.
etymology: From alarm + -ist.

definition: A white linen liturgical vestment with sleeves; worn by priests.
A simple water-soluble protein found in many animal tissues and liquids.
etymology: Borrowed from French albumine, from Latin albumen. Compare albumen.

definition: Related to or concerned with alchemy.
etymology: From alchemy + -ical.

definition: A small recess opening off a larger room.
example: The house was situated in a leafy alcove.
etymology: From French alcôve, from Spanish alcoba or Portuguese alcova, from Arabic القُبَّة (al-qubba, “vault, chamber with vaulted roof”). Doublet of qubba.

definition: Inability to perceive written words.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + λέξις (léxis, “speech”) + -ia.

definition: Sprouted alfalfa seeds.
Of or relating to alga.
etymology: From alga + -al.

definition: Place in a line or arrange so as to be parallel or straight.
etymology: From a- + line, possibly from Middle English alinen (“copulate”), Middle French aligner.

definition: Lessen the intensity of or calm.
example: To allay popular excitement.
etymology: From Middle English alayen, aleyen, aleggen, from Old English āleċġan (“to put, place, lay down, lay aside, throw down, give up, cease from, abandon; put down, allay, suppress, abolish, conquer, destroy, overcome, refute;

definition: A brisk and lively tempo.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian allegro.

definition: Any substance that can cause an allergy.
example: Pollen, dust, and spores are common allergens.
etymology: Syncopated compound of allergy + -gen, coined on the model of pharmaceutical words such as pathogen and antigen.

definition: (of pain or sorrow) made easier to bear.
example: My alleviated sorrow no longer crushes me.

definition: The feeling that comes when something burdensome is removed or reduced.
etymology: From alleviate + -ion.

definition: Use of the same consonant at the beginning of each stressed syllable in a line of verse.
etymology: From New Latin allīterātiō, from allīterātus, from allīterō, from Latin ad (“to, towards, near”) and lītera (“a letter”).

definition: Make a more or less disguised reference to.
example: He alluded to the problem but did not mention it.
etymology: From Middle French alluder, from Latin alludere (“to play with or allude”), from ad + ludere (“to play”). See also al-.

definition: Loss of hair (especially on the head) or loss of wool or feathers; in humans it can result from heredity or hormonal imbalance or certain diseases or drugs and treatments (chemotherapy for cancer).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin alōpecia, from the Ancient Greek ἀλωπεκία (alōpekía, “fox-mange”), from ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx, “fox”) + -ία (-ía, a formative ending used in Ancient Greek, especially used in naming diseases).

definition: A lipoprotein that transports cholesterol in the blood; composed of a high proportion of protein and relatively little cholesterol; high levels are thought to be associated with decreased risk of coronary heart disease and atherosclerosis.
Ovoviviparous amphibian of the Alps.
Successive change from one thing or state to another and back again.
example: A trill is a rapid alternation between the two notes.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin alternatio; compare French alternation. By surface analysis, alternate + -ion.

definition: Any of various plants of the genus Althaea; similar to but having smaller flowers than genus Alcea.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin althaea.

definition: A musician who plays the alto saxophone.
etymology: From alto saxophone + -ist.

definition: Any of various forms of aluminum oxide occurring naturally as corundum.
etymology: From the combining form of Latin alumen + -a.

definition: A branch of the maxillary artery that supplies the alveolar process.
A consonant articulated with the tip of the tongue near the gum ridge.
A particular environment or surrounding influence.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French ambiance.

definition: A mixture of nectar and pollen prepared by worker bees and fed to larvae.
etymology: From Latin ambrosia (“food of the gods”), from Ancient Greek ἀμβροσία (ambrosía, “immortality”), from ἄμβροτος (ámbrotos, “immortal”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βροτός (brotós, “mortal”).

definition: To make better.
example: They offered some compromises in an effort to ameliorate the situation.
etymology: Alteration of meliorate after French améliorer.

definition: In an amicable manner.
example: They separated amicably.
etymology: From Middle English amcabily, equivalent to amicable + -ly. Piecewise doublet of amiably.

definition: A water solution of ammonia.
Of or related to the amnion or characterized by developing an amnion.
example: Amniotic membrane.
etymology: Likely borrowed from French amniotique, from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (amníon, “vessel for collecting the blood from sacrifices”). Equivalent to amnion + -otic.

definition: The fluid-filled cavity that surrounds the developing embryo.
The serous fluid in which the embryo is suspended inside the amnion.
Thin innermost membranous sac enclosing the developing embryo of higher vertebrates (reptiles, birds and mammals).
A sulfate derivative of amphetamine that is used as a stimulant for the central nervous system.
To an ample degree or in an ample manner.
example: These voices were amply represented.
etymology: From ample + -ly.

definition: Someone who has had a limb removed by amputation.
etymology: From French amputée, (past participle of amputer (“to amputate”)), from Latin amputatus, perfect passive participle of amputare (“to amputate”).

definition: Something located at a time when it could not have existed or occurred.
Chronologically misplaced.
example: English public schools are anachronistic.
etymology: From anachronist + -ic.

definition: A lack of vitality.
Loss of bodily sensation with or without loss of consciousness.
etymology: From an- + -aesthesia.

definition: A word or phrase spelled by rearranging the letters of another word or phrase.
etymology: Late 16th century, either from Middle French anagramme or Latin anagramma, formed on Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”). Analyzable as ana- (“up, back”) + -gram (“letter”).

definition: Capable of relieving pain.
example: An analgesic effect.
etymology: From analgesia (“absence of pain”) + -ic, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ἄλγησις (álgēsis, “sense of pain”), from ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). Compare -algia.

definition: Related to the hypersensitivity known as anaphylaxis.
example: Anaphylactic shock.

definition: A severe and rapid and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reaction to a substance (especially a vaccine or penicillin or shellfish or insect venom) to which the organism has become sensitized by previous exposure.
Hypersensitivity reaction to the ingestion or injection of a substance (a protein or drug) resulting from prior contact with a substance.
Of or relating to the structure of the body.
example: Anatomical features.
etymology: From French anatomique or its etymon Latin anatomicus, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομικός (anatomikós, “skilled in anatomy”). By surface analysis, anatomy + -ic.

definition: A ring of muscle that contracts to close an opening.
With respect to anatomy.
example: Anatomically correct.
etymology: From anatomical + -ly.

definition: A male television reporter who coordinates a broadcast to which several correspondents contribute.
etymology: From anchor + man. Senses 1 and 4 derive from sense 2, sense 3 is literal.

definition: Tiny fishes usually canned or salted; used for hors d'oeuvres or as seasoning in sauces.
etymology: From Spanish anchoa, from Genoese Ligurian anciôa or related Corsican anchjuva, anciua. The term's ultimate origin is unclear;

definition: Butter blended with mashed anchovies.
Vinaigrette and mashed anchovies.
Paste made primarily of anchovies; used in sauces and spreads.
West Indian tree bearing edible fruit resembling mango.
Tomato and cheese pizza with anchovies.
Made of white sauce and mashed anchovies.
Used of a single unit or thing; not two or more.
example: ‘ane’ is Scottish.

definition: Any woodland plant of the genus Anemone grown for its beautiful flowers and whorls of dissected leaves.
etymology: From Latin anemōnē, from Ancient Greek ἀνεμώνη (anemṓnē), from ἄνεμος (ánemos, “wind”) + matronymic suffix -ώνη (-ṓnē, “daughter of”).

definition: Live associated with sea anemones.
A specialist who administers an anesthetic to a patient before they are treated.
etymology: From anesthesiology + -ist.

definition: The branch of medical science that studies and applies anesthetics.
The sound of a bell rung in Roman Catholic churches to announce the time when the Angelus should be recited.
The sound of a bell rung in Roman Catholic churches to announce the time when the Angelus should be recited.
The formation of new blood vessels.
etymology: From angio- + -genesis.

definition: Roentgenographic examination of blood vessels after injection of a radiopaque contrast medium; produces an angiogram.
etymology: From angio- + -graphy.

definition: Experiencing intense pain especially mental pain.
example: An anguished conscience.

definition: A person who owns, shows, judges, or breeds animals.
A feeling of ill will arousing active hostility.
A negatively charged ion.
Native to Egypt but cultivated widely for its aromatic seeds and the oil from them used medicinally and as a flavoring in cookery.
etymology: From Middle English anys, borrowed from Old French anis, from Latin anīsum, from Ancient Greek ἄνισον (ánison), from Egyptian jnst.

definition: Cookie made without butter and flavored with anise seed.
An essential oil extracted from the seeds of Pimpinella anisum (aniseed), having a pungent liquorice-like smell.
Native to Egypt but cultivated widely for its aromatic seeds and the oil from them used medicinally and as a flavoring in cookery.
Liquorice-flavored seeds, used medicinally and in cooking and liquors.
