etymology: From Middle English baronie, baronye, from Old French baronie, equivalent to baron + -y.

definition: Put in or stored in a barrel.
example: Barreled beer.

definition: Preventing entry or exit or a course of action.
example: A barricaded street.

definition: (Judaism) an initiation ceremony marking the 12th birthday of a Jewish girl and signifying the beginning of religious responsibility.
Any of several masses of subcortical grey matter at the base of each cerebral hemisphere that seem to be involved in the regulation of voluntary movement.
Self-consciously timid.
example: I never laughed, being bashful; lowering my head, I looked at the wall.
etymology: 16th-century apheresis of abashed + -ful (“full of”).

definition: A raised vertical board with basket attached; used to play basketball.
Smooth-haired breed of hound with short legs and long ears.
etymology: From French bassette, from Italian bassetta.

definition: A tenor clarinet; pitched in the key of F below the B-flat clarinet.
etymology: From German Bassetthorn, translation of French cor de bassette, from Italian corno di bassetto.

definition: Smooth-haired breed of hound with short legs and long ears.
etymology: From French basset (“basset hound”), nominalization of Old French adjective basset (“short-legged”), from bas (“short, low”).

definition: A double-reed instrument; the tenor of the oboe family.
etymology: Borrowed from French basson.

definition: Strong woody fibers obtained especially from the phloem of from various plants.
example: I thought I saw Him in the Long Walk there, by the bed of Nelly Roche, tending a fallen flower with a wisp of bast.
etymology: From Middle English bast, from a back-formation of Middle English bastard.

definition: Strong woody fibers obtained especially from the phloem of from various plants.
A building containing dressing rooms for bathers.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English bathhous, bathous, from Old English bæþhūs (“bathhouse”), equivalent to bath + house.

definition: A loose-fitting robe of towelling; worn after a bath or swim.
etymology: From bath + robe.

definition: A dyed fabric; a removable wax is used where the dye is not wanted.
Stuffing made of rolls or sheets of cotton wool or synthetic fiber.
Furnish with battens.
example: Batten ships.

definition: A clay-like mineral; the chief ore of aluminum; composed of aluminum oxides and aluminum hydroxides; used as an abrasive and catalyst.
etymology: Derived from the name of Les Baux in France, plus + -ite. The /ks/ in the English pronunciation is from a spelling pronunciation.

definition: A street of small shops (especially in Orient).
Herb with greyish leaves found along the east coast of North America; used as an ornamental plant.
A minor parish official who serves a ceremonial function.
etymology: From Middle English bedel, bidel, from Old English bydel (“warrant officer, apparitor”), from Proto-West Germanic *budil, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz (“herald”), equivalent to bid + -le.

definition: Larvae live in and feed on growing or stored beans.
An outstanding example of its kind.
example: His roses were beauties.
etymology: Either a back-formation from beauty or a clipping of thereof.

definition: The act of making something more beautiful.
example: Thanks to the beautification efforts, the appearance of the highway has vastly improved.
etymology: First attested in 1600, from beautify (“to make beautiful”) + -ication.

definition: Make more beautiful.
etymology: From Middle English beutifien, from Old French beaute (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fine”), + -ify, from Latin facio (“make”).

definition: The study and creation of visual works of art.
A hitch used for temporarily tying a rope to the middle of another rope (or to an eye).
Deposited or arranged in horizontal layers.
example: Three-bedded room.

definition: An upright geranium having scalloped leaves with a broad color zone inside the margin and white or pink or red flowers.
Confined to bed (by illness).
Cubes of beef cooked in hot oil and then dipped in various tasty sauces.
Cut of meat from a loin of beef.
Beef loin muscle.
Made greater or stronger.
example: Beefed-up sales efforts.

definition: Muscular and heavily built.
example: A beefy wrestler.
etymology: From beef + -y.

definition: A farmer who keeps bees for their honey.
etymology: From bee + keeper.

definition: The cultivation of bees on a commercial scale for the production of honey.
etymology: From bee + keeping.

definition: A yellow to brown wax secreted by honeybees to build honeycombs.
example: The candle was made entirely of natural beeswax.
etymology: From bee + -s- + wax.

definition: Become of; happen to.
example: He promised that no harm would befall her.
etymology: From Middle English bifallen, from Old English befeallan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifallan, from Proto-Germanic *bifallaną; equivalent to be- + fall.

definition: (of offspring) generated by procreation.
example: Naturally begotten child.

definition: Be envious of; set one's heart on.
etymology: From Middle English bigrucchen (“to grumble at”), equivalent to be- (“at, about, over”) + grudge. Compare also English begrouch.

definition: Highly attractive and able to arouse hope or desire.
example: The voice was low and beguiling.

definition: A Muslim woman of high rank in India or Pakistan.
etymology: From be- + gum.

definition: Cut the head of.
example: The French King was beheaded during the Revolution.
etymology: From Middle English beheden, bihefden, biheveden, from Old English behēafdian (“to behead”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihaubudōn, *bihaubidōn (“to behead”), equivalent to be- (“off, away”) + head.

definition: A style of operatic singing.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian bel canto (literally “beautiful singing”).

definition: A witty or clever person with a fine mind.
etymology: Borrowed from French bel esprit.

definition: Later than usual or than expected.
example: I belatedly wished her a happy birthday.
etymology: From belated + -ly.

definition: A bell tower; usually stands alone unattached to a building.
A belittling comment.
A morel whose fertile portion resembles a bell and is attached to the stipe only at the top.
Perennial Eurasian herb with reddish bell-shaped flowers and shining black berries; extensively grown in United States; roots and leaves yield atropine.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian belladonna (altered by folk etymology: bella donna (“beautiful lady”)) from Medieval Latin blādōna (“nightshade”), of Gaulish origin.

definition: Amaryllis of South Africa often cultivated for its fragrant white or rose flowers.
Perennial Eurasian herb with reddish bell-shaped flowers and shining black berries; extensively grown in United States; roots and leaves yield atropine.
Having a belly.
example: Full-bellied knife.

definition: A very loud utterance (like the sound of an animal).
example: His bellow filled the hallway.

definition: A dive in which the abdomen bears the main force of impact with the water.
Greyish-blue North American kingfisher with a chestnut band on its chest.
Valuable source of caviar and isinglass; found in Black and Caspian seas.
etymology: Borrowed from Russian белу́га (belúga), from бе́лый (bélyj, “white”). In modern standard Russian, белу́га (belúga) denotes the fish Huso huso only, while белу́ха (belúxa) denotes the cetacean.

definition: Roe of beluga sturgeon usually from Russia; highly valued.
Deeply absorbed in thought.
example: As distant and bemused as a professor listening to the prattling of his freshman class.

definition: Pantropical tree of usually seacoasts sometimes cultivated as an ornamental for its rounded heart-shaped leaves and showy yellow and purple flowers; yields valuable pink to dark red close-grained wood and oil from its seeds.
A French liqueur originally made by Benedictine monks.
A form of amphetamine.
Of or relating to or happening on the bottom under a body of water.
etymology: From benthos + -ic. By surface analysis, benth- + -ic.

definition: A region including the bottom of the sea and the littoral zones.
A severe rebuke.
example: He deserved the berating that the coach gave him.

definition: Ask for or request earnestly.
etymology: From Middle English besechen, bisechen, prefixed form of Old English sēċan (“to seek or inquire about”); compare the doublet beseek, from the same dialect that gave seek.

definition: The stupid brutal quality of a beast.
etymology: From bestial + -ity.

definition: An isomer of carotene that is found in dark green and dark yellow fruits and vegetables.
etymology: From beta + carotene.

definition: A form of interferon that is produced by fibroblasts and have antiviral effects; used in the treatment of multiple sclerosis.

A lipoprotein that transports cholesterol in the blood; composed of moderate amount of protein and a large amount of cholesterol; high levels are thought to be associated with increased risk of coronary heart disease and atherosclerosis.
A leaf of a vine from the betel pepper.
etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese bétele, from Malayalam വെറ്റില (veṟṟila) or Tamil வெற்றிலை (veṟṟilai).

definition: A leaf of a vine from the betel pepper.
Southeastern Asian palm bearing betel nuts (scarlet or orange single-seeded fruit with a fibrous husk).
Asian pepper plant whose leaves are chewed with betel nut (seed of the betel palm) by southeast Asians.
Two surfaces meeting at an angle different from 90 degrees.
example: To give a bevel to the edge of a table or a stone slab.

definition: Gears that mesh at an angle.
A hand tool consisting of two rules that are hinged together so you can draw or measure angles of any size.
A large gathering of people of a particular type.
example: He was surrounded by a bevy of beauties in bathing attire.
etymology: From Middle English bevey, of uncertain origin, possibly Anglo-Norman.

definition: Confusion resulting from failure to understand.
example: She looked around in bewilderment.
etymology: From bewilder + -ment.

definition: Capturing interest as if by a spell.
example: Bewitching smile.
etymology: From bewitch + -ing.

definition: Relating to or dealing with bibliography.
etymology: From bibliography + -ic.

definition: A salt of carbonic acid (containing the anion HCO3) in which one hydrogen atom has been replaced; an acid carbonate.
etymology: From bi- + carbonate.

definition: A quarrel about petty points.
etymology: See also Old English becca (“pickax”), Dutch bikken (“to hack”), German picken (“to peck, pick at”), Old Norse bikkja (“to plunge into water”); compare also German Low German bickern (“to nibble, gnaw”).

definition: Riding a bicycle.
Dwell.
etymology: From Middle English biden, from Old English bīdan (“to stay, continue, live, remain, delay; wait for, await, expect; endure, experience, find; attain, obtain;

definition: A tap that provides water for a bidet.
Reactive or functioning or allowing movement in two usually opposite directions.
etymology: From bi- + directional.

definition: Aromatic shrub of arid regions of western North America having hoary leaves.
Having a prominent belly.
Wild sheep of mountainous regions of western North America having massive curled horns.
etymology: From big + horn.

definition: Wild sheep of mountainous regions of western North America having massive curled horns.
A loop in a rope.
example: The bight of a horse's knee.
etymology: From Middle English bight, biȝt, byȝt (also bought, bowght, bouȝt; see bought), from Old English byht (“bend, angle, corner;

definition: Water accumulated in the bilge of a ship.
example: Complete bilge.
etymology: Likely derived from bulge. Compare Middle English bulgen (“to ground or scuttle a ship”).

definition: Either of two lengthwise fins attached along the outside of a ship's bilge; reduces rolling.
A pump to remove bilgewater.
Water accumulated in the bilge of a ship.
(nautical) a well where seepage drains to be pumped away.
The ability to speak two languages colloquially.
etymology: From bilingual + -ism.

definition: A room in which billiards is played.
A room in which billiards is played.
Characterized by great swelling waves or surges.
example: Billowy storm clouds.

definition: Occurring twice a month.
example: The organization's bimonthly meetings allow for two discussions each quarter.
etymology: From bi- + monthly.

definition: Relating to both eyes.
example: Binocular vision.
etymology: Borrowed from French binoculaire.

definition: A light microscope adapted to the use of both eyes.
Vision involving the use of both eyes.
Of or relating to or consisting of two terms.
example: Binomial expression.
etymology: Formed from Late Latin binōmium + -al. The derivation of binōmium is unclear. It was used by Gerard of Cremona in the 12th century.

definition: A theoretical distribution of the number of successes in a finite set of independent trials with a constant probability of success.
A theorem giving the expansion of a binomial raised to a given power.
Someone with special training in biochemistry.
etymology: Back-formation from biochemistry.

definition: The branch of engineering science in which biological science is used to study the relation between workers and their environments.
etymology: From bio- + engineering.

definition: The branch of ethics that studies moral values in the biomedical sciences.
etymology: From bio- + ethics.

definition: Hazard to humans or the environment resulting from biological agents or conditions.
etymology: From bio- + hazard.

definition: A loose one-piece garment worn to protect the wearer against dangerous biological or chemical agents.
Pertaining to biology or to life and living things.
etymology: From biology + -ic.

definition: The use of bacteria or viruses or toxins to destroy men and animals or food.
A branch of biology that studies biological phenomena and observations by means of statistical analysis.
etymology: From bio- + metrics.

definition: Physics as applied to biological problems.
Any of the branches of natural science dealing with the structure and behavior of living organisms.
etymology: From bio- + science.

definition: Of or relating to living organisms.
etymology: From Ancient Greek βιωτικός (biōtikós, “of life”), from βίος (bíos, “life”). Equivalent to bio- + -otic.

definition: (ecology) a group of interdependent organisms inhabiting the same region and interacting with each other.
A B vitamin that aids in body growth.
etymology: Borrowed from German Biotin, from Ancient Greek βίοτος (bíotos, “life”) + the suffix -in.

definition: Consisting of or combining two races.
example: A biracial committee.
etymology: From bi- + racial.

definition: A person with a strong interest in birds.
Wingless insect with mouth parts adapted for biting; mostly parasitic on birds.
The characteristic sound produced by a bird.
example: First a solitary blackbird started up, and soon the whole forest was alive with birdsong.
etymology: From bird + song.

definition: A regularly recurrent spasm of pain that is characteristic of childbirth.
The territorial jurisdiction of a bishop.
example: Later that year, he was appointed to the bishopric of Lindesmeere.
etymology: From Middle English bischopriche, from Old English bisċoprīċe, equivalent to bishop + -ric (compare German Reich).

definition: A heavy brittle diamagnetic trivalent metallic element (resembles arsenic and antimony chemically); usually recovered as a by-product from ores of other metals.
etymology: From German Wismuth. Often explained as a miner's contraction of wis mat "white mass" from Old High German hwiz "white".

definition: Someone who bites.
example: Not all dogs are biters.
etymology: From Middle English biter, bitere, equivalent to bite + -er. Cognate with West Frisian biter (“biter”), Dutch bijter (“biter”), German Low German Bieter (“biter”), German Beißer (“biter”).

definition: Wingless insect with mouth parts adapted for biting; mostly parasitic on birds.
Minute two-winged insect that sucks the blood of mammals and birds and other insects.
Alcoholic liquor flavored with bitter herbs and roots.
example: Tonic water dashed with bitters.

definition: Occurring every two weeks.
etymology: From bi- + week + -ly. The sense referring to twice a week can be analyzed as bi- + weekly.

definition: Important dark-colored edible food and game fish of Australia.
Widely cultivated currant bearing edible black aromatic berries.
Low shrub of the eastern United States bearing shiny black edible fruit; best known of the huckleberries.
Medium-sized larch of Canada and northern United States including Alaska having a broad conic crown and rust-brown scaly bark.
A highly venomous southern African mamba dreaded because of its quickness and readiness to bite.
etymology: Predominantly the Zulu language iMamba

definition: A morel whose pitted fertile body is attached to the stalk with little free skirt around it; the fertile body is grey when young and black in old age.
Eurasian herb naturalized in America having white flowers and poisonous hairy foliage and bearing black berries that are sometimes poisonous but sometimes edible.
Australian tree that yields tanning materials.
Brown weevil that infests stored grain especially rice.
An eraser that removes chalk marks from blackboard.
A substance used to produce a shiny protective surface on footwear.
Perennial of Arctic Europe having large white flowers with inflated calyx.
Bearing or characterized by a blade or sword; often used in combination.
example: He fought on, broken-bladed but unbowed.

definition: In a blank and uncomprehending manner.
example: She stared at him blankly.
etymology: From blank + -ly.

definition: A worker who bleaches (cloth or flour etc.).
example: There could be a rough crowd out in the bleachers.
etymology: From Middle English blechere, equivalent to bleach + -er. Compare Dutch bleker, Swedish blekare. The seating was so named because the boards were bleached by the sun.

definition: Catch unawares, especially with harmful consequences.
example: The economic downturn blindsided many investors.
etymology: From blind + side.

definition: Anesthesia of an area supplied by a nerve; produced by an anesthetic agent applied to the nerve.
Preventing entry or exit or a course of action.
example: The blockaded harbor.

definition: Resembling a block in shape.
example: The oldest video games had crude, blocky graphics.
etymology: From block + -y.

definition: North American dogtooth having solitary white flowers with yellow centers and blue or pink exteriors.
A process in which liquid blood is changed into a semisolid mass (a blood clot).
A breed of large powerful hound of European origin having very acute smell and used in tracking.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English blodhound, blodhond; equivalent to blood + hound.

definition: Destitute of blood or apparently so.
example: The bloodless carcass of my Hector sold.
etymology: From Middle English blodles, from Old English blōdlēas (“bloodless”).

definition: (of an eye) reddened as a result of locally congested blood vessels; inflamed.
example: Bloodshot eyes.
etymology: From blood + shot.

definition: A flower that blooms in a particular way.
example: A night bloomer.
etymology: From Middle English blomer, from blome (“iron ingot”) (modern English bloom), from Old English blōma.

definition: Absorbent paper used to dry ink.
Utter while crying.
Variety inhabiting the Great Lakes.
Sometimes placed in genus Scilla.
etymology: From blue + bell.

definition: Liqueur infused with blueberries, blueberry juice, or blueberry flavoring.
example: Blueberry liqueur is a flavorful, versatile alcoholic drink that goes great simply on the rocks.

definition: Of lavender tinged with blue.
Made dull or blunt.
Noisy confusion and turbulence.
example: He was awakened by the bluster of their preparations.
etymology: From Middle English blusteren (“to wander about aimlessly”); however, apparently picking up the modern sense from Middle Low German blüstren (“to blow violently”; compare later Low German blustern, blistern).

definition: A tenant in someone's house.
example: The student body consisted primarily of boarders, except for a few children belonging to the school staff.
etymology: From board + -er.

definition: Exhibiting self-importance.
example: He wrote a boastful autobiography, recording all his great deeds.
etymology: From Middle English bostful, equivalent to boast + -ful.

definition: A shed at the edge of a river or lake; used to store boats.
etymology: From boat + house.

definition: A man who drives or rides in a boat.
etymology: From Middle English boteman, botman, bateman. Equivalent to boat + -man.

definition: A winder around which thread or tape or film or other flexible materials can be wound.
example: Ignition coils using a bobbin molded from high-performance polyester withstand open-circuit bench tests to 70kV.
etymology: Borrowed from French bobine, recorded in English since 1530.

definition: A handmade lace worked on a pillow with threads wound on bobbins; the pattern is marked out on the pillow by pins.
The momentary juggling of a batted or thrown baseball.
example: The second baseman made a bobble but still had time to throw the runner out.
etymology: * (noun): from bob + -le (diminutive suffix). * (verb): from bob + -le (frequentative suffix). Compare bauble.

definition: Formerly two short sleds coupled together.
etymology: From bobs, the short runners on which the bobsleigh is based (as opposed to a usual sleigh on long runners continuing all the way along the vehicle); further etymology unclear.

definition: A small Hispanic shop selling wine and groceries.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish bodega, from Latin apothēca (“storehouse”), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of apotheke and boutique. In New York, it was popularized by the Puerto Rican community.

definition: Part of a dress above the waist.
A parasitic louse that infests the body of human beings.
A variety of aster (Oclemena nemoralis).
An imaginary monster used to frighten children.
example: The bogeyman of a Halloween-candy poisoner behind every door has animated occasional moral panics against trick-or-treating.
etymology: From bogey + -man.

definition: Standard formulations uniformly found in certain types of legal documents or news stories.
example: They put that boilerplate on all the warning labels.
etymology: From boiler + plate.

definition: A cord fastened around the neck with an ornamental clasp and worn as a necktie.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish bola (“ball”) and Portuguese bola (“ball”). First attested in 1818.

definition: A cord fastened around the neck with an ornamental clasp and worn as a necktie.
The rounded seed-bearing capsule of a cotton or flax plant.
etymology: From Middle English bolle (“pod; shell”) and Middle Dutch bolle (“round object”), from Frankish *bollo, all ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bullô (“round object; bowl”). More at bowl.

definition: A cord fastened around the neck with an ornamental clasp and worn as a necktie.
etymology: From Philippine Spanish bolo, from Tagalog bolo.

definition: Long heavy knife with a single edge; of Philippine origin.
A cord fastened around the neck with an ornamental clasp and worn as a necktie.
A small round soft mass (as of chewed food).
etymology: From Late Latin bōlus (“clod of earth, lump”), plural bōlī, from Ancient Greek βῶλος (bôlos, “clod, lump”). Doublet of bole.

definition: An instrument in a Jacquard loom that raises or lowers the harness, which carries and guides the warp thread so that the weft will either lie above or below it, which in turn creates the pattern.
Cast, hurl, or throw repeatedly with some missile.
example: The enemy's stronghold was bombarded for 3 hours straight.
etymology: From Middle English bombard, from Middle French bombarde (“a bombard, mortar, catapult"; also "a bassoon-like musical instrument”), from Latin bombus (“buzzing; booming”).

definition: Ostentatiously lofty in style.
Having bones especially many or prominent bones.
The owner or manager of an inn.
etymology: After Boniface, the innkeeper in George Farquhar's 1707 comedic play The Beaux' Stratagem.

definition: Flesh of mostly Pacific food fishes of the genus Sarda of the family Scombridae; related to but smaller than tuna.
An imaginary monster used to frighten children.
etymology: By alteration from bogeyman.

definition: Minute wingless psocopterous insects injurious to books and papers.
A gambler who accepts and pays off bets (especially on horse races).
etymology: Clipping of bookmaker + -ie.

definition: Characterized by diligent study and fondness for reading.
example: A bookish farmer who always had a book in his pocket.
etymology: From book + -ish.

definition: A maker of books; someone who edits or publishes or binds books.
etymology: From Middle English bokmakere, boke maker, equivalent to book + maker. The gambling term came from the archaic phrase make book or make a book, used in 19th century England.

definition: A person who pays more attention to formal rules and book learning than they merit.
etymology: From book + worm.

definition: A person who drinks alcohol to excess habitually.
etymology: From booze + -er (agent noun suffix) or (pub) + -er (relational noun suffix).

definition: Given to or marked by the consumption of alcohol.
example: His boozy drinking companions.
etymology: From booze + -y.

definition: A man who patrols the borders of a country.
Relating to or marked by qualities associated with the north wind.
example: Boreal forests.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin boreālis (“northern”), from Boreās, from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās, “personification of the north wind”).

definition: A drill for penetrating rock.
etymology: From bore + -er.

definition: A plant fertilizer which formula contains boron.
Causing irritation or annoyance.
example: Aircraft noise is particularly bothersome near the airport.
etymology: From bother + -some.

definition: A lady's bedroom or private sitting room.
etymology: Borrowed from French boudoir, from bouder (“to sulk”), of Germanic origin.

definition: Any of the larger branches of a tree.
example: When the bough breaks, the cradle will fall. (Rock-a-bye Baby).
etymology: PIE word *bʰeh₂ǵʰús From Middle English bough (“branch of a bush or tree, especially a main branch; limb of an animal or person; something resembling a branch (such as a plant root or branch of a nerve);

definition: A clear seasoned broth.
etymology: First attested 1656, from French bouillon, from the verb bouillir (“to boil”), from Old French boillir, from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).

definition: A cube of evaporated seasoned meat extract.
Like a bower; leafy and shady.
example: A bowery lane.
etymology: From bower + -y.

definition: A beam built up from boards; has a hollow rectangular cross section.
Creeping evergreen shrub of southeastern United States having small shiny boxlike leaves and flavorless berries.
Resembling a box in rectangularity.
etymology: From box + -y.

definition: A man who is a stupid incompetent fool.
etymology: Attested since the 1910s in American English, of uncertain origin. The term may derive from Spanish bozal, a term originally for a recently-imported slave and then "someone who speaks (Spanish) poorly".

definition: A measure of how densely information is packed on a storage medium.
Distasteful and unpleasant; spoiled by mixture.
example: A thin brackish gruel.
etymology: From Scottish brack (from Middle Dutch brac (“brackish”)) + -ish.

definition: Trimming used to decorate clothes or curtains.
etymology: From Middle English breydynge; equivalent to braid + -ing.

definition: The part of the brain continuous with the spinal cord and comprising the medulla oblongata and pons and midbrain and parts of the hypothalamus.
Persuade completely, often through coercion.
example: The propaganda brainwashed many people.
etymology: From brain + wash, a calque of Chinese 洗腦 /洗脑 (xǐnǎo), literally to wash the brain. Usage via U.S. military during the Korean War.

definition: Having or marked by unusual and impressive intelligence.
example: Our project needs brainy women.
etymology: From Middle English brayny; equivalent to brain + -y.

definition: Cooked by browning in fat and then simmering in a closed container.
Any of various rough thorny shrubs or vines.
etymology: From Middle English brembel, from Old English bræmbel, from earlier brǣmel, brēmel, from dialectal Proto-West Germanic *brāmil, diminutive of *brām (English broom).

definition: Any prickly shrub of the genus Rubus bearing edible aggregate fruits.
The property of being very new.
etymology: From brand-new + -ness.

definition: In a brazen manner.
example: He spoke brazenly.
etymology: From brazen + -ly.

definition: Large metal container in which coal or charcoal is burned; warms people who must stay outside for long times.
etymology: From Middle English brasiere, from brasen (“to cover with brass”), from Old English brasian, bræsian (“to cover with brass”). By surface analysis, bras(s) + -ier.

definition: One whose earnings are the primary source of support for their dependents.
etymology: From bread + winner, where to win = to earn. Compare West Frisian breawinning (“livelihood”, literally “bread-winning”), Dutch broodwinning (“livelihood”).

definition: Moving at very high speed.
example: A breakneck pace.
etymology: From break + neck.

definition: A protective structure of stone or concrete; extends from shore into the water to prevent a beach from washing away.
etymology: From break + water. Compare Dutch breekwater (“breakwater”). Compare firebreak.

definition: Flesh of various freshwater fishes of North America or of Europe.
etymology: Compare broom, and German brennen (as in ein Schiff brennen).

definition: A swimming stroke; the arms are extended together in front of the head and swept back on either side accompanied by a frog kick.
etymology: From breast + stroke.

definition: (used in the plural) trousers ending above the knee.
A life buoy in the form of a ring with short breeches for support; used to transfer people from a ship.
A craftsman skilled in building with bricks.
etymology: From Middle English brekelayeer, brekelayer, equivalent to brick + layer.

definition: Masonry done with bricks and mortar.
etymology: From brick + -work.

definition: A light roll rich with eggs and butter and somewhat sweet.
etymology: Borrowed from French brioche.

definition: In a brisk manner.
example: She walked briskly in the cold air.
etymology: From brisk + -ly.

definition: A brush that is made with the short stiff hairs of an animal or plant.
Any fern of the genus Trichomanes having large pinnatifid often translucent fronds; most are epiphytic on tree branches and twigs or terrestrial on mossy banks.
Grasses of grasslands and woodlands having large gracefully arching spikes with long bristles beneath each spikelet.
Pointed like bristles.
A decorative pin worn by women.
etymology: From Middle English broche, from Old French broche, from Vulgar Latin *brocca, originally a feminine form of Latin broccus, perhaps ultimately of Gaulish origin (see Scottish Gaelic bròg). Doublet of brochure.

definition: Having relatively broad rather than needlelike or scalelike leaves.
Thick heavy expensive material with a raised pattern.
etymology: From Occitan brocada and Spanish and Portuguese brocado, influenced by French brocart, from Italian broccato, from brocco, ultimately from Gaulish.

definition: A thick and heavy shoe.
etymology: An alteration of brogue.

definition: An oven or part of a stove used for broiling.
Any of the salts of hydrobromic acid; formerly used as a sedative but now generally replaced by safer drugs.
example: My adviser at college was a bromide who had not had an original thought in years.
etymology: From brom- + -ide. First used in the sense “dull person” by American artist, art critic, poet, author and humorist Gelett Burgess.

definition: A sensitive photographic paper with pure silver bromide emulsions that produce neutral black or ‘cold’ blue-black image tones.
European plant with racemes of sweet-scented flowers; widely cultivated as an ornamental.
Relating to or associated with the bronchi.
example: Bronchial tubes.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin bronchiālis. By surface analysis, bronchium + -al.

definition: Arteries that accompany the bronchioles.
Respiratory disorder characterized by wheezing; usually of allergic origin.
Pneumonia characterized by acute inflammation of the walls of the bronchioles.
Either of the two main branches of the trachea.
Veins serving the bronchi; empty into the azygos vein.
An adult, male fan of the show My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic.
(of skin) having a tan color from exposure to the sun.
example: A young bronzed Apollo.

definition: Pathology in which iron accumulates in the tissues; characterized by bronzed skin and enlarged liver and diabetes mellitus and abnormalities of the pancreas and the joints.
A cosmetic powder that comes in various shades of brown, meant to create an impression of tanned skin.
example: Sculpting your face with a bronzing powder will make it appear slimmer.
etymology: From bronze (“to tan skin”) + -er (agent noun suffix).

definition: Common large songbird of eastern United States having reddish-brown plumage.
(of skin) deeply suntanned.
Greatly annoyed; out of patience.
example: Bob was browned off when he was passed over for promotion.

definition: Having brown speckles.
A reddish brown sandstone; used in buildings.
etymology: From brown + stone.

definition: A conventional name for a bear used in tales following usage in the old epic ‘Reynard the Fox’.
etymology: From Middle Dutch bruun (“brown”) via William Caxton's 1485 translation of a Dutch version of the legend of Reynard the Fox. Bruin is the bear, named for his brown color. Doublet of brown.

definition: (of champagne) extremely dry.
etymology: From French brut (“raw”), from Middle French brut, from Old French brut, from Latin brūtus (“heavy”).

definition: Resembling a beast; showing lack of human sensibility.
example: A dull and brutish man.
etymology: From brute + -ish.

definition: Of or evidencing buboes.
example: Bubonic plague.
etymology: From Latin būbō (stem būbōn-) + English -ic.

definition: The most common form of the plague in humans; characterized by chills, prostration, delirium and the formation of buboes in the armpits and groin; does not spread from person to person.
Inspired with confidence.
example: Felt bucked up by his success.

definition: A wild horse that is vicious and difficult or impossible to break in.
A perennial that is valuable as sheep forage in the United States.
North American nightshade with prickly foliage and racemose yellow flowers.
Aspirin coated with a substance capable of neutralizing acid (trade name Bufferin).
Shaped like a bulb.
etymology: From bulb + -ous or alteration of Latin bulbosus.

definition: Any of various irises having a rootstock formed like a bulb.
Plant growing from a bulb.
A disorder of eating seen among young women who go on eating binges and then feel guilt and depression and self-condemnation.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek βουλῑμῐ́ᾱ (boulīmĭ́ā, “ravenous hunger”), from βούλῑμος (boúlīmos) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).

definition: The ratio of the change in pressure acting on a volume to the fractional change in volume.
Large powerful breed developed by crossing the bulldog and the mastiff.
Coarse prickly weed having pale yellow flowers and yellow berrylike fruit; common throughout southern and eastern United States.
A machine that cuts raw dough into small portions and rolls each to obtain balls of the same weight and shape.
A onetime custom during courtship of unmarried couples occupying the same bed without undressing.
Give a tip or gratuity to in return for a service, beyond the compensation agreed on.
etymology: Borrowed from Yagara bang (“dead”).

definition: A grass of the genus Cenchrus.
Medium to large deciduous oak of central and eastern North America with ovoid acorns deeply immersed in large fringed cups; yields tough close-grained wood.
Marsh plant having elongated linear leaves and round prickly fruit.
A loose garment (usually with veiled holes for the eyes) worn by Muslim women especially in India and Pakistan.
etymology: From Hindustani برقع / बुरक़ा (burqā), from Classical Persian برقع (burqa'), from Arabic بُرْقُع (burquʕ).

definition: Coarse jute fabric.
etymology: Uncertain. Attested since about 1695 in the spelling bore-lap, borelapp. Likely from burel (“a coarse woollen cloth”) + lap (“flap of a garment”), where the first element is from Middle English burel, borel.

definition: A bag made of burlap.
Made smooth and bright by or as if by rubbing; reflecting a sheen or glow.
example: A burnished brass knocker.

definition: A loose garment (usually with veiled holes for the eyes) worn by Muslim women especially in India and Pakistan.
example: The Taliban forced all women to wear the burqa.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi बुरक़ा (burqā) / Urdu بُرْقَع (burqa')), from Classical Persian بُرْقَع (burqa'), from Arabic بُرْقُع (burquʕ).

definition: Any of several plants of the genus Bidens having yellow flowers and prickly fruits that cling to fur and clothing.
A small fluid-filled sac located between movable parts of the body especially at joints.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursa (“purse”), from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa); compare purse and bourse, which are doublets.

definition: The treasury of a public institution or religious order.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursaria, from bursarius.

definition: Tall hat; worn by some British soldiers on ceremonial occasions.
etymology: Various theories; probably from the surname Busby.

definition: A honeysuckle shrub of southern Russia to central Asia.
An insulating liner in an opening through which conductors pass.
etymology: From bush (“metal lining of the axle hole of a wheel or touch hole of a gun”) + -ing.

definition: Stiff perennial of the eastern United States having small linear leaves and numerous tiny white flower heads.
In a busy manner.
example: They were busily engaged in buying souvenirs.
etymology: From Middle English busily, busiliche, bisili, bisiliche, equivalent to busy + -ly.

definition: Occurs in natural gas; used in the manufacture of rubber and fuels.
The business of a butcher.
etymology: From butcher + -ing.

definition: A building where animals are butchered.
etymology: From Middle English bocherie, from Old French. See butcher for more.

definition: Plant bearing somewhat drum-shaped fruit having dark green rind with greyish markings.
North American walnut tree having light-brown wood and edible nuts; source of a light-brown dye.
example: He made a delicious butternut soup.
etymology: From butter + nut.

definition: Plant bearing buff-colored squash having somewhat bottle-shaped fruit with fine-textured edible flesh and a smooth thin rind.
North American walnut tree having light-brown wood and edible nuts; source of a light-brown dye.
A hard brittle candy made with butter and brown sugar.
Reinforce with a buttress.
example: Buttress the church.
etymology: From Old French ars bouterez (noun, literally “supporting arcs”), from bouterez (adjective), oblique plural of bouteret (rare in the singular), from Frankish *bôtan, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to push”).

definition: A hydrocarbon radical (C4H9).
A flammable alcohol derived from butanes and used for solvents.
The act of purchasing back something previously sold.
etymology: Deverbal from buy back.

definition: A rule adopted by an organization in order to regulate its own affairs and the behavior of its members.
etymology: From Middle English bylawe, bilawe, partly from Old English bīlage (“bylaw”) and partly from a variant of Middle English byrelawe, birlawe, from Old Norse býjar (“town's; settlement's”) + lǫg (“laws; jurisdiction”).

definition: A small tent used as a dressing room beside the sea or a swimming pool.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish cabaña and Portuguese cabana, both from Late Latin capanna. Doublet of cabane and cabin.

definition: Low-growing fan-leaved palm of coastal southern United States having edible leaf buds.
The area for food preparation on a ship.
etymology: From Dutch kabuis, kombuis (“galley, kitchen”) or German Low German Kabüüs (“galley”), from Middle Dutch cabûse and Middle Low German kabûs, kabûse respectively.

definition: A loud harsh or strident noise.
etymology: From French cacophonie, from Ancient Greek κακοφωνία (kakophōnía), from κακός (kakós, “bad”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”), equivalent to caco- + -phony.

definition: An attendant who carries the golf clubs for a player.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from Scots caddie (“military cadet; young man; ragamuffin; person engaged to run errands; person hired to assist a golfer”), from French cadet (“army cadet; younger sibling”), from capdet (“captain;

definition: A yellow sulfide used chiefly as a pigment.
Relating to abdominal delivery.
etymology: From Caesar + -ean, but see also Caesarean section § Etymology.

definition: The delivery of a fetus by surgical incision through the abdominal wall and uterus (from the belief that Julius Caesar was born that way).
The delivery of a fetus by surgical incision through the abdominal wall and uterus (from the belief that Julius Caesar was born that way).
Small rough-haired breed of terrier from Scotland.
(Italian cuisine) squid prepared as food.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian calamari, plural of calamaro, from Latin calamarius, from calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed, ink pen”).

definition: Composed of or containing or resembling calcium carbonate or calcite or chalk.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin calcārius (“of or pertaining to lime”), derived from calx (“lime”). Similar to calcium.

definition: A common mineral consisting of crystallized calcium carbonate; a major constituent of limestone.
etymology: From Latin calx + -ite.

definition: A bicarbonate that is a major cause of hard water, with chemical formula Ca(HCO3)2.
A saltlike binary compound (CaH2) used as a reducing agent and source of hydrogen.
A white crystalline salt made by the action of lactic acid on calcium carbonate; used in foods (as a baking powder) and given medically as a source of calcium.
A white salt (CaSO4).
A large crater caused by the violent explosion of a volcano that collapses into a depression.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish caldera (“cauldron”), from Late Latin caldāria (“warm bath”), from Latin caldārium. Doublet of chowder.

definition: A machine that smooths or glazes paper or cloth by pressing it between plates or passing it through rollers.
etymology: * From Middle French calandre, from Late Latin calendra, altered from Latin cylindrus (“cylinder”), from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros). Doublet of calander and cylinder.

definition: Capturing a calf with a lasso and binding its feet.
A variety of aster (Symphyotrichum lateriflorum).
An instrument for measuring the distance between two points.
etymology: Variant of caliber.

definition: An area of skin that is thick or hard from continual pressure or friction (as the sole of the foot).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin callum (“hard skin”). Displaced Old English wearr.

definition: A highly decorated ceremonial pipe of Amerindians; smoked on ceremonial occasions (especially as a token of peace).
etymology: From a Norman variant of Old French chalumeau (imported to Canada with Norman colonists), from Latin calamellus, diminutive of calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos).

definition: A slight convexity (as of the surface of a road).
etymology: From Old French cambre (“bent”), from Latin camurum, from camur (“arched”).

definition: An arch with a straight horizontal extrados and a slightly arched intrados.
A portable television camera and videocassette recorder.
etymology: Blend of camera + recorder. Appears to be a borrowing from Japanese カムコーダー (kamukōdā), an original registered trademark filed for by Sony in 1981. First use appears c. 1982 in The Economist.

definition: Any of several shrubs or small evergreen trees having solitary white or pink or reddish flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Camellia, named after Moravian botanist Joseph Kamel (‘Camellus’) (1661–1706). The Czech surname Kamel is a variant of Kamil.

definition: Any plant of the genus Silene.
etymology: Likely from Middle English campion, a variant of champioun; see champion. In classical times, the rose campion was fitted in garlands used to crown victors.

definition: Encrusted with sugar or syrup.
example: Candied grapefruit peel.

definition: An apple that is covered with a candy-like substance (usually caramelized sugar).
Fruit cooked in sugar syrup and encrusted with a sugar crystals.
Eurasian tulip with small flowers blotched at the base.
A form of solitaire that involves gambling.
A factory where food is canned.
example: Jim had a summer job cleaning and packing salmon at the fish cannery.
etymology: From can + -ery.

definition: (Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Church) the act of admitting a deceased person into the canon of saints.
etymology: From canonize + -ation.

definition: Accorded sacrosanct or authoritative standing.
A variety of muskmelon vine having fruit with a tan rind and orange flesh.
etymology: From French cantaloup, from Italian Cantalupo (a place name), from Italian canto + lupo, literally "howl of the wolf".

definition: A variety of muskmelon vine having fruit with a tan rind and orange flesh.
Ride at a canter.
example: The men cantered away.
etymology: Short for Canterbury pace, from the supposed easy pace of medieval pilgrims to Canterbury.

definition: Project as a cantilever.
etymology: First attested in the 1660s, probably from cant (“slope, edge, corner”) + lever, but the earliest form (c. 1610) was cantlapper.

definition: Bridge constructed of two cantilevers that meet in the middle.
Of or relating to capacitance.
example: Capacitive touchscreens are all glass and designed for use in ATMs and similar kiosk-type applications.
etymology: From capacity + -ive.

definition: A sensor that detects anything that is conductive or has a dielectric different from that of air.
example: Size and spacing of the capacitive sensor are both very important to the sensor's performance.

definition: Annual of tropical South America having edible purple fruits.
Southern African herb with white bell-shaped flowers.
Any of several South African plants grown for the profusion of usually yellow daisylike flowers and mounds of aromatic foliage.
A tube of small internal diameter; holds liquid by capillary action.
Supply with capital, as of a business by using a combination of capital used by investors and debt capital provided by lenders.
Favoring or practicing capitalism.
Surrender under agreed conditions.
example: He argued and hollered for so long that I finally capitulated just to make him stop.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1537; borrowed from Medieval Latin capitulātus perfect passive participle of Medieval Latin capitulō (“(originally; of a book, text) to draw up under distinct headings;

definition: The head of a branch of an organized crime syndicate.
etymology: Shortening of capotasto, from Italian.

definition: A long overcoat with a hood that can be pulled over the head.
etymology: Borrowed from French capote. Doublet of capot and kaput.

definition: A final touch; a crowning achievement; a culmination.
etymology: From Middle English capston; equivalent to cap + stone.

definition: Attract; cause to be enamored.
etymology: See Etymology 1. Equivalent to captive + -ate (adjective-forming suffix)

definition: A person who captures and holds people or animals.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin captor, from Latin capiō. English usage began around 1688.

definition: Burnt sugar; used to color and flavor food.
Hard outer covering or case of certain organisms such as arthropods and turtles.
etymology: Compare Catalan carabassa, Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”), Latin scarabaeus (the source of scarab); also Spanish galápago (“kind of turtle”). Doublet of calipash.

definition: A toxic colorless flammable liquid (CS2); used in the manufacture of rayon and cellophane and carbon tetrachloride and as a solvent for rubber.
Relating to or containing the carbonyl group.
etymology: From carbon + -yl.

definition: The bivalent radical CO.
Relating to or containing the carboxyl group or carboxyl radical.
An organic acid characterized by one or more carboxyl groups.
Any substance that produces cancer.
etymology: From carcino- + -gen.

definition: Rhizomatous herb of India having aromatic seeds used as seasoning.
Yarn that has undergone the carding process, but not the combing process.
An abnormal rate of muscle contractions in the heart.
Inadequate blood flow to the heart muscles; can cause angina pectoris.
The valve between the distal end of the esophagus and the stomach; the physiological sphincter at the esophagogastric junction.
(grammar) A word that expresses a countable quantity.
example: Cardinal numerals expressing numbers below 100 are single words, while those expressing higher numbers are syntactically composite.

definition: Small bright red and blue aquarium fish from streams in Brazil and Colombia.
A disorder (usually of unknown origin) of the heart muscle (myocardium).
etymology: From cardio- + myopathy.

definition: Eurasian plant with pink to purple-red spice-scented usually double flowers; widely cultivated in many varieties and many colors.
etymology: From Middle French carnation (“flesh color, complexion”), either via Italian carnagione (“flesh color”) or directly from Late Latin carnātiō (“fleshiness”), from Latin carō (“flesh, meat”) + ātiō (“-ation”).

definition: Large family of herbs or subshrubs (usually with stems swollen at the nodes).
An orange isomer of an unsaturated hydrocarbon found in many plants; is converted into vitamin A in the liver.
etymology: From car(r)ot + -ene.

definition: A plexus of nerves surrounding the internal carotid artery.
Of or relating to the wrist.
example: Carpal tunnel syndrome.
etymology: From the Latin carpālis.

definition: Any of the eight small bones of the wrist of primates.
A passageway in the wrist through which nerves and the flexor muscles of the hands pass.
example: He played that rhythm game so much he got carpal tunnel.

definition: Covered with or as if with carpeting or with carpeting as specified; often used in combination.
example: The carpeted hallway.

definition: Floor covering consisting of a piece of thick heavy fabric (usually with nap or pile).
example: As part of the restoration of the house, they took up the carpeting and left the hardwood floors exposed.

definition: American vulture smaller than the turkey buzzard.
Any of various plants of the genus Stapelia having succulent leafless toothed stems resembling cacti and large foul-smelling (often star-shaped) flowers.
Any of various ill-smelling brown-capped fungi of the order Phallales.
The making of maps and charts.
etymology: From French cartographie, from carte (“map”) (ultimately from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “map”)) + -graphie (“-graphy”) (from γράφω (gráphō, “write”)); carto- (“map”) + -graphy.

definition: Covered or protected with or as if with a case.
example: Knights cased in steel.

definition: A milk protein used in making e.g. plastics and adhesives.
etymology: From French caséine, formed from Latin cāseus (“cheese”) + -ine.

definition: Made from casein; used for e.g. plywood and cabinetwork.
A water-base paint made with a protein precipitated from milk.
A window sash that is hinged (usually on one side).
A window with one or more casements.
Kidney-shaped nut edible only when roasted.
A starch made by leaching and drying the root of the cassava plant; the source of tapioca; a staple food in the tropics.
Any of various trees or shrubs of the genus Cassia having pinnately compound leaves and usually yellow flowers followed by long seedpods.
etymology: From Latin cassia (“cinnamon”), from Ancient Greek κασσία, κασία, κάσια (kassía, kasía, kásia), from Hebrew קְצִיעָה (qəṣīʿā), from Aramaic קְצִיעֲתָא (qəṣīʿătā), from קְצַע (qṣaʿ, “to cut off”). Compare Kezia.

definition: A person who is rejected (from society or home).
example: Robinson Crusoe was a famous fictional castaway.
etymology: Deverbal from cast away.

definition: A person who breeds and cares for cats.
A sudden violent change in the earth's surface.
Severely destructive.
example: Cataclysmic nuclear war.
etymology: From cataclysm + -ic.

definition: Acceleration of a chemical reaction induced by the presence of material that is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κατάλυσις (katálusis, “dissolution”), from καταλύω (katalúō, “I dissolve”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + λύω (lúō, “I loose”). By surface analysis, cata- + -lysis.

definition: Change by catalysis or cause to catalyze.
A boat with two parallel hulls held together by single deck.
Arranged into categories.
Someone who provides food and service (as for a party).
etymology: From cater + -er.

definition: (psychoanalysis) purging of emotional tensions.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κάθαρσις (kátharsis, “cleansing, purging”), from καθαίρω (kathaírō, “I cleanse”). Coined in the dramatic-emotional sense by Aristotle.

definition: Hairy aromatic perennial herb having whorls of small white purple-spotted flowers in a terminal spike; used in the past as a domestic remedy; strongly attractive to cats.
example: Some cats go bonkers over catnip; others ignore it.
etymology: Compound of cat + nep, nip (“catnip”), from Middle English nep, from Old English nepte, from Proto-West Germanic *nepetā, from Latin nepeta (“catnip”).

definition: Marked by or arising from malice.
example: A catty remark.
etymology: From cat + -y. Compare Dutch kattig, which also means “subtly hostile” and is formed the same way (kat + -ig); see also catfight.

definition: Slanted across a polygon on a diagonal line.
example: Set off in a catty-corner direction across the vacant lot.
etymology: Corruption of cater-corner under influence from catty.

definition: Regional anesthesia resulting from injection of an anesthetic into the caudal end of the spinal canal; now largely replaced by epidural anesthesia.
The tail of fishes and some other aquatic vertebrates.
A comprehensive term for any proceeding in a court of law whereby an individual seeks a legal remedy.
Producing an effect.
example: Poverty as a causative factor in crime.
etymology: From French causatif, from Latin causātīvus (“causative, pertaining to a lawsuit, accusative”), from causa (“cause”); see cause (verb) and -ive.

definition: A potassium compound often used in agriculture and industry.
A procession of people traveling on horseback.
etymology: From French cavalcade, from Old French cavalcade, from Old Italian cavalcata, from cavalcare (“to ride on horseback”), from Medieval Latin caballicō, from Vulgar Latin caballus (“horse”). Doublet of chevauchee.

definition: Either of a pair of large venous sinuses in the cranial cavity.
A hollow chamber whose dimensions allow the resonant oscillation of electromagnetic or acoustic waves.
The sound made by corvine birds.
etymology: Onomatopoeic

definition: A coral reef off the southern coast of Florida.
etymology: ] From Spanish cayo, from Taíno.

definition: Uninterrupted in time and indefinitely long continuing.
example: The ceaseless thunder of surf.
etymology: From cease + -less.

definition: The act of ceding.
The act of ceding back.
Someone who plays a violoncello.
A transparent paperlike product that is impervious to moisture and used to wrap candy or cigarettes etc.
etymology: Genericized trademark. Blend of cellulose + diaphane.

definition: Highly flammable substance made from cellulose nitrate and camphor; used in e.g. motion-picture and X-ray film; its use has decreased with the development of nonflammable thermoplastics.
etymology: Former trademark of Celluloid Manufacturing Company; from cellulose + -oid.

definition: A monument built to honor people whose remains are interred elsewhere or whose remains cannot be recovered.
example: A cenotaph was erected for him in Gaul, while his body was taken to Rome and inclosed in a magnificent tomb.
etymology: From French cénotaphe, from Ancient Greek κενός (kenós, “empty”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis ceno- + -taph.

definition: A line that bisects a plane figure.
etymology: From center + line.

definition: A metric unit of length equal to one hundredth of a meter.
etymology: Borrowed from French centimètre; equivalent to centi- + metre.

definition: Either of two gyri on either side of the central sulcus.
The property of being central.
etymology: From central + -ity.

definition: The act of consolidating power under a central control.
example: The centralization of power in the general government.
etymology: From French centralisation, equivalent to central + -ization or centralize + -ation.

definition: The central or most important feature.
etymology: From centre + piece.

definition: A major division of the vertebrate brain; situated above the medulla oblongata and beneath the cerebrum in humans.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cerebellum, diminutive of cerebrum.

definition: Of or relating to the brain and spinal cord.
example: Cerebrospinal fluid.
etymology: From cerebro- + spinal.

definition: Meningitis caused by bacteria and often fatal.
Clear liquid produced in the ventricles of the brain; fills and protects cavities in the brain and spinal cord.
A nerve plexus lying beneath the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
One of 7 vertebrae in the human spine located in the neck region.
Relating to abdominal delivery.
etymology: From Caesar + -ean, but see also Caesarean section § Etymology.

definition: The delivery of a fetus by surgical incision through the abdominal wall and uterus (from the belief that Julius Caesar was born that way).
The delivery of a fetus by surgical incision through the abdominal wall and uterus (from the belief that Julius Caesar was born that way).
Soreness or irritation of the skin caused by friction.
A metal pan over a heater; used to cook or to keep things warm at the table.
Covering (usually rope or canvas) of a line or spar to protect it from friction.
A long chair; for reclining.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French chaise. Doublet of cathedra and chair.

definition: Composed of or containing or resembling calcium carbonate or calcite or chalk.
example: A chalky texture.
etymology: From chalk + -y.

definition: Having compartmental chambers.
example: A spiral chambered seashell.
etymology: From chamber (“noun”) + -ed.

definition: Eurasian plant with apple-scented foliage and white-rayed flowers and feathery leaves used medicinally; in some classification systems placed in genus Anthemis.
The main vein of ore in a deposit.
Area around the altar of a church for the clergy and choir; often enclosed by a lattice or railing.
etymology: From Old French chancel. Doublet of cancellus.

definition: A person of subnormal intelligence.
etymology: The noun is derived from change + -ling (suffix with the sense ‘immature; small’). Sense 6 (“idiot, simpleton”) is from the idea that foolish children had been left by magical creatures (sense 1).

definition: An event that results in a transformation.
etymology: Deverbal from change over.

definition: Dense vegetation consisting of stunted trees or bushes.
etymology: From Spanish chaparral, from chaparro (“evergreen oak”) + -al, from Basque txaparro, from txapar, from sapar.

definition: Widely spreading evergreen shrub of southwestern United States with flower heads in a leafy panicle.
Speedy largely terrestrial bird found from California and Mexico to Texas.
Spiny evergreen xerophytic shrub having showy rose and purple flowers and forming dense thickets; of dry rocky mountain slopes of California.
Silvery-leaved California herb with purple flowers.
Be characteristic of.
example: What characterizes a Venetian painting?
etymology: From character + -ise.

definition: A polymer consisting of two or more different monomers.

definition: A copper salt made by the action of sulfuric acid on copper oxide.
A person employed to write advertising or publicity copy.

definition: Evergreen North American honeysuckle vine having coral-red or orange flowers.
In a hearty manner.
example: Ever most cordially yours,.

definition: Not having a cord.

etymology: From cord + -less.

definition: A cut pile fabric with vertical ribs; usually made of cotton.
etymology: Origin uncertain. Probably from cord + duroy (“a 17th century coarse fabric made in England”).

(dated slang) a remarkable or excellent thing or person.

definition: A bottle opener that pulls corks.

etymology: From cork (“stopper”) + -y.

European white-flowered weed naturalized in North America.
European herb with bright yellow flowers; a common weed in grain fields.

definition: A field planted with corn.

definition: Starch prepared from the grains of corn; used in cooking as a thickener.

definition: A goat's horn filled with grain and flowers and fruit symbolizing prosperity.

definition: A practical consequence that follows naturally.

definition: Flower arrangement consisting of a circular band of foliage or flowers for ornamental purposes.
etymology: From Middle English coronal, from Anglo-Norman coronal, from Latin corōnālis (“related to a crown”), from corōna (“a crown”).

definition: (phonetics) articulated with the flexible front part of the tongue.
The suture between the parietal and frontal bones of the skull.
Inadequate blood flow to the heart muscles; can cause angina pectoris.
Occlusion of a coronary artery caused either by progressive atherosclerosis or by a blood clot.
A small crown; usually indicates a high rank but below that of sovereign.

definition: Having material or physical form or substance.

Confirmation that some fact or statement is true through the use of documentary evidence.

etymology: From Middle English corroboracioun, borrowed from Late Latin corrōborātiō (“strengthening”).

A cataract that affects the lens cortex.
A corticosteroid hormone (trade name Cortone Acetate) normally produced by the adrenal cortex; is converted to hydrocortisone.
A curve whose equation in Cartesian coordinates is of the form y = a cos x.

definition: The practice of beautifying the face and hair and skin.
etymology: From French cosmétologie. By surface analysis, cosmetics + -ology.

definition: A person trained to travel in a spacecraft.
example: The Russians called their astronauts cosmonauts.
etymology: Borrowed from Russian космона́вт (kosmonávt), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “universe”) + ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”). By surface analysis, cosmo- + -naut.

definition: Of or relating to or near a rib.
etymology: From French costal and its etymon Medieval Latin costālis, from Latin costa (“rib”). As a Spanish unit, via Spanish costal. By surface analysis, costa + -al. Piecewise doublet of coastal.

definition: The cartilages that connect the sternum and the ends of the ribs; its elasticity allows the chest to move in respiration.
Groove between the ribs where the nerves and blood vessels are.
Dressed in clothing characteristic of a period, country, or class.
That can be counted.

etymology: From Middle English countable, equivalent to count (“to enumerate”) + -able.

definition: A weight that balances another weight.
etymology: From counter- + balance.

definition: In the direction opposite to the rotation of the hands of a clock.

definition: A culture with lifestyles and values opposed to those of the established culture.
etymology: From counter- + culture.

definition: Actions taken by a government to defeat insurgency.
example: The United States will continue to pursue a military and civilian counterinsurgency strategy in Afghanistan.
etymology: From counter- + insurgency.

definition: Intelligence activities concerned with identifying and counteracting the threat to security posed by hostile intelligence organizations or by individuals engaged in espionage or sabotage or subversion or terrorism.
etymology: From counter- + intelligence.

definition: Contrary to what common sense would suggest.

definition: The top side of a counter.
etymology: From counter + top.

definition: A weight that balances another weight.
etymology: From counter- + weight.

definition: Occurring or extending throughout a country or nation.

etymology: From country + -wide.

definition: A mechanical device that serves to connect the ends of adjacent objects.
etymology: From couple + -er.

definition: Two items of the same kind.
example: 5th Street is one-way west only and 6th Street is one-way east only. Together, they form a couplet in Downtown Los Angeles.
etymology: From French couplet, from couple + -et. Doublet of cabaletta.

definition: In a courageous manner.
etymology: From courageous + -ly.

definition: Hunting with dogs (usually greyhounds) that are trained to chase game (such as hares) by sight instead of by scent.
A woman who cohabits with an important man.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French courtisane, from Italian cortigiana, feminine of cortigiano (“courtier”), from corte (“court”), itself from Latin cohors.

definition: An attendant at the court of a sovereign.
etymology: From Middle English courteour, from Anglo-Norman corteour, Old French cortoiier, from cort (“court”). By surface analysis, court + -ier.

definition: Refined or imposing in manner or appearance; befitting a royal court.
example: A courtly gentleman.
etymology: From Middle English courtly, equivalent to court + -ly.

definition: (Middle Ages) a highly conventionalized code of conduct for lovers.
A spicy dish that originated in northern Africa; consists of pasta steamed with a meat and vegetable stew.
etymology: Borrowed from French couscous, from Arabic كُسْكُس (kuskus), from a Berber language. First use appears c. 1593.

definition: Of or relating to or characterized by covalence.
example: Covalent bond.
etymology: From co- + valent.

definition: A chemical bond that involves sharing a pair of electrons between atoms in a molecule.
(statistics) the mean value of the product of the deviations of two variates from their respective means.
etymology: From co- + variance.

definition: A small collection of people.
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English covei, covey (“brood of partridges, covey; volley of shot;

definition: A louse that infests the pubic region of the human body.
A whimsically eccentric person.

etymology: Mostly likely a back-etymology of pot, to form crack + pot. Originally, from crack + pate. Compare typologically Russian чо́кнутый (čóknutyj) (< чо́каться (čókatʹsja), onomatopoeic), see crack for the further typology.

definition: A steep rugged rock or cliff.
etymology: A variant of craw.

definition: Having hills and crags.
example: The goat climbed up the craggy rocks.
etymology: From crag + -y.

definition: An alcoholic beverage made from cranberries.
example: Awhile back, King-Man's colleague Mary told me she often makes her own cranberry liqueur this time of year.

definition: The part of the skull that encloses the brain.
etymology: From Medieval Latin crānium (“skull”), from Ancient Greek κρᾱνίον (krāníon, “skull”). By surface analysis, crani- + -um.

definition: Make a retreat from an earlier commitment or activity.
example: We'll have to crawfish out from meeting with him.

definition: A squeaking sound.
example: The creak of the floorboards gave him away.

definition: A small pitcher for serving cream.
example: Nondairy creamer.

definition: A workplace where dairy products (butter and cheese etc.) are produced or sold.
etymology: From French crémerie, reformed as cream + -ery.

definition: An organic compound of creatine and phosphoric acid; found in the muscles of vertebrates where its hydrolysis releases energy for muscular contraction.
Easy to believe on the basis of available evidence.
example: A suitor can credibly signal his love for a woman by offering her an expensive and extravagant gift.
etymology: From credible + -ly.

definition: Worthy of often limited commendation.
example: The student's effort on the essay — though not outstanding — was creditable.
etymology: From credit + -able.

definition: Perennial European herb with long creeping stolons.
Fern of rain forests of tropical Australia and New Zealand and South Africa.
Ornamental shrub from eastern India commonly planted in the southern United States.
A long narrow depression in a surface.
etymology: From Middle English crevice, from Old French crevace, from crever (“to break, burst”), from Latin crepō (“to break, burst, crack”). Doublet of crevasse.

definition: A plain straight neckline opening from shoulder to shoulder of sweaters.
A male member of a flight crew.
etymology: From crew + -man.

definition: Legislation that makes something illegal.

etymology: From criminal + -ization or criminalize + -ation.

definition: An angular or rounded shape made by folding.

etymology: Uncertain. Likely from etymology 1, above, but the historical development is not clear. Attested since the seventeenth century.

definition: Embarrassing such that it would cause cringing.

definition: Totally submissive.
Street names for methylenedioxymethamphetamine.
Someone left in charge of pets while their owners are away from home.
Tableware (eating and serving dishes) collectively.
etymology: From crocker (“(obsolete) potter”) + -ery (suffix with the sense ‘a class, group, or collection of’ forming nouns).

definition: An ugly evil-looking old woman.
etymology: From Middle English crone, from Anglo-Norman carogne (compare central Old French charogne (a term of abuse, literally “carrion, carcass, old sheep, hag”), whence modern French charogne). Doublet of carrion.

definition: A close friend who accompanies their buddies in their activities.
etymology: Coined between 1655 and 1665 from Ancient Greek χρόνιος (khrónios, “perennial, long-lasting”); see also chrono- (“time”).

definition: Small farmers and tenants.

Sports equipment used in playing croquet.

Fertilization by the union of male and female gametes from different individual of the same species.

Shaped like a cross.

definition: In a crude or unrefined manner.

Strips of gingerroot cooked in sugar syrup and coated with sugar.
Honey in which some of the glucose content has spontaneously crystallized from solution as the monohydrate.
The branch of science that studies the formation and structure of crystals.

A bee that is parasitic in the nests of bumblebees.
The galley or pantry of a small ship.

A transverse and totally enclosed drain under a road or railway.
A globular cloud.

Shaped like a wedge.
etymology: From French cunéiforme or New Latin cuneifōrmis, from Classical Latin cuneus (“wedge”) + fōrma.

definition: A wrist bone that articulates with the pisiform and hamate and lunate bones.

An edible morel with a cup-shaped or saucer-shaped fruiting body can be up to 20 cm wide; the fertile surface inside the cup has wrinkles radiating from the center; can be easily confused with inedible mushrooms.
A vertical cylindrical furnace for melting iron for casting.

etymology: Borrowed from Italian cupola, from Latin cūpula (“little tub”); from Latin cūpa, cuppa (“cup”); named for its resemblance to a cup turned over. Doublet of cupula.

definition: A cup of tea.
example: I’ve just put the kettle on – fancy a cuppa?
etymology: Contraction of cup of (with “tea” or sometimes “coffee” implied). See also a (“of”), pinta (“pint of milk”).

definition: A treatment in which evacuated cups are applied to the skin to draw blood through the surface.

etymology: From Middle English cupping, equivalent to cup + -ing.

definition: Able to be cured or healed.

definition: Tending to cure or restore to health.

definition: Of or relating to a curator or the duties of a curator.

Any of various deciduous shrubs of the genus Ribes bearing currants.
Softened by the addition of cushions or padding.
Not burdensome or demanding; borne or done easily and without hardship.

definition: By custom; according to common practice.

definition: A representation (drawing or model) of something in which the outside is omitted to reveal the inner parts.
A representation (drawing or model) of something in which the outside is omitted to reveal the inner parts.
A short heavy curved sword with one edge; formerly used by sailors.
etymology: From Middle French coutelas, from Old French coutel (“knife”) + -as (augmentative suffix).

definition: Ten-armed oval-bodied cephalopod with narrow fins as long as the body and a large calcareous internal shell.
etymology: From cuttle + fish.

definition: Of the blue-green color that is a primary subtractive color of light.
Crime committed using a computer and the internet to steal a person's identity or sell contraband or stalk victims or disrupt operations with malevolent programs.
etymology: From cyber- + crime.

definition: Of or relating the principles of cybernetics.
example: Cybernetic research.

definition: (biology) the field of science concerned with processes of communication and control (especially the comparison of these processes in biological and artificial systems).
example: […] he lost both of his arms and his jaw in a previous fight and had them replaced with cybernetics.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, guide, act as a pilot”) (whence English govern).

With cynicism; in a cynical manner.

definition: An amino acid containing sulfur that is found in most proteins; oxidizes on exposure to air to form cystine.

Dip a foot or hand briefly into a liquid.

definition: Covered with bright patches (often used in combination).

definition: Any of numerous shallow-water ducks that feed by upending and dabbling.
Small long-bodied short-legged German breed of dog having a short sleek coat and long drooping ears; suited for following game into burrows.
etymology: From German Dachshund (literally “badger dog”), from German Dachs (“badger”) + Hund (“dog”).

definition: Any of numerous varieties of Narcissus plants having showy often yellow flowers with a trumpet-shaped central crown.

A platform raised above the surrounding level to give prominence to the person on it.

A room in which photographs are developed.

definition: An imaginary line on the surface of the earth following (approximately) the 180th meridian.
etymology: From date + line.

definition: An item of factual information derived from measurement or research.
example: A datum of experience.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin datum, a nominalization of datus, perfect passive participle of dō, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, reduplication of *deh₃-, or from *-ti. Doublet of die.

definition: Invulnerable to fear or intimidation.
etymology: From daunt + -less.

definition: A schoolchild at a boarding school who has meals at school but sleeps at home.
By right; according to law.
example: De jure recognition of the new government.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dē jūre (literally “according to law”).

definition: Breaking up a military unit (by transfers or discharges).
etymology: From de- + activation.

definition: Foul-smelling perennial Eurasiatic herb with a green creeping rhizome.
A weight training exercise in which a loaded barbell is lifted off the ground to the hips, then lowered back to the ground.

Deliberately impassive in manner.

Expose while ridiculing; especially of pretentious or false claims and ideas.

A sentence (in the indicative mood) that makes a declaration.
Interpret (a text or an artwork) by the method of deconstructing.

definition: Legislation that makes something legal that was formerly illegal.

definition: Express strong disapproval of.

definition: Convert code into ordinary language.

definition: The activity of making clear or converting from code into plain text.

etymology: Verbal noun of decrypt, from de- + crypt (only attested in compounds, such as cryptogram) from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”).
