definition: Reasoning from the general to the particular (or from cause to effect).
Having deep bilateral lobes.
Charge falsely or with malicious intent; attack the good name and reputation of someone.
example: The journalists have defamed me!
etymology: From Middle English defamen, from Anglo-Norman defamer (verb), defame (noun), and its source, Latin diffāmō, from fāma (“fame; rumour; reputation”).

definition: A person who abandons their duty (as on a military post).
An electronic device that administers an electric shock of preset voltage to the heart through the chest wall in an attempt to restore the normal rhythm of the heart during ventricular fibrillation.
etymology: From defibrillate + -or.

definition: Place under suspicion or cast doubt upon.
example: To urinate on someone’s grave is an example of a way to defile it.
etymology: From Late Middle English defilen (“to make dirty, befoul; rape; abuse; destroy; injure; oppress”) [and other forms], a variant of defoulen (“to make dirty, defile, pollute; have sexual intercourse with; rape;

definition: Morally blemished; stained or impure.
Collapse by releasing contained air or gas.
example: Deflate a balloon.
etymology: From de- + (in)flate. Coined in 1891, in reference to balloons. Equivalent to Latin dē- (“away, from”) + Latin flō (“blow”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: A device intended to turn aside the flow of something (water or air or smoke etc.).
etymology: From deflect + -or.

definition: Make formless.
example: The heat deformed the plastic sculpture.
etymology: From Middle English deformen (“to disfigure, distort, or mar; (figuratively) to disfigure morally; to defame;

definition: Make or become free of frost or ice.
example: Defrost the car window.
etymology: From de- + frost.

definition: Remove gas from.
etymology: From de- + gas.

definition: Extremely pleasing to the sense of taste.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:delectable.
etymology: From Middle English delectable, from Middle French délectable, from Old French delectable, from Medieval Latin delectare (“to delight”). By surface analysis, delect + -able. Piecewise doublet of delightable.

definition: Authorizing subordinates to make certain decisions.
Harmful to living things.
example: Deleterious chemical additives.
etymology: Adapted borrowing (1640s;

definition: A style of glazed earthenware; usually white with blue decoration.
etymology: After the Dutch city of Delft.

definition: Involved in or characterized by deliberation and discussion and examination.
example: A deliberative body.
etymology: From Middle French délibératif, from Latin deliberativus.

definition: An assembly of people for the purpose of unhurried consideration and discussion.
Show the form or outline of.
etymology: First attested in 1559;

definition: Represented accurately or precisely.
A graphic or vivid verbal description.
Reduce in worth or character, usually verbally.
etymology: (1595) From de- + mean (“lowly, base, common”), from Middle English mene, aphetic variation of imene (“mean, base, common”), from Old English ġemǣne (“mean, common”). Compare English bemean.

definition: (behavioral attributes) the way a person behaves toward other people.
Make into a demon.
example: Power had demonized him.
etymology: From Medieval Latin daemonizō, from daemon + -izō. Compare Ancient Greek δαιμονίζομαι (daimonízomai, “to be possessed by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn, “demon”). By surface analysis, demon + -ize.

definition: Necessarily or demonstrably true.
example: Demonstrable truths.
etymology: From Middle English demonstrable, from Old French.

definition: Given to or marked by the open expression of emotion.
example: An affectionate and demonstrative family.
etymology: From Middle English demonstratif, from Middle French démonstratif, from Latin dēmōnstrātīvus. Equivalent to demonstrate + -ive.

definition: Serving to prove or demonstrate.
example: The oath of office is … demonstrative of the legislative opinion on this subject.

definition: A pronoun that points out an intended referent.
example: In the sentence I like this, the word this is a demonstrative pronoun.

definition: Made less hopeful or enthusiastic.
example: Desperate demoralized people looking for work.

definition: Destructive of morale and self-reliance.
Act of lowering in rank or position.
Affectedly modest or shy especially in a playful or provocative way.
example: She is a demure young lady.

definition: (neuroscience) of or relating to or resembling a dendrite.
example: Dendritic fiber.
etymology: From dendrite + -ic, from Ancient Greek δενδρίτης (dendrítēs, “of or pertaining to a tree”).

definition: Cause to seem less serious; play down.
example: You have no right to denigrate people and things that you have no personal experience with.
etymology: Derived from Latin dēnigrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēnigrō (“to blacken”) [see -ate (verb-forming suffix)], from dē- (“of; from”) + nigrō (“to blacken”) [from niger (“black”)].

definition: Someone trained to provide preventive dental service (cleaning teeth or taking x-rays).
A dental appliance that artificially replaces missing teeth.
example: After the mouth surgery, she was fitted with a denture.
etymology: From French denture (“set of teeth”), from Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + -urus, -ura, -urum, a suffix implying a set.

definition: A public act of denouncing.
The quality of being dependable or reliable.
etymology: From depend + -ability.

definition: Use up (resources or materials).
example: The winter storm quickly depleted the salt supply of the county.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēplētus (“empty”), from depleō. First attested in 1716; originally a medical term.

definition: Force to leave (an office).
example: A deposed monarch may go into exile as pretender to the lost throne, hoping to be restored in a subsequent revolution.
etymology: Recorded since c.1300, from Middle English, from Old French deposer, from de- (“down”) + poser (“to put, place”).

definition: Capable of depressing physiological or psychological activity or response by a chemical agent.
etymology: From depress + -ant.

definition: An accident in which a train runs off its track.
etymology: Borrowed from French déraillement.

definition: A tendency to be negligent and uncaring.
example: His derelictions were not really intended as crimes.
etymology: From Latin dērelictiō (“neglect, abandonment”), from dērelinquō (“to neglect, abandon”), from dē- + re- + linquō (“to leave”).

definition: Appearing silly or stupid especially in a cute manner.
etymology: Probably from dur, a British informal exclamation for “stupid” or from duh, an exclamation indicating faltering speech and assumed stupidity, glottalized for emphasis.

definition: Blasphemous behavior; the act of depriving something of its sacred character.
example: Desecration of the Holy Sabbath.
etymology: From desecrate + -ion.

definition: Small long-tailed lizard of arid areas of southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico.
Most common paintbrush of western United States dry lands; having erect stems ending in dense spikes of bright orange to red flowers.
An infection of the lungs and skin characterized by excessive sputum and nodules.
A disloyal person who betrays or deserts their cause or religion or political party or friend etc.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin desertor (“deserter”), from desero (“to forsake, to abandon”); or from desert + -er.

definition: The quality of being worthy of desiring.
etymology: Morphologically desirable + -ity and desire + -ability.

definition: Having or expressing desire for something.
example: Desirous of high office.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French desirrous, from desirrer + -ous.

definition: Changing from an adsorbed state on a surface to a gaseous or liquid state.
Arising from or marked by despair or loss of hope.
example: A despairing view of the world situation.
etymology: From Middle English despeyringe, equivalent to despair + -ing.

definition: An official report (usually sent in haste).
Without or almost without hope.
example: Despondent about his failure.
etymology: From Latin dēspondēns, from the verb despondere (“to give up, to abandon”).

definition: A cruel and oppressive dictator.
etymology: From Middle French despote, from Old French despote, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”). Cognate with Sanskrit दम्पति (dámpati).

definition: Belonging to or having the characteristics of a despot.
example: This despotic age of the empire ended in a revolt.
etymology: From Ancient Greek δεσποτικός (despotikós) via French despotique, equivalent to despot + -ic.

definition: An event that causes a loss of equilibrium (as of a ship or aircraft).
etymology: From de- + stabilization or destabilize + -ion.

definition: A mechanical or electrical explosive device or a small amount of explosive; can be used to initiate the reaction of a disrupting explosive.
A fuse containing an explosive.
A mechanical or electrical explosive device or a small amount of explosive; can be used to initiate the reaction of a disrupting explosive.
etymology: From detonate + -or.

definition: A treatment for addiction to drugs or alcohol intended to remove the physiological effects of the addictive substances.
etymology: From de- + toxification.

definition: The remains of something that has been destroyed or broken up.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dētrītus (“(that which is) rubbed away”), from dēterō (“rub away”).

definition: An isotope of hydrogen which has one neutron (as opposed to zero neutrons in hydrogen).
example: Heavy water is "heavy" because it contains deuterium.
etymology: From deutero- + -ium. Coined by American physical chemist Harold Urey, from Ancient Greek δεύτερος (deúteros, “second”).

definition: Water containing a substantial proportion of deuterium atoms, used in nuclear reactors.
Remove the value from; deprive of its value.
etymology: From de- + value.

definition: Cause extensive destruction or ruin utterly.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēvastātus, perfect passive participle of dēvastō (“to lay waste, devastate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)); from dē- (augmentative prefix) + vastō (“to destroy, lay waste”). See vast.

definition: With respect to development.
example: Developmentally retarded.
etymology: From developmental + -ly.

definition: Abnormal displacement of any wall that separates two chambers (usually in the nasal cavity).
A stinging herb of tropical America.
Wet with dew.
example: The dewy grass was too slick for football.
etymology: From Middle English dewy, deuhy, from Old English dēawiġ, from Proto-West Germanic *dauwag, *dauwīg, equivalent to dew + -y.

definition: Exhibiting childlike simplicity and credulity.
example: Dewy-eyed innocence.
etymology: From dewy + eyed.

definition: Any formal system of reasoning that arrives at the truth by the exchange of logical arguments.
example: This situation created the inner dialectic of American history.
etymology: From Latin dialecticus, from Ancient Greek δῐᾰλεκτῐκός (dĭălektĭkós).

definition: Of or relating to or employing dialectic.
example: The dialectical method.
etymology: From Latin dialecticus + -al. By surface analysis, dialectic + -al or dialect + -ical.

definition: As from opposite ends of a diameter.
example: Three of these brushes were approximately 120 feet apart and the fourth diametrically opposite to one of the three.
etymology: From diametrical + -ly.

definition: Thunderous verbal attack.
example: To throw a diatribe.

definition: A tranquilizer (trade name Valium) used to relieve anxiety and relax muscles; acts by enhancing the inhibitory actions of the neurotransmitter GABA; can also be used as an anticonvulsant drug in cases of nerve agent poisoning.
etymology: From (benzo)diazep(ine) + am(ide).

definition: Of uncertain outcome; especially fraught with risk.
example: An extremely dicey future on a brave new world of liquid nitrogen, tar, and smog.
etymology: From dice + -y.

definition: Small bird; adults talking to children sometimes use these words to refer to small birds.
example: We've not heard a dicky-bird about anything relating to his birthday.

definition: A small third seat in the back of an old-fashioned two-seater.
An authoritative direction or instruction to do something.
example: Since I learned shorthand, I can take dictation at eighty words a minute.
etymology: From Late Latin dictātiō, noun of action from dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō. By surface analysis, dictate + -ion.

definition: The articulation of speech regarded from the point of view of its intelligibility to the audience.
Instructive (especially excessively).
example: Didactic poetry.
etymology: From French didactique, from Ancient Greek διδακτικός (didaktikós, “skilled in teaching”), from διδακτός (didaktós, “taught, learnt”), from διδάσκω (didáskō, “to teach, educate”). By surface analysis, didact + -ic.

definition: Someone who makes dies.
A specialist in the study of diet and nutrition.
etymology: Irregular spelling of diet + -ician, probably influenced by dietetic.

definition: In a differential manner.
example: Hubel and Wiesel have found cells that respond differentially according to the direction in which a stimulus is moved across the retina.
etymology: From differential + -ly.

definition: (of light rays) subjected to scattering by reflection from a rough surface or transmission through a translucent material.
example: Diffused light.

definition: Capable of being converted into assimilable condition in the alimentary canal.
etymology: From Old French digestible, equivalent to digest + -ible.

definition: Conversion of analog information into digital information.
etymology: From digitize + -ation.

definition: A compound whose molecules are composed of two identical monomers.
etymology: From di- + -mer.

definition: A rheostat that varies the current through an electric light in order to control the level of illumination.
etymology: From dim (verb) + -er.

definition: A chad that has been punched or dimpled but all four corners are still attached.
etymology: Cognate with German Low German Dümpel, German Tümpel (“pond, pool”). Related also to Old English dyppan (“to dip”).

definition: 100 dinars equal 1 rial in Iran.
etymology: From Arabic دِينَار (dīnār) and Serbo-Croatian динар (also from Arabic), derived from the Latin dēnārius. Doublet of denar, denarius, denier, diner, dinero, and dinheiro.

definition: A small wooded hollow.
etymology: From Middle English dingle (“a deep hollow; dell”), from Old English *dyngel, a diminutive of Old English dung (“dungeon; pit”), equivalent to dung + -le (diminutive suffix).

definition: Small and unimpressive.
example: We stayed in a dinky old hotel.
etymology: 1780-90; compare Scots dink (“neatly dressed, trim”) (of obscure origin); sense shift perhaps: trim > dainty > small > insignificant; + -y.

definition: Interchangeable with ‘means’ in the expression ‘by means of’.
etymology: From Middle English dint, dent, dünt, from Old English dynt (“dint, blow, strike, stroke, bruise, stripe; the mark left by a blow;

definition: Acute contagious infection caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae; marked by the formation of a false membrane in the throat and other air passages causing difficulty in breathing.
With diplomacy; in a diplomatic manner.
example: He answered very diplomatically.
etymology: From diplomatic + -ally or diplomatical + -ly.

definition: Not to your liking.
example: A disagreeable situation.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English disagreable, from Middle French desagreable, from Old French desagraable (compare French désagréable). By surface analysis, dis- + agreeable.

definition: A person who is not pleasant or agreeable.
Command against.
example: The prisoners were disallowed to contact with a lawyer.
etymology: From Middle English disallowen, desallowen, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman desalouer, Old French desalöer. By surface analysis, dis- + allow.

definition: Expressing or manifesting disapproval.
example: The word "lazy", when used to describe a person's unwillingness to work, is a disapproving word.

definition: Take apart into its constituent pieces.
example: To perform the repair it was necessary to disassemble most of the mechanism.
etymology: From dis- + assemble.

definition: The act of taking something apart (as a piece of machinery).
etymology: From dis- + assembly.

definition: Refuse to acknowledge; disclaim knowledge of; responsibility for, or association with.
example: Her husband disavowed her after 30 years of marriage and six children.
etymology: From dis- + avow, or from Old French desavouer.

definition: Reject as false; refuse to accept.
example: If you disbelieve such people, then keep disbelieving them for as long as you live or want.
etymology: Coined circa 1640, from dis- + believe. Compare misbelieve.

definition: Amounts paid for goods and services that may be currently tax deductible (as opposed to capital expenditures).
etymology: From disburse + -ment.

definition: The position of disciple.
etymology: From disciple + -ship.

definition: The act of discontinuing or breaking off; an interruption (temporary or permanent).
etymology: From dis- + continuation.

definition: Lack of connection or continuity.
example: Structural discontinuity.
etymology: From Late Latin discontinuitās, from discontinuus, equivalent to dis- + continuity.

definition: Of a function or curve; possessing one or more discontinuities.
etymology: From dis- + continuous.

definition: Not in agreement or harmony.
example: Views discordant with present-day ideas.
etymology: From Late Middle English discordaunt (“(adjective) not in accord or harmony; dissonant;

definition: The feeling of despair in the face of obstacles.
etymology: From discourage + -ment.

definition: Someone who is the first to think of or make something.
etymology: From Middle English discoverour, dyscowerer, partly from Middle French descouvreur and partly equivalent to discover + -er.

definition: Proceeding to a conclusion by reason or argument rather than intuition.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French discursif, formed from the stem of Latin discursus and the suffix -if, and in part borrowed from Medieval Latin discursivus. By surface analysis, discourse + -ive.

definition: Go ashore.
example: The passengers disembarked at Southampton.
etymology: From dis- + embark.

definition: Not having a material body.
Any incorporeal supernatural being that can become visible (or audible) to human beings.
Freed from enchantment.
The act of releasing from an attachment or connection.
example: Moral disengagement.
etymology: From dis- + engage + -ment.

definition: In a disgusting manner or to a disgusting degree.
example: The beggar was disgustingly filthy.
etymology: From disgusting + -ly.

definition: Shaped like a dish or pan.
example: Bicycle and cart wheels are often dished.

definition: In disarray; extremely disorderly.
example: Her clothing was disheveled.

definition: Lacking honor or integrity; deserving dishonor.
example: Dishonorable in thought and deed.

definition: Suffering shame.
Bring shame or dishonor upon.
example: He dishonored his family by committing a serious crime.
etymology: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honour.

definition: Destroy microorganisms or pathogens by cleansing.
example: Disinfect a wound.
etymology: From English dis- + infect, from Middle French desinfecter.

definition: Treatment to destroy harmful microorganisms.
etymology: From dis- + infection.

definition: Tolerance attributable to a lack of involvement.
example: She eyed him over her martini with cool disinterest.
etymology: From dis- + interest.

definition: The quality of being disloyal.
etymology: From Old French desloiauté (Modern French déloyauté), from des- + loiauté (“loyalty”).

definition: The removal of limbs; being cut to pieces.
etymology: From dismember + -ment.

definition: The act of dismounting (a horse or bike etc.).
example: Nice dismount!
etymology: From dis- + mount, probably a calque of Old French desmonter.

definition: Not obeying or complying with commands of those in authority.
example: Disobedient children.
etymology: From Middle English disobedient, dysobedyent, from Old French desobedient; morphologically, from dis- + obedient.

definition: A wild delusion (especially one induced by a hallucinogenic drug).
etymology: From dis- + orientation or perhaps disorientate + -ation.

definition: Prevent deliberately (as by making a will) from inheriting.
example: Lord Capulet and his wife threatened to disown their daughter Juliet if she didn’t go through with marrying Count Paris.
etymology: From dis- + own.

definition: Express a negative opinion of.
example: She disparaged her student's efforts.
etymology: From Middle English disparage (noun), disparagen (verb), from Old French desparage (noun), desparagier (verb), from des- (“dis-”) + parage (“equal rank, rank”).

definition: Unaffected by strong emotion or prejudice.
example: A journalist should be a dispassionate reporter of fact.
etymology: From dis- + passionate.

definition: (computer science) an electronic device that converts information in memory to video output to a display.
Depriving of legal right; rendering legally disqualified.
example: Certain disabling restrictions disqualified him for citizenship.

definition: A feeling of mild anxiety about possible developments.
etymology: From dis- + quiet.

definition: Disagreement among those expected to cooperate.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

definition: Tending to produce dissociation.
example: It was a lonely, dissociative time in my life, when I stayed holed up in my apartment for weeks on end.
etymology: From dissociate + -ive.

definition: Dissociation so severe that the usually integrated functions of consciousness and perception of self break down.
Characterized by musical dissonance; harmonically unresolved.
example: The music was filled with dissonant chords.
etymology: From Middle French dissonant.

definition: From or at a distance.
example: Dimly, distantly, voices sounded in the stillness.
etymology: From distant + -ly.

definition: Serving to distribute or allot or disperse.
example: If function f is distributive with respect to function g, then f(a,g(b,c))=g(f(a,b),f(a,c)).
etymology: From Middle French distributif, from Latin distribūtīvus.

definition: Shock caused by poor distribution of the blood flow.
Having or showing distrust.
example: A man of distrustful nature.
etymology: From distrust + -ful.

definition: In a disturbing manner.
example: The details of the kidnapper's letter had sounded disturbingly convincing.
etymology: From disturbing + -ly.

definition: A short simple song (or the words of a poem intended to be sung).
etymology: From Middle English dite, ditee, from Old French ditie or dité, from ditier, from Latin dictāre (participle dictatus).

definition: Kit used by sailors and soldiers.
etymology: Suggested to be a clipping of commodity bag, a British naval term.

definition: Fluctuations that occur during each day.
A long backless sofa (usually with pillows against a wall).
etymology: Borrowed from French, from Ottoman Turkish دیوان (divan), from Classical Persian دیوان (dēwān), from Middle Persian d(p)ywʾn' (dēwān, “archive, collected writings”), from Sumerian 𒁾 (dub).

definition: An armless couch; a seat by day and a bed by night.
Tending to move apart in different directions.
A lens such that a parallel beam of light passing through it is caused to diverge or spread out.
By divine means.
example: The divinely appointed means of rescue from temporal existence.
etymology: From divine + -ly.

definition: Capable of being or liable to be divided or separated.
example: Even numbers are divisible by two.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English divisible, from Old French, from Late Latin divisibilis, from the verb Latin divido.

definition: An establishment on the waterfront where vessels are built or fitted out or repaired.
etymology: From dock + yard.

definition: A person who acts and gets things done.
example: When you want something done, get a doer.
etymology: From Middle English doer, doar, doere, from Old English dōere (“a doer; worker”), equivalent to do + -er.

definition: A fiercely disputed contest.
example: Their rancor dated from a political dogfight between them.
etymology: From dog + fight.

definition: Relentless and indefatigable in pursuit or as if in pursuit.
example: Impossible to escape the dogging fears.

definition: Outbuilding that serves as a shelter for a dog.
example: He's out of the doghouse now that he's bought his wife some flowers.
etymology: Compound of dog + house.

definition: A tree of shrub of the genus Cornus often having showy bracts resembling flowers.
etymology: From dag + wood, from dag (“a sharp object”).

definition: A rosid dicot family of the order Umbellales including: genera Aucuba, Cornus, Corokia, Curtisia, Griselinia, Helwingia.
A tree of shrub of the genus Cornus often having showy bracts resembling flowers.
A strong liqueur prepared by infusing vodka with the fruit of Cornelian cherry.
example: I tried dogwood vodka on my trip to Armenia.

definition: A small measure (usually of food).
example: Each pancake comes with a dollop of suspiciously soft butter in a tiny plastic cup.
etymology: From earlier East Anglian dialectal dallop (“patch, tuft (of grass, etc.)”), of unknown origin. Compare dialectal Norwegian dolp (“lump”).

definition: A kind of sedimentary rock resembling marble or limestone but rich in magnesium carbonate.
etymology: From French dolomite, coined March 1792 by Nicolas de Saussure, named after French mineralogist and engineer Déodat de Dolomieu (1750–1801) who described the stone in 1791 by adding -ite, from place name Dolomieu, Isère.

definition: (Roman Catholic Church) a priest who is an honorary member of the papal household.
Adaptation to intimate association with human beings.
etymology: From domesticate + -ion.

definition: Tending to domineer.
Any of several games played with small rectangular blocks.
A clergyman; especially a settled minister or parson.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dominus (“master”). Doublet of dan, dom, domine, dominie, and don.

definition: (computer science) an electronic device that must be attached to a computer in order for it to use protected software.
etymology: Unknown. Likely a descendant of dangle, reflecting that electronic accessories such as computer peripherals often are plugged in via a flexible cable (although wirelessness is also often relevant).

definition: Having or revealing stupidity.
example: A dopey answer.
etymology: From dope (“stupid person”) + -y.

definition: A ghostly double of a living person that haunts its living counterpart.
etymology: Borrowed from German Doppelgänger (“ghostly spirit”, literally “double-walker”).

definition: Of or pertaining to the Doric style of architecture.
A gabled extension built out from a sloping roof to accommodate a vertical window.
etymology: From Middle French dormoir (“sleeping room”), from dormir (“to sleep”).

definition: The window in a gabled extension built to accommodate a window.
One of 12 vertebrae in the human vertebral column; thoracic vertebrae extend from the seventh cervical vertebra down to the first lumbar vertebra.
Treated with some kind of application.
example: A mustache dosed with bear grease.

definition: Sleep in a convenient place.
example: I am going to doss tomorrow when the match is on.
etymology: Perhaps from Latin dorsum (“the back”), i.e. what one lies on when sleeping; perhaps from English dialect doss (“a hassock”).

definition: Sleep in a convenient place.
example: After the party, John let me doss down on the living-room floor.

definition: Extravagantly or foolishly loving and indulgent.
example: Deceiving her preoccupied and doting husband with a young captain.
etymology: From Middle English dotynge; equivalent to dote + -ing.

definition: Informal or slang terms for mentally irregular.
example: Look at the dotty pattern on that cheetah's fur.
etymology: See dote, or compare totty (“unsteady, dizzy”).

definition: The bassoon that is the largest instrument in the oboe family.
Having two barrels mounted side by side.
example: A double-barreled shotgun.

definition: Having a double bed.
example: A double-bedded room.

definition: Having unusually flexible joints especially of the limbs or fingers.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From double (adjective) + jointed (adjective), from the fact that a body part of a person with the condition appears to have two joints bending in different directions.

definition: Marked by deliberate deceptiveness especially by pretending one set of feelings and acting under the influence of another.
example: A double-dealing double agent.
etymology: From Middle English doubultongud, dowbyl townged, dubble tungyd, equivalent to double + tongued.

definition: Two games instead of one (especially in baseball when the same two teams play two games on the same day).
Stubbornly unyielding.
example: Dour determination.
etymology: Borrowed from Scots dour, possibly from Latin dūrus (“hard, stern”), via Middle Irish dúr. Compare French dur, Catalan dur, Italian duro, Portuguese duro, Romanian dur, Spanish duro. Doublet of dure.

definition: Put out, as of a candle or a light.
example: Douse the lights.
etymology: Probably of North Germanic origin, related to Swedish dunsa (“to plumb down, fall clumsily”), Danish dunse (“to thump”). Compare Old English dwǣsċan (“to extinguish”) and douse below.

definition: The first beat of a musical measure (as the conductor's arm moves downward).
etymology: From down + beat.

definition: Located at, or relatively closer to, the defending team's end of the playing field.
example: He threw to a downfield receiver.
etymology: From down- + field.

definition: Dismiss from work.
example: Three secretaries were downsized during the financial crisis.
etymology: From down- + size.

definition: Abused or oppressed by people in power.
example: A patch of downtrodden soil.

With the wind; in the direction the wind is blowing.
example: They flew downwind.

definition: Like down or as soft as down.
example: The chick's downy coat of feathers formed almost immediately to keep it warm.

European birch with dull white to pale brown bark and somewhat drooping hairy branches.

Annual or winter annual grass with softly hairy leaves of the Mediterranean.

A bridge that can be raised to block passage or to allow boats or ships to pass beneath it.
example: Drawbridge mentality.

definition: A tie consisting of a cord that goes through a seam around an opening.

definition: Battleship that has big guns all of the same caliber.

definition: Resembling a dream.
example: Night invested the lake with a dreamlike quality.
etymology: From dream + -like.

definition: Sediment that has settled at the bottom of a liquid.
example: The dregs of society.

definition: Wood that is floating or that has been washed ashore.

definition: Suitable for drinking.

definition: A worthless message.

definition: Comical in an odd or whimsical manner.

definition: An unchanging intonation.

definition: Droop, sink, or settle from or as if from pressure or loss of tautness.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English droupen, from Old Norse drúpa (“to droop”), from Proto-Germanic *drūpaną, *drupōną (“to hang down, drip, drop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewb- (“to drip, drop”). Doublet of drip and drop.

definition: Weak from exhaustion.
example: Drooping flowers.

etymology: Inherited from Middle English drupi, from drup (“sad”), from Old Norse drúpr (“drooping sadness”); related to Middle English drupen, droupen (“to sag, droop”), also from Old Norse. By surface analysis, droop + -y.

definition: A scone made by dropping a spoonful of batter on a griddle.
A tiny drop.
etymology: From drop + -let.

definition: Pipet consisting of a small tube with a vacuum bulb at one end for drawing liquid in and releasing it a drop at a time.
example: She used an eye dropper to administer medication to the eyes.
etymology: From drop + -er.

definition: A very sleepy state.
etymology: From drowsy + -ness.

definition: Hard monotonous routine work.
etymology: From drudge (“person who works in a low servile job”) + -ery (suffix meaning ‘the art, craft, or practice of’ forming nouns).

definition: An unlicensed dealer in illegal drugs.
An unlicensed dealer in illegal drugs.
The administration of a sedative agent or drug.
example: Alleged druggings of horses.

definition: A chronic drinker.
Showing effects of much strong drink.
example: He sang drunkenly.
etymology: From drunken + -ly.

definition: Dry pale amber variety.
The activity of building stone walls without mortar.
The doctrine that reality consists of two basic opposing elements, often taken to be mind and matter (or mind and body), or good and evil.
etymology: From dual + -ism.

definition: Leader.
example: Mussolini was called Il Duce.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian duce. Doublet of doge, duc, duke, and dux.

definition: Flesh of a young domestic duck.
etymology: From Middle English dokeling, dukling, dookelynge (“duckling”), equivalent to duck + -ling.

definition: A warm coat made of duffel; usually has a hood and fastens with toggles.
etymology: After the Belgian town of Duffel, which produced the thick cloth from which early duffel coats were made.

definition: Having lost or been caused to lose interest because of overexposure.

A stupid person; these words are used to express a low opinion of someone's intelligence.

definition: A cone-shaped paper hat formerly placed on the head of slow or lazy pupils.
A fraudulent or duplicitous representation.
etymology: From Latin duplicare (double). Equivalent to duplex + -ity.

definition: The outermost (and toughest) of the 3 meninges.
etymology: Ellipsis of dura mater.

definition: Tree of southeastern Asia having edible oval fruit with a hard spiny rind.
Tree of southeastern Asia having edible oval fruit with a hard spiny rind.
A bin that holds rubbish until it is collected.
etymology: From dust + bin, as used for disposing of dust (originally ash from domestic fires) and other rubbish.

definition: Willingly obedient out of a sense of duty and respect.

etymology: From duty + -ful.

definition: Out of a sense of duty; in a dutiful manner.

etymology: From dutiful + -ly.

definition: Become smaller or lose substance.

example: Her savings dwindled down.

definition: The capacity of a system to reproduce loud sounds without distortion.
Of or relating to or symptomatic of dyslexia.
etymology: By surface analysis, dyslexia + -ic. Piecewise doublet of dyslectic.

definition: Abnormal depression and discontent.
example: Body dysphoria.
etymology: From Ancient Greek δυσφορία (dusphoría, “excessive pain”), from δύσφορος (dúsphoros, “grievous”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + φέρω (phérō, “I bear, carry”).

definition: Abnormal development (of organs or cells) or an abnormal structure resulting from such growth.
etymology: * From dys- + -plasia. * (psychology): Introduced by John Curtis Gowan in 1974.

definition: Resembles a thimble on a finger; the surface of the fertile portion is folded into wrinkles that extend from the top down; fruiting begins in spring before the leaves are out on the trees.
Electro-acoustic transducer for converting electric signals into sounds; it is held over or inserted into the ear.
example: Holding the earpiece to my ear, I could hear him speaking clearly.
etymology: From ear + piece.

definition: The range within which a voice can be heard.
example: The children were told to stay within earshot.
etymology: From ear + shot.

definition: Confined to the earth.
etymology: From earth + -bound.

definition: Ceramic ware made of porous clay fired at low heat.
example: Earthenware bowl.
etymology: From earthen + -ware, first recorded appearance in 1673. Compare Dutch aardewerk (“earthenware”).

An upright tripod for displaying something (usually an artist's canvas).
etymology: Borrowed from Dutch ezel (“donkey;

Toward the east.
example: They migrated eastward to Sweden.
etymology: From east + -wards.

definition: Not hurried or forced.
example: At a leisurely (or easygoing) pace.
etymology: From easy + going.

definition: Tableware implements for cutting and eating food.
A biologist who studies the relation between organisms and their environment.
etymology: From eco- + -logist. The less common sense “environmentalist” might be from association with deep ecology, or influenced by Romance-language equivalents such as Spanish ecologista (“environmentalist”).

definition: Of or relating to econometrics.
example: Econometric theories.
etymology: From econo- + -metric.

definition: The application of mathematics and statistics to the study of economic and financial data.
etymology: An adaptation of the French économétrie. Coined by Norwegian economist Ragnar Frisch in 1926.

definition: Mobilization of the economy.
Exhibiting ectopia.
etymology: From ectopia + -ic.

definition: Pregnancy resulting from gestation elsewhere than in the uterus.
Pregnancy resulting from gestation elsewhere than in the uterus.
A mussel with a dark shell that lives attached to rocks.
One who brings about a result or event; one who accomplishes a purpose.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin effector. By surface analysis, effect + -or.

definition: Having unsuitable feminine qualities.
etymology: From Middle English effeminat, effemynat, from Latin effēminātus, past participle of effēminō, from fēmina (“woman”).

definition: Used of wines and waters; charged naturally or artificially with carbon dioxide.
etymology: From Latin effervescentem, from effervescere, from ex- + fervescere, from fervere. By surface analysis, ef- + Latin ferv- + -escent.

definition: Marked by qualities giving the power to produce an intended effect.
example: Written propaganda is less efficacious than the habits and prejudices … of the readers.
etymology: From Old French efficacieux (whence -acious), from Latin efficāx (“efficacious”) + -ous, from efficere (“to effect, to accomplish”); see effect.

definition: That is flowing outward.
etymology: From French effluent, from Latin effluens, effluentis. By surface analysis, e- + fluent.

etymology: From Middle English evete, from Old English efete, of unknown origin.

etymology: From French ellipse. Learned borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis). Doublet of ellipsis.

definition: The quality of being elongated.

etymology: From Anglo-Norman aloper (“to abduct, run away”), itself borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *andihlaupan (“to run away”). Equivalent to and- + lope as well as and- + leap (these being doublets). First attested in 1593.

definition: Make clear and (more) comprehensible.
etymology: From Late Latin ēlūcidātus (“lightened, enlightened”), see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

definition: Very thin especially from disease or hunger or cold.

definition: Proceed or issue forth, as from a source.

definition: Free from traditional social restraints.

definition: Unmoved by feeling.

definition: Showing empathy or ready comprehension of others' states.

definition: Needing nourishment.

definition: Of or relating to endoscopy.

definition: Visual examination of the interior of a hollow body organ by use of an endoscope.

definition: Malignant tumor in bone marrow (usually in the pelvis or in long bones).

definition: Call forth.

definition: A skilled worker who can inscribe designs or writing onto a surface by carving or etching.

definition: Capable of arousing and holding the attention.

definition: Of or relating to the biological science of entomology.

definition: Something that provides access (to get in or get out).

definition: A numbered list.

definition: Surrounding and closing in on or hemming in.

definition: The philosophical doctrine that environment is more important than heredity in determining intellectual growth.

definition: Form a mental image of something that is not present or that is not the case.

definition: Visual imagery.
The longest division of geological time.
example: It’s been eons since we last saw each other.
etymology: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

definition: Something transitory; lasting a day.

The outer layer of the skin covering the exterior body surface of vertebrates.

The act of making equal or uniform.

definition: Compensate; make the score equal.
example: To equalize accounts, burdens, or taxes.
etymology: From equal + -ize.

definition: Encephalitis caused by a virus that is transmitted by a mosquito from an infected horse.
A cgs unit of work or energy; the work done by a force of one dyne acting over a distance of one centimeter.

definition: Of or relating to ergonomics.
etymology: Dated 1950 C.E.; ergo- + -nomy + -ic, from Ancient Greek: ἔργον (érgon, “work”) and νόμος (nómos, “distribution”).

definition: In an erratic unpredictable manner.
example: Economic changes are proceeding erratically.
etymology: From erratic + -ally.

definition: An act of scaling by the use of ladders (especially the walls of a fortification).

etymology: Borrowed from French escapade (“the act of escaping; a trick”), itself borrowed from Old Spanish escapada, from escapar (“to escape”), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre.

definition: An inclination to retreat from unpleasant realities through diversion or fantasy.
example: Romantic novels were her escape from the stress of daily life.

Alimentary tract smear of material obtained from the esophagus.
Small veins from the esophagus emptying into the brachiocephalic vein or the azygos veins.
Surpassing what is common or usual or expected.

definition: Choose and follow; as of theories, ideas, policies, strategies or plans.

definition: A writer of literary works.

definition: Additional unspecified odds and ends; more of the same; entity, other pronoun; pronoun, entity; quantifier: other.

The cause of a disease.

A short composition for a solo instrument; intended as an exercise or to demonstrate technical virtuosity.

definition: Reddish-brown dried gummy exudation from any of several trees of the genus Eucalyptus especially Eucalyptus camaldulensis.

At any future time; in the future.

etymology: From Middle English evermore (written as two words before 14th century), equivalent to ever + -more.

definition: Turn inside out; turn the inner surface of outward.
example: Evert the eyelid.
etymology: From Late Latin ēvertere (“to turn (an item of clothing) inside out”), Latin ēvertere, present active infinitive of ēvertō (“to turn upside down; to overturn;

definition: Pertaining to or constituting evidence.
example: Evidentiary technique.
etymology: From Latin ēvidentia + -ary.

definition: Imaginative re-creation.
etymology: From Middle French évocation.

definition: Without previous consideration.
etymology: From Latin ex (“immediately after”) + tempore, ablative singular of tempus (“time", "opportunity", "occasion”).

definition: A male person who has served in the armed forces.
etymology: From ex- + serviceman.

definition: Making worse.
Praise, glorify, or honor.
example: The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high.
etymology: From Middle English exalten, from Old French exalter, from Latin exaltō.

definition: An exasperated feeling of annoyance.
Recover through digging.
example: Schliemann excavated Troy.
etymology: From a substantivization of Latin excavātus through the associated taxon's name (Excavata), see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

definition: A workman who excavates for foundations of buildings or for quarrying.
example: The excavators of an ancient Egyptian tomb.
etymology: From excavate + -or.

definition: The omission that is made when an editorial change shortens a written passage.
example: Both parties agreed on the excision of the proposed clause.
etymology: From Middle French excision, from Latin excīsiō(n).

definition: Easily excited.
example: The excitable puppy jumped all over the furniture.
etymology: From excite + -able.

definition: The cortical area that influences motor movements.
An abrupt excited utterance.
example: She gave an exclamation of delight.

definition: A rule that provides that otherwise admissible evidence cannot be used in a criminal trial if it was the result of illegal police conduct.
The bodily process of discharging waste matter.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French excrétion, or Late Latin excretio, excretionis, from Latin excerno.

definition: An explanation or critical interpretation (especially of the Bible).
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “to explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead, guide”).

definition: Something to be imitated.
example: An exemplar of success.
etymology: From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplair, and its source, Latin exemplar, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

definition: Be typical of.
example: This compositional style is exemplified by this fugue.
etymology: From Middle English exemplifien, from Middle French exemplifier and its etymon Medieval Latin exemplificō, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

definition: Someone who organizes an exhibit for others to see.
example: The exhibitors at the aviation conference included the inventor of a new kind of light aircraft.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin exhibitor. First attested in 1654. By surface analysis, exhibit + -or.

definition: The feeling of lively and cheerful joy.
etymology: From exhilarate + -ion.

definition: A communication intended to urge or persuade the recipients to take some action.
etymology: From Middle English exhortacioun, from Old French exhortacion, from Latin exhortātiōnem, accusative singular of exhortātiō (“encouraging;

definition: (philosophy) a 20th-century philosophical movement chiefly in Europe; assumes that people are entirely free and thus responsible for what they make of themselves.
example: The heyday of existentialism occurred in the mid-twentieth century.
etymology: From existential + -ism (suffix forming the names of schools of thought, systems, or theories), modelled after German Existentialismus.

definition: Derived or originating externally.
etymology: From exo- + -genous.

definition: An inappropriate state of depression that is precipitated by events in the person's life (to be distinguished from normal grief).
Obesity caused by overeating.
Sequence of a gene's DNA that transcribes into protein structures.
example: Exons are interspersed with introns.
etymology: Apparently an attempt to express the pronunciation of French exempt.

definition: Pronounce not guilty of criminal charges.
etymology: From Middle English exoneraten (attested in past participle exonerated), from Latin exonerātus, past perfect participle of exonerō (“to discharge, unload; to exonerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: The exterior protective or supporting structure or shell of many animals (especially invertebrates) including bony or horny parts such as nails or scales or hoofs.
etymology: From exo- + skeleton.

definition: Able to expand or be expanded.
example: An expandable baton.
etymology: From expand + -able.

definition: Of or involving or guided by expansionism.
etymology: From expansion + -ist.

definition: The quality of being suited to the end in view.
The act of spending money for goods or services.
example: Expendings of time and energy.

definition: Serving to expound or set forth.
example: Clean expository writing.
etymology: From exposit(ion) + -ory.

definition: Produce laughter.
An art movement early in the 20th century; the artist's subjective expression of inner experiences was emphasized; an inner feeling was expressed through a distorted rendition of reality.
etymology: Borrowed from French expressionnisme, equivalent to expression + -ism.

definition: Of or relating to expressionism.
example: Expressionist art.
etymology: From expression + -ist.

definition: Aphasia in which expression by speech or writing is severely impaired.
Taking out of an owner's hands (especially taking property by public authority).
etymology: From expropriate + -ion.

definition: Capable of being protruded or stretched or opened out.
example: An extensile tongue.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin extēnsibilis, from extendō (“to extend”).

definition: Partially excusing or justifying.
example: Extenuating circumstances.
etymology: From Latin ex (“to delete, to cross out”) and tenuatus, past participle of tenuare (“to make thin”) + Middle English -ing. By surface analysis, ex- + tenuate + -ing.

definition: Someone who exterminates (especially someone whose occupation is the extermination of troublesome rodents and insects).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin exterminātor. By surface analysis, exterminate + -or.

definition: The act of extinguishing; causing to stop burning.
example: The extinction of the lights.

definition: Involving the removal of substances from the ground.
example: Most of the skeptics in the geology community are either older or employed in the extractive industries.
etymology: From extract + -ive.

definition: An instrument for extracting tight-fitting components.
Hand over to the authorities of another country.
example: They extradited the fugitive to his native country so he could be tried there.
etymology: Back-formation from extradition.

definition: Beyond the usual course of legal proceedings; legally unwarranted.
example: An extrajudicial penalty.
etymology: From extra- + judicial.

definition: Characterized by adultery.
example: Extramarital affairs.

definition: Extraordinary in a particular capacity.
example: A woodworker extraordinaire.
etymology: Borrowed from French extraordinaire. Doublet of extraordinary.

definition: Draw from specific cases for more general cases.
etymology: From extra- + (inter)polate.

definition: (mathematics) calculation of the value of a function outside the range of known values.
etymology: Morphologically extrapolate + -ion

definition: Release from entanglement of difficulty.
example: I cannot extricate myself from this task.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin extrīcātus, past participle of extrīcō. Compare intricate.

definition: Not forming an essential part of a thing or arising or originating from the outside.
example: Extrinsic evidence.
etymology: From French extrinsèque, from Latin extrinsecus (“from without, without, on the outside”), from *extrim, an assumed adverbial form of exter (“outer, outward”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

definition: Fraud that prevents a party from knowing their rights or from having a fair opportunity of presenting them at trial.
Being concerned with the social and physical environment.
etymology: Alteration of earlier extravert (by influence of introvert), from German Extravert, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's 1918 "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte". By surface analysis, extro- + -vert.

definition: Release (a liquid) in drops or small quantities.
example: Exude sweat through the pores.
etymology: Latin exudāre, exsudāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- (“out, out of”) + sudāre (“to sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

definition: Pipet consisting of a small tube with a vacuum bulb at one end for drawing liquid in and releasing it a drop at a time.
example: She used an eye dropper to administer medication to the eyes.

definition: Exceedingly; extremely.
example: She plays fabulously well.
etymology: From fabulous + -ly.

definition: The act of putting your hand to cover your face to show disappointment or despair.
etymology: From face + palm. Attested since at least 2001.

definition: Cleverly amusing in tone.
example: Facetious remarks.
etymology: From French facétieux, from Latin facētia (“jest, wit, humor”), from facētus (“witty, jocose, facetious”).

definition: Solid excretory product evacuated from the bowels.
A small being, human in form, playful and having magical powers.
etymology: A deliberately archaic spelling of fairy (attested since the 1300s in spellings like fairye, fayre), based on Old French faerie, used in 1590 by Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene.

definition: Having made preparations.
etymology: From Middle English fain (“enjoyable, pleasing; fond of; glad, pleased; good, suitable;

definition: An open area for holding fairs or exhibitions or circuses.
etymology: From fair + ground.

definition: Very small Argentine armadillo with pale silky hair and pink plates on head and neck.
Having the character of, or characteristic of, a traitor.
example: The faithless Benedict Arnold.
etymology: From Middle English feithles, equivalent to faith + -less.

definition: Meaningless syllables in the refrain of a partsong.
Containing or based on a fallacy.
example: Fallacious reasoning.
etymology: From Old French fallacieux (whence -acious), from Latin fallācia, from fallāx, from fallere.

definition: To break off a military action with an enemy.
example: A failure of one of the rocket's first-stage engines just after liftoff would result in a destructive pad fallback.
etymology: From the verb fall back.

definition: Likely to fail or make errors.
example: Everyone is fallible to some degree.
etymology: From Middle English fallible, from Medieval Latin fallibilis (“liable to err, also deceitful”), from Latin fallere (“to deceive”).

definition: Any of various autumn-flowering perennials having white or pink to purple flowers that resemble asters; wild in moist soils from New Jersey to Florida and Texas.
Evergreen of tropical America having pulpy fruit containing saponin which was used as soap by Native Americans.
A fungus of the family Helvellaceae.
Any of several flowering weeds of the genus Boehmeria lacking stinging hairs.
(law) an offense involving intent to defraud and false representation and obtaining property as a result of that misrepresentation.
Artificially high; above the normal voice range.
example: A falsetto voice.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian falsetto, from falso (“false”).

definition: Any evidence that helps to establish the falsity of something.
etymology: From false + -ification.

definition: Make false by mutilation or addition; as of a message or story.
example: To falsify a record or document.
etymology: From French falsifier, from Late Latin falsificāre (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”), corresponding to false + -ify.

definition: The act of determining that something is false.
Unsteady in speech or action.
etymology: From falter + -ing.

definition: An elaborate system of vaulting in which the ribs diverge like fans.
Having fan-shaped leaves.
Excessive intolerance of opposing views.
etymology: From fanatic + -ism.

definition: A person having a strong liking for something.
example: She's definitely a cat fancier: she has nine of them in her home and the walls are covered with pictures of more.
etymology: From fancy (verb) + -er.

definition: A provocative Spanish courtship dance in triple time; performed by a man and a woman playing castanets.
example: What’s that fandango you’re using?
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish fandango, of uncertain origin. Possibly related to Portuguese fado, or of West African origin.

definition: Especially spread in a fan shape.
example: The peacock's fanned tail.

definition: Broadly or extravagantly humorous; resembling farce.
example: The wild farcical exuberance of a clown.
etymology: From farce + -ical, after comical etc.

definition: Fine meal made from cereal grain especially wheat; often used as a cooked cereal or in puddings.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin farīna (“flour, meal”), from far (“kind of grain”).

definition: A card game in which players bet against the dealer on the cards they will draw from a dealing box.
etymology: Presumably an alteration of pharaoh, itself a transcription of French pharaon, perhaps as a name for the King of Hearts.

definition: A former British bronze coin worth a quarter of a penny.
Cause to be interested or curious.
example: The flickering TV fascinated the cat.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fascinātus, perfect passive participle of fascinō (“to enchant, bewitch, fascinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fascinum (“a phallus-shaped amulet worn around the neck in Ancient Rome;

definition: A person who fastens or makes fast.
example: He found the door fastened and wondered who the fastener was.

definition: Giving careful attention to detail; hard to please; excessively concerned with cleanliness.
example: A fastidious and incisive intellect.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fastīdiōsus (“passive: that feels disgust, disdainful, scornful, fastidious;

definition: Having no living father.
etymology: From Middle English faderles, federles, from Old English fæderlēas, from Proto-Germanic *fadērlausaz, equivalent to father + -less. Cognate with German vaterlos.

definition: Like or befitting a father or fatherhood; kind and protective.
example: Fatherly advice.
etymology: From Middle English faderly, from Old English fæderlīċ (“fatherly, paternal”), from Proto-West Germanic *faderlīk, from Proto-Germanic *fadurlīkaz (“fatherly, paternal”), equivalent to father + -ly.

definition: Military uniform worn by military personnel when doing menial labor.
example: Ross: … why do you have to wear underwear tonight? Joey: It's a rented tux, 'kay? I'm not gonna go commando in another man's fatigues.

definition: Make fat or plump.
example: We must fatten the turkey in time for Thanksgiving.
etymology: From fat + -en.

definition: Make fat or plump.
Make fat or plump.
Subject to or used in the process of finishing or fattening up for slaughter.
example: A fattening hog.

definition: A ruling on a point of Islamic law that is given by a recognized authority.
example: The website contains fatwas on points of Islamic law that arise in court cases.

definition: (geology) a crack in the earth's crust resulting from the displacement of one side with respect to the other.
example: They built it right over a geological fault.

definition: Without fault or error.
example: Faultless logic.
etymology: From fault + -less.

definition: Attempting to win favor from influential people by flattery.
The loyalty that citizens owe to their country (or subjects to their sovereign).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English feaute, feute, from Anglo-Norman fëauté, fëuté, from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness”; “homage, fealty” in Medieval Latin), from fidēlis (“faithful”) + -tās (noun suffix);

definition: Without fear.
example: Fearlessly, he led the troops into combat.
etymology: From fearless + -ly.

definition: Eurasian aromatic oak-leaved goosefoot with many yellow-green flowers; naturalized North America.
An amateur boxer who weighs no more than 126 pounds.
etymology: From feather + weight.

definition: Of or relating to or characterized by fever.
example: A febrile reaction caused by an allergen.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrīlis, from Latin febris (“fever”). By surface analysis, Latin febr- + -ile.

definition: The raw material that is required for some industrial process.
example: Bio-materials may be substituted for petrochemical feedstocks as petroleum prices rise.
etymology: From feed + stock.

definition: Make believe with the intent to deceive.
example: He feigned that he was ill.
etymology: From Middle English feynen, feinen, borrowed from Old French feindre (“to pretend”), from Latin fingere (“to form, shape, invent”). Compare French feignant (present participle of feindre, literally “feigning”).

definition: Not genuine.
example: Feigned sympathy.

definition: Pretending with intention to deceive.
Any distracting or deceptive maneuver (as a mock attack).
etymology: Borrowed from French feint, the past participle of feindre (“to fake, feign”): see etymology 1.

definition: A person who fells trees.
etymology: From Middle English fellere, feller; equivalent to fell + -er.

definition: The biceps muscle of the thigh; it flexes the knee and rotates the leg laterally.
Small terrestrial orchid of eastern North America and Europe having two nearly basal leaves and dull yellow-green racemose flowers.
A process in which an agent causes an organic substance to break down into simpler substances; especially, the anaerobic breakdown of sugar into alcohol.
Transport by boat or aircraft.
Creation by the physical union of male and female gametes; of sperm and ova in an animal or pollen and ovule in a plant.
etymology: From the French; equivalent to fertilise + -ation.

definition: Provide with fertilizers or add nutrients to.
example: We should fertilize soil if we want to grow healthy plants.
etymology: From French fertiliser; equivalent to fertile + -ize.

definition: (heraldry) an ordinary consisting of a broad horizontal band across a shield.
etymology: Clipping of confess.

definition: Admit or acknowledge a wrongdoing or error.
etymology: Clipping of confess up.

definition: (medicine) the formation of morbific matter in an abscess or a vesicle and the discharge of pus.
Any joyous diversion.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English festivite, from Middle French festivité, from Latin festīvitas, equivalent to festive + -ity.

definition: An elaborate party (often outdoors).
etymology: * The noun derives from French fête. Doublet of feast, fiesta, and fest. * The verb derives from French fêter.

definition: A day designated for feasting.
In a feverish manner.
example: She worked feverishly.
etymology: From feverish + -ly.

definition: A trivial lie.
example: He told a fib about eating his spinach.
etymology: Unknown. Probably from fable; compare fible-fable (“nonsense”).

definition: A covering material made of glass fibers in resins.
etymology: Compound of fibre + glass.

definition: The outer and thinner of the two bones of the human leg between the knee and ankle.
A feeling of agitation expressed in continual motion.
example: He's got the fidgets.
etymology: From fidge (“to fidget”) + *-et (frequentative ending), possibly from Middle English *-ten, from Old English -ettan.

definition: European white-flowered weed naturalized in North America.
European wormwood similar to common wormwood in its properties.
The ordinal number of fifty in counting order.
etymology: From earlier fifteth, from Middle English fiftithe, fyftith; equivalent to fifty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.

definition: Any of several South African plants of the genus Mesembryanthemum cultivated for showy pink or white flowers.
A contrived or fantastic idea.
example: A figment of the imagination.
etymology: From Late Latin figmentum (“anything made, a fiction”), from fingō (“make, form, feign”); see fiction, feign, feint.

definition: (computer science) the name given to a computer file in order to distinguish it from other files; may contain an extension that indicates the type of file.
example: Meronyms: filename extension, extension.
etymology: From file + name.

definition: A string of characters beginning with a period and followed by one or more letters; the optional second part of a PC computer filename.
example: Most BASIC files use the filename extension .BAS.

definition: Designating the generation or the sequence of generations following the parental generation.
etymology: From Middle English filial, from Latin fīliālis, from fīlius (“son”) / fīlia (“daughter”) + -al.

definition: Duty of a child to its parents.
The love of a child for a parent.
Delicate and intricate ornamentation (usually in gold or silver or other fine twisted wire).
etymology: From French filigrane, from Italian filigrana, from Latin fīlum (“thread”) + grānum (“grain”).

definition: The quality of being final or definitely settled.
example: The finality of death.

definition: Having fine leaves.

(used in the plural) a percussion instrument consisting of a pair of hollow pieces of wood or bone (usually held between the thumb and fingers) that are made to click together (as by Spanish dancers) in rhythm with the dance.
The nail at the end of a finger.
etymology: From Middle English finger neil(e); equivalent to finger + nail. Compare Middle English nayl of fynger (“fingernail”) and Old English handnæġl (“fingernail”).

definition: The procedure of taking inked impressions of a person's fingerprints for the purpose of identification.
The end (tip) of a finger.
etymology: From finger + tip. Compare tiptoe and toetip.

definition: An upright hydrant for drawing water to use in fighting a fire.
Difficult to burn.
Difficult to burn.
The male is bright red with black wings and tail.
etymology: From fire + bird, so called because of their bright red or orange plumage.

definition: A piece of wood that has been burned or is burning.
example: The crowd cheered as a firebrand was tossed onto the huge pile of wood to start the traditional homecoming bonfire.
etymology: From Middle English fyr-brand, furbrond, equivalent to fire + brand. Cognate with German Feuerbrand (“firebrand”).

definition: Firework consisting of a small explosive charge and fuse in a heavy paper casing.
etymology: From fire + cracker.

definition: An area near a fireplace (usually paved and extending out into a room).
etymology: From fire + side.

definition: Eggs beaten with milk or cream and cooked until set.
The apparent surface of the imaginary sphere on which celestial bodies appear to be projected.
example: The international fashion firmament.
etymology: From Middle English firmament, furmament (“heaven; sky”), from Old French firmament (“firmament”), or from its etymon Latin firmāmentum (“support;

definition: A chisel with a thin blade for woodworking.
Someone habitually a spectator at the openings of theatrical productions.
etymology: From first night + -er.

definition: An upright geranium having scalloped leaves with a broad color zone inside the margin and white or pink or red flowers.
A kind of copepod.
etymology: From fish + louse.

definition: Capable of undergoing nuclear fission.
example: A fissionable nucleus.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fissilis.

definition: The quantity that can be held in the hand.
etymology: From fist (noun) + -ful.

definition: A chronic inflammation of the withers of a horse.
example: Communicating fistula.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin fistula (“pipe, ulcer, catheter”). Doublet of fester.

definition: In accordance with what is appropriate or suitable for the circumstances.
etymology: From fitting + -ly.

definition: Having five lobes.
A United States bill worth 5 dollars.
example: Do you have a fiver I could borrow? I can pay you back tomorrow.
etymology: From five + -er (measurement suffix) or + -er (“supporter”).

definition: A fricative sound (especially as an expression of disapproval).
etymology: Attested in English since 1525-35. From earlier fysel (“to fart”). Related to fīsa (“to fart”). Compare with Swedish fisa (“to fart (silently)”). See also feist.

definition: End weakly.
As if struck dumb with astonishment and surprise.
example: The flabbergasted aldermen were speechless.
etymology: Past tense of flabbergast.

definition: Out of condition; not strong or robust; incapable of exertion or endurance.
example: Flabby around the middle.
etymology: From a variant of flappy, from flap (“to hang loose”). Compare English dialectal flapsy (“flabby”), Middle Dutch flabbe (“a slap in the face; a fan-blade; a hair ribbon;

definition: Drooping without elasticity; wanting in stiffness.
example: A flaccid penis.

definition: Weakness or loss of muscle tone resulting from injury or disease of the nerves innervating the muscles.
An extreme bellicose nationalist.
etymology: From flag + waver.

definition: Surveying instrument consisting of a straight rod painted in bands of alternate red and white each one foot wide; used for sightings by surveyors.
etymology: From flag + pole. Cognate with West Frisian flaggepeal (“flagpole”), Dutch vlaggenpaal (“flagpole”), Low German Flaggenpohl (“flagpole”), German Flaggenpfahl (“flagpole”).

definition: Give a thrashing to; beat hard.
example: He was flailing wildly, but didn't land a blow.
etymology: From Middle English flayle, from earlier fleil, fleyl, fleȝȝl, from Old English fligel, *flegel (“flail”), from Proto-West Germanic *flagil, of uncertain origin.

definition: Any of various Old World tropical plants of the genus Coleus having multicolored decorative leaves and spikes of blue flowers.
Resistant to catching fire.
A back stationed wide of the scrimmage line; used as a pass receiver.
etymology: From flank + -er. The verb is from the noun (sense 3).

definition: A back stationed wide of the scrimmage line; used as a pass receiver.
Streaming or flapping or spreading wide as if in a current of air.
example: Ran quickly, her flaring coat behind her.

definition: Lacking a prominent belly.
Freight car without permanent sides or roof.
etymology: From flat + bed.

definition: A printing press where the type is carried on a flat bed under a cylinder that holds paper and rolls over the type.
Food fish of the Indonesian region of the Pacific; resembles gurnards.
etymology: From flat + head.

definition: Large catfish of central United States having a flattened head and projecting jaw.
An associate who shares an apartment with you.
etymology: From flat + -mate.

definition: Full of flavor.
etymology: From flavor + -ful.

definition: A small fragment of something broken off from the whole.
example: A fleck of hope.
etymology: From Middle English *flekk, *flekke (attested in Middle English flekked (“spotted, flecked”)), from Old Norse flekkr (“spot”), from Proto-Germanic *flekka-. Cognate with Dutch vlek, German Fleck, Swedish fläck.

definition: Given substance or detail; completed.
example: A plan fleshed out with statistics and details.

definition: A skeletal muscle whose contraction bends a joint.
etymology: From New Latin flexor, agent noun of flectō (“to bend”).

definition: A skeletal muscle whose contraction bends a joint.
Showing inappropriate levity.
etymology: 1595, from Northern English dialectal flippand (“prattling, babbling, glib”), present participle of flip (“to babble”), of North Germanic origin.

definition: A low plain adjacent to a river that is formed chiefly of river sediment and is subject to flooding.
example: Tidal floodplain.
etymology: From flood + plain.

definition: An insect that infests flour and stored grains.
A diagram of the sequence of operations in a computer program or an accounting system.
Aphasia characterized by fluent but meaningless speech and severe impairment of the ability understand spoken or written words.
Souffle-like omelet made by beating and adding the whites separately.
A nonmetallic univalent element belonging to the halogens; usually a yellow irritating toxic flammable gas; a powerful oxidizing agent; recovered from fluorite or cryolite or fluorapatite.
example: An octahedron of fluorines.
etymology: From Latin fluor (“flow”) + English -ine. Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1813.

definition: An applicator for applying flux (as in soldering).
Erect deciduous North American shrub with yellow-white flowers.
A buttress that stands apart from the main structure and connected to it by an arch.
Arboreal nocturnal mammal of southeast Asia and the Philippines resembling a lemur and having a fold of skin on each side from neck to tail that is used for long gliding leaps.
Of or relating to a fetus.
etymology: From foetus + -al, the former from Latin foetus, alternative form of fētus, and the latter from Latin -alis.

definition: The system of blood vessels and structures through which blood moves in a fetus.
An abnormal condition of a fetus; usually discovered during pregnancy and characterized by an abnormal heart rhythm.
An electronic monitor that monitors fetal heartbeat and the mother's uterine contractions during childbirth.
Motion of a fetus within the uterus (usually detected by the 16th week of pregnancy).
A pate made from goose liver (marinated in Cognac) and truffles.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French foie gras (literally “fat liver”).

definition: A B vitamin that is essential for cell growth and reproduction.
etymology: From folic acid + -ate (“salt or ester”).

definition: Capable of being folded up and stored.
example: A foldaway bed.
etymology: From fold + -able.

definition: A B vitamin that is essential for cell growth and reproduction.
etymology: From Latin folium (“leaf”), from its occurrence in leafy vegetables.

definition: Of or relating to or constituting a follicle.
Candy made of a thick creamy sugar paste.
example: Fondant chocolate.
etymology: 19th century. Unadapted borrowing from French fondant (“melting”), from fondre (“to melt”), from Latin fundere (“to melt”).

definition: Touch or stroke lightly in a loving or endearing manner.
example: They fondled in the back seat of the taxi.
etymology: From fond (“love, admire”) + -le (frequentative suffix).

definition: Cubes of meat or seafood cooked in hot oil and then dipped in any of various sauces.
example: A Swiss fondue.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French fondue (“melted”), from fondre (“to melt”).

definition: Marked by defiant disregard for danger or consequences.

definition: A bridge designed for pedestrians.

The part of the seashore between the highwater mark and the low-water mark.

example: In the female genitalia, the clitoral hood is homologous to the foreskin.
etymology: From fore- + skin, a loose calque of Latin praepūtium. Compare German Vorhaut, etc. First attested in c. 1535.

definition: Keep from happening or arising; make impossible.

definition: Someone who operates a forge.
etymology: From Middle English forger, forgere, from Old French forgiere; equivalent to forge + -er.

definition: Tendency to forget.

etymology: From Middle English forgetfulnes, forgetfulnesse, forȝetfulnesse, equivalent to forgetful + -ness.

definition: The place where something divides into branches.
example: The forkings of a road, or of a deer's antlers.

definition: The doctrine that formal structure rather than content is what should be represented.
etymology: From formal + -ism.

definition: Characterized by or in accordance with some formula.

definition: Having no cause or apparent cause.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin fortuītus (“happening by chance, accidental, random, fortuitous”), from *fortu- (“chance, fortune, luck”) + -ītus (suffix forming adjectives).

definition: A concavity in a surface (especially an anatomical depression).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin fossa (“a ditch, trench, fosse”). Doublet of fosse.

definition: Largest carnivore of Madagascar; intermediate in some respects between cats and civets.

example: The building stood foursquare.
etymology: From Middle English foure square; equivalent to four + square.

definition: An irregular ventricle between the third ventricle and the central canal of the spinal cord.
A ballroom dance in quadruple time; combines short and long and fast and slow steps fixed sequences.
etymology: From fox + trot.

etymology: From German Frankfurter, the demonym of Frankfurt. Specifically, a reference to Frankfurt-am-Main.

definition: A long bun shaped to hold a frankfurter.
The quality of being honest and straightforward in attitude and speech.
example: Complete frankness.
etymology: From frank + -ness.

definition: Changeable.
example: Freakish weather.
etymology: From freak + -ish.

definition: Done by hand without mechanical aids or devices.
example: A freehand drawing.
etymology: From free + hand.

definition: A natural or instinctive fellowship between people of similar interests.
example: He enjoyed the freemasonry of the Press.
etymology: From freemason + -ry.

definition: Standing apart; not attached to or supported by anything.
example: A freestanding bell tower.

definition: Software that is provided without charge.
etymology: From free + -ware (clipping of "software"). Coined by Andrew Fluegelman.

definition: Excessively agitated; distraught with fear or other violent emotion.
example: Frenetic screams followed the accident.

definition: Anything that freshens.
example: I sprayed freshener around the bathroom.
etymology: From freshen + -er.

definition: Flesh of various freshwater fishes of North America or of Europe.
Bivalve mollusk abundant in rivers of central United States.
Having frets.
example: The dulcimer and sitar are fretted instruments.

definition: In a terrifying manner.
example: The disturbing thing about the Minister's behavior is that far from being artificial, it too often rings frighteningly true.
etymology: From frightening + -ly.

definition: Having decorative ruffles or frills.
etymology: From frill + -y.

definition: A gecko that has membranous expansions along the sides of its body and limbs and tail that enable it to glide short distances.
Any of several summer-flowering American orchids distinguished by a fringed or lacerated lip.
Playful like a lively kitten.
example: He had his hands full, with three frisky kittens in the house.
etymology: From frisk + -y.

definition: (of hair) in small tight curls.
example: The wet weather made her hair frizzy and untidy.
etymology: From frizz + -y.

definition: Gay or light-hearted recreational activity for diversion or amusement.
example: Their frolic in the surf threatened to become ugly.
etymology: From Dutch vrolijk (“cheerful”), from Middle Dutch vrolijc, from Old Dutch frōlīk, from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz. Compare German fröhlich (“blitheful, gaily, happy, merry”).

definition: Emitting or filled with bubbles as from carbonation or fermentation.

etymology: From froth + -y.

definition: Showing displeasure or anger.
Prudence in avoiding waste.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French frugalité. By surface analysis, frugal + -ity.

definition: Capable of bearing fruit.
An organ specialized for producing spores.
Any of various tropical shrubs widely cultivated for their showy drooping purplish or reddish or white flowers; Central and South America and New Zealand and Tahiti.
etymology: From New Latin, after the genus Fuchsia, itself named after German botanist Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566).

definition: The activity of supplying or taking on fuel.

Dissociative disorder in which a person forgets who they are and leaves home to create a new life; during the fugue there is no memory of the former life; after recovering there is no memory for events during the dissociative state.
etymology: Borrowed from French fugue, from Italian fuga (“flight, ardor”), from Latin fuga (“act of fleeing”), from fugiō (“to flee”); compare Ancient Greek φυγή (phugḗ).

definition: A dive in which the diver throws the feet forward to complete a full backward somersault and enters the water feet first and facing away from the diving board.
Be mad, angry, or furious.
etymology: From Middle English fume, from Old French fum (“smoke, steam, vapour”), from Latin fūmus (“vapour, smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós (“smoke”), from *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, raise dust”).

definition: Of or for or relating to a funeral.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerārius, from Latin funus.

definition: In a strange manner.
example: Who, Bob? I just ran into him last week, funnily enough.
etymology: From funny + -ly.

definition: An interest followed with exaggerated zeal.
