etymology: From Middle English furour, from Middle French fureur, from Old French furor, from Latin furor, from furō (“To rage, to be out of one's mind”).

definition: Hollow out in the form of a furrow or groove.

definition: Encouragement of the progress or growth or acceptance of something.
etymology: From further + -ance.

definition: Mattress consisting of a pad of cotton batting that is used for sleeping on the floor or on a raised frame.
A theologian who believes that the Scripture prophecies of the Apocalypse (the Book of Revelation) will be fulfilled in the future.
etymology: From future + -ist.

definition: A sharp metal spike or spur that is fastened to the leg of a gamecock.
example: We politely ignored his gaff.
etymology: From Middle English gaffe, from Old French gaffe, from Old Occitan gaf (“hook”), derivative of gafar (“to seize”), from 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌰𐌽 (giban, “to give”). Doublet of gaffe.

definition: A socially awkward or tactless act.
example: Make a gaffe.
etymology: From French gaffe (“blunder”), in turn from Old Occitan gaf (“clasp”). Ultimately derived from Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍆𐌰𐌷 (gafah, “clasp”, noun) (𐌲𐌰- (ga-, intensifier) + 𐍆𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (fahan, “to catch”)). Doublet of gaff.

definition: A gay feeling.
example: There was much gaiety at the ball.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French gaieté, from gai. By surface analysis, gay + -ety.

definition: A person who gains weight.
etymology: From gain + -er. Compare German Gegner (“opponent, adversary”).

definition: Soft blue-grey mineral; lead sulfide; a major source of lead.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin galēna (“dross from smelting lead”).

definition: Fragile mosquito-like flies that produce galls on plants.
A large square-rigged sailing ship with three or more masts; used by the Spanish for commerce and war from the 15th to 18th centuries.
etymology: From Middle French galion or Spanish galeón.

definition: Causing irritation or annoyance.
example: Found it galling to have to ask permission.
etymology: From gall + -ing. The adjective follows from the verb.

definition: A rare silvery (usually trivalent) metallic element; brittle at low temperatures but liquid above room temperature; occurs in trace amounts in bauxite and zinc ores.
etymology: Borrowed from French gallium, named by its discoverer Lecoq, after Latin Gallia (“Gaul”).

definition: A form of interferon that is produced by T cells and macrophages; involved in the activation of phagocytes.
Underworld organizations.
etymology: From gang + land.

definition: An encapsulated neural structure consisting of a collection of cell bodies or neurons.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek γᾰγγλῐ́ον (gănglĭ́on, “encysted tumour on a tendon or aponeurosis”).

definition: A nerve cell whose body is outside the central nervous system.
example: Damage to ganglion cells in the retina may play a role in the development of glaucoma.

definition: Necrotic tissue; a mortified or gangrenous part or mass.

etymology: Borrowed from French gangrène, from Latin gangraena, from Ancient Greek γάγγραινα (gángraina, “gangrene”).

definition: A temporary passageway of planks (as over mud on a building site).
example: The new fleet of trains comes with widened gangways and improved seating.
etymology: From Middle English gangway, from Old English gangweġ (“passageway; thoroughfare”), equivalent to gang + way. Related to Dutch gang (“hallway”) and Norwegian gang (“hallway”).

definition: A strong-smelling plant whose dried leaves can be smoked for a pleasant effect or pain reduction.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi गांजा (gāñjā), ultimately from Sanskrit गञ्जा (gañjā, “hemp”). First use appears c. 1800.

definition: A framework of steel bars raised on side supports to bridge over or around something; can display railway signals above several tracks or can support a traveling crane etc.

Lacking orderly continuity.
Improved garden variety of black nightshade having small edible orange or black berries.
Low perennial with small silvery-green ovate to hastate leaves.
Of great mass; huge and bulky.

definition: Befitting a man of good breeding.

Someone who cuts flat glass to size.

definition: A momentary flash of light.

definition: Having brief brilliant points or flashes of light.
example: Bugle beads all aglitter.

definition: Tasteless showiness.
example: The glitz of the award ceremony was obvious.
etymology: Back-formation from glitzy, in turn from German glitzern (“glint”). Cognate with Old Norse glitra, glita (“glitter”) and Gothic 𐌲𐌻𐌹𐍄𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌾𐌰𐌽 (glitmunjan, “glisten”).

definition: Dwell on with satisfaction.
example: You did well to win the game, but there's no need to gloat about it.

definition: Malicious satisfaction.
Loss of all ability to communicate.
Mediterranean thistlelike plant widely cultivated for its large edible flower head.
Having the shape of a sphere or ball.
example: Little globular houses like mud-wasp nests.
etymology: From French globulaire or Medieval Latin globulāris.

definition: Having the hands covered with gloves.
example: Holding your gloved right hand under the cuff of the left glove, insert your left hand in the left glove.

definition: Moody and melancholic.

definition: A crystalline amino acid occurring in proteins; important in protein metabolism.

A sweet syrupy trihydroxy alcohol obtained by saponification of fats and oils.

definition: The simplest amino acid found in proteins and the principal amino acid in sugar cane.

definition: A conjugated protein having a carbohydrate component.
etymology: From glyco- + protein.

definition: Glyptic art in the form of a symbolic figure carved or incised in relief.

etymology: First attested in 1727. Borrowed from French glyphe, from Ancient Greek γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carving”), from γλύφω (glúphō, “I carve, engrave”).

definition: Bite or chew on with the teeth.
example: Gnaw an old cracker.
etymology: From Middle English gnawen, gnaȝen, from Old English gnagan, from Proto-West Germanic *gnagan, from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą (“to gnaw”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʰnēgʰ- (“to gnaw, scratch”).

definition: Become ground down or deteriorate.
Relative large gnawing animals; distinguished from rodents by having two pairs of upper incisors specialized for gnawing.
Give heart or courage to.

definition: Having no points scores.
etymology: From goal + -less.

definition: A person who tends a flock of goats.

etymology: From goat + -ee (diminutive suffix), referring to the tuft of hair on the chin of many domestic goats.

definition: A man who serves as a sailor.
example: He spat a big ball of gob on to the pavement.

definition: Expletives used informally as intensifiers.
example: I'll be damned (or blessed or darned or goddamned) if I'll do any such thing.
etymology: From French goddam (“English person”), from English goddamn.

definition: Appropriate to or befitting a god.
example: A man of godlike sagacity.
etymology: From god + -like.

definition: Piety by virtue of being a godly person.
etymology: From godly + -ness.

definition: A male godchild.
etymology: From Middle English godsone, gossone, from Old English godsunu (“godson”), equivalent to god- + son. Cognate with Danish gudsøn (“godson”), Swedish gudson (“godson”), Icelandic guðsonur (“godson”).

definition: Someone who leaves.

definition: A compound of telluride and gold with the chemical formula AuTe2.
Chinese deciduous conifer resembling a larch with golden yellow leaves.

Plovers of Europe and America having the backs marked with golden-yellow spots.
Shiner of eastern North America having golden glints; sometimes also called ‘bream’.
Shrubby Australian tree having clusters of fragrant golden yellow flowers; widely cultivated as an ornamental.
Greyish woolly leafy perennial with branched stems ending in leafless stalks bearing golden-yellow flower heads; dry areas western North America.
etymology: From the resemblance of its flowers to yarrows'.

definition: A variety of green lacewing.
etymology: From golden + eye.

definition: Early-flowering perennial of southern and southeastern Europe with flower heads resembling those of goldenrod.
etymology: From goldy + locks. Goldilocks is a traditional children's story and its protagonist.

definition: A good source of something that is desired.
An attendant who carries the golf clubs for a player.
The evasion of work or duty.
A cricket ball bowled as if to break one way that actually breaks in the opposite way.
example: His weakness in batting is against googly.
etymology: Unknown; perhaps derived from googie (“an egg, in reference to the unusual direction of bounce”).

definition: Stalked barnacle that attaches to ship bottoms or floating timbers.
Spiny Eurasian shrub having greenish purple-tinged flowers and ovoid yellow-green or red-purple berries.
In some classifications considered a part of the family Saxifragaceae: plants whose fruit is a berry.
Burrowing edible land tortoise of southeastern North America.
etymology: By surface analysis, gopher (“burrowing rodent”, compare translingual Gopherus) + tortoise.

etymology: Borrowed from Scots hod (“to jog along on horseback”), probably related to hotch (“(verb) to move up and down jerkily, bob; to jog along on horseback; to hop like a frog; to fidget; to shrug; to heave with laughter;

definition: A very loud utterance (like the sound of an animal).

definition: A very loud utterance (like the sound of an animal).
The original specimen from which the description of a new species is made.
etymology: From holo- + -type.

definition: An informal term for a youth or man.
example: That gunslinger is one bad hombre.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish hombre (“man; human being”). Doublet of gome, homo, ombre, and omi.

definition: An alcoholic beverage (especially beer) made at home.

definition: A classroom in which all students in a particular grade (or in a division of a grade) meet at certain times under the supervision of a teacher who takes attendance and does other administrative business.
Oriented toward home.
example: In a homeward direction.

definition: Oriented toward home.
example: In a homeward direction.

definition: A sermon on a moral or religious topic.
etymology: From Middle English omelī, omelīe, omelye, from Old French omelie and directly from Late Latin homīlia (“homily”), from Ancient Greek ὁμῑλίᾱ (homīlíā, “homily;

definition: The quality of being similar or comparable in kind or nature.

example: Because of their connection with both homology and cohomology, chain complexes are an important topic of study in homological algebra.
etymology: From Latin homologia, from Ancient Greek ὁμολογία (homología, “agreement, assent”); compare French homologie. By surface analysis, homo- + -logy.

definition: Thorny deep-rooted drought-resistant shrub native to southwestern United States and Mexico bearing pods rich in sugar and important as livestock feed; tends to form extensive thickets.
Social bee often domesticated for the honey it produces.
etymology: From honey + bee.

definition: Lining of the reticulum (or second stomach) of a ruminant used as food.
Shrub or vine of the genus Lonicera.
etymology: From Middle English honysokel, honisokel, honysocle, hunisuccle, perhaps an alteration of Middle English honysoke, honysouke (“honeysuckle”) (whence honeysuck), from Old English huniġsūce, huniġsūge (“honeysuckle”);

definition: Shrubs and small trees and woody vines.
An illicitly distilled (and usually inferior) alcoholic liquor.
etymology: Abbreviation of hoochinoo, name of a specific liquor, from Tlingit Xutsnoowú Ḵwáan, the group that produced it, from Hutsnuwu (“grizzly bear fort”), the name of the village on Admiralty Island in which they lived.

definition: (geology) a column of weathered and unusually shaped rock.
example: A tall sandstone hoodoo.
etymology: Apparently an alteration of voodoo.

definition: A wrench with a hook that fits over a nut or bolt head.
A cruel and brutal fellow.
etymology: Probably a variant of the Irish surname Houlihan, 1890s.

definition: Blatant or sensational promotion.
etymology: Earlier houp-la, hoop la, first attested in c.

definition: Having the frame made of horn or tortoise shell or plastic that simulates either.
example: Horn-rimmed glasses.

definition: Highly venomous viper of northern Africa and southwestern Asia having a horny spine above each eye.
Catfish common in eastern United States.
Northern Pacific puffin.
etymology: So called because of the significant fleshy "horn" above each eye.

definition: Small pale-colored desert rattlesnake of southwestern United States; body moves in an s-shaped curve.
Screamer having a hornlike process projecting from the forehead.
An ointment containing horse chestnut extract, used to relieve muscle pain and joint pain.
example: I use horse balsam after working out to soothe muscle pain.

A person who breeds and cares for horses.
Coarse prickly weed having pale yellow flowers and yellow berrylike fruit; common throughout southern and eastern United States.
The root of the horseradish plant; it is grated or ground and used for seasoning.

definition: The root of the horseradish plant; it is grated or ground and used for seasoning.
Creamy white sauce with horseradish and mustard.
Socks and stockings and tights collectively (the British include underwear).
etymology: From hosier + -y.

definition: A mixed drink made of liquor and water with sugar and spices and served hot.
A situation that is ideal for rapid development (especially of something bad).
example: It was a hotbed of vice.
etymology: From hot + bed.

definition: A long bun shaped to hold a frankfurter.
The presence of heat.
etymology: From Middle English hotnes, from Old English hātnes (“hotness, heat”), equivalent to hot + -ness.

definition: Someone who is dazzlingly skilled in any field.
example: She sure was a hotshot on the keyboard, 93 words per minute!
etymology: From hot + shot.

definition: A barge that is designed and equipped for use as a dwelling.
etymology: From house + boat.

definition: A craft capable of moving over water or land on a cushion of air created by jet engines.
etymology: From hover + -craft. Originally a trademark by Saunders-Roe Limited, a British aero- and marine-engineering company.

definition: A joke that seems extremely funny.
example: A howler is a glaring mistake, a mistake that cries out to be noticed.
etymology: From howl + -er. Some senses are derivatives of the intensifier "howling", as in "howling wilderness", (Deuteronomy 32:10)

definition: Monkey of tropical South American forests having a loud howling cry.
Any plant of the genus Hoya having fleshy leaves and usually nectariferous flowers.
etymology: From the genus name.

definition: Loud confused noise from many sources.
etymology: In early use, the noun is often mentioned as a cry by Irish people, and so is possibly borrowed from Irish;

definition: Any of various dark-fruited as distinguished from blue-fruited blueberries.
example: I'm your huckleberry.
etymology: Probably an alteration of Middle English hurtilbery (“whortleberry”). American English from 1660s.

definition: A low spreading or prostrate shrub of southwestern United States with small acorns and leaves resembling those of the huckleberry.
An act of forcible exhalation.
etymology: From huff + -ing.

definition: A Polynesian rain dance performed by a woman.
Of great size and bulk.
example: A hulking figure of a man.
etymology: From hulk + -ing.

definition: In a humane manner.
example: Let's treat the prisoners of war humanely.
etymology: From Middle English humanly; equivalent to humane + -ly. Piecewise doublet of humanly.

definition: Pretentious or silly talk or writing.
etymology: Origin unknown; the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) states that “the facts as to its origin appear to have been lost, even before the word became common enough to excite attention”.

definition: Bone extending from the shoulder to the elbow.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin humerus, from umerus. Cognate with Spanish hombro (“shoulder”).

definition: (used informally) very large.
etymology: Of expressive origin, likely inspired by huge, with the termination of monstrous.

definition: In a humorous manner.
example: Dickens had humorously suggested a special service of intercession at St. Paul's Cathedral.
etymology: From humorous + -ly.

definition: Being satisfactory or in satisfactory condition.
A woman hunter.
etymology: A variant of hunteress, from Middle English hunteras, hunteres, hunteresse, equivalent to hunter + -ess, possibly on the model of the likes of mistress.

definition: Moving with great haste.
example: Affection for this hurrying driving … little man.

definition: A red transparent variety of zircon used as a gemstone.
A faucet for drawing water from a pipe or cask.
etymology: An irregular formation: hydr- + -ant, originally US English. By surface analysis, hydrate + -ant.

definition: Any binary compound formed by the union of hydrogen and other elements.
etymology: From hydro- + -ide.

definition: An aqueous solution of hydrogen chloride; a strongly corrosive acid.
example: Near-synonyms: gastric acid, stomach acid, gastric juice (which is mostly hydrochloric acid).

definition: A complex consisting of an organic base in association with hydrogen chloride.

definition: A colorless gas that yields hydrobromic acid in solution with water.
A colorless gas that yields hydroiodic acid in aqueous solution.
Of or relating to the science of hydrography.
etymology: From hydrography + -ic.

definition: Having a strong affinity for water; tending to dissolve in, mix with, or be wetted by water.
etymology: From hydro- + -philic.

definition: Relating to fluids at rest or to the pressures they exert or transmit.
example: Hydrostatic pressure.

definition: The pressure at a given point in a liquid measured in terms of the vertical height of a column of the liquid needed to produce the same pressure.
Being or containing a hydroxyl group.
etymology: From hydro- + oxy.

definition: Any acid that has hydroxyl groups in addition to the hydroxyl group in the acid itself.
The monovalent group -OH in such compounds as bases and some acids and alcohols.

definition: The monovalent group -OH in such compounds as bases and some acids and alcohols.
The anion OH having one oxygen and one hydrogen atom.
The monovalent group -OH in such compounds as bases and some acids and alcohols.
A medical specialist in hygiene.

definition: Machine-readable text that is not sequential but is organized so that related items of information are connected.

definition: A database management system that allows strings of text (‘objects’) to be processed as a complex network of nodes that are linked together in an arbitrary way.
Abnormal enlargement of a body part or organ.
etymology: From French hypertrophie, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over, excessive”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”), equivalent to hyper- + -trophy.

definition: A punctuation mark (‘-’) used between parts of a compound word or between the syllables of a word when the word is divided at the end of a line of text.
A person who induces hypnosis.

definition: Induce hypnosis in.
example: Hypnotize a subject.
etymology: Derived from hypnot(ic) + -ize (verbal derivational suffix).

definition: A compound used as a fixing agent in photographic developing.
etymology: Clipping of various terms beginning with hypo-, from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “under”).

definition: Abnormally low blood sugar usually resulting from excessive insulin or a poor diet.
etymology: From hypo- + glycemia or hypo- + glyc- + -emia.

definition: Abnormally low blood pressure.

definition: A basal part of the diencephalon governing autonomic nervous system.
etymology: From hypo- + thalamus.

definition: To believe especially on uncertain or tentative grounds.
etymology: From hypothesis + -ize.

definition: An underactive thyroid gland; a glandular disorder resulting from insufficient production of thyroid hormones.
etymology: Coined c. between 1900 and 1905 from hypo- (“under”) + thyroid + -ism.

definition: Neurotic disorder characterized by violent emotional outbreaks and disturbances of sensory and motor functions.
An attack of hysteria.

definition: Frozen dessert containing cream and sugar and flavoring.
The process of forming and relating ideas.
example: Suicidal ideation.
etymology: From ideate + -ion.

definition: In the Roman calendar: the 15th of March or May or July or October or the 13th of any other month.
etymology: From Middle English ides, idus, from Anglo-Norman and Old French ides, from Latin īdūs, a fourth-declension plurale tantum, from the Latin practice of treating most recurring calendrical days as plurals.

Any disease arising from internal dysfunctions of unknown cause.

Unlawfulness by virtue of violating some legal statute.

definition: (of handwriting, print, etc.) not legible.

definition: With impatience; in an impatient manner.

definition: Having or showing arrogant superiority to and disdain of those one views as unworthy.

definition: Someone who (fraudulently) assumes the appearance of another.

definition: Characterized by a lightly pert and exuberant quality.

definition: Characterized by undue haste and lack of thought or deliberation.

etymology: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).

definition: Incapable of being placated.

In an impulsive or impetuous way; without taking cautions.

definition: Worthless or dangerous material that should be removed.

etymology: From impure + -ity. From Middle French impurité, from Latin impuritas.

definition: While absent; although absent.

definition: In the uterus.
example: The child was infected in utero from the mother.

definition: In an inaccurate manner.

definition: In an inadequate manner or to an inadequate degree.
example: The temporary camps were inadequately equipped.
etymology: From inadequate + -ly.

definition: Incapable of being repudiated or transferred to another.
example: An inalienable right is a right that cannot be given away nor taken away.

etymology: Attested since 1430. From Middle English incredulite, from Old French incredulité, from Late Latin incredulitas, from Latin incredulus (“unbelieving”) + -itas (“-ity”), equivalent to incredulous + -ity.

definition: Suggest that someone is guilty.
example: The newspapers incriminated the innocent man unjustly.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incrīminātus, perfect passive participle of Latin incrīminō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). First attested in 1736. By surface analysis, in- + criminate.

definition: The quality of being indecent.

A concave cut into a surface or edge (as in a coastline).
etymology: From Anglo-Norman endenture, from Old French endenteure, from endenter (“to dent”).

definition: Poor enough to need help from others.
etymology: From Middle English indigent, from Old French indigent, from Latin indigēns, present participle of indigeō (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egeō (“to be in need, want”).

definition: An affront to one's dignity or self-esteem.
example: Public indignity.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin indignitās, indignitātem. Equivalent to indign + -ity.

definition: The trait of being injudicious.
example: Political indiscretion.
etymology: From Old French, from Late Latin indiscrētiō.

definition: Marked by or expressing individuality.

definition: Marked by or expressing individuality.

definition: Stupefied or excited by a chemical substance (especially alcohol).

definition: Not suitable for food.
example: Inedible dinner.
etymology: From in- + edible.

definition: Unskillfulness resulting from a lack of training.
etymology: From Latin ineptitūdō. By surface analysis, inept + -itude.

definition: Injustice by virtue of not conforming with rules or standards.
example: The intended purpose of antidiscrimination laws is to counteract and reduce inequity.
etymology: From in- + equity. Piecewise doublet of iniquity.

definition: That cannot be entirely consumed or used up.
example: An inexhaustible supply of coal.
etymology: From in- + exhaustible.

definition: Not to be placated or appeased or moved by entreaty.
example: Russia's final hour, it seemed, approached with inexorable certainty.
etymology: From Middle French inexorable, from Latin inexōrābilis (“relentless, inexorable”) (or directly from the Latin word), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + exōrābilis (“that may be moved or persuaded by entreaty; exorable”).

definition: In an inexorable manner.
example: Time marches on inexorably.
etymology: From inexorable + -ly.

definition: An abnormal state in which development has stopped prematurely.
An acute viral disease marked by inflammation of nerve cells of the brain stem and spinal cord.
Invade in great numbers.
example: The roaches infested our kitchen.
etymology: From Middle English infesten, from Old French infester (“to infest”), from Latin īnfestō (“assail, molest”, verb), from īnfestus (“hostile”), of uncertain origin.

definition: (baseball) a person who plays a position in the infield.
example: The infielder run in to field the bunt.
etymology: From infield + -er.

definition: Infinitely or immeasurably small.
example: Do you ever get the feeling that you are but an infinitesimal speck, swallowed by the vastness of the universe and beyond?
etymology: From New Latin īnfīnītēsimus + -al. Displaced earlier coordinate term fluxion.

definition: The branch of mathematics that is concerned with limits and with the differentiation and integration of functions.
The uninflected form of the verb.
etymology: From Middle English infenitife (“without end, in perpetuity”), from Late Latin īnfīnītīvus (“unlimited, indefinite”), from Latin īnfīnītus (“unlimited, infinite”). By surface analysis, infinite + -ive.

definition: Lacking bodily or muscular strength or vitality.
example: He was infirm of body but still keen of mind, and though it looked like he couldn't walk across the room, he crushed me in debate.

definition: Cause inflammation in.
example: The repetitive motion inflamed her joint.
etymology: From Middle English inflammen, enflamen, enflaumen (“to set (something) on fire; to be on fire; (figurative) to enrage (someone); to become enraged; to incite (someone) to do evil; to inspire (someone);

definition: (of the voice) altered in tone or pitch.
example: His southern Yorkshire voice was less inflected and singing than her northern one.

definition: The time and process of budding and unfolding of blossoms.
etymology: From Latin inflōrēscentia, from inflōrēscō (“to begin to flower”), inchoative verb of flōreō (“to flower”).

definition: Someone who intervenes with authorities for a person in trouble (usually using underhand or illegal methods for a fee).
A television commercial presented in the form of a short documentary.
etymology: Blend of information + commercial.

definition: A film or TV program presenting the facts about a person or event.
etymology: Blend of information + entertainment.

definition: Any tree or shrub of the genus Inga having pinnate leaves and showy usually white flowers; cultivated as ornamentals.
etymology: Borrowed from Brazilian Portuguese ingá, borrowed from Old Tupi ingá, from Proto-Tupi-Guarani *iŋa.

definition: A gas that produces general anesthesia when inhaled.
The quality of lacking compassion or consideration for others.
etymology: From Middle French inhumanité, from Latin inhumanitas, equivalent to inhuman + -ity.

definition: Defying imitation; matchless.
example: An inimitable style.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French inimitable, from Latin inimitabilis, corresponding to in- + imitable.

definition: Morally objectionable behavior.
etymology: From Middle English iniquite, jniquite (“evil, wickedness, iniquity; evil act; hostility, malevolence; hostile act;

definition: (computer science) the format of sectors on the surface of a hard disk drive so that the operating system can access them and setting a starting position.
etymology: From initialize + -ation.

definition: A person who initiates a course of action.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin initiātor. By surface analysis, initiate + or.

definition: (used of drugs) capable of being injected.
etymology: From inject + -able.

definition: Harmful to living things.
etymology: From Middle English injurious, from Anglo-Norman enjurius, from Latin iniūriōsus; analysable as injury + -ous.

definition: A block of absorbent material saturated with ink; used to transfer ink evenly to a rubber stamp.
Of the color of black ink.
etymology: From ink + -y.

definition: Having a cap that melts into an inky fluid after spores have matured.
Of the color of black ink.
Adorned by inlays.
(dentistry) a filling consisting of a solid substance (as gold or porcelain) fitted to a cavity in a tooth and cemented into place.
etymology: From in- + lay.

definition: Internal organs collectively (especially those in the abdominal cavity).
example: He took the cover off his computer and looked at the innards.
etymology: Alteration of inwards.

definition: The owner or manager of an inn.
etymology: From Middle English inkeper; equivalent to inn + keeper. Compare Middle English inholder (“innkeeper”).

definition: Taking a vaccine as a precaution against contracting a disease.
etymology: From Latin inoculātio. Equivalent to inoculate + -ion.

definition: Not causing anger or annoyance.
example: Inoffensive behavior.
etymology: From in- + offensive.

definition: Beyond normal limits.
example: A book of inordinate length.
etymology: From Middle English inordinat, from Latin inōrdinātus (“not arranged, disordered, irregular”), from in- + ordinatus, past participle of ōrdināre (“to arrange, order”).

definition: Of an obscure nature.
example: The inscrutable workings of Providence.
etymology: Borrowed into late Middle English from Late Latin īnscrūtābilis, from in- (“not”) + scrūtō (“to examine”), corresponding to in- + scrutable

definition: The inability to respond to affective changes in your interpersonal environment.
etymology: From in- + sensitivity.

definition: (of winds) coming from the sea toward the land.
example: An inshore breeze.

definition: Caliper for measuring inside dimensions (the size of a cavity or hole); points on its legs curve outward.
Lacking sincerity.
example: A charming but thoroughly insincere woman.
etymology: From Latin insincerus.

definition: Introduce or insert (oneself) in a subtle manner.
example: He insinuated himself into the conversation of the people at the nearby table.
etymology: First attested in 1529;

definition: An indirect (and usually malicious) implication.
example: Slander may be conveyed by insinuations.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French insinuation, from Old French, from Latin insinuatio, from īnsinuō (“to push in, creep in, steal in”), from in (“in”) + sinus (“a winding, bend, bay, fold, bosom”).

definition: Lacking taste or flavor or tang.
example: Insipid hospital food.
etymology: From French insipide, from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”). In some senses, perhaps influenced by insipient (“unwise, foolish, stupid”).

definition: The trait of being rude and impertinent; inclined to take liberties.
example: They are fond of fun and therefore witty, wit being well-bred insolence.
etymology: From Middle French insolence, from Latin īnsolentia.

definition: Marked by casual disrespect.
example: Insolent behaviour.

definition: Experiencing or accompanied by sleeplessness.
example: Insomniac old people.
etymology: From insomnia + -ac.

definition: The verbal act of urging on.
etymology: From Middle English instigacioun, from Old French instigacïon and Latin instīgātio.

definition: Someone who deliberately foments trouble.
example: She was the instigator of their quarrel.
etymology: From Latin īnstīgātor (“stimulator”), from īnstīgāre (present infinitive of īnstīgō (“to incite, set on, stimulate, rouse or urge”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp, to stab; to puncture;

definition: Teaching or impressing upon the mind by frequent instruction or repetition.
Someone who plays a music as a profession.
etymology: From instrumental + -ist.

definition: Defiance of authority.
etymology: From in- + subordination, on the model of French insubordination.

definition: A lack of competence.
example: Pointed out the insufficiencies in my report.
etymology: From in- + sufficiency.

definition: A material such as glass or porcelain with negligible electrical or thermal conductivity.
example: To isolate electrical wires from the pylons supporting them, one often uses glass insulators.
etymology: From insulate + -or.

definition: A financial institution that sells insurance.
A measuring instrument for measuring the area of an irregular plane figure.
etymology: From integrate + -or.

definition: An educated and intellectual elite.
etymology: From Russian интеллиге́нция (intelligéncija) or Polish inteligencja, from Latin intellegentia (“intelligence”). Doublet of intelligence.

definition: Provision of logistic (or administrative) support by one or more of the military services to one or more departments or agencies of the United States government.
A loan from one bank to another.
Act between parties with a view to reconciling differences.
example: He interceded in the family dispute.
etymology: First attested in c. 1570. From Middle French intercéder, from Latin intercēdō, from inter- (“between”) + cēdō (“I go”) (English cede), literally “to (act as) go-between”.

definition: Used of competition between colleges or universities.
example: Intercollegiate basketball.
etymology: From inter- + collegiate.

definition: Be interwoven or interconnected.
example: The bones are interconnected via the muscle.
etymology: From inter- + connect.

definition: A reciprocal relation between interdependent entities (objects or individuals or groups).
etymology: From inter- + dependence.

definition: Mutually dependent.
etymology: From inter- + dependent.

definition: Authoritative prohibition.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from French interdiction, itself a borrowing from Latin interdictiō.

definition: Fire directed to an area to prevent the enemy from using that area.
Any measuring instrument that uses interference patterns to make accurate measurements of waves.
etymology: From interfer(e) + -o- + -meter.

definition: Having a pattern of fretwork or latticework.
Coordinate in such a way that all parts work together effectively.
etymology: From inter- + lock.

definition: Marriage to a person belonging to a tribe or group other than your own as required by custom or law.
Tiresomely long; seemingly without end.
example: An interminable sermon.
etymology: From Middle English interminable, from Middle French interminable and its etymon Late Latin interminābilis. By surface analysis, in- + terminable.

definition: Incorporate within oneself; make subjective or personal.
example: Internalize a belief.
etymology: From internal + -ize.

definition: An advocate of internationalism.
etymology: From international + -ist.

definition: The act of bringing something under international control.
etymology: From international + -ization.

definition: Reciprocally connected.
etymology: From inter- + related.

definition: A questioner who is excessively harsh.
etymology: From Latin interrogātor. By surface analysis, interrogate + -or.

definition: Chronic lung disease affecting the interstitial tissue of the lungs.
A person who is interviewed.
etymology: From interview + -ee.

definition: Acute abdominal pain (especially in infants).
An uprising by Palestinian Arabs (in both the Gaza Strip and the West Bank) against Israel in the late 1980s and again in 2000.
example: The first intifada ended when Israel granted limited autonomy to the Palestine National Authority in 1993.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic اِنْتِفَاضَة (intifāḍa, “shaking off, uprising, insurrection”).

definition: Within the skull.
etymology: From intra- + cranial.

definition: An aneurysm of a cranial artery.
The cavity enclosed by the cranium.
Carried on within the bounds of an institution or community.
example: Most of the students participated actively in the college's intramural sports program.
etymology: From Latin intramuralis, from intra (“within”) + muralis (“of a wall”).

definition: A restricted computer network; a private network created using World Wide Web software.
etymology: From intra- + net.

definition: In an intravenous manner.
example: The patient had to be fed intravenously.
etymology: From intravenous + -ly.

definition: With elaboration.
etymology: From intricate + -ly.

definition: Projecting inward.
The insertion of a cannula or tube into a hollow body organ.
etymology: Probably coined in 1880–1884 by Joseph O'Dwyer, M.D.; in widespread publication in 1887.

definition: Establishing as invalid or untrue.
The power of creative imagination.
etymology: From inventive + -ness.

definition: Make an inversion (in a musical composition).
example: Here the theme is inverted.
etymology: From Middle French invertir.

definition: A mixture of equal parts of glucose and fructose resulting from the hydrolysis of sucrose; found naturally in fruits; sweeter than glucose.
Any of various organs of locomotion or attachment in invertebrates.
Designed to find information or ascertain facts.
example: Investigative reporting.
etymology: From investigate + -ory.

definition: Imparting strength and vitality.
example: The invigorating mountain air.

definition: Immune to attack; impregnable.
example: Gunners raked the beach from invulnerable positions on the cliffs.
etymology: From Middle French invulnérable, from Latin invulnerābilis, from vulnerābilis, from vulnerō (“to wound”), from vulnus (“wound”), equivalent to in- + vulnerable.

definition: With respect to private feelings.
example: Inwardly, she was raging.
etymology: From inward + -ly.

definition: A salt or ester of hydriodic acid.
etymology: From iodine + -ide.

definition: Converted totally or partly into ions.
A heavy brittle metallic element of the platinum group; used in alloys; occurs in natural alloys with platinum or osmium.
etymology: New Latin iridium, from Classical Latin iris + -ium, from Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris, “rainbow”), because of the bright colour of many of the element's salts.

definition: A compound containing two atoms of sulfur combined with iron.
A common mineral (iron disulfide) that has a pale yellow color.
Sheathed in iron plates for protection.
example: Unlike the average vehicle, cash delivery vans are ironclad and almost unstoppable.
etymology: From iron + clad.

definition: In an irrational manner.
example: They acted irrationally.
etymology: From irrational + -ly.

definition: Impossible to reconcile.
example: Irreconcilable differences.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French irréconciliable, from Late Latin irreconciliābilis, from in- (“not”) + reconciliō (“to reconcile”) + -ābilis (“-able”). By surface analysis, ir- + reconcilable.

definition: Incapable of being made smaller or simpler.
example: An irreducible minimum.
etymology: From ir- + reducible.

definition: Impossible to deny or disprove.
example: An irrefutable argument.
etymology: From Late Latin irrefūtābilis, from ir- (“not”) + refūtābilis (“refutable”), from refūtō (“to refute”) + -bilis (“-able”), equivalent to ir- + refutable.

definition: Behavior that breaches the rule or etiquette or custom or morality.
example: An irregularity of surface.
etymology: From Middle French irrégularité, from Medieval Latin irregularitas. Morphologically irregular + -ity.

definition: The lack of a relation of something to the matter at hand.
In an irreparable manner or to an irreparable degree.
etymology: From irreparable + -ly.

definition: Impossible to repress or control.
example: An irrepressible chatterbox.
etymology: From ir- + repressible.

definition: Incapable of being resisted.
etymology: From irresistible + -ly.

definition: A form of untrustworthiness; the trait of lacking a sense of responsibility and not feeling accountable for your actions.
etymology: From ir- + responsibility or irresponsible + -ity.

definition: In an irresponsible manner.
example: He acted irresponsibly.
etymology: From irresponsible + -ly or ir- + responsibly.

definition: In an irreversible manner.
example: This old tradition is irreversibly disappearing.
etymology: From irreversible + -ly or ir- + reversibly.

definition: Supply with water, as with channels or ditches or streams.
example: We need to irrigate the land before we plant the crops.
etymology: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin irrigātus, perfect passive participle of irrigō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). See also Middle English irrigat(e) (“watered, irrigated”).

definition: Something that causes irritation and annoyance.
etymology: From French irritant, equivalent to irritate + -ant.

definition: Hypoxia resulting from slow peripheral circulation (such as follows congestive cardiac failure).
California evergreen wild plum with spiny leathery leaves and white flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish islay.

definition: A policy of nonparticipation in international economic and political relations.
etymology: From isolation + -ism.

definition: Of or relating to isolationism.
etymology: From isolation + -ist.

definition: Of or relating to or having the relation of an isotope.
etymology: From isotope + -ic.

definition: Invariant with respect to direction.
etymology: From iso- + -tropic, from Ancient Greek ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + τροπικός (tropikós, “of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure; tropic; tropical; etc.”).

definition: A style of handwriting with the letters slanting to the right.
etymology: Named after the nation of Italy, as it was first used by an Italian printer, Aldo Manuzio, around 1500. Literally Italy + -ic.

definition: To say, state, or perform again.
example: She kept reiterating her request.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1533, the noun in 1941;

definition: Any of various coarse shrubby plants of the genus Iva with small greenish flowers; common in moist areas (as coastal salt marshes) of eastern and central North America.
A commonly cultivated trailing South American plant with peltate leaves and rosy flowers.
A highly figured fabric woven on a Jacquard loom.
example: The White House has jacquard drapes in the East Room.
etymology: Eponym, from Joseph Marie Jacquard, inventor of the Jacquard loom.

definition: Someone who guards prisoners.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English gayoler, gayler, jayler, from Old French jaiolier, gaiolier, from jaiole. By surface analysis, jail + -er.

definition: A correctional institution used to detain persons who are in the lawful custody of the government (either accused persons awaiting trial or convicted persons serving a sentence).
etymology: From jail + house.

definition: Immense East Indian fruit resembling breadfruit; it contains an edible pulp and nutritious seeds that are commonly roasted.
A small outbuilding with a bench having holes through which a user can defecate.
etymology: From Middle English Jake (variant of “Jack”) or Jakke (variant of “Jacques” and “Jack”). Use as a place to urinate and defecate first attested in the form jacques.

definition: Plant bearing very hot and finely tapering long peppers; usually red.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish jalapeño.

definition: Hot green or red pepper of southwestern United States and Mexico.
A gay festivity.
etymology: Unknown 19th-century American slang. Chosen by Baden-Powell in 1919 for use in the Scout Movement.

definition: A transmitter used to broadcast electronic jamming.
etymology: From jam + -er.

definition: Yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes caused by an accumulation of bile pigment (bilirubin) in the blood; can be a symptom of gallstones or liver infection or anemia.
etymology: From Middle English jaundis, jaunis, from Middle French jaunisse, from jaune (“yellow”) + -isse (“-ness”). Jaune, from Old French jalne, from Latin galbinus (“yellowish”), from galbus (“yellow”).

definition: A journey taken for pleasure.
etymology: Origin uncertain. Perhaps a palatalised alteration of daunt (“to discourage”). Compare Scots jaunder (“to ramble, jaunt to taunt, jeer”), dialectal Swedish ganta (“to play the buffoon, romp, jest”);

definition: Marked by up-to-dateness in dress and manners.
example: A jaunty red hat.
etymology: Formerly spelt janty, from French gentil. See gentle, and compare genty. Doublet of genteel, gentile, and gentle.

definition: An open two-wheeled one-horse cart formerly widely used in Ireland.
The jaw in vertebrates that is hinged to open the mouth.
etymology: From Middle English jawe bone, a partial calque of earlier Middle English chawlbone, chawylbon, chavylbone, chawle boon, chavyl bon (“jaw bone”, literally “chavel bone”), see chavel-bone; equivalent to jaw + bone.

definition: Of animals having jaws of a specified type.
etymology: From jaw + -ed.

definition: With jealousy.
example: He guarded his privacy jealously.
etymology: From jealous + -ly.

definition: Become gelatinous.
example: The liquid jelled after we added the enzyme.
etymology: The verb is a back-formation from jelly. The later noun is from the verb. Reinforced by gel. Compare obsolete geal.

definition: Throw away, of something encumbering.
example: The ballooners had to jettison all of their sand bags to make it over the final hill.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman getteson, from Old French getaison, from geter, jeter (modern French: would be *jetaison like pendaison); possibly from a Vulgar Latin *iectātiō, from *iectātus < iectāre, from Latin iactō.

definition: Someone who makes jewelry.
A very short time (as the time it takes the eye to blink or the heart to beat).
example: I’ll be back in a jiffy.
etymology: Origin unknown; said to have been thieves’ cant for “lightning”. Also formerly written "giffy", to which a connection with gliff has been proposed. As a kind of envelope, a genericization of Jiffy bag.

definition: A slight irregular shaking motion.
example: Give the key a jiggle and see if it opens.
etymology: From jig + -le (frequentative suffix).

definition: Rebuffed (by a lover) without warning.
example: Jilted at the altar.

definition: Characterized by jerky movements.
example: A jittery ride.
etymology: From jitter + -y.

definition: A short riding boot that fastens with a buckle at the side.
A short riding boot that fastens with a buckle at the side.
A short riding boot that fastens with a buckle at the side.
Someone who runs a steady slow pace (usually for exercise).
etymology: From jog + -er.

definition: A person who likes to join groups.
etymology: From Middle English joynour (“maker of furniture, small boxes, etc.”), from Old French joigneor (“joiner, carpenter”), agent noun from joindre (“to join”), equivalent to join + -er.

definition: Fine woodwork done by a joiner.
etymology: From joiner + -y; see also -ery.

definition: Having joints or jointed segments.
etymology: From joint (“noun”) + -ed.

definition: Rush of Australia.
The act of traveling from one place to another.
etymology: From Middle English journeyinge; equivalent to journey + -ing.

definition: A heavy plate armor not intended for free combat, produced in the late 15th to 16th century.
example: The jousting armour could weigh as much as 50 kg (100 pounds).

definition: A heavy plate armor not intended for free combat, produced in the late 15th to 16th century.
example: The jousting armour could weigh as much as 50 kg (100 pounds).

definition: Full of or showing high-spirited merriment.
example: A jovial old gentleman.
etymology: First attested in 1590; borrowed from Middle French jovial (“under the influence of Jupiter; of Jove;

definition: In a joyous and gleeful manner.
etymology: From Middle English joifulliche, joyfully, equivalent to joyful + -ly.

definition: A ride in a car taken solely for pleasure.
example: They took their girlfriends for joyrides in stolen cars.
etymology: From joy + ride.

definition: Joyful and proud especially because of triumph or success.
example: Be in jubilant mood.
etymology: From Latin iubilans ("shouting for joy").

definition: A feeling of extreme joy.
example: I knew it had been a victory when I heard the jubilations coming from that neighborhood.
etymology: From Old French jubilacion, from Latin iūbilātiō (“a shouting for joy”). Cognate with Spanish jubilación (“retirement”).

definition: Marked by the exercise of good judgment or common sense in practical matters.
example: Judicious use of one's money.
etymology: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.

definition: A performer who juggles objects and performs tricks of manual dexterity.
etymology: From Middle English jogeler, jogelour, iogular, partly continuing Old English ġeogolere (“juggler; magician;

definition: Veins in the neck that return blood from the head.
A person who drinks alcoholic beverages (especially to excess).
example: A keen juicer, she has tried all kinds of fruits and vegetables.
etymology: From juice + -er.

definition: In utter disorder.
Being in a tense state.
etymology: From jump + -y.

definition: Weighs no more than 122 pounds.
A legal scholar versed in civil law or the law of nations.
example: Distinguished jurist.
etymology: From Middle French juriste.

definition: Something that bulges out or is protuberant or projects from its surroundings.
etymology: From Middle English jutten (“to project, jut out”), an alteration of jetten (“to strut, be showy”). More at English jet.

definition: Extend out or project in space.
example: His sharp nose jutted out.

definition: Extending out above or beyond a surface or boundary.
example: The jutting limb of a tree.

definition: A small benign growth on the faces of hands of children.
An esoteric or occult matter resembling the Kabbalah that is traditionally secret.
Large brownish-green New Zealand parrot.
etymology: Borrowed from Māori kea.

definition: Having a ridge or shaped like a ridge or suggesting the keel of a ship.
example: It was a deep-keeled yacht.

definition: Something of sentimental value.
etymology: From keep + sake.

definition: A fibrous scleroprotein that occurs in the outer layer of the skin and in horny tissues such as hair, feathers, nails, and hooves.
etymology: Borrowed from German Keratin, from Ancient Greek κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + -in. Doublet of carat.

definition: An edge between a sidewalk and a roadway consisting of a line of curbstones (usually forming part of a gutter).
etymology: From curb (“raised border or frame”) [from mid-17th c.]. Doublet of curve.

definition: Any of a class of organic compounds having a carbonyl group linked to a carbon atom in each of two hydrocarbon radicals.
example: Methyl ethyl ketone R₁ = CH₃, R₂ = C₂H₅.
etymology: From German Keton, from Aketon (“acetone”), from French acétone (“acetone”). See acetone.

definition: A group having the characteristic properties of ketones.
A musician who plays a keyboard instrument.
etymology: From keyboard + -ist.

definition: A military uniform made of khaki fabric.
A collective farm or settlement owned by its members in modern Israel; children are reared collectively.
etymology: From Hebrew קִבּוּץ (kibúts), derived from the verb קָבַץ (kaváts, “to gather, collect, assemble”). Not related to kibitz.

definition: A commercial bribe paid by a seller to a purchasing agent in order to induce the agent to enter into the transaction.
etymology: Deverbal from kick back.

definition: Material for starting a fire.
example: Go and collect some kindling.
etymology: From kindle + -ing.

definition: A male relative.
etymology: From Middle English kynnesman, equivalent to kin + -s- + -man.

definition: Someone who kisses.
example: She's a great kisser!
etymology: Agent noun of kiss: from kiss + -er.

definition: A utensil used in preparing food.
Excessively garish or sentimental art; usually considered in bad taste.
etymology: From German Kitsch, from dialectal kitschen (“to coat, to smear”); the word and concept were popularized in the 1930s by several critics who contrasted it with avant-garde art.

definition: A deceitful and unreliable scoundrel.
etymology: From Middle English knave, knafe, from Old English cnafa (“child, boy, youth; servant”), from Proto-West Germanic *knabō. Cognate to Dutch knaap and German Knabe.

definition: (used in the plural) trousers ending above the knee.
A small flat triangular bone in front of the knee that protects the knee joint.
etymology: From knee + cap.

definition: Knitted clothing.
etymology: From knit + -wear.

definition: Making great mental demands; hard to comprehend or solve or believe.
example: I faced the knotty problem of what to have for breakfast.
etymology: From Middle English knotti, knotty (“having a knot in it; full of knots; tied together (?); resembling a knot, knotlike; having knobs or protuberances; bulging, convex; of a tree, branch, etc.: full of knots, gnarled;

definition: Pine lumber with many knots; used especially for paneling and furniture.
100 kobos equal 1 naira in Nigeria.
etymology: Ultimately from English copper, probably via one or more West African languages (compare Igbo kọbọ̀ and Fula kobo).

definition: Tree bearing large brown nuts containing e.g. caffeine; source of cola extract.
etymology: Presumably from a West African language. Compare Hausa gōr̃ò, Bambara goro, Temne kola, Mandinka kolo (“kola nut”).

definition: Bitter brown seed containing caffein; source of cola extract.
example: The local people here believe that kola nut tea -- or as they call it, bissy tea -- is a cure for all ailments.
etymology: Compound of kola + nut

definition: Someone regarded as eccentric or crazy and standing out from a group.
etymology: Possibly from cuckoo.

definition: Informal or slang terms for mentally irregular.
example: His kooky behavior seemed charming at first, but soon got on our nerves.
etymology: From kook + -y.

definition: The ratio of the distance traveled (in kilometers) to the time spent traveling (in hours).
Shrimp-like planktonic crustaceans; major source of food for e.g. baleen whales.
etymology: From Norwegian krill (“fry of fish”).

definition: The basic unit of money in China.
Doing arduous or unpleasant work.
example: The bent backs of laboring slaves picking cotton.

definition: Lacking natural ease.
example: At the end of the marathon, her laboured breathing told us she was exhausted.

definition: Doing arduous or unpleasant work.
A torn ragged wound.
example: The doctor sewed up the laceration in his arm.
etymology: From Latin lacerātiō, first attested in 1598. By surface analysis, lacerate + -tion. Compare lacerate.

definition: A small amount of liquor added to a food or beverage.
example: A light lacing of rum goes into the cake batter.

definition: A salt or ester of lactic acid.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lactātus, perfect passive participle of lactō (“to suckle, give suck, contain milk”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from lac (“milk”), cognate to Ancient Greek γάλα (gála, “milk”).

definition: Producing or secreting milk.
example: Lactating cows.

definition: Put (a liquid) into a container by means of a ladle.
example: Ladle soup into the bowl.

definition: Small round bright-colored and spotted beetle that usually feeds on aphids and other insect pests.
etymology: From lady + bird. Lady here refers to the Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus.

definition: Small round bright-colored and spotted beetle that usually feeds on aphids and other insect pests.
Small round bright-colored and spotted beetle that usually feeds on aphids and other insect pests.
etymology: From lady + bug, the “lady” here referring to Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus. Compare German Marienkäfer, Danish mariehøne, Latvian mārīte, Macedonian бубамара (bubamara) and Spanish mariquita.

definition: The syllable naming the sixth (submediant) note of a major or minor scale in solmization.
etymology: An anglicised spelling of la.

definition: The doctrine that government should not interfere in commercial affairs.
etymology: Borrowed from French laissez faire (“leave it be”, literally “let do”).

definition: A document indicating permission to do something without restrictions.
With minimally restricted freedom in commerce.
Found in the Great Lakes and north to Alaska.
Land bordering a lake.
example: Property on the lakefront is very expensive.
etymology: From lake + front.

definition: The shore of a lake.
etymology: From lake + shore.

definition: Support column consisting of a steel cylinder filled with concrete.
Support column consisting of a steel cylinder filled with concrete.
Arranged in or consisting of laminae.
etymology: From Latin lāmina (“thin sheet of material”) + English -ar.

definition: Nonturbulent streamline flow in parallel layers (laminae).
A quadrille for 8 or 16 couples.
Owning no land.
example: The landless peasantry.
etymology: From Middle English londlees, from Old English landlēas, equivalent to land + -less. Cognate with Dutch landeloos (“landless”), German landlos (“landless”), Icelandic landlaus (“landless”).

definition: Atlantic salmon confined to lakes of New England and southeastern Canada.
A large continuous extent of land.
etymology: From land + mass.

definition: Lacking spirit or liveliness.
example: A languid mood.
etymology: * Portuguese lânguido (“languid; listless”)

definition: Lose vigor, health, or flesh, as through grief.
example: He languished without his girlfriend.
etymology: From Middle English languysshen, from the present participle stem of Anglo-Norman and Middle French languir, from Late Latin languīre, alteration of Latin languēre (“to be faint, unwell”).

definition: A small pinion having cylindrical bars instead of teeth, used chiefly in inexpensive clocks.
Having a protruding jaw giving the face a gaunt appearance.
Jointed so as to produce a flush surface.
Having overlapping hull planks.
Wood of a larch tree.
Any of numerous conifers of the genus Larix all having deciduous needlelike leaves.
A supply of food especially for a household.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English larder, from Anglo-Norman larder and Old French lardier, from Latin lardārium. By surface analysis, lard + -er.

definition: Having relatively large leaves.
A cartilaginous structure at the top of the trachea; contains elastic vocal cords that are the source of the vocal tone in speech.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin larynx, from Ancient Greek λᾰ́ρῠγξ (lắrŭnx, “larynx; windpipe; gullet, throat”).

definition: Baked dish of layers of lasagna pasta with sauce and cheese and meat or vegetables.
etymology: From Italian.

definition: A girl or young woman who is unmarried.
example: [Bhuvan, English captions, Radha Kaise Na Jale]: O my lovely lassie...
etymology: From lass + -ie.

definition: A long noosed rope used to catch animals.
etymology: From Spanish lazo, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lace.

definition: A relay that maintains either contact position indefinitely without power applied to the coil.
example: A latching relay allows remote control of building lighting without the hum that may be produced from a continuously (AC) energized coil.

definition: Of plants that ripen in the fall.

definition: Advancing as if in the child's game, by leaping over obstacles or competitors.

The rind of a lemon.
Running or extending in the direction of the length of a thing.

Cause of leprosy.

etymology: Coined in 1564, from Latin levitās (“lightness, frivolity”), from levis (“lightness (in weight)”). Cognate to lever, and more distantly, light.

The property of having one dimension.

definition: The quality of being luminous; emitting or reflecting light.

definition: Having the properties of a magnet; i.e. of attracting iron or steel.

definition: A magician or sorcerer of ancient times.

definition: A great raja; a Hindu prince or king in India ranking above a raja.

definition: Injure or wound seriously and leave permanent disfiguration or mutilation.

definition: The chief steward or butler of a great household.
Any unwholesome or desperate condition.
example: What maladies afflict our nation?
etymology: From Middle English maladie, from Old French maladie (“sickness, illness, disease”), from malade (“ill, sick”), from Latin male habitus (“ill-kept, not in good condition”), 1st century AD. See also malice and habit.

definition: A kind of mantis shrimp.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish mariposa (“a butterfly”).

definition: Skill in shooting.

definition: A loose and crumbling earthy deposit consisting mainly of calcite or dolomite; used as a fertilizer for soils deficient in lime.

definition: Soup cooked in a large pot.
etymology: Borrowed from French marmite.

definition: Cut off or left behind.
example: Travelers marooned by the blizzard.

definition: A name given to a product or service.
etymology: Borrowed from French marque. Doublet of mark. Ultimately cognate with marquee.

definition: A noblewoman ranking below a duchess and above a countess.
etymology: Borrowed from French marquise.

definition: Old World harrier frequenting marshy regions.
Swamp plant of Europe and North America having bright yellow flowers resembling buttercups.
(of soil) soft and watery.
example: A marshy coastline.
etymology: From Middle English mersshy, mershi, equivalent to marsh + -y.

definition: Agile slender-bodied arboreal mustelids somewhat larger than weasels.
etymology: From Middle English martren, martryn, from Old French martrine (“marten fur”), from Old Dutch *marthrīn (“of marten fur”), from *marthar (“marten”). Displaced related Old English mearþ, from Proto-Germanic *marþuz.

definition: Agile slender-bodied arboreal mustelids somewhat larger than weasels.
Commonest shrew of moist habitats in North America.
A party of guests wearing costumes and masks.
example: Mud masque; clay masque.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French masque. Doublet of mask and mesh.

definition: A female massager.
example: Oh! I'm a masseuse. I give people massages and stuff.
etymology: Borrowed from French masseuse, feminine of masseur.

definition: A block of the earth's crust bounded by faults and shifted to form peaks of a mountain range.
etymology: Borrowed from French massif, from Middle French massif, ultimately from Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “barley-cake, lump (of dough)”).

definition: In a skillfully masterful manner; with the skill of a master.
example: The young boy played the violin sonata masterfully.

definition: An old breed of powerful deep-chested smooth-coated dog used chiefly as a watchdog and guard dog.
A soft-furred chocolate-brown bat with folded ears and small wings; often runs along the ground.
etymology: These bats' faces are supposed to resemble those of mastiff dogs.

definition: Extinct elephant-like mammal that flourished worldwide from Miocene through Pleistocene times; differ from mammoths in the form of the molar teeth.
A box for holding matches.
etymology: From match + box.

definition: Someone with great regard for material possessions.
etymology: From material + -ist.

definition: (used colloquially) having the relationship of friends or pals.
example: You've been very matey with that new bird.
etymology: From mate + -y.

definition: A female head of a family or tribe.
Admission to a group (especially a college or university).
The interchange of each row of a square matrix with the corresponding column.
Of a pale to moderate greyish violet color.
etymology: Borrowed from French mauve (“mallow”), from Latin malva, which has a purple colour. Doublet of mallow. Coined in 1856 by the chemist William Henry Perkin, when he accidentally created the first aniline dye.

definition: Of blue tinged with mauve.
Of pink tinged with mauve.
Of or relating to the upper jaw.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin māxillāris (“of or belonging to the jaw”), from māxilla (“the jawbone, jaw”) + -āris (“-ar, -ary”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to maxilla + -ary.

definition: Either of two arteries branching from the external carotid artery and supplying structure of the face.
Posterior continuation of the pterygoid plexus; joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein.
Making as great as possible.
Perennial European buttercup with yellow spring flowers widely naturalized especially in eastern North America.
Tall perennial Old World salvia with violet-blue flowers; found in open grasslands.
Widely distributed in grasslands of northern United States and Canada.
A bend or curve, as in a stream or river.
example: The meanders of an old river, or of the veins and arteries in the body.
etymology: From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course (modern Turkish Menderes).

definition: Explained in terms of physical forces.
example: A mechanistic universe.
etymology: From mechan(ism) + -istic.

definition: Esteemed for its flavor; usually preserved or used for sauces and relishes.
In a submissive or spiritless manner.
example: Meekly bowed to his wishes.
etymology: From Middle English mekely, mekeliche, equivalent to meek + -ly. Compare Old Norse mjúkliga.

definition: Announce for a score; of cards in a card game.
example: One can meld copper and zinc together to form brass.
etymology: The verb is probably derived: * from a blend of melt + weld; or * from melled (“blended; mingled”), the past participle of mell. The noun is derived from the verb. Compare also melting pot.

definition: Having a musical sound; especially a pleasing tune.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English melodious, from Middle French melodieus, melodieux. By surface analysis, melod(i) + -ous.

definition: Learning so as to be able to remember verbatim.
example: The actor's memorization of his lines.
etymology: From memorize + -ation.

definition: Of or relating to the menopause.
etymology: From menopause + -al.

definition: A decent responsible person with admirable characteristics.
etymology: From Yiddish מענטש (mentsh, “an honorable person”), from Middle High German mensch, mensche, mennische, from Old High German mennisko (“man, human being”), from Proto-Germanic *manniskaz (“human”).

definition: The healthy psychological state of someone with good judgment.
In a compassionate manner.
example: He dealt with the thief mercifully.
etymology: From merciful + -ly.

definition: An ointment containing mercury.
Properly deserved.
example: A merited success.

definition: A form of social system in which power goes to those with superior intellects.
example: As a small nation without natural resources, Singapore relies on education and meritocracy to develop its economy.

definition: A gay feeling.
etymology: From merry + -ment.

definition: A form of carcinoma of the mesothelium lining lungs or abdomen or heart; usually associated with exposure to asbestos dust.
etymology: From mesothelium + -oma.

definition: Any of several small spiny trees or shrubs of the genus Prosopis having small flowers in axillary cylindrical spikes followed by large pods rich in sugar.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish mezquite, mizquite, from Nahuatl mizquitl (“the mesquite tree”).

definition: A gum obtained from mesquite pods; resembles gum arabic.
The activity of making things out of metal in a skillful manner.
example: Metalworking industry.
etymology: From metal + working.

definition: Of or relating to metamorphosis (especially of rocks).
example: Metamorphic stage.
etymology: From metamorphosis + -ic.

definition: Rock altered by pressure and heat.
Given out in portions.
Of or pertaining to atmospheric phenomena, especially weather and weather conditions.
example: Meteorological factors.
etymology: From meteor + -ic.

definition: An antidiabetic drug (trade name Glucophage) prescribed to treat type II diabetes.
etymology: From meth- + -formin (“phenformin derivative”).

definition: A crystalline amino acid containing sulfur; found in most proteins and essential for nutrition.
etymology: From methyl + thio- + -n- + -ine.

definition: A poisonous gas or liquid (CH3Br) used to fumigate rodents, worms, etc.
Any of three poisonous colorless isomeric phenols; derived from coal or wood tar; used as a disinfectant.
The scientific study of measurement.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure”) + English -logy.

definition: Clicking pendulum indicates the exact tempo of a piece of music.
etymology: Coined in English from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure”) + νόμος (nómos, “regulation, law”).

definition: The pace of music measured by the number of beats occurring in 60 seconds.
The courage to carry on.
etymology: From figurative use of metal (since 16th century). The two spellings were originally interchangeable variants, but came to be distinguished by sense in the 18th century.

definition: The common gull of Eurasia and northeastern North America.
Street lined with buildings that were originally private stables but have been remodeled as dwellings.
example: She lives in a Chelsea mews.
etymology: From Mewes, the name of the royal stables at Charing Cross, which is the plural of mew (“falcon cage”).

definition: A soprano with a voice between soprano and contralto.
etymology: (music): Clipping of mezzo-soprano

definition: A soprano with a voice between soprano and contralto.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian mezzosoprano.

definition: A minute life form (especially a disease-causing bacterium); the term is not in technical use.
Film on which materials are photographed at greatly reduced size; useful for storage; a magnification system is used to read the material.
etymology: From micro- + film.

definition: Some point in the air; above ground level.
example: The planes collided in midair.
etymology: From mid (adjetive) + air (noun).

definition: The median plane of the body (or some part of the body).
etymology: From mid- + line.

definition: The middle area of the human torso (usually in front).
etymology: From mid- + section.

definition: A male temporary rank held by young naval officers in training.
The middle of winter.
etymology: From Middle English midwinter, mydwinter, mydwynter, from Old English midwinter, from Proto-West Germanic *midiwintru, from Proto-Germanic *midjawintruz (“midwinter”), equivalent to mid- + winter.

definition: Aroused to impatience or anger.
etymology: From miff + -ed.

definition: (used only in combinations) the length of something in miles.
example: The race was a 30-miler.
etymology: From mile + -er.

definition: A militant aggressiveness.
Imbued with militarism.
etymology: From militarist + -ic or military + -istic.

definition: Act of assembling and putting into readiness for war or other emergency:.
etymology: From militarize + -ation.

definition: Issued military arms.
An attache who is a specialist in military matters.
A female member of the military police who polices soldiers and guards prisoners.
Nonvenomous tan and brown king snake with an arrow-shaped occipital spot; southeastern ones have red stripes like coral snakes.
A man who delivers milk.
etymology: From milk + -man.

definition: A metric unit of length equal to one thousandth of a meter.
etymology: From French millimètre, equivalent to milli- + metre.

definition: One thousandth (10^-3) of a second.
etymology: From milli- + second.

definition: (figurative) something that hinders or handicaps.
example: Paying the mortgage every month is a millstone round their necks.
etymology: From Middle English mylneston, milneston, from Old English mylenstān (“millstone”), from Proto-West Germanic *mulīnu + *stain; equivalent to mill + stone;

definition: Fish sperm or sperm-filled reproductive gland; having a creamy texture.
The act of mimicking; imitative behavior.
example: They say that mimicry is the sincerest form of flattery, but I still think I'm being mocked when he acts just like me.
etymology: From mimic + -ry.

definition: Evergreen Australasian tree having white or silvery bark and young leaves and yellow flowers.
etymology: From New Latin mimosa, from Latin mimus (“mime, actor”), referring to Mimosa pudica and its habit of shrinking back when touched.

definition: Tropical American thorny shrub or small tree; fragrant yellow flowers used in making perfumery.
The act of reducing something to the least possible amount or degree or position.
example: Companies should engage in risk minimization.
etymology: From minimize + -ation.

definition: Extremely small.
etymology: Likely a conflation between miniature and minuscule.

definition: Very small European freshwater fish common in gravelly streams.
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English menew, menowe (“small fish; (specifically) common minnow (Phoxinus phoxinus);

definition: Tansy-scented Eurasian perennial herb with buttonlike yellow flowers; used as potherb or salad green and sometimes for potpourri or tea or flavoring; sometimes placed in genus Chrysanthemum.
Relating to or suggestive of mint.
etymology: From mint + -y.

definition: Entrap.
example: Our people should not be mired in the past.
etymology: From Middle English mire, a borrowing from Old Norse mýrr, from Proto-Germanic *miuzijō, whence also Swedish myr, Norwegian myr, Icelandic mýri, Dutch *mier (in placenames, for example Mierlo).

definition: New Zealand conifer used for lumber; the dark wood is used for interior carpentry.
etymology: Borrowed from Māori miro.

definition: Great merriment.
etymology: From Middle English merth, myrthe, murhthe, from Old English myrgþ (“mirth, joy”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgiþu (“briefness, brevity”); equivalent to merry + -th (abstract nominal suffix).

definition: The fraudulent appropriation of funds or property entrusted to your care but actually owned by someone else.
etymology: From mis- + appropriation.

definition: Behave badly.
example: The children misbehaved all morning.
etymology: From Middle English misbehaven, equivalent to mis- + behave.

definition: Improper or wicked or immoral behavior.
example: The teacher did not tolerate misbehavior in his classroom.
etymology: From mis- + behavior.

definition: A mistake in calculating.
etymology: From mis- + calculation.

definition: A collection containing a variety of sorts of things.
example: A monthly miscellany of literature.
etymology: Borrowed from French miscellanées, from Latin mīscellānea, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“to mix”).

definition: An incorrect charge to a jury given by a judge.
example: The magician used misdirection to get us to watch his left hand while he did something with his right hand.
etymology: From mis- + direction.

definition: Interpret falsely.
etymology: From mis- + interpret.

definition: Putting the wrong interpretation on.
example: His misinterpretation of the question caused his error.
etymology: From mis- + interpretation or misinterpret + -ation.

definition: An incorrect or unsuitable name.
example: The name Chinese checkers is a misnomer since the game has nothing to do with China.
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English misnoumer (“(law) mistaken identification of a person;

definition: Misinterpretation caused by inaccurate reading.
Represent falsely.
example: This statement misrepresents my intentions.
etymology: From mis- + represent.

definition: So badly formed or out of shape as to be ugly.
example: Misshapen old fingers.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English mysshapen, misse shapen, mysshape, mysshap; equivalent to mis- + shapen.

definition: A spelling that is incorrect.
example: Accomodation is a common misspelling of accommodation.
etymology: From mis- + spelling.

definition: An unintentional but embarrassing blunder.
example: Confusion caused his unfortunate misstep.
etymology: From mis- + step.

definition: A plant of the genus Rhipsalis.
etymology: Like mistletoe, it grows on larger plants and produces white fruits.

definition: Large European thrush that feeds on mistletoe berries.
A strong north wind that blows in France during the winter.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French mistral, from Occitan. Doublet of magistral.

definition: A trial that is invalid or inconclusive.
etymology: From mis- + trial.

definition: Of or relating to or located in or near the mitral valve.
example: Mitral insufficiency.
etymology: From mitre + -al.

definition: Valve with two cusps; situated between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
Joint that forms a corner; usually both sides are bevelled at a 45-degree angle to form a 90-degree corner.
etymology: From Middle English mytre, from Old French mitre, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”). Its use in reference to a counterfeit coin derived from the bishop's mitre stamped upon it.

definition: Hand tool for guiding handsaws in making crosscuts or miter joints.
Joint that forms a corner; usually both sides are bevelled at a 45-degree angle to form a 90-degree corner.
Of or relating to or involved the practice of aiding the memory.
example: Mnemonic device.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, “pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives).

definition: Act of marshaling and organizing and making ready for use or action.
example: Mobilization of the country's economic resources.
etymology: From French mobilisation or mobilise + -ation.

definition: Call to arms; of military personnel.
etymology: From French mobiliser.

definition: A sweater with a short turtleneck collar that does not fold down.
In a disrespectful jeering manner.
etymology: From mocking + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to a popularization of art deco that used bright colors and rectangular shapes.
Become technologically advanced.
example: Viet Nam is modernizing rapidly.

definition: Brought up to date.
example: Modernized methods.

definition: A small or moderate or token amount.
example: England still expects a modicum of eccentricity in its artists.
etymology: From Middle English modicum, from Latin modicum (“a little, a small amount”), a noun use of the neuter form of modicus (“moderate; restrained, temperate; reasonable”) + -cum (suffix forming neuter nouns).

definition: An unvarying or habitual method or procedure.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin modus operandī, from modus (“manner, method”) and operandī (“of working”).

definition: One of two (approximately) equal parts.
example: Aniline has both a phenyl and an amino moiety.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French moytié, from Old French meitié (“half”) (modern French moitié (“half”)), from Late Latin medietās (“centre, midpoint; half”), from Latin medius (“half;

definition: Make (more) humid.
example: Moisturize your skin.
etymology: From moisture + -ize.

definition: Taffy made of molasses.
Covered with or smelling of mold.
example: Moldy bread.
etymology: From mold + -y.

definition: Brownish-black burrowing salamander of southeastern United States.
A polyvalent metallic element that resembles chromium and tungsten in its properties; used to strengthen and harden steel.
example: A quadruple bond between molybdenums.
etymology: Attested since the last quarter of 18th century.

definition: Steel containing 10-15% molybdenum; properties are similar to tungsten steel.
Establishing something (e.g. gold or silver) as the legal tender of a country.
etymology: From monetize + -ation.

definition: Someone who purchases and maintains an inventory of goods to be sold.
