etymology: Origin uncertain, possibly from monger (“dealer or trader in a specific commodity”) (etymology 1); or related to Middle English mangbot (“type of fishing boat used on the Thames”).

definition: 100 mongo equal 1 tugrik in Mongolia.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish mongo . Compare Tagalog munggo. Doublet of mung.

definition: Agile grizzled Old World viverrine; preys on snakes and rodents.
etymology: First attested in the 1690s. Borrowed from Portuguese manguço, from Marathi मुंगूस (muṅgūs), from Old Marathi 𑘦𑘳𑘽𑘐𑘳𑘭 (muṃgusa).

definition: Of or relating to monochromatism.
etymology: From mono- + chromatic, mono- from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”), chromatic from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”).

definition: Complete color blindness; colors can be differentiated only on the basis of brightness.
A simple compound whose molecules can join together to form polymers.
etymology: From mono- + -mer.

definition: Having exclusive control over a commercial activity by possession or legal grant.
example: The antitrust laws try to prevent monopolistic behavior.
etymology: From monopoly + -istic.

definition: A railway having a single track.
etymology: Borrowed from French monorail, equivalent to mono- + rail.

definition: Belief in a single God.
etymology: The term was coined by Henry More, ca. 1660, in explicit juxtaposition with both atheism and polytheism. It was redefined through etymological fallacy by Daniel Webster ca. 1828.

definition: Believing that there is only one god.
etymology: From mono- + theistic.

definition: Lighted by moonlight.
example: The moonlit landscape.
etymology: From moon + lit. Compare Saterland Frisian mouneljoacht (“moonlit”), West Frisian moanneljocht (“moonlit”), Dutch maanverlicht (“moonlit”), Danish månelys (“moonlit”), Swedish månljus (“moonlit”).

definition: Open land usually with peaty soil covered with heather and bracken and moss.
etymology: From Middle English morelond, equivalent to moor + land. Compare Old Norse mýrlendi (“moorland”).

definition: Accumulated earth and stones deposited by a glacier.
In a morbid manner or to a morbid degree.
example: He was morbidly fascinated by dead bodies.
etymology: From morbid + -ly.

definition: Any of various edible mushrooms of the genus Morchella having a brownish spongelike cap.
etymology: From Middle English morel, morell, from Anglo-Norman and Old French morel, morele, morelle and their etymon Medieval Latin maurella, morella, from Late Latin maurus, morus (“black”) + Latin -ella (diminutive suffix).

definition: Any of several cultivated sour cherry trees bearing fruit with dark skin and juice.
etymology: Probably either: * an alteration of morel with Italian -ello substituted for the ending, perhaps after Italian morello (“dark-coloured”);

definition: Not growing or changing; without force or vitality.
etymology: From Latin moribundus (“dying”).

definition: In a morphological manner; with regard to morphology.
example: These two plants are morphologically related.
etymology: From morphological + -ly.

definition: A small quantity of anything.
example: A morsel of paper was all he needed.
etymology: From Middle English morsel, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, perfect passive participle of mordeo (“to bite”).

definition: Burdened with legal or financial obligations.
example: His house, his business, indeed, his whole life was heavily mortgaged.

definition: Dance the slam dance.
etymology: Possibly an alteration or deformation of mash.

definition: Tuft- or mat-forming dwarf perennial of Arctic regions of western and central Europe and North America.
Overgrown with moss.
etymology: From Middle English mossy, equivalent to moss + -y.

definition: (nontechnical usage) a tiny piece of anything.
example: A wardmote in the city of London.
etymology: From Middle English mot, from Old English mot (“grain of sand; mote; atom”), from Proto-West Germanic *mot (“grain of dirt or sand, speck”). Perhaps linked to English mud.

definition: The main vein of ore in a deposit.
etymology: Probably a calque of Spanish veta madre (“mother lode”).

definition: Befitting a mother; warm and nurturing.
etymology: From Middle English moderly, from Old English mōdorlīċ (“motherly, maternal”), from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlīkaz (“motherly, maternal”), equivalent to mother + -ly.

definition: Ability to move spontaneously and independently.
etymology: From motile + -ity.

definition: Aphasia in which expression by speech or writing is severely impaired.
Inability to coordinate voluntary muscle movements; unsteady movements and staggering gait.
A boat propelled by an internal-combustion engine.
etymology: From motor + boat.

definition: A procession of people traveling in motor cars.
example: JFK was assassinated in a motorcade.
etymology: Blend of motor + cavalcade.

definition: A female policeman who rides a motorcycle (and who checks the speeds of motorists).
A traveler who rides a motorcycle.
etymology: From motorcycle + -ist or motor + cyclist.

definition: Equipped with a motor or motors.
example: A motorized wheelchair.

definition: A chute through which supraglacial water enters a glacier, boring either to the bedrock or to the depth of common crevasse formation.
example: The icy river plunged, roaring, into the moulin's blue depths.
etymology: Borrowed from French moulin, from Late Latin molinum (“mill”). Doublet of moline and mill.

definition: Silky-foliaged herb of the Rocky Mountains with bluish-white flowers.
A rodent native to the mountains of Chile and Peru and now bred in captivity.
Expressing sorrow.
etymology: From mourn + -ful.

definition: Old World annual having fragrant purple to deep crimson flower heads; naturalized in United States.
A medicated solution used for gargling and rinsing the mouth.
etymology: From mouth + wash.

definition: Meat from a mature domestic sheep.
etymology: Borrowed from French mouton (“sheep”). Doublet of mutton.

definition: A religious holiday that falls on different dates in different years.
Fortitude and determination.
etymology: First recorded use in 1930.

definition: Slow-growing procumbent evergreen shrublet of northern North America and Japan having white flowers and numerous white fleshy rough and hairy seeds.
Mucus-secreting membrane lining all body cavities or passages that communicate with the exterior.
Of or relating to mucous membranes.
etymology: From mucosa + -al.

definition: Recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhea (often alternating with periods of constipation); often associated with emotional stress.
Mucus-secreting membrane lining all body cavities or passages that communicate with the exterior.
Grassy-leaved North American aquatic plant with yellow star-shaped blossoms.
A tubular acoustic device inserted in the exhaust system that is designed to reduce noise.
A photograph of someone's face (especially one made for police records).
A military force of Muslim guerilla warriors engaged in a jihad.
example: Some call the mujahidin international warriors but others just call them terrorists.
etymology: From Arabic مُجَاهِدِين (mujāhidīn), plural of مُجَاهِد (mujāhid, “fighter, freedom fighter, warrior, struggler”).

definition: An alcoholic beverage made by infusing mulberries in strong alcohol.
example: My aunt makes the best mulberry liqueur.

definition: Wine heated with sugar and spices and often citrus fruit.
A recorder with two or more channels; makes continuous records of two or more signals simultaneously.
Having sections or patches colored differently and usually brightly.
etymology: From multi- + colored.

definition: Of a building having more than one level.
etymology: From multi- + level.

definition: Tending or having the power to multiply or increase in number or quantity or degree.
example: The multiplicative tendency of proportional representation.
etymology: From 6th-century Latin multiplicativus, from Classical Latin multiplicāre (“to multiply”).

definition: Made up of or involving or acting on behalf of various races.
example: A multiracial society.
etymology: From multi- + racial.

definition: Language or ritual causing, or intending to cause, confusion.
example: Rev. Quack's healing services are little more than mumbo jumbo.
etymology: Probably from Mandinka maamajomboo (“mask; masked dancer”); or perhaps from /l/-vocalization in the words mumble and jumble.

definition: Of or relating to or transmitted by a member of the family Muridae (rats and mice).
example: A murine plague.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mūrīnus (“mouselike”).

definition: The muscular system of an organism.
etymology: Borrowed from French musculature.

definition: Artistry in performing music.
etymology: From musician + -ship.

definition: Deeply or seriously thoughtful.
Plain-woven cotton fabric.
example: Fitting this pattern is tricky, so we recommend you make a muslin first.

definition: Black marine bivalves usually steamed in wine.
etymology: From Middle English muscle (“mussel”), from Old English muscle, from Proto-West Germanic *muskulā, from Late Latin muscula, from Latin mūsculus (“mussel, muscle”, literally “little mouse”). Doublet of muscle.

definition: Tiny marine and freshwater crustaceans with a shrimp-like body enclosed in a bivalve shell.
Undergo mutation.
example: Cells mutate.
etymology: First attested in 1796; back-formation from mutation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Latin mūtō (“to exchange; to change, to vary”). Doublet of moult.

definition: Similar to and often marketed as ‘red snapper’.
A white fatty substance that forms a medullary sheath around the axis cylinder of some nerve fibers.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós, “marrow”).

definition: Of or relating to bone marrow.
etymology: From myelo- + -oid.

definition: Chronic leukemia characterized by granular leukocytes; more common in older people.
Destruction of heart tissue resulting from obstruction of the blood supply to the heart muscle.
etymology: From Late Latin infarctus + French myocarde < from Greek ἔμφραγμα (obstacle) του (of) μυοκαρδίου (heart muscle).

definition: (ophthalmology) eyesight abnormality resulting from the eye's faulty refractive ability; distant objects appear blurred.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μυωπία (muōpía, “shortsightedness”), from μύω (múō, “to shut, close”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”) + -ία (-ía).

definition: Unable to see distant objects clearly.
example: Corrective lenses compensate for the excessive positive diopters of the myopic eye.
etymology: From myopia + -ic.

definition: Aromatic resin that is burned as incense and used in perfume.
etymology: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from Semitic.

definition: Tree of eastern Africa and Asia yielding myrrh.
Similar to Audubon's warbler.
Totally perplexed and mixed up.
Leavened bread baked in a clay oven in India; usually shaped like a teardrop.
etymology: From Hindi नान (nān) / Urdu نان (nān), from Classical Persian نان (nān), from Middle Persian LHMA (nān, “bread, food”).

definition: The basic unit of money in Nigeria.
etymology: A contraction of Nigeria, coined by Federal Commissioner for Finance Obafemi Awolowo.

definition: In a naive manner.
example: He believed, naively, that she would leave him her money.
etymology: From naive + -ly.

definition: Lack of sophistication or worldliness.
etymology: From naive + -ity, English analogue of naïveté (naïf + -eté) borrowed from French.

definition: Someone who pretends that famous people are his/her friends.
A plate bearing a name.
example: The nameplate on a locomotive.
etymology: From name + plate.

definition: The mother of your father or mother.
etymology: Possibly derived from Proto-Celtic *nana (“grandmother”); probably from a Proto-Indo-European root imitative of a child babbling, similar to Ancient Greek νάννα (nánna). See also nanny.

definition: The back side of the neck.
etymology: From Middle English nape, naape, of uncertain origin.

definition: Bulbous plant having erect linear leaves and showy yellow or white flowers either solitary or in clusters.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos), ultimately either from Pre-Greek or related to νάρκη (nárkē).

definition: Money (especially in the form of US dollars) obtained from narcotrafficking.
An area that has been taken over and is controlled and corrupted by drug cartels and where law enforcement is effectively nonexistent.
example: This Mexican town has become a narco-state that ships 100 pounds of cocaine to the United States every day.
etymology: From narco- + state.

definition: A sleep disorder characterized by sudden and uncontrollable episodes of deep sleep.
example: He believes that narcolepsy is attributable to an inability to suppress REM sleep during waking.
etymology: From French narcolepsie. By surface analysis, narco- + -lepsy, from Ancient Greek ναρκόω (narkóō, “put to sleep”) + λῆψις (lêpsis, “seizure”).

definition: Corduroy with narrow ribs.
(used with singular count nouns) colloquial for ‘not a’ or ‘not one’ or ‘never a’.
example: Heard nary a sound.
etymology: Univerbation of ne'er + a.

definition: Exaggerated nasality in speech (as in some regional dialects).
A state characterized by foul or disgusting dirt and refuse.
etymology: From nasty + -ness.

definition: The action of forming or becoming a nation.
example: The nationalisation of India.
etymology: From French nationalisation. By surface analysis, nationalise + -ation.

definition: The action of forming or becoming a nation.
etymology: From national + -ization.

definition: Erect deciduous shrub or tree to 10 feet with maroon flowers; New Zealand.
A logarithm to the base e.
example: The natural logarithm can be used to integrate ¹⁄ₓ.
etymology: From New Latin logarithmus nātūrālis, coined in 1668 by Nicholas Mercator in his book Logarithmo-technica.

definition: Causing or able to cause nausea.
example: A nauseating smell.

definition: A military attache who is a commissioned or warrant officer in a navy.
A governor in India during the Mogul empire.
etymology: From Hindi नवाब (navāb)/Urdu نواب (navāb), from Persian نوّاب (navvâb), ultimately from Arabic نُوَّاب (nuwwāb), plural of نَائِب (nāʔib, “naib”).

definition: The line formed by the edge of a garment around the neck.
etymology: From neck + line.

definition: Neckwear consisting of a long narrow piece of material worn (mostly by men) under a collar and tied in knot at the front.
example: He stood in front of the mirror tightening his necktie.

definition: One who practices magic or sorcery.
etymology: An alteration of nigromancer after necromancy, equivalent to necromancy + -er.

definition: Relating to or affected by necrosis.
example: Necrotic tissue.

definition: Necessary for relief or supply.
example: Provided them with all things needful.
etymology: From Middle English needeful, nedeful, from Old English nēodful (“necessary; earnest; zealous”). Equivalent to need + -ful. Cognate with Dutch noodvol, German notvoll.

definition: A creation created or assembled by needle and thread.
etymology: From needle + -work.

definition: Of one mind; without dissent.
etymology: Abbreviation of Latin nemine contradicente.

definition: Unsegmented worms with elongated rounded body pointed at both ends; mostly free-living but some are parasitic.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Nematoda, from Ancient Greek νηματώδης (nēmatṓdēs, “fibrous, in filaments”), from νῆμα (nêma, “thread, yarn”) + -ώδης (-ṓdēs, “-like”).

definition: Unsegmented worms with elongated rounded body pointed at both ends; mostly free-living but some are parasitic.
A synthetic rubber that is resistant to oils and aging; used in waterproof products.
etymology: US, 1930s; genericized trademark for DuPont brand of polychloroprene. neo- (“new”) + isoprene (dropping the iso-), the latter from terpene. Originally called duprene (blend of DuPont and isoprene);

definition: Extremely irritating to the nerves.
example: Nerve-racking noise.
etymology: 1867, following earlier nerve-racking (1812).

definition: Sting with or as with nettles and cause a stinging pain or sensation.
example: The children were badly nettled after playing in the field.

definition: An itchy skin eruption characterized by weals with pale interiors and well-defined red margins; usually the result of an allergic response to insect bites or food or drugs.
Any of various trees of the genus Celtis having inconspicuous flowers and small berrylike fruits.
The branch of biology that deals with the anatomy and physiology and pathology of the nervous system.
etymology: From neuro- + biology.

definition: Of or relating to or used in or practicing neurology.
example: Neurological evidence.
etymology: From neurology + -ic.

definition: Affecting or characteristic of both neural and muscular tissue.
example: Multiple sclerosis is a neuromuscular disease.
etymology: From neuro- + muscular.

definition: The junction between a nerve fiber and the muscle it supplies.
A neurobiologist who specializes in the study of the brain.
etymology: From neuro- + scientist.

definition: A mental or personality disturbance not attributable to any known neurological or organic dysfunction.
etymology: From neuro- + -sis.

definition: A particular situation that is radically different from the preceding situation.
example: HDTV looks the same but it's really a whole new ballgame.

definition: Someone recently married.
etymology: From newly + wed.

definition: The quality of being new; the opposite of oldness.
example: The newness of the car meant it still had that funny smell.
etymology: From Middle English newenesse, possibly from Old English nīewnes (“newness, novelty”), equivalent to new + -ness.

definition: A broadcast of news or commentary on the news.
etymology: From news + -cast, from broadcast.

definition: Someone who broadcasts the news.
etymology: From newscast + -er.

definition: A short news announcement concerning some on-going news story.
example: Television programmes were interrupted by a newsflash announcing that the Prime Minister had resigned.
etymology: From news + flash.

definition: Cheap paper made from wood pulp and used for printing newspapers.
example: They used bales of newspaper every day.
etymology: From news + print.

definition: Someone who reads out broadcast news bulletin.
etymology: From news + reader.

definition: A short film and commentary about current events.
etymology: From news + reel.

definition: A stall where newspapers and other periodicals are sold.
etymology: From news + stand.

definition: Someone who sells newspapers.
A B vitamin essential for the normal function of the nervous system and the gastrointestinal tract.
etymology: in 1942 derived from nicotinic + acid + vitamin, chosen to dissociate it from nicotine, to avoid the perception that vitamins or niacin-rich food contains nicotine, or that cigarettes contain vitamins.

definition: Terrestrial worm that burrows into and helps aerate soil; often surfaces when the ground is cool or wet; used as bait by anglers.
etymology: From night + crawler.

definition: Lingerie consisting of a loose dress designed to be worn in bed by women.
etymology: From Middle English nyght gowne. By surface analysis, night + gown.

definition: A person who likes to be active late at night.
etymology: From night + hawk.

definition: Extremely alarming.
etymology: From nightmare + -ish.

definition: Any of numerous shrubs or herbs or vines of the genus Solanum; most are poisonous though many bear edible fruit.
etymology: From Middle English nyȝtschade, niȝteschode, nyght shade, from Old English nihtsċada, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtskadō (“nightshade”), corresponding to night + shade.

definition: A revolutionary doctrine that advocates destruction of the social system for its own sake.
etymology: Probably borrowed from French nihilisme, German Nihilismus, or Late Latin nihilismus;

definition: Of or relating to nihilism.
etymology: From nihilist + -ic.

definition: A dark grey cloud bearing rain.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nimbus (“dark cloud”). Doublet of nimb. Sense 2 (“grey rain cloud”) was coined by the British chemist and amateur meteorologist Luke Howard (1772–1864): see the 1803 quotation.

definition: A dark grey cloud bearing rain.
Capable of wounding.
A face veil covering the lower part of the face (up to the eyes) worn by observant Muslim women.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic نِقَاب (niqāb).

definition: Any of the nitrobacteria that oxidize nitrites into nitrates.
A compound containing nitrogen and a more electropositive element (such as phosphorus or a metal).
etymology: From nitr(ogen) + -ide.

definition: The radical -NO2 or any compound containing it (such as a salt or ester of nitrous acid).
Any of the nitrobacteria that oxidize ammonia into nitrites.
The choicest or most essential or most vital part of some idea or experience.
example: He gave a short summary without getting into the nitty-gritty of the problem.
etymology: Of uncertain origin;

definition: A pensive lyrical piece of music (especially for the piano).
etymology: Borrowed from French nocturne (literally “nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus. Doublet of notturno.

definition: The normal cardiac rhythm when the heart is controlled by the atrioventricular node.
Informal terms for a human head.
etymology: Uncertain. First use appears c. 1588. Appears in publications in the 1600s (e.g.

definition: Inability to name objects or to recognize written or spoken names of objects.
Serving as or indicating the subject of a verb and words identified with the subject of a copular verb.
example: Nominative noun endings.
etymology: From Middle English nominatyf, either via Old French nominatif or directly from Latin nōminātīvus (“pertaining to naming, nominative”).

definition: The category of nouns serving as the grammatical subject of a verb.
Marked by blithe unconcern.
example: Drove his car with nonchalant abandon.
etymology: Borrowed from French nonchalant, from Old French nonchaloir (“to be unconcerned”), from non- (“not”) + chaloir (“to have concern for”), from Latin non (“not”) + calēre (“to be warm”).

definition: In a composed and unconcerned manner.
etymology: From nonchalant + -ly.

definition: Not connected with or engaged in commercial enterprises.
example: A noncommercial organization.
etymology: From non- + commercial.

definition: Lacking distinct or individual characteristics; dull and uninteresting.
example: Women dressed in nondescript clothes.
etymology: From non- + descript (from Latin dēscrīptus, past participle of dēscrībō).

definition: Not human; not belonging to or produced by or appropriate to human beings.
example: Nonhuman primates such as chimpanzees.
etymology: From non- + human.

definition: Not conforming to or in accord with tradition.
example: Nontraditional designs.
etymology: From non- + traditional.

definition: Being other than verbal communication.
example: Art like gesture is a form of nonverbal expression.
etymology: From non- + verbal.

definition: Intelligence that is manifested in the performance of tasks requiring little or no use of language.
Peaceful resistance to a government by fasting or refusing to cooperate.
etymology: From non- + violence.

definition: A catecholamine precursor of epinephrine that is secreted by the adrenal medulla and also released at synapses.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:norepinephrine.
etymology: From nor- + epinephrine.

definition: Common harrier of North America and Europe; nests in marshes and open land.
Situated farthest north.
example: Alaska is our northernmost state.
etymology: From northern + -most.

definition: Any region lying in or toward the north.
etymology: From north + land.

definition: In a northern direction.
example: They earn more up north.
etymology: From north + -wards.

definition: Bleeding from the nose.
etymology: From nose + bleed.

definition: A person who meddles in the affairs of others.
Not based on fact; existing only in the imagination.
example: To create a notional world for oneself.
etymology: From notion + -al.

definition: Nuts or fruit pieces in a sugar paste.
A bar of nougat candy often dipped in chocolate.
A mathematical element that when added to another number yields the same number.
example: 0.335 cm is nought/zero point three three five of a centimeter.
etymology: From Middle English nought, noght, noȝt, from Old English nōwiht, nāwiht, which in turn comes from ne-ā-wiht, which was a phrase used as an emphatic "no", meaning "not anything".

definition: A school of French cooking that uses light sauces and tries to bring out the natural flavors of foods instead of making heavy use of butter and cream.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French nouvelle cuisine (“new cuisine”).

definition: (law) the removal or termination or destruction of something that has been found to be a nuisance.
The states'-rights doctrine that a state can refuse to recognize or to enforce a federal law passed by the United States Congress.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin nullificatio, from nullifico, equivalent to null + -ification.

definition: Skill with numbers and mathematics.
etymology: From numerate + -cy, from Latin numerus; coined with numerate in 1959 by the UK Committee on Education, presided over by Sir Geoffrey Crowther.

definition: The convent of a community of nuns.
etymology: From Middle English nonnery, nonnerie, equivalent to nun + -ery. (brothel): Compare typologically Czech nevěstinec (< nevěstka < nevěsta).

definition: Of or relating to a wedding.
example: Nuptial day.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”), from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”).

definition: The social event at which the ceremony of marriage is performed.
California evergreen having a fruit resembling a nutmeg but with a strong turpentine flavor.
With regard to nutrition.
example: Nutritionally, her new diet is suicide.
etymology: From nutritional + -ly.

definition: Confusion resulting from failure to understand.
example: You need to turn on obfuscation for these classes.
etymology: From Middle English obfuscacioun, from Latin obfuscātiō, obfuscātiōnem, from obfuscāre (“to darken”), from ob (“over”) + fuscāre (“to make dark”), from fuscus (“dark”).

definition: The act of representing an abstraction as a physical thing.
etymology: From object + -ification, following objectify.

definition: A person who dissents from some established policy.
etymology: Partly from Latin obiector and partly from object + -or.

definition: Force somebody to do something.
etymology: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Latin obligātus, perfect passive participle of obligō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of oblige, taken through French.

definition: Showing a cheerful willingness to do favors for others.
example: The obliging waiter was in no hurry for us to leave.

definition: To, toward or at one side.
etymology: From oblique + -ly.

definition: A slender double-reed instrument; a woodwind with a conical bore and a double-reed mouthpiece.
etymology: An earlier form in English is hautboy, but the spelling oboe was adopted into English ca.

definition: The process of becoming obsolete; falling into disuse or becoming out of date.
example: A policy of planned obsolescence.
etymology: From Latin obsolēscēns (present participle of obsolēscere).

definition: Of or relating to or used in or practicing obstetrics.
example: Obstetric hospital.
etymology: From Medical Latin obstetricus (“belonging to a midwife”), from Latin obstetrīx (“midwife”).

definition: A physician specializing in obstetrics.
etymology: From obstetrics + -ician.

definition: Tenaciously unwilling or marked by tenacious unwillingness to yield.
example: An obstinate blockage in the pipe.

definition: The more conspicuous of two alternatives or cases or sides.
example: The obverse of this issue.
etymology: From Latin obversus, 1650s.

definition: Of or relating to the occiput.
example: Occipital bone.
etymology: Borrowing from Middle French occipital, from Medieval Latin occipitālis, from occiput (“the back of the head, occiput”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent of occiput + -al. Doublet of occipitalis.

definition: A saucer-shaped membrane bone that forms the back of the skull.
etymology: From Latin occiput; compare ob- (“towards, against”) and caput (“head”)

definition: That part of the cerebral cortex in either hemisphere of the brain lying in the back of the head.
That part of the cerebral cortex in either hemisphere of the brain lying in the back of the head.
A vein that drains the occipital region.
Someone who lives at a particular place for a prolonged period or who was born there.
etymology: From Middle English occupier, occupiour, from occupien + -er (equivalent to occupy + -er) or Middle French occupier, occupiour.

definition: Any of various earths containing silica and alumina and ferric oxide; used as a pigment.
etymology: From Old French ocre and its source Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”), from ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale, ocher”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).

definition: Of or relating to or shaped like an octagon.
etymology: From octagon + -al.

definition: Viscera and trimmings of a butchered animal often considered inedible by humans.
etymology: From Middle English offal, offall, offalle (“offal, refuse, scrap waste”), equivalent to off- + fall.

definition: With little or no preparation or forethought.
example: Offhand excuses.
etymology: From Middle English *ofhande, *ofhende, from Old English ofhende (“absent, lost”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *abahandijaz. Equivalent to (and re-formed as) off- + hand. Cognate with Icelandic afhendur.

definition: Act in an official capacity in a ceremony or religious ritual, such as a wedding.
example: Who officiated at your wedding?
etymology: Borrowed from Latin officiātus, perfect participle of Late Latin officior (“to perform a function”) and of Medieval Latin officiō (“to officiate, say mass (9th cent.); to serve a church (13th cent.);

definition: The near or foreseeable future.
example: There was a wedding in the offing.
etymology: From off + -ing. Attested since before 1600. Early texts also spell the term offin and offen.

definition: Offset printing by lithography.
Situated or taking place in the area of a stage not visible to the audience.
example: Offstage noises.
etymology: From off + stage.

definition: Look at with amorous intentions.
etymology: 17th century.

definition: A region rich in petroleum deposits (especially one with producing oil wells).
A Turkish unit of weight equal to about 2.75 pounds.
example: Dram (49·5 grains), 100=chequi, 4=oka (2·8286 ℔); dram (49·5 grains), 180=rotl, 100=kintal or kantar (127·29 ℔).
etymology: From Italian oca, from French oque, from Ottoman Turkish اوقه (okka). Doublet of ounce, inch, uncia, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

definition: An endorsement.
Long green edible beaked pods of the okra plant.

Tall coarse annual of Old World tropics widely cultivated in southern United States and West Indies for its long mucilaginous green pods used as basis for soups and stews; sometimes placed in genus Hibiscus.
A common long-tailed sea duck of the northern parts of the United States.
A song that was formerly popular.
example: An oldies radio station.
etymology: From old + -ie.

definition: The faculty that enables us to distinguish scents.
One of the rulers in an oligarchy.
etymology: From French oligarque, olygarche, from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs). By surface analysis, olig- (“few”) + -arch (“ruler, leader”).

definition: Beaten eggs or an egg mixture cooked until just set; may be folded around e.g. ham or cheese or jelly.
Pan for cooking omelets.
In an ominous manner.
example: The sun darkened ominously.
etymology: From ominous + -ly.

definition: Infinitely wise.
example: The story was narrated from an omniscient point of view.
etymology: From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).

definition: Having a single cell (and thus not divided into cells).
etymology: From one + celled.

definition: One part in a thousand equal parts.
Belonging to some prior time.
example: The additional funds included the FBI’s support of the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City, Utah (a onetime increase) […].
etymology: From one + time.

definition: Injurious to onion plants and sometimes tobacco.
Of or relating to ontology.
example: Ontological speculations.
etymology: From ontology + -ical.

definition: Capable of being treated by surgical operation.
example: An operable cancer.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin operābilis.

definition: In respect to operation.
example: Reported the machine operationally satisfactory.
etymology: From operational + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to ophthalmology.
example: Ophthalmic surgery.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ophthalmicus, from Ancient Greek ὀφθᾰλμῐκός (ophthălmĭkós, “of or for the eyes”), from ὀφθᾰλμός (ophthălmós, “eye”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”, adjectival suffix).

definition: A branch of the internal carotid artery that supplies the eye and neighboring structures.
Either of two veins that serve the eye; empties into the cavernous sinus.
A medical doctor specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases of the eye.
etymology: From ophthalmology + -ist.

definition: Suitable or at a time that is suitable or advantageous especially for a particular purpose.
example: An opportune place to make camp.
etymology: From Old French opportun, from Latin opportunus.

definition: Taking advantage of opportunities without regard for the consequences for others.
etymology: From French opportunisme, equivalent to opportune + -ism.

definition: A person of authority who subjects others to undue pressures.
etymology: From Middle English oppressour, from Old French opressor and Latin oppressor; equivalent to oppress + -or.

definition: In an optical manner.
example: Optically distorted.
etymology: From optical + -ly.

definition: The act of rendering optimal.
example: The simultaneous optimization of growth and profitability.
etymology: From optimise + -ation.

definition: Make optimal; get the most out of; use best.
example: Optimize your resources.

definition: A person skilled in testing for defects of vision in order to prescribe corrective glasses.
etymology: From optometry + -ist.

definition: The practice of an optometrist.
etymology: From opto- + -metry.

definition: Wealth as evidenced by sumptuous living.
etymology: From French opulence, from Latin opulentia.

definition: Large long-armed ape of Borneo and Sumatra having arboreal habits.
North American annual plant with usually yellow or orange flowers; grows chiefly on wet rather acid soil.
Having the color of ripe oranges.
An instance of oratory.
example: He delivered an oration on the decline of family values.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōrātiō, ōrātiōnem, from ōrō (“to orate”) + -tiō (“action (nominalizer)”). Cognate with and doublet of orison.

definition: A musical composition for voices and orchestra based on a religious text.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian oratorio (“oratorical”), from Latin ōrātōrius. Doublet of oratory.

definition: Write an orchestra score for.
example: Sergio Leone orchestrated "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly".
etymology: From orchestra + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French orchestrer.

definition: An arrangement of a piece of music for performance by an orchestra or band.
etymology: From French orchestration. Equivalent to orchestrate + -ion.

definition: Of or relating to a taxonomic order.
example: Family and ordinal names of animals and plants.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōrdinālis, adjective formed from noun ōrdō (“order”), + adjective suffix -ālis.

definition: The number designating place in an ordered sequence.
A hard compact kind of calcite.
An event that is a beginning; a first part or stage of subsequent events.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin orīginātiō, from orīgō (“to act, to commence”, stem as origin-) + -tiō.

definition: A fee charged to a borrower (especially for a mortgage loan) to cover the costs of initiating the loan.
The branch of zoology that studies birds.
etymology: From New Latin ornithologia, coined by Ulisse Aldrovandi from Ancient Greek ὀρνιθολόγος (ornithológos), from ὄρνις (órnis) and λόγος (lógos). See also ornitho- + -logy.

definition: A dentist specializing in the prevention or correction of irregularities of the teeth.
etymology: From orthodontic + -ist.

definition: A method of representing the sounds of a language by written or printed symbols.
Large African antelope with long straight nearly upright horns.
etymology: From Latin ory̆x, from Ancient Greek ὄρῠξ (órŭx, “a pickax; an oryx (the antelope)”).

definition: Appearing as such but not necessarily so.
example: The ostensible truth of their theories.

definition: Intended to attract notice and impress others.
example: An ostentatious sable coat.
etymology: Originated 1590; from Latin ostentātus + -ious.

definition: Amphibious African insectivorous mammal that resembles an otter.
A person who ousts or supplants someone else.
etymology: From Old French ouster, oustre, a nominalization of Anglo-Norman oustre (“to oust”).

definition: The act of ejecting someone or forcing them out.
Bid over an opponent's bid when one's partner has not bid or doubled.
etymology: From out- + bid.

definition: Decisively surpassed by something else so as to appear to be of a lower class.
Be or do something to a greater degree.
example: She outdoes all other athletes.
etymology: From out- + do.

definition: Situated at the farthest possible point from a center.
example: He lived on the outermost edge of the city.
etymology: From Middle English uttermost, uttirmest, uttermast, outemast, alteration (due to Middle English outre (“outer”)) of Old English ūtemest, ȳtemest (“outermost”), equivalent to outer + -most. Doublet of uttermost.

definition: Clothing for use outdoors.
etymology: From outer + -wear.

definition: Grow too large or too mature for.
example: I have outgrown these clothes.
etymology: From out- + grow.

definition: A natural consequence of development.
etymology: From out- + growth.

definition: A small outbuilding with a bench having holes through which a user can defecate.
etymology: From Middle English outhous, equivalent to out- + house. Compare Old Norse úthús (“outhouse”).

definition: Live longer than.
example: She outlived her husband by many years.
etymology: From Middle English outliven, equivalent to out- + live.

definition: Out of fashion.
example: Demode (or outmoded) attire.

definition: Shine brighter than.
example: What star outshines the sun?
etymology: From out- + shine.

definition: Caliper for measuring outside dimensions; points on its legs curve inward.
Beat through cleverness and wit.
etymology: From out- + smart.

definition: Of a leaf shape; egg-shaped with the broader end at the base.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōvātus, from ōvum (“an egg”) + -ātus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

definition: An egg-shaped leaf with the broader end at the base.
More active than normal.
etymology: From over- + active.

definition: Eating to excess (personified as one of the deadly sins).
Excessive size; usually caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone from the pituitary gland.
etymology: From over- + growth.

definition: Hear, usually without the knowledge of the speakers.
example: We overheard the conversation at the next table.
etymology: From Middle English overheren, from Old English oferhīeran (“to overhear, hear, disobey, disregard, neglect”), equivalent to over- + hear.

definition: Get excessively and undesirably hot.
example: The car engines overheated.
etymology: From Middle English overheten. Cognate with German überheizen, überhitzen (“to overheat”), Swedish överhetta (“to overheat”). By surface analysis, over- + heat.

definition: Placed on or over something else.
example: An overlying image.
etymology: From over- + lying.

definition: Too much population.
Overly protective.
example: Overprotective parents.
etymology: From over- + protective.

definition: Fail by aiming too high or trying too hard.
etymology: The verb is from Middle English overrechen (“to rise above; to extend beyond or over; to encroach; to catch, overtake; to reach; to obtain wrongfully (?);

definition: Rule against.
example: The Republicans were overruled when the House voted on the bill.
etymology: From over- + rule.

definition: Be greater in significance than.
example: The tragedy overshadowed the couple's happiness.
etymology: From Middle English overschadwen, overschadewe, from Old English ofersċeadwian (“to overshadow”), equivalent to over- + shadow.

definition: Shoot beyond or over (a target).
example: When you drive, you must remember to not overshoot the parking space and end up with two wheels over the line.
etymology: From Middle English overshoten, oversheten (“to shoot beyond, shoot past, pour down from above”), perhaps continuing Old English ofersċēotan (“to shoot down”), equivalent to over- + shoot.

definition: Larger than normal for its kind.
etymology: From over- + size.

definition: To enlarge beyond bounds or the truth.
example: He was suggested not to overstate at the interview.
etymology: From over- + state.

definition: To spend to much time considering something and thus reach the wrong conclusion.
etymology: From Middle English *overthenken, *overthenchen (compare Middle English overthinken (“to grieve; have regrets; be sorry; be anxious”)), from Old English oferþenċan (“to think over; consider”), equivalent to over- + think.

definition: Use too much.
example: This play has been overworked.
etymology: From Middle English overwerken, possibly from Old English oferwyrċan (“to overwork, overlay”), equivalent to over- + work. Cognate with Dutch overwerken (“to overwork”).

definition: Marked by excessive enthusiasm for and intense devotion to a cause or idea.
example: With his overzealous attempts to impress, he only managed to annoy her.
etymology: From over- + zealous.

definition: An occupant who owns the home that he/she lives in.
Any of the enzymes that catalyze biological oxidation.
etymology: From oxide + -ase introduced by Gabriel Bertrand.

definition: A substance that oxidizes another substance.
Conjoining contradictory terms (as in ‘deafening silence’).
etymology: First attested in the 17th century, noun use of 5th century Latin oxymōrum (adjective), neut. nom.

definition: A horse used to set the pace in racing.
etymology: From pace + -er.

definition: The act of appeasing someone or causing someone to be more favorably inclined.
example: A wonderful skill in the pacification of crying infants.
etymology: From Middle English pacificacion, from Old French pacification.

definition: Someone who tries to bring peace.
etymology: From pacify + -er.

definition: The doctrine that all violence is unjustifiable.
Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of.
example: Near-synonyms: peacify, repacify, allay, locarnize.
etymology: From Middle French pacifier, from Latin pāx (“peace”) + faciō (“to do, make”). Cognate with pay and peacify.

definition: A detachable lock; has a hinged shackle that can be passed through the staple of a hasp or the links in a chain and then snapped shut.
example: He secured the gate with a heavy padlock.
etymology: From earlier pad lock (19th c.); Middle English padlock, padlokke, from pad-, of unknown origin, + lok (“lock”).

definition: A rich and spectacular ceremony.
example: Pomp and pageantry.
etymology: From pageant + -ry.

definition: An electronic device that generates a series of beeps when the person carrying it is being paged.
etymology: From page + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (measurement suffix) (sense 3).

definition: A brush used as an applicator (to apply paint).
etymology: From paint + brush.

definition: Perennial aromatic herb of southeastern Asia having large usually bright-colored or blotched leaves and spikes of blue-violet flowers; sometimes placed in genus Solenostemon.
Relating to or being a palace.
example: The palatial residence.
etymology: Borrowed from French palatial, formed from the root of Latin palātium (“a palace”), from Palātium (“Palatine Hill”).

definition: One of several arteries supplying the face.
Having a pale color.
Of or relating to the second period of the Stone Age (following the eolithic).
example: Paleolithic artifacts.

definition: A specialist in paleontology.
etymology: From paleontology + -ist.

definition: Fortification consisting of a strong fence made of stakes driven into the ground.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French palissade, from Old French, from Old Occitan palissada, from palissa (“stake”), probably from pal (“stake”), or possibly from Gallo-Romance *pālīcea, from Latin pālus (“stake”) + -ade.

definition: Any of several low-growing palms with fan-shaped leaves.
etymology: From Spanish palmito, diminutive of palma (“palm tree”), from Latin palma. Doublet of palmite and palmito.

definition: Tall fan palm of Africa and India and Malaysia yielding a hard wood and sweet sap that is a source of palm wine and sugar; leaves used for thatching and weaving.
Tall fan palm of Africa and India and Malaysia yielding a hard wood and sweet sap that is a source of palm wine and sugar; leaves used for thatching and weaving.
Gratifying tastes, appetites, or desires.
example: Pampering parents often have spoilt children.

definition: Distinctive and stylish elegance.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French panache, from Middle French pennache (“plume of feathers”), from Italian pennacchio, from Late Latin pinnāculum. Doublet of pinnacle.

definition: Inflammation of the pancreas; usually marked by abdominal pain.
etymology: From pancreas + -itis.

definition: Yield (to); give satisfaction to.
example: His latest speech panders to the worst instincts of the electorate.
etymology: From Middle English pandare, from Chaucer’s character Pandare (in Troilus and Criseyde;

definition: Fitted or decorated with panels or wainscoting.
etymology: From panel + -ed.

definition: A panel or section of panels in a wall or door.
A member of a panel.
etymology: From panel + -ist.

definition: Fitted or decorated with panels or wainscoting.
etymology: From panel + -ed.

definition: A panel or section of panels in a wall or door.
Thrown into a state of intense fear or desperation.
example: Became panicky as the snow deepened.
etymology: From panic + -y.

definition: Any of various orchids of the genus Miltonia having solitary or loosely racemose showy broadly spreading flowers.
Common violet of the eastern United States with large pale blue or purple flowers resembling pansies.
A woman's undergarment that combines a girdle and panties.
Electrophoresis carried out on filter paper.
A fastener for holding a sheet of paper in place.
A machine used for aligning uneven stacks of paper.
Small slender toy spaniel with erect ears and a black-spotted brown to white coat.
etymology: From French papillon (“butterfly”), from Latin pāpiliō (“butterfly, moth”). Doublet of papilio and pavilion.

definition: A concave reflector used to produce a parallel beam when the source is placed at its focus or to focus an incoming parallel beam.
From crude petroleum; used for candles and for preservative or waterproof coatings.
etymology: From Latin paraffinum, from parum (too little) + affinis (related, affinity). Therefore low affinity or being chemically neutral.

definition: (British usage) kerosine.
Partly refined paraffin wax.
A series of non-aromatic saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH(2n+2).
From crude petroleum; used for candles and for preservative or waterproof coatings.
Similarity by virtue of corresponding.
etymology: From parallel + -ism and from Late Latin parallelismus.

definition: Make powerless and unable to function.
example: The bureaucracy paralyzes the entire operation.
etymology: Partly a borrowing from French. Probably partly either (i) formed within English, by derivation. Or partly (ii) a borrowing from French, combined with an English element. Etymons: Middle English paralysie, -ize suffix;

definition: Any statistic computed by procedures that assume the data were drawn from a particular distribution.
A low wall along the edge of a roof or balcony.
etymology: From Middle French parapet, from Italian parapetto.

definition: Suffering complete paralysis of the lower half of the body usually resulting from damage to the spinal cord.
etymology: From para- + -plegic.

definition: A variety of jaeger.
A handheld collapsible source of shade.
etymology: From French parasol, from Italian parasole, from para- (“to shield”) + sole (“sun”).

definition: Edible long-stalked mushroom with white flesh and gills and spores; found in open woodlands in autumn.
A soldier in the paratroops.
etymology: Blend of parachute + trooper.

definition: Either of two punctuation marks ‘(’ or ‘)’ used to enclose textual material.
etymology: The plural is also a learned borrowing from Late Latin parenthesēs.

definition: That part of the cerebral cortex in either hemisphere of the brain lying below the crown of the head.
That part of the cerebral cortex in either hemisphere of the brain lying below the crown of the head.
A thin fragment or slice (especially of wood) that has been shaved from something.
A small sharp knife used in paring fruits or vegetables.
Large ground squirrel of the North American far north.
etymology: So called because the Eskimos use the pelts of these squirrels to make parkas.

definition: A series of wagers in which the winnings from one wager are used as a stake for the subsequent wagers.
etymology: The verb is derived from paroli (“cumulative bet in card games”), possibly modified under the influence of French parler (“to speak, talk”).

definition: A negotiation between enemies.
etymology: From Middle English parlai (“speech, parley”), from Old French parler (“to talk;

definition: A computer program that divides code up into functional components.
example: Compilers must parse source code in order to translate it into object code.
etymology: From parse + -er.

definition: An official residence provided by a church for its parson or vicar or rector.
etymology: From parson + -age.

definition: A denture replacing one or more teeth in a dental arch.
A non-finite form of the verb; in English it is used adjectivally and to form compound tenses.
etymology: From Middle English participle, from Old French participle (1388), variant of participe, from Latin participium.

definition: Someone who spoils the pleasure of others.
Of or relating to Passover or Easter.
example: Paschal lamb.

definition: Out of fashion.
A person who passes by casually or by chance.
The trait of remaining inactive; a lack of initiative.
etymology: From passive + -ity.

definition: A participle that expresses completed action.
A musical composition consisting of a series of songs or other musical pieces from various sources.
example: This supposed research paper is a pastiche of passages from unrelated sources.

definition: An informal use of the Latin word for father; sometimes used by British schoolboys or used facetiously.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pater (“father”). Doublet of ayr, faeder, father, padre, and père.

definition: In a manner arousing sympathy and compassion.
example: The sick child cried pathetically.
etymology: From pathetic + -ally.

definition: A fine coating of oxide (produced by oxidation over a long period of time) on the surface of a metal (particularly copper).
example: He enjoys a patina of respect by the police, despite being an ex-criminal.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian patina, from Latin patina (“dish, pan”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē), either from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread”) or from Pre-Greek.

definition: Befitting a person of noble origin.
example: A patrician nose.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French patricien, from Latin patricius, derived from patrēs cōnscrīptī (“Roman senators”). May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian

definition: A church endowment.
example: The museum holds an important part of the country's cultural patrimony.
etymology: From earlier patrimoyne, from patremoyne, from Middle French patrimoine/patremoine, semilearned borrowing from Latin patrimōnium, from pater (“father”) + -mōnium (“state, condition”). First attested in 1513.

definition: A male policeman who patrols a given region.
etymology: From patrol + -man.

definition: (used of behavior or attitude) characteristic of those who treat others with condescension.
Assume sponsorship of.
etymology: From patron + -ize (verb ending); or from Old French patroniser, from Medieval Latin patronizāre (“to lead a galley as patron”). Piecewise doublet of patternize.

definition: An insufficient quantity or number.
etymology: From Middle English paucete, paucite, paucyte, partly from Middle French paucité and partly from its etymon, Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”). Related to few.

definition: Plant with an elongated head of broad stalked leaves resembling celery; used as a vegetable in east Asia.
Larvae live in and feed on seeds of the pea plant.
A member of a military force that is assigned (often with international sanction) to preserve peace in a trouble area.
etymology: From peace + keeper.

definition: Someone who tries to bring peace.
etymology: Compound of peace + maker. First attested in the Tyndale Bible from 1526, as a translation of Koine Greek εἰρηνοποιοί (eirēnopoioí, “peacemaker”), a hapax legomenon found in the New Testament.

definition: Cephalopod of the Indian and Pacific oceans having a spiral shell with pale pearly partitions.
A pudding made with strained split peas mixed with egg.
Either of two large muscles of the chest.
A skeletal support to which the forelimbs of vertebrates are attached.
An odd or unusual characteristic.
example: The peculiarity of meeting six people on a usually deserted trail only struck me later on.
etymology: From peculiar + -ity.

definition: Uniquely or characteristically.
example: These peculiarly cinematic elements.
etymology: From peculiar + -ly.

definition: (used in the plural) snug trousers ending at the calves; worn by women and girls.
etymology: From pedal pusher (“cyclist”) + -s (suffix forming pluralia tantum and regular plurals of nouns), as they were originally worn by cyclists.

definition: Marked by a narrow focus on or display of learning especially its trivial aspects.
etymology: From pedant + -ic.

definition: Someone who travels about selling their wares (as on the streets or at carnivals).
etymology: From Middle English pedlere, pedlare, pedeler, alteration of Middle English peddere (“hawker, peddler”), of uncertain origin. Compare Medieval Latin pedārius, from Latin pedāre (“to furnish with feet; prop up”).

definition: Professional care for the feet and toenails.
etymology: From French pédicure, from Latin pes (“foot”).

definition: Expressing disapproval.
etymology: From Late Latin peiōrātus (“worsened”, past participle of peiōrāre (“worsen”), from Latin peior (“worse”)) + -ive. Compare French péjoratif (“depreciative, disparaging”). By surface analysis, pejorate + -ive.

definition: Relating to or occurring or living in or frequenting the open ocean.
example: Pelagic organisms.
etymology: From Latin pelagicus (and possibly pelagus); from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”). By surface analysis, -pelag + -ic.

definition: Bird of the open seas.
The structure of the vertebrate skeleton supporting the lower limbs in humans and the hind limbs or corresponding parts in other vertebrates.
Impose a penalty on; inflict punishment on.
example: The students were penalized for showing up late for class.
etymology: From penal + -ize.

definition: A rotary implement for sharpening the point on pencils.
An implant that creates an artificial erection.
Feeling or expressing remorse for misdeeds.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin paenitēns, poenitēns (“penitent”), present participle of paeniteō, poeniteō (“to cause to repent; to regret, repent”). Doublet of penitente.

definition: The act of creating written works.
example: The idle pennings of a poetic daydreamer.

definition: Deeply or seriously thoughtful.
example: He sat in pensive silence, weighing his options carefully.
etymology: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).

definition: A star with 5 points; formed by 5 straight lines between the vertices of a pentagon and enclosing another pentagon.
etymology: From Ancient Greek πεντάγραμμον (pentágrammon), noun form of the adjectives πεντάγραμμος (pentágrammos) and πεντέγραμμος (pentégrammos, “five-lined, having five lines”). Equivalent to penta- + -gram.

definition: Any of numerous plants widely cultivated for their showy single or double red or pink or white flowers.
etymology: From Old English peonie, peonia et al., from Latin paeōnia;

definition: Perennial rhizomatous herbs and shrubs; of temperate Europe and North America.
Marked by lively action.
example: The peppy and interesting talk.
etymology: From pep + -y.

definition: Capable of being perceived by the mind or senses.
example: A perceptible limp.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin perceptibilis, from Latin percipio.

definition: Through chance.
example: To sleep, perchance to dream ….
etymology: From Middle English parchaunce, from Old French par cheance (“by chance”).

definition: Involving percussion or featuring percussive instruments.
example: Percussive music.
etymology: From percuss + -ive.

definition: A musical instrument in which the sound is produced by one object striking another.
A participle that expresses completed action.
A disposition to feel that anything less than perfect is unacceptable.
example: His perfectionism seemed excessive to his students.
etymology: From perfection + -ism.

definition: A line of small holes for tearing at a particular place.
A verb that explicitly conveys the kind of speech act being performed.
Filled or impregnated with perfume.
example: Perfumed boudoir.
etymology: From perfume (noun and verb) + -ed.

definition: Pumping a liquid into an organ or tissue (especially by way of blood vessels).
etymology: From Middle French perfusion, from Latin perfūsiō (“the act of pouring over”).

definition: A pale green variety of chrysolite; used as a gemstone.
etymology: From Middle English peritot, from Anglo-Norman peridou, peridout, Middle French perido, peridon, of uncertain origin; later reborrowed from modern French péridot.

definition: Occurring during the period around birth (5 months before and 1 month after).
example: Perinatal mortality.
etymology: From peri- + natal.

definition: The quality of recurring at regular intervals.
etymology: From French périodicité. By surface analysis, periodic + -ity.

definition: Of or relating to or involving or practicing periodontics.
example: Periodontal disease.
etymology: From Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around”) + ὀδούς (odoús, “a tooth”).

definition: A disease that attacks the gum and bone and around the teeth.
Of or relating to or affecting the peritoneum.
example: Peritoneal cancer.
etymology: From peritone(um) + -al. Compare New Latin peritonaeālis.

definition: Spread or diffuse through.
example: An atmosphere of distrust has permeated this administration.
etymology: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Latin permeātus, perfect passive participle of permeō (“to pass through”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

definition: An event in which one thing is substituted for another.
example: Which permutation for completing our agenda items makes the most sense?
etymology: From Middle English permutacioun, permutacyoun, from Old French permutacïon, promutatïon and Medieval Latin permūtātiōnem, accusative of permūtātiō. Morphologically permute + -ation.

definition: A chronic progressive anemia of older adults; thought to result from a lack of intrinsic factor (a substance secreted by the stomach that is responsible for the absorption of vitamin B12).
Quietly and steadily persevering especially in detail or exactness.
example: With persevering (or patient) industry she revived the failing business.

definition: Any of several tropical trees of the genus Diospyros.
Any of several tropical trees of the genus Diospyros.
Relentless and indefatigable in pursuit or as if in pursuit.
(of persons) pleasant in appearance and personality.
Personal as opposed to real property; any tangible movable property (furniture or domestic animals or a car etc.).
Make personal or more personal.
example: Personalized service.
etymology: From personal + -ize.

definition: Salty fluid secreted by sweat glands.
etymology: Borrowed from late Middle French perspiration, from perspirer (“perspire”), from Latin perspirare (“to blow or breathe constantly”), from per (“through”) + spirare (“to breathe, blow”). Morphologically perspire + -ation.

definition: Characterized by a lightly pert and exuberant quality.
example: Pert breasts.
etymology: From Middle English pert, perte, aphetic form of apert.

definition: An unhappy and worried mental state.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French perturbation, from Old French perturbacion, from Latin perturbatio.

definition: Thrown into a state of agitated confusion; (‘rattled’ is an informal term).
example: The equation x² − 3.0001x + 2 = 0 is a perturbed version of x² − 3x + 2 = 0.

definition: A disease of the respiratory mucous membrane.
etymology: From New Latin, from Latin per- (“thorough”) + tussis (“cough”).

definition: Examine or consider with attention and in detail.
example: Please peruse this report at your leisure.
etymology: From either Medieval Latin perūtor, perūsitō (“wear out”) or Anglo-Norman peruser (“use up”), originally leading to two concurrent meanings, but only those derived from "to examine" survive today.

definition: Reading carefully with intent to remember.
etymology: From peruse + -ing.

definition: A member of a Kurdish guerilla organization that fights for a free Kurdish state.
etymology: Borrowed from Kurdish پێشمەرگە (pêşmerge) / pêşmerge (literally “those who face death”), from pêş (“front”) + merg (“death”) + e (“is”).

definition: A person who expects the worst.
etymology: From French pessimiste, from Latin pessimus (“worst”) + -ist.

definition: Annoy persistently.
example: He pestered me with questions.
etymology: In the senses of “overcrowd (a place)” and “impede (a person)”: from Middle French and Old French empestrer (“encumber”), influenced by English pest. The modern sense is an extension of the sense “infest”.

definition: Causing irritation or annoyance.
example: Swarms of pestering gnats.

definition: Machine consisting of a heavy bar that moves vertically for pounding or crushing ores.
example: A pestle of pork.
etymology: From Middle English pestel, pestell, from Old French pestel, from Latin pistillum, from pīnsō (“pound, beat”). Doublet of pistil and pistillum.

definition: Undergarment worn under a skirt.
etymology: From Middle English petticote, petycote, peticote, petite cote, equivalent to petty + coat.

definition: Narrowness of mind or ideas or views.
example: The pettiness of the accounting department asking me to save a receipt from a fast-food restaurant was absurd.
etymology: From petty + -ness.

definition: Unarmed woody rhizomatous perennial plant distinguished from wild sarsaparilla by more aromatic roots and panicled umbels; southeastern North America to Mexico.
Easily irritated or annoyed.
example: Lack of sleep is causing Dave's recent petulant behavior.
etymology: From Middle French, from Latin petulāns, akin to petō (“to ask for”).

definition: A small spineless globe-shaped cactus; source of mescal buttons.
etymology: From Spanish peyote, from Classical Nahuatl peyotl.

definition: A virus that is parasitic (reproduces itself) in bacteria.
etymology: Clipping of bacteriophage from bacterio- (“bacteria”) + -phage (“eater”); latter suffix from Ancient Greek -φάγος (-phágos, “eater”), from φαγ- (phag-), aorist stem of ἐσθίω (esthíō) or ἔδω (édō, “to eat, to consume”).

definition: Relating to a phallus especially as an embodiment of generative power.
example: A phallic cult.
etymology: From phallus (“penis”) + -ic.

definition: Any of a class of weakly acidic organic compounds; molecule contains one or more hydroxyl groups.
etymology: From French phène, from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “to clear”), as it was used for illumination, name given by Auguste Laurente in 1836.

definition: A thermosetting resin.
etymology: From phenol + -ic.

definition: A plastic consisting of phenolic resins.
A thermosetting resin.
To a phenomenal degree.
example: His reaction was phenomenally quick.
etymology: From phenomenal + -ly.

definition: A philosophical doctrine proposed by Edmund Husserl based on the study of human experience in which considerations of objective reality are not taken into account.
etymology: From phenomenon + -logy, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”), hence "the study of what shows itself (to consciousness)".

definition: Of or relating to or constituting a phenotype.
example: Phenotypical profile.
etymology: From phenotype + -ic.

definition: A chemical substance secreted externally by some animals (especially insects) that influences the physiology or behavior of other animals of the same species.
etymology: From φέρω (phérō, “I bring, bear, carry”) and hormone.

definition: The humanistic study of language and literature.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English Philologie, from Latin philologia, from Ancient Greek φιλολογίᾱ (philologíā, “love of argument or reasoning, love of learning and literature”).

definition: Apathy demonstrated by an absence of emotional reactions.
etymology: From Middle English flewme, fleume, fleme, from Old French fleume, Middle French flemme (French flegme), and their source, Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; inflammation;

definition: Suffering from irrational fears.
example: Anything can become a phobic stimulus.
etymology: From phobia + -ic, see -phobic.

definition: An anxiety disorder characterized by extreme and irrational fear of simple things or social situations.
example: Phobic disorder is a general term for all phobias.

definition: Someone who wiretaps a telephone or telegraph wire.
By phonetics.
example: Phonetically realized.
etymology: From phonetic + -ally.

definition: The branch of acoustics concerned with speech processes including its production and perception and acoustic analysis.
example: This dictionary shows the phonetics of the words.
etymology: From phonetic + -s. By surface analysis, phone (“linguistic unit of sound”) + -etic + -s.

definition: Fraudulent; having a misleading appearance.
Teaching reading by training beginners to associate letters with their sound values.
etymology: From phon- + -ics.

definition: Machine in which rotating records cause a stylus to vibrate and the vibrations are amplified acoustically or electronically.
etymology: From phono- + -graph.

definition: An album for holding phonograph records.
A stylus that formerly made sound by following a groove in a phonograph record.
Sound recording consisting of a disk with a continuous groove; used to reproduce music by rotating while a phonograph needle tracks in the groove.
Sound recording consisting of a disk with a continuous groove; used to reproduce music by rotating while a phonograph needle tracks in the groove.
Of or relating to phonology.
example: The phonological component of language.
etymology: From phonology + -ical.

definition: The system of phones used in a particular language.
The study of the sound system of a given language and the analysis and classification of its phonemes.
etymology: From phono- (prefix denoting sound) + -logy (suffix denoting a branch of learning, or a study of a particular subject).

definition: Any of a group of enzymes that act as a catalyst in the hydrolysis of organic phosphates.
etymology: From phosphate + -ase.

definition: A synthetic substance that is fluorescent or phosphorescent; used to coat the screens of cathode ray tubes.
etymology: From Medieval Latin phosphorus.

definition: A corrosion-resistant bronze containing phosphorus; used in bearings and gears.
Containing or characteristic of phosphorus.
example: Phosphoric acid.
etymology: From phosphorus + -ous.

definition: A clear or yellow monobasic acid (H3PO2).
A photographic copy of written or printed or graphic work.
etymology: From photo- + copy.

definition: Of or relating to photometry.
etymology: From photo- + -metric.

definition: Relating to or using or formed by photosynthesis.
etymology: From photo- + synthetic.

definition: (biology) the sequence of events involved in the evolutionary development of a species or taxonomic group of organisms.
example: Understanding the phylogeny of this musical group helps us understand its music.

definition: A purging medicine; stimulates evacuation of the bowels.
etymology: From Middle English phisik, from Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape;

definition: Of or relating to physiological processes; with respect to physiology.
example: Physiologically ready.
etymology: From physiological + -ly.

definition: A biologist specializing in physiology.
Therapist who treats injury or dysfunction with exercises and other physical treatments of the disorder.
etymology: From physio- + therapist or physiotherapy + -ist.

definition: An eating disorder, frequent in children, in which non-nutritional objects are eaten persistently.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pīca (“jay; magpie”). Doublet of pie (“magpie”). * (pathology): From the idea that magpies will eat almost anything.

definition: A linear unit (1/6 inch) used in printing.
The act of someone who picks up or takes something.
example: The pickings were easy.

definition: A thief who steals from the pockets or purses of others in public places.
etymology: From pick + pocket.

definition: An artificial language used for trade between speakers of different languages.
etymology: From pidgin English, from Chinese Pidgin English pidgin, a pronunciation of English business during trade in the Far East.

definition: Relating to or involving piezoelectricity.
example: Piezoelectric plates.
etymology: From piezo- + electric.

definition: A crystal that can be used as a transducer.
Electricity produced by mechanical pressure on certain crystals (notably quartz or Rochelle salt); alternatively, electrostatic stress produces a change in the linear dimensions of the crystal.
example: Human bones display a piezoelectric effect.

definition: A material that accumulates an electric charge in response to mechanical stress.
Ride on someone's shoulders or back.
example: They tried to piggyback that proposal on the rivers and harbors bill.
etymology: A corruption of pickaback, itself a corruption of pick-pack, like a pack.

definition: Vigorous perennial herb with flowers in erect racemes and having young plants develop at the junction of a leaf blade and the leafstalk.
Small short-eared burrowing mammal of rocky uplands of Asia and western North America.
etymology: From French, from an Evenki word which Peter Simon Pallas transcribes as piika or peeka, but which cannot be found in modern dictionaries. Probably ultimately onomatopoeic.

definition: A common cyst of the skin; filled with fatty matter (sebum) that is secreted by a sebaceous gland that has been blocked.
Wrongfully emptied or stripped of anything of value.
The act of stealing valuable things from a place.
Bed linen consisting of a cover for a pillow.
example: The burglar carried his loot in a pillowcase.
etymology: From pillow + case.

definition: A fine cloth made from pineapple fibers.
Erect clematis of Florida having pink to purple flowers.
Dark brown marten of northern Eurasian coniferous forests.
Short-tailed glossy-furred burrowing vole of the eastern United States.
Relating to the pineal body.
example: Pineal hormone.
etymology: From French pinéal, from Middle French, from Latin pīnea (“pine cone, pine nut”), from pīneus (“of the pine”).

definition: A small endocrine gland in the brain; situated beneath the back part of the corpus callosum; secretes melatonin.
A sensory structure capable of light reception located on the dorsal side of the diencephalon in various reptiles.
Dark-green kiwi-sized tropical fruit with white flesh; used chiefly for jellies and preserves.
A gear with a small number of teeth designed to mesh with a larger wheel or rack.
etymology: From Middle English pynyon, from Old French pignon, from Latin penna (“feather”).

definition: White Australian cockatoo with roseate tinged plumage.
Of a light shade of red.
etymology: From pink + -ish.

definition: Of lavender tinged with pink.
Of orange tinged with pink.
Of purple tinged with pink.
Of white tinged with pink.
A kind of guan.
Nut of Mediterranean trees having an edible green kernel.
An unforeseen or unexpected or surprising difficulty.
example: It's usually a simple task, but you should know the pitfalls before you attempt it yourself.

definition: Concise and full of meaning.
example: Welcomed her pithy comments.
etymology: From Middle English pithy, pythy, equivalent to pith + -y.

definition: A man who works in a coal mine.
etymology: From pit + -man.

definition: An inadequate payment.
example: They work all day for a mere pittance.
etymology: From Middle English pitaunce, from Old French pitance, pitence, from Medieval Latin *pietāntia, from Latin pietās (“piety”).

definition: A window that opens by pivoting either horizontally or vertically.
A chest in which coins from the mint are held to await assay.
Post in a public place.
example: To placard a sale.

definition: Pertaining to or having or occurring by means of a placenta.
example: All mammals except monotremes and marsupials are placental mammals.
etymology: From post-classical Latin placentalis, corresponding to placenta + -al.

definition: Mammals having a placenta; all mammals except monotremes and marsupials.
Copied and passed off as your own.
example: Used plagiarized data in his thesis.

definition: An inhabitant of a plains region (especially the Great Plains of North America).
A building housing an instrument for projecting the positions of the planets onto a domed ceiling.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin planētārium. Equivalent to planet + -arium.

definition: Planks collectively; a quantity of planks.
etymology: From plank + -ing.

definition: Any of several small insects especially aphids that feed by sucking the juices from plants.
Any of numerous plants of the genus Plantago; mostly small roadside or dooryard weeds with elliptic leaves and small spikes of very small flowers; seeds of some used medicinally.
etymology: From Spanish plantano (obsolete variant of plátano), from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).

definition: Cosmopolitan family of small herbs and a few shrubs; most are troublesome weeds.
Any of numerous perennials having mounds of sumptuous broad ribbed leaves and clusters of white, blue, or lilac flowers; used as ground cover.
A banana tree bearing hanging clusters of edible angular greenish starchy fruits; tropics and subtropics.
Relating to or occurring on the undersurface of the foot.
example: Plantar warts can be very painful.
etymology: From Latin plantāris, from planta (“sole of the foot”) + -āris. By surface analysis, planta + -ar.

definition: Flexion of the toes when the sole of the foot is stroked firmly on the outer side from the heel to the front in persons over the age of 2 years; under 2 years the results should be extension of the toes (Babinski reflex).
A small cellular inclusion consisting of a ring of DNA that is not in a chromosome but is capable of autonomous replication.
etymology: From plasma + -id, coined by American molecular biologist Joshua Lederberg in 1952.

definition: The application of plaster.
A machine for wall rendering.
Apparent validity.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin plausibilitās.

definition: Easy to believe on the basis of available evidence.
example: He talked plausibly before the committee.
etymology: From plausible + -ly.

definition: A festive merry feeling.
etymology: From playful + -ness.

definition: A recreation room for noisy activities (parties or children's play etc.).
etymology: From play + room.

definition: An artifact designed to be played with.
etymology: From play + thing.

definition: A pleasing entertainer.
example: He is quite the crowd pleaser.
etymology: From Middle English plesere, equivalent to please + -er.

definition: A diplomat who is fully authorized to represent his or her government.
etymology: From Medieval Latin plēnipotentiārius (“having full power”), Late Latin plēnipotēns, from plēnus (“full”) + potēns (“mighty, powerful”).

definition: Of or relating to the pleura or the walls of the thorax.
example: Pleural muscles.
etymology: From pleura + -al.

definition: The cavity in the thorax that contains the lungs and heart.
The small potential space between the parietal and visceral layers of the pleura.
Susceptible to being led or directed.
example: You will find the clay perfectly pliable as long as it stays moist.
etymology: From Middle French, from Old French ploiable, from ploiier (“to fold”). By surface analysis, ply + -able. Compare pliant.

definition: An architectural support or base (as for a column or statue).
example: The queen placed the vase on the plinth so the cupbearer could fill it with flowers.
etymology: From French plinthe, from Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).

definition: Hard monotonous routine work.
Drop something with a plopping sound.
example: He plopped down on the sofa to watch TV.
etymology: Imitative of the sound, or perhaps a variant of plap.

definition: Any of numerous chiefly shorebirds of relatively compact build having straight bills and large pointed wings; closely related to the sandpipers.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English plover, from Anglo-Norman plover, plovier, from Medieval Latin plovarius, pluviārius, of disputed origin; perhaps from Latin pluvia (“rain”).

definition: Marked by courage and determination in the face of difficulties or danger; robust and uninhibited.
etymology: From pluck (“nerve, persistence”) + -y.

definition: Any of a variety of alcoholic liqueurs made from plums.
Given to taking by force what is desired.
Of or relating to the philosophical doctrine of pluralism.
example: A pluralistic culture.
etymology: From plural + -istic.

definition: Hunt illegally.
example: People are poaching elephants for their ivory.
etymology: From Middle English pochen (“to poach (eggs)”), from Old French pocher "to put (egg yolks) in pockets" (i.e. in bags formed by the whites), from Old French poche (“pocket”).

definition: Someone who hunts or fishes illegally on the property of another.
