etymology: From poach + -er.

definition: Your personal financial means.
example: That car is too expensive for my pocketbook.

definition: An issue whose settlement will affect financial resources.
Small brown bat of California and northern Mexico.
Of or relating to poetry.
example: Poetic works.
etymology: From Middle English poetical, possibly equivalent to poet + -ical.

definition: In such a manner as to make something clearly evident.
example: He pointedly ignored the question.
etymology: From pointed + -ly.

definition: Having a pointed toe.
example: Pointy-toed shoes.

definition: Smooth American swamp shrub with pinnate leaves and greenish flowers followed by greenish white berries; yields an irritating oil.
Poisonous perennial Old World vine having violet flowers and oval coral-red berries; widespread weed in North America.
An agaric regarded as poisonous.
Wasting time.
The condition of having or giving polarity.
etymology: Borrowed from French polarisation. By surface analysis, polarise + -ation or polar + -isation.

definition: A competition that involves jumping over a high crossbar with the aid of a long pole.
A writer who argues in opposition to others (especially in theology).
etymology: From French polémique, from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós, “of war”), from πόλεμος (pólemos, “war”). By surface analysis, polem- + -ic.

definition: A thick mush made of cornmeal boiled in stock or water.
A female member of a police force.
etymology: From police + -woman.

definition: An official of the Communist Party who was assigned to teach party principles to a military unit.
Waste matter that contaminates the water or air or soil.
etymology: From pollute + -ant.

definition: A ghost that announces its presence with rapping and the creation of disorder.
example: A poltergeist haunts the house by moving objects around, making chain-rattling noises and throwing things.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from German Poltergeist, from poltern (“to rumble”) + Geist (“ghost”), cognates with English boulder and ghost, respectively.

definition: Having more than one mate at a time; used of relationships and individuals.
example: That Mormon community no longer practises polygamous relationships.
etymology: From poly- + -gamous.

definition: Having many sides or relating to a surface marked by polygons.
example: Polygonal structure.
etymology: From polygon + -al.

definition: In geometry, a connected series of line segments.
example: The upper convex hull is a polygonal chain that connects the leftmost point in P to the rightmost one.

definition: A closed plane figure bounded by straight sides.
Of or relating to or consisting of a polymer.
example: A polymeric compound.
etymology: From polymer + -ic.

definition: (genetics) the genetic variation within a population that natural selection can operate on.
etymology: * (object-oriented programming) Coined by British computer scientist Christopher Strachey in 1967. By surface analysis, poly- + -morphism.

definition: A peptide containing 10 to more than 100 amino acids.
etymology: From poly- + peptide.

definition: A polymer of propylene used as a thermoplastic molding material.
etymology: From poly- + propylene.

definition: A foam made by adding water to polyurethane plastics.
Common and widely distributed tall timber pine of western North America having dark green needles in bunches of 2 to 5 and thick bark with dark brown plates when mature.
etymology: From the specific epithet, New Latin ponderōsa (“heavy”), in reference to the wood.

definition: Common and widely distributed tall timber pine of western North America having dark green needles in bunches of 2 to 5 and thick bark with dark brown plates when mature.
A band of nerve fibers linking the medulla oblongata and the cerebellum with the midbrain.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pōns (“bridge”). Doublet of Pontus.

definition: Proceeding from or ordered by or subject to a pope or the papacy regarded as the successor of the Apostles.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pontificālis.

definition: Administer a pontifical office.
etymology: From Latin pontificatus, from pontifex (“high priest”), from pons (“bridge”) + facere (“make”).

definition: (nautical) a floating structure (as a flat-bottomed boat) that serves as a dock or to support a bridge.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French ponton, from Old French ponton, from Latin pontō, pontōnem (“ferryboat”), from pōns (“bridge”).

definition: A temporary bridge built over a series of pontoons.
A seaplane equipped with pontoons for landing or taking off from water.
Of an event that is taking place and is lively.
Meat from a loin of pork.
Pork loin muscle.
The property of being porous; being able to absorb fluids.
etymology: From porous + -ity.

definition: Any of several small gregarious cetacean mammals having a blunt snout and many teeth.
A yellow fatty oil obtained from porpoises and used as a fine lubricant.
A porch or entrance to a building consisting of a covered and often columned area.
etymology: From Italian portico, from Latin porticus (“porch”), from porta (“gate”). Doublet of porch, portego, and porticus.

definition: A new word formed by joining two others and combining their meanings.
example: ‘motel’ is a portmanteau word made by combining ‘motor’ and ‘hotel’.

definition: A new word formed by joining two others and combining their meanings.
example: ‘motel’ is a portmanteau word made by combining ‘motor’ and ‘hotel’.
etymology: First used by Lewis Carroll in 1871, based on the concept of two words packed together, like a portmanteau (“a travelling case having two halves joined by a hinge”).

definition: That state of an adverb indicating simple quality, without comparison or relation to increase or diminution.
example: An example using a positive-degree adverb that doesn't end in ‘-ly’ would be the adverb ‘fast’ in the sentence, ‘She drove fast’.

definition: An elementary particle with positive charge; interaction of a positron and an electron results in annihilation.
example: The notion of a positron weapon remains the stuff of science fiction.
etymology: From positive + -tron (electron). Coined by American physicist Carl Anderson in 1932 to replace the earlier term antielectron.

definition: A person who owns something.
etymology: From possess + -or.

definition: Deciduous shrub of southeastern and central United States.
Closed horse-drawn carriage with four wheels; formerly used to transport passengers and mail.
etymology: From post + chaise (“type of carriage”) or its etymon, French chaise.

definition: A grant that funds postdoctoral study or research.
etymology: Clipping of postdoctoral.

definition: Subsequent to menopause.
etymology: From post- + menopausal.

definition: Genre of art and literature and especially architecture in reaction against principles and practices of established modernism.
etymology: From post- + modernism.

definition: Occurring immediately after birth.
example: Postnatal development.
etymology: From post- + natal. First use appears c. 1831.

definition: Happening or done after a surgical operation.
example: Postoperative complications.
etymology: From post- + operative.

definition: Of or relating to or involving posture.
example: Postural exercises.
etymology: From posture + -al.

definition: The common European annual marigold.
etymology: From pot + marigold.

definition: A white crystalline double sulfate of aluminum: the potassium double sulfate of aluminum.
etymology: From potash + alum.

definition: A crystalline salt (KHCO3) that is used in baking powder and as an antacid.
A white crystalline salt (KBr) used as a sedative and in photography.
A crystalline salt in organic synthesis and in making photographic emulsions and in iodized table salt.
A pit or hole produced by wear or weathering (especially in a road surface).
etymology: From dialectal pot (“pit, hollow, cavity”) + hole.

definition: Whatever happens to be available especially when offered to an unexpected guest or when brought by guests and shared by all.
example: Having arrived unannounced we had to take potluck.
etymology: From pot + luck. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, sense 3 (“a shared meal consisting of whatever guests have brought”) is unlikely to have been influenced by potlatch.

definition: A Canadian dish made with french fries and cheese curds topped with a light brown gravy.
example: Jean made an eight-hour trip across the border into Quebec just to satisfy his craving for poutine.
etymology: Borrowed from Canadian French poutine (“French fries with cheese curds and gravy; any of various kinds of pudding”);

definition: Any of various fungi of the genus Erysiphe producing powdery conidia on the host surface.
A large vertical steel tower supporting high-tension power lines.
example: Power pylons are a favorite target for terrorists.

definition: The quality of lacking strength or power; being weak and feeble.
etymology: From powerless + -ness.

definition: Sleep fully clothed in the same bed with one's betrothed.
Short hairy perennial with early spring blue-violet or lilac flowers; North America and Siberia.
Perennial herb of North American prairies having dense heads of small white flowers.
Typical vole of the extended prairie region of central United States and southern Canada.
Someone who plays practical jokes on others.
example: A skilled prankster.
etymology: From prank + -ster.

definition: The fleshy part of the human body that you sit on.
example: Pratt, a Buttock.
etymology: Unknown. Perhaps a specialised use of Etymology 1 (see above).

definition: Designed or having the power to deter or prevent an anticipated situation or occurrence.
In a precarious manner.
example: Being a precariously dominant minority is a difficult position for human nature to cope with.
etymology: From precarious + -ly.

definition: Of structural members especially of concrete; cast into form before being transported to the site of installation.
example: The bridge used precast concrete girders.
etymology: From pre- + cast.

definition: Rule of personal conduct.
example: Precept guides, but example draws.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin praeceptum, form of praecipiō (“to teach”), from Latin prae (“pre-”) + capiō (“take”).

definition: Done with very great haste and without due deliberation.
example: Wondered whether they had been rather precipitate in deposing the king.
etymology: From obsolete French précipiteux, from Vulgar Latin *praecipitōsus, from praeceps, praecipit- (“ precipice”) + -ōsus (“-ful, -ous”), from prae- (“before”) + caput (“head”).

definition: Of or relating to the early phases of a disease when accurate diagnosis is not possible because symptoms of the disease have not yet appeared.
etymology: From pre- + clinical.

definition: A laboratory test of a new drug or a new invasive medical device on animal subjects; conducted to gather evidence justifying a clinical trial.
A laboratory test of a new drug or a new invasive medical device on animal subjects; conducted to gather evidence justifying a clinical trial.
A laboratory test of a new drug or a new invasive medical device on animal subjects; conducted to gather evidence justifying a clinical trial.
An assumption on which rests the validity or effect of something else.
example: A marriage licence is a precondition for a wedding.
etymology: From pre- + condition.

definition: Be earlier in time; go back further.
example: The Chinese use of Pascal's Triangle predates its discovery by Blaise Pascal.
etymology: From pre- + date.

definition: Previous determination as if by destiny or fate.
etymology: From Middle English predestinacion, from Old French predestination, from Late Latin praedēstinātiō. By surface analysis, predestine + -ation. Displaced native Old English foreteohhung.

definition: A predisposition in favor of something.
example: A predilection for expensive cars.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedīlēctiō.

definition: A dehydrogenated analogue of cortisol (trade names Orasone or Deltasone or Liquid Pred or Meticorten); used as an anti-inflammatory drug in the treatment of arthritis and as an immunosuppressant.
etymology: From pre(gnane) + d(ie)ne + (cort)isone.

definition: Be larger in number, quantity, power, status or importance.
example: Hispanics predominate in this neighborhood.
etymology: From Latin praedominātus, past participle of praedominor. By surface analysis, pre- + dominate.

definition: In a preferential manner.
example: He was treated preferentially.
etymology: From preferential + -ly.

definition: Form into a shape resembling the final, desired one.
etymology: From pre- + form.

definition: The anterior part of the frontal lobe.
(sometimes followed by ‘to’) causing harm or injury.
example: The reporter's coverage resulted in prejudicial publicity for the defendant.
etymology: From Middle English prejudiceele, prejudicial, prejudiciall, prejudiciel, prejudiciell, prejudycyall, from Old French prejudicial, prejudiciel and Medieval Latin prēiūdiciālis.

definition: A senior clergyman and dignitary.
etymology: From Old French prelat (French prélat), from Medieval Latin praelātus, perfect passive participle of praeferō (“to carry before, prefer, exceed”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix). Doublet of prefer.

definition: A minor match preceding the main event.
etymology: Clipping of preliminary. Sense 2 ("clipping of preliminary examination") was originally Oxford University slang, now in common use.

definition: Written matter preceding the main text of a book.
example: Are you done with prelims yet?

definition: Relating to events before a marriage.
example: Premarital sex is now far more common than it was in the 1920s.
etymology: From pre- + marital.

definition: A feeling of evil to come.
etymology: First use appears c. 1533.

definition: Payment in advance.
etymology: From pre- + payment.

definition: Superiority in power or influence.
example: The preponderance of good over evil.
etymology: From preponderant + -ance.

definition: A function word that combines with a noun or pronoun or noun phrase to form a prepositional phrase that can have an adverbial or adjectival relation to some other word.
etymology: From Middle English preposicioun, from Old French preposicion, from Latin praepositio, praepositionem, from praepono (“to place before”), equivalent to pre- + position. Compare French préposition.

definition: Perceiving the significance of events before they occur.
example: Extraordinarily prescient memoranda on the probable course of postwar relations.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin praesciēns (“foreknowing; foretelling, predicting”), present participle of) Latin praesciō (“to foreknow”), from prae- (prefix meaning ‘before;

definition: A participle expressing present action; in English is formed by adding ‘-ing’.
A fortress established in the southwestern United States by the Spanish in order to protect their missions and other holdings.
example: Tucson was first settled as a walled presidio.
etymology: From Spanish presidio (“garrison”), from Latin praesidium, 1763. Doublet of praesidium and presidium.

definition: Of or relating to or designed for children between the ages of 9 and 12.
example: A preteen party.
etymology: From pre- + teen.

definition: A false or unsupportable quality.
An infant that is born prior to 37 weeks of gestation.
(law) a conference held before the trial begins to bring the parties together to outline discovery proceedings and to define the issues to be tried; more useful in civil than in criminal cases.
example: As a result, another pretrial review was to be held on 17 February.
etymology: From pre- + trial.

definition: (law) a conference held before the trial begins to bring the parties together to outline discovery proceedings and to define the issues to be tried; more useful in civil than in criminal cases.
Existing or belonging to a time before a war.
example: Prewar levels of industrial production.
etymology: From pre- + war.

definition: Pricing above the market price when no alternative retailer is available.
example: The farmers aren't really guilty of price gouging, but they are trying to recoup some of their losses from the flooding earlier this spring.

definition: Having prickly leaves.
As it seems at first sight.
example: A prima facie case of murder.
etymology: From Latin prīmā (“first”) + faciē (“shape, figure”), literally “at the first appearance.”

definition: Having existed from the beginning; in an earliest or original stage or state.
example: The forest primeval.
etymology: From Latin primaevus (“in the first or earliest period of life”) + -al, from primus (“first”) + aevum (“time, age”); see prime and age.

definition: The presiding bishop of the Episcopal Church of Scotland.
etymology: From Latin prīmus (“[the] first”); related to prior, the comparative form. Partially cognate to foremost, from Proto-Indo-European [Term?]. Doublet of prime and primo.

definition: Artistic design and manufacture of prints as woodcuts or silkscreens.
etymology: From print + making.

definition: The output of a computer in printed form.
etymology: Deverbal from print out.

definition: (microbiology) an infectious protein particle similar to a virus but lacking nucleic acid; thought to be the agent responsible for scrapie and other degenerative diseases of the nervous system.
etymology: From (a reordering of) the initial letters of proteinaceous infectious particle. Coined by American neurologist and biochemist Stanley B. Prusiner in 1982.

definition: An officer or crew member of a privateer.
etymology: From private + -eer probably after volunteer, shortened from the original term "private man-of-war".

definition: Change from governmental to private control or ownership.
example: The oil industry was privatized.
etymology: From private + -ize.

definition: In a way that agrees in amount, magnitude or degree.
example: Tenants who have given 30 days' notice who do not leave on the last day of the month will be charged on a pro rata basis.
etymology: From Latin prō (“according to”) + ratus (“calculated”).

definition: For the time being.
example: He is the president pro tem.
etymology: From the Latin prō tempore (literally “for a time”).

definition: Under terms not final or fully worked out or agreed upon.
example: Probationary employees.
etymology: From probation + -ary.

definition: A beneficial bacterium found in the intestinal tract of healthy mammals; often considered to be a plant.
Postpone doing what one should be doing.
example: He did not want to write the letter and procrastinated for days.

definition: Have offspring or produce more individuals of a given animal or plant.
example: The Bible tells people to procreate.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in the first part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English, the verb in 1525;

definition: A person authorized to act for another.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English procuratour, from Anglo-Norman procuratour, from Latin prōcūrātor, from prōcūrō (“to procure”) (English procure). Equivalent to procure + -ator and a doublet of proctor and procurer.

definition: A verbalization that encourages you to attempt something.
example: The ceaseless prodding got on his nerves.

definition: In a productive way.
example: They worked together productively for two years.
etymology: From productive + -ly.

definition: An open avowal (true or false) of some belief or opinion.
example: A profession of disagreement.

definition: The position of professor.
etymology: From professor + -ship.

definition: Making the profit as great as possible.
example: The profit-maximizing price.

definition: In a productive way.
etymology: From profitable + -ly.

definition: The property of being extremely abundant.
example: The profusion of detail.
etymology: From Middle French profusion, from Late Latin profusio.

definition: Of or relating to prediction; having value for making predictions.
The process of modifying a software system to make some aspect of it work more efficiently or use fewer resources.
The political orientation of those who favor progress toward better conditions in government and society.
etymology: From progressive + -ism.

definition: To a prohibitive degree.
example: It is prohibitively expensive.
etymology: From prohibitive + -ly.

definition: Any personality test designed to yield information about someone's personality on the basis of their unrestricted response to ambiguous objects or situations.
The geometry of properties that remain invariant under projection.
Any personality test designed to yield information about someone's personality on the basis of their unrestricted response to ambiguous objects or situations.
Any personality test designed to yield information about someone's personality on the basis of their unrestricted response to ambiguous objects or situations.
The slipping or falling out of place of an organ (as the uterus).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prolapsus.

definition: Grow rapidly.
example: Pizza parlors proliferate in this area.
etymology: Back-formation from proliferation.

definition: Relating to or having the character of a promise.
example: Promissory note.
etymology: From Middle English promissorye, from Medieval Latin prōmissōrius. By surface analysis, promise + -ory.

definition: A promise to pay a specified amount on demand or at a certain time.
A natural elevation (especially a rocky one that juts out into the sea).
etymology: From Medieval Latin prōmontōrium, from prōmineō, from prō- + *mineō (“to project or jut”, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stand out”)) + -tōrium (“place”).

definition: An authoritative declaration.
example: The trial concluded with the pronouncement of a guilty verdict.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman and Old French prononcement. By surface analysis, pronounce + -ment. Doublet of pronunciamento.

definition: Read for errors.
example: I should proofread my manuscripts.
etymology: From proof + read.

definition: Of or relating to or characterized by propaganda.
etymology: From propaganda + -ist, after French propagandiste.

definition: Predict or reveal through, or as if through, divine inspiration.
etymology: From Middle English prophecien; partly from prophecie, and partly from Middle French prophecier, prophesier, from prophecie (“prophecy”). Doublet of prophecy.

definition: Capable of preventing conception or impregnation.

definition: A ratio of two quantities that is constant.

definition: Italian salt-cured ham usually sliced paper thin.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian prosciutto (meaning 'ham', in general), from asciutto, with a change of prefix, or from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from per + Latin exsūctus.

definition: Excluded from use or mention.

definition: Someone who prowls or sneaks about; usually with unlawful intentions.

definition: Make brighter and prettier.
example: We refurbished the guest wing.
etymology: 1605, from re- + furbish, from Middle English furbishen, from Middle French forbir (stem furbiss-, “to clean, polish”), from Frankish *furbēn (“to clean, polish”).

definition: The speech act of answering an attack on your assertions.
example: His refutation of the charges was short and persuasive.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French refutation (compare French réfutation, Spanish refutación, Portuguese refutação, Italian refutazione) or its etymon Latin refūtātiō, from refūtō + -ātiō. By surface analysis, refute + -ation.

definition: Paraphernalia indicative of royalty (or other high office).
example: To be dressed in full regalia (dressed up).
etymology: From Middle English regalie, from Medieval Latin rēgālia (“royal powers”), substantivisation of the neuter plural of rēgālis (“of a king”), from rēx (“king”). By surface analysis, regal + -ia.

definition: Loss of sensation in a region of the body produced by application of an anesthetic agent to all the nerves supplying that region (as when an epidural anesthetic is administered to the pelvic region during childbirth).
A person who is formally entered (along with others) in a register (and who obtains certain rights thereby).
Go back to a statistical means.
example: Your nightmares stopped when you were eight years old, but after the house burned down, you regressed.
etymology: (verb) From Latin regressus, past participle of regredior (“to go back”), from re- (“back”) + gradior (“to go”). Doublet of regressus.

definition: Feeling or expressing regret or sorrow or a sense of loss over something done or undone.
example: Felt regretful over his vanished youth.
etymology: From regret + -ful.

definition: With regret (used in polite formulas).
example: I must regretfully decline your kind invitation.
etymology: From regretful + -ly.

definition: Present or use over, with no or few changes.
example: Today's parliamentary session only rehashed last week's arguments.
etymology: From re- + hash.

definition: Heat again.
example: Please reheat the food from last night.
etymology: From re- + heat.

definition: An erect greyish branching lichen of Arctic and even some north temperate regions constituting the chief food for reindeer and caribou and sometimes being eaten by humans.
A new or different meaning.
etymology: From re- + interpretation.

definition: Introduce anew.
example: We haven't met in a long time, so let me reintroduce myself.
etymology: From re- + introduce.

definition: An act of renewed introduction.
etymology: From re- + introduction.

definition: Cause (a stream or river) to erode, as by an uplift of the land.
etymology: From re- (“again”) + Latin iuvenis (“young”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare Old French rejuvener.

definition: Kindle anew, as of a fire.
example: After being abroad for a decade, when he came back he rekindled his obsession with cricket.
etymology: From re- + kindle.

definition: A failure to maintain a higher state.

Marked by recurring high fever and transmitted by the bite of infected lice or ticks; characterized by episodes of high fever and chills and headache and muscle pain and nausea that recur every week or ten days for several months.
(philosophy) the philosophical doctrine that all criteria of judgment are relative to the individuals and situations involved.
etymology: From relative + -ism.

definition: Give in, as to influence or pressure.
example: He had planned to ground his son for a month, but relented and decided to give him a stern lecture instead.
etymology: From Middle English relenten, from Anglo-Norman relentir, from Latin re- + lentare (“to bend”), from lentus (“soft, pliant, slow”). Earliest recording dates to 1526. The noun is from the verb.

definition: The relation of something to the matter at hand.
etymology: From relevant + -cy.

definition: Exaggerated or affected piety and religious zeal.
etymology: From religio(u)s + -ity, from Latin religiositas.

definition: A verbal act of renouncing a claim or right or position etc.
Taking a small amount into the mouth to test its quality.
The act of marrying again.
etymology: From re- + marriage.

definition: Marry, not for the first time.
example: After her divorce, she remarried her high school sweetheart.
etymology: From re- + marry.

definition: A mental impression retained and recalled from the past.
etymology: From Late Latin reminīscentiae (“remembrances”), from Latin reminīscēns, present active participle of reminīscor (“remember”); see reminiscent.

definition: Failing in what duty requires.
example: Remiss of you not to pay your bills.
etymology: From Middle English remisse, remysse, from Latin remissus (“languid, negligent”), perfect passive participle of remittō (“remit”).

definition: A payment of money sent to a person in another place.
example: Remittance advice.
etymology: From remit + -ance.

definition: A male exile living on money sent from home.
An exile living on money sent from home.
A female exile living on money sent from home.
Feeling or expressing pain or sorrow for sins or offenses.
example: He was so remorseful that he voluntarily paid full restitution.
etymology: From remorse + -ful.

definition: The property of being remote.
etymology: From remote + -ness.

definition: Sharp pain in the lower back that radiates into the groin; associated with the passage of a renal calculus through the ureter.
Insufficient excretion of wastes by the kidneys.
Negociate anew.
example: The two warring parties will have to renegociate.
etymology: From re- + negotiate.

definition: Rejecting or disowning or disclaiming as invalid.
example: The President's renunciation of the treaty has upset Congress.
etymology: From Latin renūntiātiō. Compare renounce.

definition: Paint a particular subject again.
example: He repainted the same scenery many times during his life.
etymology: From re- + paint (“verb”).

definition: A male skilled worker whose job is to repair things.
etymology: From repair + -man.

definition: Compensation (given or received) for an insult or injury.
example: An act for which there is no reparation.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin reparātiō, reparātiōnis.

definition: Able or fit to be repeated or quoted.
example: What he said was not repeatable in polite company.
etymology: From repeat + -able.

definition: Filling again by supplying what has been used up.
etymology: From replenish + -ment.

definition: The news as presented by reporters for newspapers or radio or television.
Change place or direction.
etymology: From re- + position.

definition: The act of placing in a new position.
(used especially of art) depicting objects, figures,or scenes as seen.
example: Representational art.
etymology: From representation + -al.

definition: Restrictive of action.
example: A repressive regime.

definition: Capable of being reproduced.
example: Astonishingly reproducible results can be obtained.
etymology: From reproduce + -ible.

definition: The political orientation of those who hold that a republic is the best form of government.
etymology: From republican + -ism.

definition: Rejecting or disowning or disclaiming as invalid.
example: Congressional repudiation of the treaty that the President had negotiated.
etymology: From Latin repudiātiōnem, equivalent to repudiate + -ion.

definition: Force or drive back.
example: To repulse an assault; to repulse the enemy.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English repulsen, a learned borrowing from Latin repulsus, from repellō.

definition: The force by which bodies repel one another.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French répulsion, from Late Latin repulsio, repulsionem, from Latin repulsus.

definition: By repute; according to general belief.
example: Fish with reputedly poisonous flesh.
etymology: From reputed + -ly.

definition: The act of requiring; an authoritative request or demand, especially by a military or public authority that takes something over (usually temporarily) for military or public use.
example: A lab requisition for blood tests.
etymology: From Middle English requisicion, from Old French requisicion, from Medieval Latin requisitio. By surface analysis, requisit(e) + -ion.

definition: An official form on which a request is made.
example: First you have to fill out the requisition.

definition: A person who rescues you from harm or danger.
etymology: From rescue + -er.

definition: A colloquium at which the results of (scientific) research are reported.
Settled in a new location.
An occurrence of rebounding or springing back.
etymology: From Latin resiliō (“to spring back”) + English -ency.

definition: Exhibiting or relating to electrical resistance.
example: Resistive load.
etymology: From resist + -ive.

definition: Characterized by resonance.
example: A resonant voice.

definition: A hollow chamber whose dimensions allow the resonant oscillation of electromagnetic or acoustic waves.
The quality of being able to cope with a difficult situation.
example: A man of great resourcefulness.
etymology: From resourceful + -ness.

definition: A breathing device for administering long-term artificial respiration.
example: Any N95 respirator is designed to filter out 95 percent of particles 0.3 microns or larger.
etymology: From respirate + -or.

definition: Having great beauty and splendor.
example: The resplendent sun rose over the horizon.
etymology: From the obsolete sense of the English verb splendish (“to shine”), from Latin splendere (“to shine”), or from resplend + -ent, from Latin resplendere (“to shine back, glitter”).

definition: The proprietor of a restaurant.
Reappear on the surface.
example: His body finally resurfaced after three years underwater.
etymology: From re- + surface.

definition: Rising again as to new life and vigor.
example: Resurgent nationalism.
etymology: From re- + surgent.

definition: Cause to regain consciousness.
example: To resuscitate a drowned person.
etymology: From Latin resuscitātus, past participle of resuscitō (“to raise up again, revive”), from re- (“again”) + suscitō (“to raise up”), from sub- (“up, under”) + citō (“to summon, rouse”).

definition: The act of taking something back.
An eviction in reprisal for the tenant's good-faith complaints against the landlord; illegal in many states.
Any agent that retards or delays or hinders.
example: Flame-retardant.
etymology: Borrowed from French retardant, equivalent to retard (“to slow down”) + -ant.

definition: The trait of being uncommunicative; not volunteering anything more than necessary.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from Middle French réticence (“act of keeping silent, silence; reserve;

definition: Temperamentally disinclined to talk.
example: She's rather reticent on the subject of her finances.
etymology: Latin reticēns, present participle of reticeō (“to keep silence”).

definition: Any fine network (especially one in the body composed of cells or blood vessels).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin rēticulum (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticule, and Reticulum.

definition: The group following and attending to some important person.
example: The queen’s retinues.
etymology: From Middle English retenue, from Old French retenue, past participle of retenir (“retain”). Doublet of ritenuto.

definition: To go back over again.
example: We retraced the route we took last summer.
etymology: From French retracer, from Middle French retracier.

definition: Teach new skills.
example: We must retrain the linguists who cannot find employment.
etymology: From re- + train.

definition: Hear or try a court case anew.
etymology: From re- + try.

definition: Unrestrained merrymaking.
etymology: From Middle English revelrye; equivalent to revel + -ry.

definition: Absentminded dreaming while awake.
etymology: Borrowed from French rêverie.

definition: Restored to new life and vigor.
example: A revitalized economy.

definition: Tending to impart new life and vigor to.
Intense aversion.
etymology: Partly from Middle French révulsion and partly from Latin revulsiō.

definition: Of southern Asia; used in medical research.
etymology: From New Latin rhēsus, arbitrary formation from Latin Rhēsus, from Ancient Greek Ῥῆσος (Rhêsos), mythical Thracian king.

definition: A blood group antigen possessed by Rh-positive people; if an Rh-negative person receives a blood transfusion from an Rh-positive person it can result in hemolysis and anemia.
Of southern Asia; used in medical research.
In a rhetorical manner.
example: ‘What can be done?’ he asked rhetorically.
etymology: From Middle English retorycally; equivalent to rhetorical + -ly.

definition: Of or pertaining to arthritis.
example: Rheumy with age and grief.

definition: A severe disease chiefly of children and characterized by painful inflammation of the joints and frequently damage to the heart valves.
Any painful disorder of the joints or muscles or connective tissues.
Canadian dogbane yielding a tough fiber used as cordage by Native Americans; used in folk medicine for pain or inflammation in joints.
An imitation diamond made from rock crystal or glass or paste.
example: Lucinda sewed rhinestones into her scarf to add a bit of flair.
etymology: From Rhine + stone; a calque of French caillou du Rhin (“Rhine pebble”).

definition: A white hard metallic element that is one of the platinum group and is found in platinum ores; used in alloys with platinum.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin rhodium, from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”), because of the colour of its salts' solutions.

definition: Any shrub of the genus Rhododendron: evergreen shrubs or small shrubby trees having leathery leaves and showy clusters of campanulate (bell-shaped) flowers.
etymology: The obsolete sense derives from Latin rhododendron (“oleander”), from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (rhodódendron, “oleander”), from ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + δένδρον (déndron, “tree”).

definition: Having corresponding sounds especially terminal sounds.
example: Rhymed verse.

definition: In a rhythmic manner.
example: The chair rocked rhythmically back and forth.
etymology: From rhythmical + -ly.

definition: A framework of ribs.
etymology: From rib (“tease”, verb) + -ing; from the common practice of tickling the ribs to cause laughter.

definition: Brown weevil that infests stored grain especially rice.
Inclined to shake as from weakness or defect.
example: A rickety table.
etymology: From dialectal ricket (“unstable, rickety”) + -y, and/or ricket (“to move noisily and in a reckless way”) + -y. Alternatively, and perhaps less likely, from rickets + -y.

definition: A mixed drink made of sweetened lime juice and soda water usually with liquor.
Soft Italian cheese like cottage cheese.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian ricotta (literally “cooked again”), from Latin recocta.

definition: A message whose content is at variance with reason.
etymology: From ridiculous + -ness.

definition: (used in the plural) flared trousers ending at the calves; worn with riding boots.
A man skilled in the use of a rifle.
example: She was quite the rifleman and could pick off a squirrels with a .22 from across the field with amazing accuracy.
etymology: From rifle + -man.

definition: Small green-and-bronze bird.
The chamber on the right side of the heart that receives venous blood from the right atrium and pumps it into the pulmonary trunk.
Preference for using the right hand.
etymology: From right-handed + -ness.

definition: In a rigid manner.
example: The body was rigidly erect.
etymology: From rigid + -ly.

definition: The quality of being valid and rigorous.
etymology: From Middle English rigour, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French rigor, from Latin rigor (“stiffness, rigidity, rigor, cold, harshness”), from rigere (“to be rigid”). Compare French rigueur.

definition: Ice crystals forming a white deposit (especially on objects outside).
example: Samuel Taylor Coleridge wrote The Rime of the Ancient Mariner in 1797–1798.
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English rim, rime, rym, ryme (“hoar frost; rime”), from Old English hrīm (“frost”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrīm (“rime;

definition: A person who leads (especially in illicit activities).
example: The police arrested the ringleaders of the smuggling operation.
etymology: From ring + leader.

definition: The removal of soap with clean water in the final stage of washing.
example: The cloth will need frequent rinsings as you wash the car.

definition: Produced or growing in extreme abundance.
example: Their riotous blooming.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English riotous, from Anglo-Norman riotous; equivalent to riot + -ous.

definition: Cause to ripen or develop fully.
example: The sun ripens the fruit.
etymology: From Middle English *ripenen, extended form of ripen, from Old English rīpian. In the modern form, equivalent to ripe + -en (inchoative and factitive suffix).

definition: Coming to full development; becoming mature.
A small wave on the surface of a liquid.
A stretch of turbulent water in a river or the sea caused by one current flowing into or across another current.
example: This beach suffers from a riptide that can easily sweep you out to sea.
etymology: From rip + tide.

definition: Of or characterized by or adhering to ritualism.
example: A feudal or ritualistic society.
etymology: From ritual + -istic.

definition: A channel occupied (or formerly occupied) by a river.
etymology: From river + bed. Compare Dutch rivierbedding (“riverbed”), German Flussbett (“riverbed”), Swedish flodbädd (“riverbed”).

definition: Direct one's attention on something.
example: Terror riveted him to the spot.
etymology: From Old French rivet (13th century), from the verb Old French river (“to fetter [a person]”) (12th century), from Old French rive (“rim, edge”) (ca. 1100), which is ultimately from Latin ripa (“riverbank”).

definition: A line of rivets at a seam.
example: The fuselage cracked along the rivet line.

definition: An inn (usually outside city limits on a main road) providing meals and liquor and dancing and (sometimes) gambling.
etymology: From road + house.

definition: A soft sheepskin leather that is colored and finished to resemble morocco; used in bookbinding.
etymology: From Middle French roan, probably from Spanish roano, from Old Spanish raudano, itself probably of Germanic origin (compare Gothic *𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌰𐌽 (*raudan), accusative of 𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌸𐍃 (rauþs, “red”). Compare rowan.

definition: Barnacle that attaches to rocks especially in intertidal zones.
Plant with basal leaves mottled with white and flowers in lax panicles on erect stems.
Slender long-legged Australian wallabies living in caves and rocky areas.
A fusion of black music and country music that was popular in the 1950s; sometimes described as blues with a country beat.
etymology: Blend of rock + hillbilly.

definition: Having excessive asymmetrical ornamentation.
example: An exquisite gilded rococo mirror.
etymology: Borrowed from French rococo.

definition: Male roe deer.
etymology: From Middle English roobukke; equivalent to roe + buck (“male deer”). Doublet of rhebok.

definition: The act of forcing the enemy to withdraw.
etymology: The noun is a deverbal from roll back. The verb is a back-formation from the noun despite being redundant to roll back.

definition: Lettuce with long dark-green leaves in a loosely packed elongated head.
etymology: Ellipsis of romaine lettuce, from French laitue romaine, and direct borrowing of French romaine, from its supposed association with Rome.

definition: Lettuce with long dark-green spoon-shaped leaves.
etymology: A partial calque of French laitue romaine (“Roman lettuce”), from its supposed association with Rome.

definition: Representation of the cross on which Jesus died.
etymology: From Middle English rode, rood (“cross”), from Old English rōd (“cross”), from Proto-Germanic *rōdō, *rōdǭ (“rod, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *rōt-, *reh₁t- (“bar, beam, stem”).

definition: A screen in a church; separates the nave from the choir or chancel.
etymology: rood (“cross; crucifix”) + screen.

definition: Representation of the cross on which Jesus died.
etymology: From Middle English rodetre.

definition: A house where rooms are rented.
(of buildings and rooms) having ample space.
example: A roomy but sparsely furnished apartment.
etymology: From room + -y.

definition: Capturing cattle or horses with a lasso.
example: Ropings were a popular part of the rodeo show.

definition: An old cottage garden plant of southeastern Europe widely cultivated for its attractive white woolly foliage and showy crimson flowers.
Any of several southern African geraniums having fragrant three-lobed to five-lobed leaves and pink flowers.
Of mauve tinged with rose.
Shrub or tree native to Japan cultivated as an ornamental for its rose-pink flowers.
Orchid of central and northern South America having 1- to 3-blossomed racemes of large showy rose-colored flowers; sometimes placed in genus Pogonia.
An ornament or pattern resembling a rose that is worn as a badge of office or as recognition of having won an honor.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French rosette (in sense 15) and (modern) French rosette. By surface analysis, rose + -ette.

definition: Any of a class of solid or semisolid viscous substances obtained either as exudations from certain plants or prepared by polymerization of simple molecules.
etymology: From Old French raisine, rousine, variants of résine. Doublet of resin.

definition: A bag filled with rosin; used by baseball pitchers to improve their grip on the ball.
Erect plant with small clusters of pink trumpet-shaped flowers of southwestern United States.
A platform raised above the surrounding level to give prominence to the person on it.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin rōstrum (“beak, snout”), from rōd(ō) (“gnaw”) + -trum, from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- + *-trom.

definition: A roster of names showing the order in which people should perform certain duties.
example: On a rota basis.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin rota (“wheel”). Doublet of rotor and ruote.

definition: (computer science) the actuator that moves a read/write head to the proper data track.
An electro-mechanical device that converts the angular position or motion of a shaft or axle to an analog or digital code.
A supporting structure of the shoulder consisting of the muscles and tendons that attach the arm to the shoulder joint and enable the arm to move.
An oven or broiler equipped with a rotating spit on which meat cooks as it turns.
etymology: From French rôtisserie, from rôtir ‘to roast’. Doublet of rosticceria and roastery.

definition: A difficulty that can be overcome with effort.
example: Analysts predicted rough sledding for handset makers.

definition: Hew roughly, without finishing the surface.
example: Rough-hew stone or timber.
etymology: From rough + hew.

definition: A whitefish with a bronze back; of northern North America and Siberia.
An English ball game similar to baseball.
etymology: From round + -er + -s, presumably for the circuit that batters make around the field.

definition: In a round manner.
example: She was roundly slim.
etymology: From Middle English roundly, roundely, roundliche, equivalent to round + -ly.

definition: In a royal manner.
example: They were royally treated.
etymology: From royal + -ly.

definition: Having an elastic texture resembling rubber in flexibility or toughness.
example: What a bad restaurant! The beef was so rubbery I thought I'd never finish chewing it.
etymology: From rubber + -y.

definition: A contagious viral disease that is a milder form of measles lasting three or four days; can be damaging to a fetus during the first trimester.
etymology: From Latin rubellus (“reddish”), diminutive of ruber (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

definition: The basic unit of money in Tajikistan.
etymology: Borrowed from Russian рубль (rublʹ). Doublet of rubel and rubl.

definition: A bag carried by a strap on your back or shoulder.
etymology: Borrowed from German Rucksack.

definition: Woodland flower native to eastern North America having cup-shaped flowers reminiscent of anemone but more delicate.
Extremely harmful; bringing physical or financial ruin.
example: A ruinous course of action.
etymology: From Middle English ruynous, from Old French ruinos, ruineus, from Latin ruīnōsus. By surface analysis, ruin + -ous.

definition: Syncopated music in duple time for dancing the rumba.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish rumba.

definition: A jumble of things to be given away.
example: Have a rummage through the attic and see if you can find anything worth selling.
etymology: From Middle English ronage, from Old French arrumage (compare French arrimage), from arrumer (“to arrange the cargo in the hold”) (compare French arrimer and Spanish arrumar).

definition: A sale of donated articles.
Go against, as of rules and laws.
Slice of sweet raised bread baked again until it is brown and hard and crisp.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish or Portuguese rosca (“a twist or roll of bread”)

definition: The formation of reddish-brown ferric oxides on iron by low-temperature oxidation in the presence of water.
Make a dry crackling sound.
example: Rustling silk.
etymology: From Middle English rustelen, russelen, of uncertain origin, but probably from Old English hrūxlian, hristlan, hrystlan, hristlian (“to make a noise”). Compare also Scots reesle (“to crackle; rattle;

definition: Mercilessness characterized by a lack of pity.
etymology: From ruthless + -ness.

definition: Large black East African antelope with sharp backward-curving horns.
etymology: probably from its sable black coloring

definition: A native-born Israeli.
Having teeth that resemble sabers.
Of or relating to or near the sacrum.
etymology: From Modern Latin sacrālis, from Latin sacrum (“sacred, holy”) + -ālis.

definition: Any of five pairs of spinal nerves emerging from the sacral region of the spinal cord.
Vein of the sacral region.
Of or relating to or involving a sacrament.
etymology: From Old French sacramental, from Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentālis.

definition: A consecrated ointment consisting of a mixture of oil and balsam.
Used in a communion service.
Blasphemous behavior; the act of depriving something of its sacred character.
etymology: Circa 1300, original sense “stealing something sacred”. From Middle English sacrilege, from Old French sacrilege, from Latin sacrilegium, from sacrilegus (“sacrilegious”). Sense of “profanation” from late 14th century.

definition: Someone who obtains pleasure from inflicting pain on others.
etymology: From the name of the Marquis de Sade; see sadism.

definition: The responsibility of a guardian or keeper.
example: I locked the documents in my bureau for safekeeping.
etymology: From safe + keeping.

definition: Any of several North American composite subshrubs of the genera Artemis or Seriphidium.
etymology: From sage + brush, from resemblance in odor and appearance to Salvia officinalis.

definition: A ground dweller that prefers open ground and scattered low bushes; of United States west between Rocky and Sierra Nevada Mountains.
Marked by utter benignity; resembling or befitting an angel or saint.
example: A saintly concern for his fellow men.
etymology: From Middle English *saintli (suggested by seyntly (adverb)), equivalent to saint + -ly. Compare saintlike.

definition: Japanese alcoholic beverage made from fermented rice; usually served hot.
etymology: Compare French saki and Portuguese saki, ultimately probably from a Tupian name sagui, compare sagoin.

definition: European garden herb with purple-tinged flowers and leaves that are sometimes used for salads.
A white crystalline substance with a bitter aftertaste; used as a fungicide or in making aspirin or dyes or perfumes.
etymology: From translingual Salix (“the willow”), from whose bark it can be obtained.

definition: Salicylic alcohol, also called saligenin, is a crystalline phenolic alcohol with the chemical formula C7H8O2, that is obtained usually by hydrolysis of salicin.
example: Salicylic alcohol acts as a local anesthetic and relieves pain and fever.

definition: Of or relating to saliva.
example: Salivary gland.
etymology: From saliva + -ary.

definition: A stone formed in the salivary gland.
A duct through which saliva passes from the salivary gland into the mouth.
Any of three pairs of glands in the mouth and digestive system that secrete saliva for digestion.
Any of various plants of the genus Salvia; a cosmopolitan herb.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Salvia, in turn from Latin salvia (“sage”). Doublet of sage.

definition: A winged often one-seed indehiscent fruit as of the ash or elm or maple.
example: The fruit is a nut, samara or drupe, containing a single seed with a straight embryo and little or no endosperm.
etymology: From Latin samara (“elm seed”), from a Gaulish term derived from Proto-Celtic *samos (“summer”).

definition: A religious ceremony in which something is made holy.
etymology: From Old French sanctificacion, from ecclesiastical Latin sanctificātionem, from sanctificāre (“to sanctify”).

definition: Made or declared or believed to be holy; devoted to a deity or some religious ceremony or use.
example: Sanctified wine.

definition: Excessively or hypocritically pious.
example: A sickening sanctimonious smile.
etymology: From sanctimony + -ous.

definition: Close-grained fragrant yellowish heartwood of the true sandalwood; has insect repelling properties and is used for carving and cabinetwork.
Chiefly tropical herbs or shrubs or trees bearing nuts or one-seeded fruit.
Parasitic tree of Indonesia and Malaysia having fragrant close-grained yellowish heartwood with insect repelling properties and used, e.g., for making chests.
Stiff paper coated with powdered emery or sand.
example: They like to finish it off with a piece of 600-grit sandpaper before cleaning and painting.
etymology: From sand + paper.

definition: A windstorm that lifts up clouds of dust or sand.
etymology: From sand + storm.

definition: Sweetened red wine and orange or lemon juice with soda water.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish sangría, from sangre (“blood”) + -ía.

definition: A hospital for recuperation or for the treatment of chronic diseases.
etymology: Perhaps a blend of sanitary + sanatorium. Coined by John Harvey Kellogg.

definition: Made sanitary.
A typeface in which characters have no serifs.
etymology: From sans + serif.

definition: Abounding in sap.
example: Sappy maple trees.
etymology: From Middle English sappy, sapy, from Old English sæpiġ (“full of sap, succulent”), equivalent to sap + -y.

definition: Any of various thermoplastic resins used to make things.
etymology: From a trade name coined by the Dow Chemical Co. for a number of monomers and polymers made from vinylidene chloride (especially polyvinylidene chloride).

definition: A usually malignant tumor arising from connective tissue (bone or muscle etc.); one of the four major types of cancer.
etymology: From Latin sarcoma, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”) + -ωμα (-ōma, “process”) or from Ancient Greek σαρκόω (sarkóō), itself from σάρξ (sárx); by surface analysis, sarc- + -oma.

definition: Small fatty fish usually canned.
etymology: Borrowed from French sardine (cognate with Spanish sardina, Italian sardina), Latin sardīna; from Ancient Greek σαρδίνη (sardínē).

definition: Oil obtained from sardines and used chiefly as a lubricant and in soap.
Disdainfully or ironically humorous; scornful and mocking.
example: His rebellion is the bitter, sardonic laughter of all great satirists.

definition: A dress worn primarily by Hindu women; consists of several yards of light material that is draped around the body.
A lock attached to the sashes of a double hung window that can fix both in the shut position.
Very thinly sliced raw fish.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 刺身(さしみ) (sashimi, “sticking into; slicing + flesh, meat”), from the way the flesh of the fish is sliced

definition: Fill to satisfaction.
example: I am sated.
etymology: From Middle English sate, satte, from Old English sæt, first and third person singular preterite of sittan (“to sit”).

definition: A humorist who uses ridicule and irony and sarcasm.
etymology: From satire + -ist.

definition: Cause (a chemical compound, vapour, solution, magnetic material) to unite with the greatest possible amount of another substance.
example: Rain saturated their clothes.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in the second part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English, the verb in 1538, the noun in 1921;

definition: Oil and vinegar with mustard and garlic.
Someone who has been admitted to membership in a scholarly field.
etymology: Borrowed from French savant, from Latin sapiō. Doublet of sapient. Sense 3 is a clipping of idiot savant, literally ‘wise idiot’.

definition: A condition in which a person with a mental disability, such as an autism spectrum disorder, demonstrates profound and prodigious capacities or abilities far in excess of what would be considered normal.
example: Individuals diagnosed with savant syndrome boast unparalleled ability in certain skills and subject areas.

definition: Procumbent or spreading juniper.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English savyne, from Old French savine, from Latin sabīna. Compare Old English safine.

definition: Small hardy clump-forming spiny palm of southern United States.
etymology: The edges of the leaflets of this palm have strong spines, like a saw.

definition: Well below average height.
A musician who plays the saxophone.
etymology: From saxophone + -ist.

definition: A shell of a scallop.
Having a margin with rounded scallops.
etymology: From scallop + -ed. In culinary sense, originally referred to a seafood dish baked and served in a scallop shell, but now used more generally.

definition: Small European fern with chaffy leathery fronds.
Having a scaly tail.
In a skimpy manner.
example: Scantily clad.
etymology: From scanty + -ly.

definition: Inadequately clothed.
Erect leafless flower stalk growing directly from the ground as in a tulip.
etymology: From Latin scāpus, from Doric Greek σκᾶπος (skâpos). Doublet of native English shaft.

definition: Clean refuse from.
example: Scavenge a street.
etymology: Back-formation from scavenger. Compare messenger and passenger.

definition: An actor who draws more attention than other actors in the same scene.
example: Babies are natural scene-stealers.

definition: The imperial authority symbolized by a scepter.
Someone who habitually doubts accepted beliefs.
The imperial authority symbolized by a scepter.
etymology: From Middle English septre, sceptre, from Old French sceptre, from Latin scēptrum, from Ancient Greek σκῆπτρον (skêptron, “staff, stick, baton”), from σκήπτω (skḗptō, “to prop, to support, to lean upon a staff”).

definition: Computer hardware that arranges jobs to be done by the computer in an appropriate order.

definition: The yard associated with a school.
etymology: From school + yard.

definition: Brilliantly clever.
example: Scintillating wit.
etymology: From scintillate + -ing.

definition: An abnormal lateral curve to the vertebral column.
etymology: From Latin scoliosis, from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis, “twisting; torsion”).

definition: Small biscuit (rich with cream and eggs) cut into diamonds or sticks and baked in an oven or (especially originally) on a griddle.
etymology: Originally Scots, possibly from Middle Low German schö̂ne (“fine flour bread”), or Middle Dutch schoonbroot (“fine bread; a kind of flat angular loaf”), from schoon (“fine”) + broot (“bread”).

definition: Subject to harsh criticism.
example: Your invectives scorched the community.
etymology: From Middle English scorchen, scorcnen (“to make dry; parch”), perhaps an alteration of earlier *scorpnen, from Old Norse skorpna (“to shrivel up”).

definition: A facial expression of dislike or displeasure.
example: She made a scowl.
etymology: From Middle English scowlen, scoulen, skoulen (also as Middle English schoulen), probably of North Germanic origin. Compare Danish skule (“to scowl”), Norwegian skule (“to scowl”).

definition: Being very thin.
example: A long scrawny neck.
etymology: A variant of dialectal scranny (“thin; lean; scraggy; poor; scanty; of inferior quality”), perhaps from Old Norse skran (“rubbish; junk”) + -y. Compare Norwegian skran (“lean, thin, skinny”), English scrannel (“lean;

definition: Someone who communicates vocally in a very loud voice.

definition: Poor handwriting.

definition: Pad for preliminary or hasty writing or notes or sketches etc.; ‘scribbling block’ is a British term.
A firm open-weave fabric used for a curtain in the theater.
etymology: Attested since the end of the 18th century. Origin unknown.

definition: A certificate whose value is recognized by the payer and payee; scrip is not currency but may be convertible into currency.
example: Depositing his scrip in the outhouse the cowherd glanced around.
etymology: From Middle English scrippe, an aphetism of Old French escrepe (“purse, alms-bag”), a variant of escharpe, from Old Norse skreppa. Cognate with Danish skreppe (“scrip”), Norwegian skreppa (“bag”). Doublet of scarf.

definition: Small hardy clump-forming spiny palm of southern United States.
Transmitted by larval mites and widespread in Asia.
The back side of the neck.
example: That candidate will never get the job: he's a right scruff.
etymology: 1790, from earlier (1787) scuft and dialect scuff, influenced by scruff (“crust”). Related to North Frisian skuft (“back of the neck of a horse”) and Dutch schoft (“withers (of a horse)”), from Proto-Germanic.

definition: Extremely pleasing to the sense of taste.
example: What a scrumptious treat!
etymology: Probably from scrimp (“to put on short allowance, limit, straiten;

definition: Motivation deriving logically from ethical or moral principles that govern a person's thoughts and actions.
Having scruples; arising from a sense of right and wrong; principled.

etymology: From Middle French scrupuleux, from Latin scrupulosus.

definition: A hoe that is used by pushing rather than pulling.
Rushing about hastily in an undignified way.

definition: Moving with great haste.

definition: A widely distributed Arctic cress reputed to have value in treatment or prevention of scurvy; a concentrated source of vitamin C.
Container for coal; shaped to permit pouring the coal onto the fire.
etymology: From Middle English scuttel, scutel, from Old English scutel (“dish, platter”), from Latin scutella, diminutive form of Latin scutra (“flat tray, dish”), perhaps related to Latin scutum (“shield”);

definition: Marine polyps that resemble flowers but have oral rings of tentacles; differ from corals in forming no hard skeleton.

The work of a sailor.

definition: The waterfront of a seaside town.

definition: Either of two large northern marine mammals having ivory tusks and tough hide over thick blubber.

definition: A kind of sealing material that is used to form a hard coating on a porous surface (as a coat of paint or varnish used to size a surface).

definition: An airplane that can land on or take off from water.
etymology: From sea + plane. Supposedly coined by Winston Churchill.

definition: Make very hot and dry.

etymology: From Middle English seren, seeren, from Old English sēarian (“to become sere, to grow sear, wither, pine away”), from Proto-West Germanic *sauʀēn (“to dry out, become dry”);

definition: A light source with reflectors that projects a beam of light in a particular direction.
etymology: From search + light. Compare West Frisian sykljocht (“searchlight”), Dutch zoeklicht (“searchlight”), Danish søgelys (“searchlight”), Swedish sökarljus (“searchlight”).

definition: A lane at sea that is a regularly used route for vessels.
etymology: From Middle English seewey, from Old English sǣweġ (“a seaway, a path through the sea”), equivalent to sea + way. Compare Saterland Frisian Seegong (“seaway, swell”), German Seegang (“seaway, swell”).

definition: An advocate of secessionism.
example: Gustav Klimt was of the Viennese secessionist school.
etymology: From secession + -ist.

definition: Of or relating to a secretary or to a secretary's work.
etymology: From a Latin-type formation *sēcrētāriālis, from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius + Latin -ālis. By surface analysis, secretary + -al.

definition: An assistant who handles correspondence and clerical work for a boss or an organization.
A school where secretarial skills (typing and shorthand and filing etc.) are taught.

definition: A narrow-minded adherence to a particular sect or party or denomination.

definition: Consisting of or divided into sections.

definition: The phenomenon of sediment or gravel accumulating.

Arousing to action or rebellion.

definition: In a tempting seductive manner.
example: She smiled at him seductively.
etymology: From seductive + -ly.

definition: A small beetle that infests the seeds of legumes.
Leaking out slowly.
Separate by race or religion; practice a policy of racial segregation.

etymology: From Latin sēgregātus, perfect passive participle of sēgregō (“to separate”), from sē- (“apart”) + gregō (“to flock or group”), from grex (“flock”). Compare gregarious, aggregate.

definition: The act of changing smoothly from one state or situation to another.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian segue (“it follows”), from seguire (“to follow”), from Latin sequor; originally a term used in a musical score to indicate that the next movement or passage is to follow without a break.

definition: Aggressive self-assurance; given to making bold assertions.

definition: Fertilization by the union of male and female gametes from the same individual.
Fertilized by its own pollen.
Renunciation of your own interests in favor of the interests of others.

definition: Growing from seed dispersed by natural agency such as wind or birds.
In an egotistical manner.

definition: In an altruistic manner.

definition: The quality of unselfish concern for the welfare of others.

definition: A system of conveying information by means of visual signals, using towers with pivoting shutters; information is encoded by the position of the mechanical elements.

Imperfectly prostrate; prostrate for part of its length.

The organic process of growing older and showing the effects of increasing age.

definition: An unelaborated elementary awareness of stimulation.
Aphasia characterized by fluent but meaningless speech and severe impairment of the ability understand spoken or written words.
Capable of being divided or dissociated.
example: The siamese twins were not considered separable.

definition: A social system that provides separate facilities for minority groups.
example: She wrote an essay expounding the tenets of Scottish separatism.
etymology: From separate + -ism.

definition: A chamber that is used as a grave.
etymology: From Middle English sepulchre, sepulcre, sepulker, from late Old English sepulcer, Old French sepulchre, sepulcre, and their etymon Latin sepulchrum, sepulcrum (“grave, burial place”).

definition: (chemistry) an apparatus that can determine the sequence of monomers in a polymer.
example: A MIDI sequencer.
etymology: From sequence + -er.

definition: Requisition forcibly, as of enemy property.
example: The estate was sequestered.

definition: Providing privacy or seclusion.
example: Sat close together in the sequestered pergola.

definition: Adornment consisting of a small piece of shiny material used to decorate clothing.
etymology: Borrowed from French sequin, from Italian zecchino, from zecca (“mint”), from Arabic سِكَّة (sikka, “die for coining, coin”). Doublet of zecchin.

definition: A succession of short monogamous relationships (as by someone who undergoes multiple divorces).
A short line at the end of the main strokes of a character.
etymology: From earlier ceriph, seriph, surryph, of obscure derivation.

definition: A sweetish crystalline amino acid involved in the synthesis by the body of cysteine.
etymology: From Latin sericus (“silken”). The compound was first obtained from silk protein, a particularly rich source, in 1865. See also serge.

definition: Albumin occurring in blood serum; serves to maintain the somatic pressure of the blood.
A man who serves in the armed forces; a member of a military force.
Having seven units or components.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English sevenfold, sevenefold, from Old English seofonfeald. Equivalent to seven + -fold.

definition: Trying to maintain dignity and self respect despite shabbiness.
A restraint that confines or restricts freedom (especially something used to tie down or restrain a prisoner).

Roe of shad; may be parboiled or baked or sauteed gently.
An electro-mechanical device that converts the angular position or motion of a shaft or axle to an analog or digital code.
A louse parasitic on poultry.
Arabic term for holy martyrs.
etymology: From Arabic شَهِيد (šahīd, “martyr, witness”).

definition: Initial adjustments to improve the functioning or the efficiency and to bring to a more satisfactory state.
example: The new industry's economic shakedown.
etymology: Deverbal from shake down. An improvised bed would originally have been made by shaking down straw.

definition: In a dishonorable manner or to a dishonorable degree.
example: I looked shamefully at the floor.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English schamefully. By surface analysis, shameful + -ly.

definition: Having a well-proportioned and pleasing shape.
example: A slim waist and shapely legs.

definition: A person who makes things.
example: One's birth is a shaper of one's fortunes.

definition: Any implement that is used to make something (an edge or a point) sharper.

definition: An alert and energetic person.
etymology: From sharp + -ie (“diminutive suffix”).

definition: An athlete noted for accurate aim.
etymology: sharp + shooter, a calque of German Scharfschütze.

definition: A package of several things tied together for carrying or storing.
example: A sheaf of paper.

definition: Having the hair or wool cut or clipped off as if with shears or clippers.

Lac purified by heating and filtering; usually in thin orange or yellow flakes but sometimes bleached white.
etymology: From shell + lac, calque of French laque en écailles (literally “lac in scales/shells”).

definition: A hard wax separated from shellac by its insolubility in alcohol.
A frozen dessert made primarily of fruit juice and sugar, but also containing milk or egg-white or gelatin.
etymology: Doublet of sorbet and sharbat, related to syrup.

definition: An abnormal wobble in a motor vehicle (especially in the front wheels).
example: He could feel the shimmy in the steering wheel.
etymology: A back-formation from chemise (mistaken for a plural).

definition: Painful inflammation of the muscles around the shins; frequent among runners.
A swollen bruise caused by a blow to the eye.
etymology: From Middle English schyner, equivalent to shine + -er. Compare Old English sċīnere (“one who produces deceptive appearances, magician”).

definition: Avoid (one's assigned duties).
example: The derelict soldier shirked his duties.
etymology: First use appears c. 1633, in the publications of Shackerley Marmion, apparently from association with shark (verb), or otherwise directly from German Schurke (“rogue, knave”).

definition: A mechanical damper; absorbs energy of sudden impulses.
example: The old car needed a new set of shocks.

definition: A lace used for fastening shoes.
example: Your shoestring is untied.
etymology: The noun is derived from shoe + string. The adjective is derived from the noun, while the verb is derived from terms such as shoestring catch and shoestring tackle.

definition: (baseball) a running catch made near the ground.
example: Jones races in... and makes a fine shoestring catch in shallow center.

definition: Any of several fungi of the genus Armillaria that form brown stringy rhizomorphs and cause destructive rot of the roots of some trees such as apples or maples.
Having the hair or wool cut or clipped off as if with shears or clippers.

A failing or deficiency.

Slender mole having a long snout and tail.
Having the approximate size of a shrew.
An area where a number of shrubs are planted.

Deliberately avoiding; keeping away from or preventing from happening.
Provided with shutters or shutters as specified; often used in combination.

European medic naturalized in North America having yellow flowers and sickle-shaped pods.

definition: A ring bearing a signet.
A sturdy twill-weave cotton fabric; used for pockets and linings.

example: Dogs were heard howling and there was a rustle in the silver wattle.

definition: Having silvery leaves.
Expressing yourself readily, clearly, effectively.

definition: Having silvery leaves.

definition: Relating to or resembling an ape.
example: Simian features.
etymology: From Latin sīmia (“ape, monkey”), from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “snub-nosed”).

definition: A preposition consisting of a single word.
example: In the English language we have approximately 70 simple prepositions.

definition: A broadcast that is carried simultaneously by radio and television (or by FM and AM radio).
etymology: From simul(taneous) + -cast, from broadcast.

definition: Having one barrel.
example: Most guns are single-barreled.

definition: Having single beds.
Having a single cell (and thus not divided into cells).
A collarless men's undergarment for the upper part of the body.
etymology: From single + -let.

definition: One by one; one at a time.
example: They were arranged singly.
etymology: From Middle English senglely. Equivalent to single + -ly.

definition: A small ring-shaped friedcake.

definition: Curved or curving in and out.

A long pin for holding meat in position while it is being roasted.

Any of various small boats propelled by oars or by sails or by a motor.

definition: The sport of riding on a sled or sleigh.
A very sleepy state.
example: Sleepiness causes many driving accidents.
etymology: From sleepy + -ness.

definition: Walking by a person who is asleep.
Any of several small slim salamanders of the Pacific coast of the United States.
Having a small waist.
A detective who follows a trail.
etymology: Clipping of sleuthhound.

definition: A golfer whose shots typically curve right (for right-handed golfers).
etymology: From slice + -er.

definition: A fastener for locking together two toothed edges by means of a sliding tab.
Having a small waist.
A knot at the end of a cord or rope that can slip along the cord or rope around which it is made.
A decrease of transmitted power in a mechanical system caused by slipping.
example: Supply-chain problems led to a slippage in production last week.
etymology: From slip + -age.

definition: The flow of air that is driven backwards by an aircraft propeller.
etymology: Compound of slip + stream. Fiction sense coined by cyberpunk author Bruce Sterling in 1989.

definition: To pass or move unobtrusively or smoothly.
A bowl into which the dregs of teacups and coffee cups are emptied at the table.
Commissary maintained aboard merchant ships to sell merchandise to the crew.
A large pail used to receive waste water from a washbasin or chamber pot.
A dealer in cheap ready-made clothing.
An incompetent person; usually used in negative constructions.
example: He's no slouch when it comes to baseball.
etymology: Unclear. Perhaps from Middle English slugge, from Old Norse slókr (“lazy fellow”). See also Swedish sloka (“to slouch, wilt”), related to Swedish slak (“slack, soft and flexible”) and Latin laxus (“loose, slack”).

definition: A soft felt hat with a wide flexible brim.
Unskillfulness resulting from a lack of training.
etymology: From slow + -ness.

definition: Pour as if from a sluice.
example: An aggressive tide sluiced across the barrier reef.

definition: Pour as if from a sluice.
example: An aggressive tide sluiced across the barrier reef.

definition: Regulator consisting of a valve or gate that controls the rate of water flow through a sluice.
Eat noisily.
example: He slurped his soup.
etymology: From Middle Dutch slurpen, slorpen (“to sip, slurp”), from Old Dutch *slurpan, from Proto-West Germanic *slurp- (“to sip, slurp”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ-, *srobʰ- (“to sip, slurp, gulp”).

definition: Spoken as if with a thick tongue.
example: His words were slurred.

definition: Rather small.
etymology: From Middle English smalish, equivalent to small + -ish.

definition: A small number or amount.
example: She knows a smattering of Greek, but not enough to carry on a conversation.
etymology: From smatter + -ing.

definition: A workplace where metal is worked by heating and hammering.
example: Traditionally a village smithy was a busy place because the smith's work was so necessary.
etymology: From Middle English smythy, from Old Norse smiðja, from Proto-Germanic *smiþjǭ. Cognate with Old English smiþþe (whence the obsolete modern doublet smithe, smythe (“the workshop of a smith, forge”)).

definition: A loose coverall (coat or frock) reaching down to the ankles.
etymology: From Middle English smok, from Old English smocc, smoc, from Proto-Germanic *smukkaz (“something slipped into”).

definition: Emitting or containing little or no smoke.
example: Smokeless factory stacks.
etymology: From smoke + -less.

definition: An explosive (trade name Ballistite) that burns with relatively little smoke; contains pyrocellulose and is used as a propellant.
(military) screen consisting of a cloud of smoke that obscures movements.
example: All that talk is just a smokescreen to disguise the fact that he has nothing to say.
etymology: From smoke + screen.

definition: Fished for the hides and vitamin-rich liver.
Artfully persuasive in speech.
example: A smooth-tongued hypocrite.

definition: Causing difficulty in breathing especially through lack of fresh air and presence of heat.
example: The smothering soft voices.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English smorþering.

definition: Snarled or stalled in complete confusion.
A performer who uses movements and music to control snakes.
A fastener used on clothing; fastens with a snapping sound.
example: Children can manage snaps better than buttons.

definition: A garden plant of the genus Antirrhinum having showy white or yellow or crimson flowers resembling the face of a dragon.
etymology: (1570s) From snap + dragon, from a fancied resemblance, especially by playing children that the flower is a dragon that opens its "mouth" when squeezed on the sides.

definition: Utter in an angry, sharp, or abrupt tone.
example: The guard snarled at us.
etymology: From Middle English snarlen, frequentative of snaren (“to trap, tangle”). Equivalent to snare + -le.

definition: Make more complicated or confused through entanglements.
A number of vehicles blocking one another until they can scarcely move.
Tangled in knots or snarls.
example: Snarled thread.

definition: Flashily stylish.
example: A snazzy outfit.
etymology: Origin unknown; the following etymologies have been suggested: * A blend of sna(ppy) + (ja)zzy. * From Irish snas (“finish, polish;

definition: A person who sniffs.
etymology: From sniff + -er.

definition: The trait of condescending to those of lower social status.
etymology: From snob + -ery (noun-forming suffix).

definition: Befitting or characteristic of those who incline to social exclusiveness and who rebuff the advances of people considered inferior.
etymology: From snob + -ish.

definition: Befitting or characteristic of those who incline to social exclusiveness and who rebuff the advances of people considered inferior.
example: His tastes are snobby.
etymology: From snob + -y.

definition: (used colloquially) overly conceited or arrogant.
example: Sir Sydney was an arrogant, snooty, bigoted prig, so it was with some satisfaction that I wrote out his parking ticket.
etymology: The adjective is derived from snoot (“(UK, dialectal, and slang) snout;

definition: Breathing device consisting of a bent tube fitting into a swimmer's mouth and extending above the surface; allows swimmer to breathe while face down in the water.
example: They wore snorkels while exploring the coral reef.
etymology: Borrowed from German Schnorchel (“(submarine) snorkel”), related to schnarchen (“to snore”). Thus named because of the submarine snorkel's functional similarity to a nose and because of its noise when in use.

definition: Air passage provided by a retractable device containing intake and exhaust pipes; permits a submarine to stay submerged for extended periods of time.
Skin diving with a snorkel.
Skin diving with a snorkel.
(used colloquially) overly conceited or arrogant.
example: A snotty little scion of a degenerate family.
etymology: From snot + -y.
