definition: Someone who slides down snow-covered slopes while standing on a snowboard.
etymology: From snowboard + -er.

definition: Having a blunt nose.
example: A snub-nosed automatic.

definition: Drawn or pressed close to someone or something for or as if for affection or protection.
example: Like a baby snuggled in its mother's arms.

definition: Fitting closely.
example: The vest fit snugly.
etymology: From snug + -ly.

definition: Take part in social activities; interact with others.
example: He never socializes with his colleagues.
etymology: From social + -ise.

definition: The act of meeting for social purposes.
example: There was too much socialization with the enlisted men.

definition: Of or relating to a sociopathic personality disorder.
etymology: From socio- + -pathic.

definition: A white soluble compound (NaHCO3) used in effervescent drinks and in baking powders and as an antacid.
A flammable grey crystalline binary compound (NaH).
A crystalline salt used like potassium iodide.
Nitrite used to preserve and color food especially in meat and fish products; implicated in the formation of suspected carcinogens.
A viscous glass consisting of sodium silicate in solution; used as a cement or as a protective coating and to preserve eggs.
A solid white bitter salt used in manufacturing glass and paper and dyes and pharmaceuticals.
A substance added to another to make it less hard.
etymology: From Middle English softener, equivalent to soften + -er.

definition: The process of modifying a software system to make some aspect of it work more efficiently or use fewer resources.
Medium-sized five-needled pine of southwestern California having long cylindrical cones.
A trait of dignified seriousness.
example: The solemnity of a funeral.
etymology: From solemn + -ity, from Middle English solemnity (“observance of formality and ceremony”), frequently in the phrases in solemnity, with solemnity, which from Old French solemnite, from Latin sollemnitās, from sollemnis.

definition: A coil of wire around an iron core; becomes a magnet when current passes through the coil.
etymology: From French solénoïde, from Ancient Greek σωληνοειδής (sōlēnoeidḗs) (from σωλήν (sōlḗn, “channel, pipe”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs); see -oid).

definition: The process of becoming hard or solid by cooling or drying or crystallization.
The consistency of a solid.
etymology: From solid + -ity, from Middle French solidité, from Latin soliditās.

definition: A person who is a respected leader in national or international affairs.
etymology: From Ancient Greek Σόλων (Sólōn), the name of an influential Athenian statesman.

definition: The dissolved matter in a solution; the component of a solution that changes its state.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin solutus, past participle of solvo.

definition: Capable of being solved.
example: Such problems are perfectly solvable.
etymology: From solve + -able. Piecewise doublet of soluble.

definition: The ability to meet maturing obligations as they come due.
etymology: From solvent + -cy.

definition: The difference between the assets and liabilities of a given insurance company (the amount of assets exceeding liabilities), regulated by law.
A straw hat with a tall crown and broad brim; worn in American southwest and in Mexico.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish sombrero (“hat”), from sombra (“shadow, shade”) + -ero, literally, "shade-maker". The drink was named after the hat.

definition: Any bird having a musical call.
etymology: From song + bird.

definition: A book containing a collection of songs.
example: The great American songbook.
etymology: From Middle English song boke, from Old English sangbōc (“a music book; songbook”), equivalent to song + book.

definition: Of the blackest black; similar to the color of jet or coal.
etymology: From Middle English sooty, soty, equivalent to soot + -y. Probably influenced by similar Middle English suti (“dirty, filthy”), derived from the same root as Old English besūtian (“to befoul”).

definition: Of the black color of soot.
An ice containing no milk but having a mushy consistency; usually made from fruit juice.
example: After dinner we had an orange sorbet that was very refreshing.
etymology: Doublet of sherbet and sharbat, related to syrup.

definition: Made from juice of sweet sorghum.
Any plant or flower of the genus Oxalis.
etymology: From Middle English sorel, from Old French sorel, surele (“sorrel”), from Old French sur (“sour”), of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sūraz (“sour”); equivalent to sour + -el (diminutive suffix).

definition: Deciduous shrubby tree of eastern North America having deeply fissured bark and sprays of small fragrant white flowers and sour-tasting leaves.
Experiencing or marked by or expressing sorrow especially that associated with irreparable loss.
example: Sorrowful widows.
etymology: From Middle English sorweful, from Old English sorhful, sorgful (“full of care; anxious; sorrowful”), from Proto-Germanic *surgafullaz (“full of care; anxious”), equivalent to sorrow + -ful.

definition: A military action in which besieged troops burst forth from their position.
etymology: PIE word *upó The noun is borrowed from French sortie (“act of exiting; exit, way out;

definition: A state or condition free from damage or decay.
etymology: From Middle English soundenes, soundnes, from Old English *sundnes, *ġesundnes (attested in onsundnes), from Proto-West Germanic *sundnassī (“soundness, health”); equivalent to sound + -ness.

definition: A ladle for serving soup.
Slang for a mustache.
A baseball pitcher who throws the ball with the left hand.
example: Since home plate is generally in the southwest corner to avoid glare in the batter's eyes, a southpaw's pitching hand is to the south.
etymology: From south + paw. The original derivation is unclear: although now best known from the sport of baseball, the term is first attested in 1813, before baseball was founded.

definition: Toward the south.
example: The ship turned southerly.
etymology: From south + -wards.

definition: Erect bushy hairy annual herb having trifoliate leaves and purple to pink flowers; extensively cultivated for food and forage and soil improvement but especially for its nutritious oil-rich seeds; native to Asia.
etymology: Borrowed from Dutch soja;

definition: A source of oil; used for forage and soil improvement and as food.
etymology: From soya + bean.

definition: A milk substitute containing soybean flour and water; used in some infant formulas and in making tofu.
A hand tool that is used to hold or twist a nut or bolt.
etymology: From span + -er.

definition: A buoy resembling a vertical log.
Recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhea (often alternating with periods of constipation); often associated with emotional stress.
A loss or deficiency of motor control with involuntary spasms caused by permanent brain damage present at birth.
(of a female animal) having the ovaries removed.
(during prohibition) an illegal barroom.
etymology: Deverbal from speak easy (= speak quietly [interj.]); for the history, see Wikipedia at speakeasy § Etymology.

definition: (biology) the structural adaptation of some body part for a particular function.
etymology: From specialise + -ation.

definition: The evolution of a biological species.
Common shrub of Canada and northeastern United States having shoots scattered with rust-colored down.
Markings vary but usually harmonize with background; of southwestern Arizona and Baja California.
A fast motorboat.
etymology: From speed + boat.

definition: A meter fixed to a vehicle that measures and displays its speed.
etymology: From speed + -o- + -meter; by surface analysis, speed + -ometer.

definition: Having your attention fixated as though by a spell.
example: The story left the children spellbound.
etymology: From spell + bound.

definition: (mathematics) the trigonometry of spherical triangles.
Replay (as a melody).
etymology: Borrowed from German Spiel (“game, performance”) or Yiddish שפּיל (shpil), both from Middle High German spil, from Old High German spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil. Cognate with Old English spilian (“to revel, play”).

definition: Recite volubly or extravagantly.
An attacker who sheds or spills blood.
example: A great hunter and spiller of blood.
etymology: From Middle English spiller, from spill + -er.

definition: (economics) any indirect effect of public expenditure.
example: The spillover from the dam due to the heavy rains will run down this channel and harmlessly dump into that river, we hope.
etymology: From spill + over.

definition: A channel that carries excess water over or around a dam or other obstruction.
etymology: From spill + way.

definition: Anesthesia of the lower half of the body; caused by injury to the spinal cord or by injecting an anesthetic beneath the arachnoid membrane that surrounds the spinal cord.
Having spines.
etymology: From spine + -y.

definition: Desert lizard that feeds on ants.
Warm-water lobsters without claws; those from Australia and South Africa usually marketed as frozen tails; caught also in Florida and California.
Having the back covered with spines.
Having a spiny border.
Having a spiny stem.
(theology) any doctrine that asserts the separate existence of God.
etymology: From spiritual + -ism. In Allan Kardec's book The Spirits Book (1857) (Le Livre des Esprits in the original French), in which a distinction between spiritism and spiritualism is defined.

definition: Any of various stocky heavy-coated breeds of dogs native to northern regions having pointed muzzles and erect ears with a curled furry tail.
etymology: From German Spitz, from spitz (“pointed”); so called from the tapering shape of its muzzle.

definition: Give off the sound of a bullet flattening on impact.
example: The egg splatted onto the floor.
etymology: From earlier splat (“to spread flat”), from Middle English splatten, splaten (“to stretch out, extend", also "to split”). Compare dialectal English splat (“flat”).

definition: Covered with bright patches (often used in combination).
example: Kitchen walls splattered with grease.

definition: Wonderfully.
example: He did splendidly in the exam.
etymology: From splendid + -ly.

definition: A thin sliver of wood.
example: He lit the fire with a burning splint.
etymology: From Middle English splint, splent, splente, from Middle Low German splinte, splente or Middle Dutch splint, splinte. Cognate with Old High German splinza (“bar, bolt, latch”).

definition: A rudimentary metacarpal or metatarsal bone on either side of the cannon bone in the leg of a horse or related animal.
An infinitive with an adverb between ‘to’ and the verb (e.g., ‘to boldly go’).
An edible and choice morel with a globular to elongate head with an irregular pattern of pits and ridges.
Easily squashed; resembling a sponge in having soft porous texture and compressibility.
example: Spongy bread.
etymology: From spong(e) + -y.

definition: Glossy black North American salamander with yellow spots.
A worker who applies spray to a surface.
example: Graffiti often includes the sprayer’s name.
etymology: From spray + -er.

definition: A hand tool for spreading something.
example: He used his knife as a spreader.
etymology: From spread + -er.

definition: A below-the-hook beam used for lifting, fitted with a number of ropes at different points along its length.
A South African gazelle noted for springing lightly into the air.
etymology: Borrowed from Afrikaans springbok, from Dutch springbok, from springen (“to jump, spring”) + bok (“buck, billy goat, antelope”).

definition: Roller that has teeth on the rims to pull film or paper through.
example: Suppose we have a widget factory that produces 100 widgets per year, and a sprocket factory that produces 200 sprockets per year.
etymology: Unknown. First attested in the 16th century. Perhaps related to Italian rocchetto (“spool”), spoletta (“spool”), sprone (“spur”), or English spoke, spike, spur.

definition: Thin wheel with teeth that engage with a chain.
Moving quickly and lightly.
example: The old dog was so spry it was halfway up the stairs before we could stop it.
etymology: From British dialectal sprey, from Old Norse sprækr (“nimble, lively”) from Proto-Germanic *sprēkiz (“lively”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)preg- (“to strew, jerk, sprinkle, scatter”).

definition: An edible tuber native to South America; a staple food of Ireland.
etymology: From Middle English spudde (“small knife”). Origin unknown; probably related to Danish spyd, Old Norse spjót (“spear”), German Spieß (“spear; spike; skewer”). Compare English spit (“sharp, pointed rod”).

definition: Showing courage.
etymology: From spunk + -y.

definition: Rebuffed (by a lover) without warning.
A verbalization that encourages you to attempt something.
Computer software that obtains information from a user's computer without the user's knowledge or consent.
etymology: From spy + -ware.

definition: A quarrel about petty points.
example: The children got into a squabble about who should ride in the front of the car.
etymology: The noun form first appears c. 1602, while the verbal form first appears c. 1616. Probably of North Germanic origin and ultimately imitative.

definition: Morally degraded.
example: The squalid atmosphere of intrigue and betrayal.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin squālidus, from squālēre (“to be rough or dirty”).

definition: Make high-pitched, whiney noises.
etymology: From Middle English *squalen and squelen (“to cry, scream, squall”), from Old Norse skvala (“to cry out”), probably ultimately imitative with influence from squeal and bawl.

definition: A cold front along which squalls or thunderstorms are likely.
Sordid dirtiness.
etymology: From the Latin squālor.

definition: An epithelial cell that is flat like a plate and form a single layer of epithelial tissue.
Spend thoughtlessly; throw away.
example: You squandered the opportunity to get an advanced degree.
etymology: Earliest uses (late 16th c.) "to spend recklessly or prodigiously", also "to scatter over a wide area". Of unknown origin. Perhaps a blend of scatter + wander.

definition: Having a relatively square jaw.
A game played in an enclosed court by two or four players who strike the ball with long-handled rackets.
A small racket with a long handle used for playing squash.
Someone who settles lawfully on government land with the intent to acquire title to it.
etymology: From squat + -er.

definition: Corn having kernels almost entirely of soft starch.
Plant of western North America having woody rhizomes and tufts of stiff grasslike basal leaves and spikes of creamy white flowers.
Tall herb of eastern North America and Asia having blue berrylike fruit and a thick knotty rootstock formerly used medicinally.
Deciduous shrub of California with unpleasantly scented usually trifoliate leaves and edible fruit.
Having or making a high-pitched sound such as that made by a mouse or a rusty hinge.
Having or making a high-pitched sound such as that made by a mouse or a rusty hinge.
Excessively fastidious and easily disgusted.
example: So squeamish he would only touch the toilet handle with his elbow.
etymology: Origin obscure. Likely a merger of earlier squeamous (“squeamish”), from Middle English squaimous, queimous, from Anglo-Norman escoimus, escoymous, of unknown origin;

definition: Having eyes half closed in order to see better.
example: Squinched eyes.

definition: Mediterranean vine having oblong fruit that when ripe expels its seeds and juice violently when touched.
etymology: So named because when the fruit is fully ripe it squirts a stream of mucilaginous liquid containing its seeds.

definition: The act of making something (as a vessel or aircraft) less likely to overturn.
Support or hold steady and make steadfast, with or as if with a brace.
etymology: From stable + -ise.

definition: Made stable or firm.
(music) marked by or composed of disconnected parts or sounds; cut short crisply.
example: Staccato applause.

definition: Hypoxia resulting from slow peripheral circulation (such as follows congestive cardiac failure).
example: Low cardiac output due to heart failure can lead to stagnant hypoxia.

definition: Characterized by dignity and propriety.
etymology: From an obsolete spelling of stayed, the past participle of stay, used as an adjective.

definition: The condition in which a standard has been successfully established.
example: Standardization of nuts and bolts had saved industry millions of dollars.
etymology: From standardise + -ation.

definition: Cause to conform to standard or norm.
example: The weights and measures were standardized.
etymology: From standard + -ize.

definition: Spherical Gram-positive parasitic bacteria that tend to form irregular colonies; some cause boils or septicemia or infections.
etymology: Shortening of staphylococcus.

definition: Spherical Gram-positive parasitic bacteria that tend to form irregular colonies; some cause boils or septicemia or infections.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Staphylococcus. By surface analysis, staphylo- + -coccus.

definition: A machine that inserts staples into sheets of paper in order to fasten them together.
etymology: From staple (verb) + -er.

definition: Small tree of China and Vietnam bearing anise-scented star-shaped fruit used in food and medicinally as a carminative.
Foodstuff rich in natural starch (especially potatoes, rice, bread).
Consisting of or containing starch.
example: Starchy foods.
etymology: From starch + -y.

definition: In a stark manner.
example: He was starkly unable to achieve coherence.
etymology: From Middle English starkli, starcliche, sterkliche, stercliche, from Old English stearclīċe (“strongly; stoutly; vigorously; vehemently; fiercely; strictly”), from Proto-Germanic *starkulīka (“strongly;

definition: A young (film) actress who is publicized as a future star.
etymology: From star + -let.

definition: To stimulate to action.
example: The loud noise startled him awake.
etymology: From Middle English startlen (“to rush, jump”), from Old English steartlian (“to kick with the foot, struggle, stumble”), equivalent to start + -le.

definition: A complicated involuntary reaction to a sudden unexpected stimulus (especially a loud noise); involves flexion of most skeletal muscles and a variety of visceral reactions.
A normal reflex of young infants; a sudden loud noise causes the child to stretch out the arms and flex the legs.
A complicated involuntary reaction to a sudden unexpected stimulus (especially a loud noise); involves flexion of most skeletal muscles and a variety of visceral reactions.
A variety of aster (Symphyotrichum lateriflorum).
A medicine that lowers blood cholesterol levels by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase.
etymology: From the suffix -statin, which was used for inhibiting hormone names before it was used for HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor drug names (but, like statin, has since become much better known in the latter sense).

definition: A medicine that lowers blood cholesterol levels by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase.
Mechanical device consisting of the stationary part of a motor or generator in or around which the rotor revolves.
etymology: From stationary or static by analogy with rotor; alternatively from a hypothetical Latin stātor (literally “stander”); all ultimately from stāre (“to stand”).

definition: Mechanical device consisting of the stationary part of a motor or generator in or around which the rotor revolves.
Of or relating to or suitable for statues.
etymology: From Latin statuāria (ars) (“(art) of sculpture”), feminine of the adjective statuārius (“of statues”).

definition: A small carved or molded figure.
etymology: Borrowed from French statuette, from statue f + -ette (feminine of the diminutive suffix -et). By surface analysis, statue + -ette (diminutive suffix).

definition: In a staunch manner.
example: He staunchly defended his principles.
etymology: From staunch + -ly.

definition: With resolute determination.
example: He steadfastly refuses to go out with her.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English stedefastly, stedefastliche; equivalent to steadfast + -ly.

definition: A criminal who takes property belonging to someone else with the intention of keeping it or selling it.
example: A child-stealer.
etymology: From Middle English stelere, equivalent to steal + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Steler (“thief”), West Frisian steller, stelder (“stealer”), Dutch steler (“stealer, thief”), Danish stjæler (“stealer”).

definition: In a stealthy manner.
example: Stealthily they advanced upstream.
etymology: From stealthy + -ly.

definition: A tall tower that forms the superstructure of a building (usually a church or temple) and that tapers to a point at the top.
A footrace of usually 3000 meters over a closed track with hurdles and a water jump.
etymology: Compound of steeple + chase, from horse races in 18th century Ireland in which orientation of the course was by reference to a church steeple.

definition: Capturing a steer with a lasso.
A watch that is wound by turning a knob at the stem.
etymology: US, mid-late 19th century, originally referring to then-recent stem-wind watches (invented in 1840s, commercialized initially 1850s by Patek Philippe & Co.).

definition: Of or relating to a stereoscope.
example: Stereoscopic lenses.

definition: Two photographs taken from slightly different angles that appear three-dimensional when viewed together.
Three-dimensional vision produced by the fusion of two slightly different views of a scene on each retina.
(of non-living objects) the state of being free of pathogenic organisms.
etymology: From Middle English sterylite, sterylyte, from Latin sterilitās. By surface analysis, sterile + -ity.

definition: Make free from bacteria.
etymology: From sterile + -ize.

definition: With sternness; in a severe manner.
example: ‘No,’ she said sternly.
etymology: From Middle English sternly, sternely, sterneliche, sturnely, sturneliche, from Old English stirnlīċe, styrnlīċe, stiernlīċe (“harshly; severely; sternly”), equivalent to stern + -ly.

definition: A medical instrument for listening to the sounds generated inside the body.
etymology: Borrowed from French stéthoscope, a word coined by its inventor, physician René Laennec, equivalent to stetho- + -scope.

definition: Any plant of the genus Stevia or the closely related genus Piqueria having glutinous foliage and white or purplish flowers; Central and South America.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Stevia, after 16th century Spanish botanist Pedro Jaime Esteve (latinized as Petrus Jacobus Stevus).

definition: A woman steward on an airplane.
etymology: From steward + -ess (feminine suffix).

definition: Cooked in hot water.
etymology: From stew + -ed.

definition: Someone who insists on something.
example: A stickler for promptness.
etymology: From Middle English stighteler, stytelere, equivalent to stickle + -er. The judges at Cornish wrestling matches do indeed carry sticks which serve for signalling and as a badge of their office.

definition: Geranium of western North America having pinkish-purple flowers in open clusters.
A small dagger with a tapered blade.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Italian stiletto. By surface analysis, stilus + Italian -etto. Doublet of stilet and stylet.

definition: A very high narrow heel on women's shoes.
Failing to accomplish an intended result.
example: A stillborn plot to assassinate the President.
etymology: From English still + born. First attested in 1597.

definition: Infant who shows no signs of life after birth.
Artificially formal.
example: A stilted letter of acknowledgment.
etymology: From stilt + -ed.

definition: Perennial Eurasian nettle established in North America having broad coarsely toothed leaves with copious stinging hairs.
Disease of wheat characterized by replacement of the grains with greasy masses of smelly smut spores.
Rare small evergreen of northern Florida; its glossy green leaves have an unpleasant fetid smell when crushed.
Supporting stalk or stem-like structure especially of a pistil or fern frond or supporting a mushroom cap.
etymology: From French stipe, from Latin stīpes (“a stock, post, branch”).

definition: A corporation's purchase of its own outstanding stock; increases earnings/share so stock price rises (which can discourage a takeover attempt).
Fortification consisting of a fence made of a line of stout posts set firmly for defense.
etymology: From French estocade, equivalent to stock + -ade.

definition: Someone who holds shares of stock in a corporation.
example: Zumbeco are stockholders of round bar, flat bar and plate.
etymology: From stock + holder.

definition: Male farmer who breed or raises livestock.
etymology: From stock + -man.

definition: Accumulating and storing a reserve supply.
example: The stockpiling of war materials.

definition: Having a short and solid form or stature.
example: Stocky legs.
etymology: From stock + -y.

definition: An indifference to pleasure or pain.
etymology: From Latin stōicismus. By surface analysis, stoic + -ism. First attested in the 1620s.

definition: European trailing bramble with red berrylike fruits.
Ceramic ware that is fired in high heat and vitrified and nonporous.
etymology: From stone + -ware.

definition: Masonry done with stone.
etymology: From Middle English stonewerk, stonwerk, ston-werke, stoonwerk, from Old English stānweorc; equivalent to stone + -work.

definition: Cruise in slow or routine flights.
etymology: Perhaps an abbreviation of Russian студе́нт (studént) [stʊˈdʲent]; the original meaning was “stage assistant, actor who assists a comedian”. It may have been a Yiddish vaudeville term.

definition: Having the back and shoulders rounded; not erect.
example: A little oldish misshapen stooping woman.

definition: A stopping place on a journey.
example: There is a stopover to change planes in Chicago.
etymology: Deverbal from stop over.

definition: A timepiece that can be started or stopped for exact timing (as of a race).
etymology: From stop + watch.

definition: A depository for goods.
example: Storehouses were built close to the docks.
etymology: From store + house.

definition: A room in which things are stored.
etymology: From store + room.

definition: A system of watercourses or drains for carrying off excess water.
The dried stalks and leaves of a field crop (especially corn) used as animal fodder after the grain has been harvested.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman estovers (“necessities”) via Middle English estover (“allowance”), ultimately from Latin est opus (“there is need”). Compare estover.

definition: A person who hides aboard a ship or plane in the hope of getting free passage.
etymology: From stow away, from stow and away.

definition: Performed with little or no delay.
example: A straightaway denial.

definition: A filter to retain larger pieces while smaller pieces and liquids pass through.
etymology: From Middle English strener, streynour, strenyour, equivalent to strain + -er.

definition: Any of several tropical annual climbers having large yellow flowers and edible young fruits; grown commercially for the mature fruit's dried fibrous interior that is used as a sponge.
Unusualness as a consequence of not being well known.
etymology: From Middle English straungenesse; equivalent to strange + -ness.

definition: Complete power over a person or situation.
example: Corporations have a stranglehold on the media.
etymology: From strangle + hold.

definition: Having no straps.
example: A strapless evening gown.
etymology: From strap + -less. The noun sense is by analogy of strap-on.

definition: The population is divided into subpopulations (strata) and random samples are taken of each stratum.
The branch of geology that studies the arrangement and succession of strata.
etymology: From stratum + -graphy c. 1841–1865.

definition: One of several parallel layers of material arranged one on top of another (such as a layer of tissue or cells in an organism or a layer of sedimentary rock).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin strātum (“a spread for a bed, coverlet, quilt, blanket; a pillow, bolster; a bed”), neuter singular of strātus, perfect passive participle of sternō (“spread”). Doublet of estrade and street.

definition: Eastern Asiatic saxifrage with racemes of small red-and-white flowers; spreads by numerous creeping stolons.
Small tropical shrubby tree bearing small yellowish fruit.
Unable to find your way.
example: Found the straying sheep.

definition: In a strenuous manner; strongly or vigorously.
example: He objected strenuously to the stand his party was taking.
etymology: From strenuous + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to or caused by streptococci.
etymology: Clipping of streptococcus.

definition: An infection of the oral pharynx and tonsils by streptococcus.
Spherical Gram-positive bacteria occurring in pairs or chains; cause e.g. scarlet fever and tonsillitis.
etymology: Morphologically a compound of strepto- + -coccus. They grow in chains or pairs, thus the name — from Ancient Greek στρεπτός (streptós, “twisted, pliant”), like a chain. Compare the genus name Streptococcus.

definition: A person who walks rapidly with long steps.
example: He was such a strider that she couldn't keep up without running.
etymology: From stride + -er. Compare Dutch strijder (“fighter”).

definition: A musical instrument in which taut strings provide the source of sound.
Lean and sinewy.
example: The meat was quite stringy.
etymology: From string + -y.

definition: Maple of eastern North America with striped bark and large two-lobed leaves clear yellow in autumn.
Of northern Africa and Arabia and India.
A soft silver-white or yellowish metallic element of the alkali metal group; turns yellow in air; occurs in celestite and strontianite.
etymology: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1808, after the earlier term strontianite, for the name of the Scottish town Strontian.

definition: Short and blunt.
example: Stubby fingers.
etymology: From stub + -y.

definition: Marked by care and effort.
example: Made a studious attempt to fix the television set.
etymology: From Latin studiōsus. First recorded in English c. 1350.

definition: A sharp hand shovel for digging out roots and weeds.
The performance of stunts while in flight in an aircraft.
The feeling of distress and disbelief that you have when something bad happens accidentally.
example: He fell into a drunken stupor.
etymology: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin stupor (“insensibility, numbness, dullness”). Distantly related (from Proto-Indo-European, via Proto-Germanic) to stint, stub, and steep.

definition: Using artistic forms and conventions to create effects; not natural or spontaneous.
example: A stylized mode of theater production.

definition: In a rhetorically stylistic manner.
example: Stylistically complex.
etymology: From stylistic + -ally.

definition: A colorless oily liquid; the monomer for polystyrene.
etymology: From Latin styrax (or storax) + -ene.

definition: Of or relating to constituents of the atom or forces within the atom.
example: Subatomic particles.
etymology: From sub- + atomic.

definition: A body having finite mass and internal structure but negligible dimensions.
Someone who enters into a subcontract with the primary contractor.
etymology: From sub- + contractor.

definition: (biology) a taxonomic category below a family.
etymology: From sub- + family.

definition: In a subjective way.
example: You cannot look at these facts subjectively.
etymology: From subjective + -ly.

definition: Reduced to submission.
example: Subjugated peoples.

definition: Forced submission to control by others.
etymology: From Latin subiugātiō, from Latin subiugō (“to subjugate”). By surface analysis, subjugate + -ion.

definition: Relating to a mood of verbs.
example: Subjunctive verb endings.
etymology: From Latin subiunctīvus (“serving to join, connecting, in grammar applies to the subjunctive mode”), from subiungō (“to add, join, subjoin”), from sub- (“under”) + iungō (“to join, yoke”). See join.

definition: A mood that represents an act or state (not as a fact but) as contingent or possible.
etymology: From subjunctive (from Latin subjunctivus, from sub- (“under”) + junctus (“joined”), perfect passive participle of jungere (“to join”) + adjective suffix -ivus) + mood (from Latin modus).

definition: (chemistry) a change directly from the solid to the gaseous state without becoming liquid.
etymology: From Middle English sublimacioun, sublimacion, from Medieval Latin sublīmātiō, from Latin sublīmō (“to raise, to elevate”, verb). Synchronically, sublimate + -ion.

definition: Sink below the surface; go under or as if under water.
example: The submarine submerged in the water.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin submergere, from sub (“under”) + mergere (“to plunge”). By surface analysis, sub- + merge.

definition: A warship designed to operate under water.
A set sequence of steps, part of larger computer program.
etymology: From sub- + routine.

definition: (computing) a collection of standard programs and subroutines that are stored and available for immediate use.
An abatement in intensity or degree (as in the manifestations of a disease).
etymology: Latin subsidens, subsidentis, present participle of subsidere. Equivalent to subside + -ence.

definition: Support oneself.
example: Many people in the world have to subsist on $1 a day.
etymology: From Latin subsistō (“halt, stop”), from sub (“below”) + sistō (“stand, place”). Compare consist, desist, exist, insist, persist.

definition: (of speed) less than that of sound in a designated medium.
example: Aircraft flying at subsonic speeds.
etymology: From sub- + sonic.

definition: Something intended to misrepresent the true nature of an activity.
example: He wasn't sick — it was just a subterfuge.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French subterfuge m, from Medieval Latin subterfugium n, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugiō (“to flee”).

definition: Wingless usually flattened bloodsucking insect parasitic on warm-blooded animals.
Whole young pig suitable for roasting.
A number puzzle in which the numbers 1 through 9 must be placed into a grid of cells so that each row or column contains only one of each number.
The froth produced by soaps or detergents.
example: We went out for some pizza and suds.
etymology: From the plural of sud, a variant of sod (“a bubbling or boiling”), equivalent to sud + -s. Related to seethe.

definition: A fabric used for suits.
Plant of moist highland meadows having ragged clusters of pale yellow flowers.
(H2SO4) a highly corrosive acid made from sulfur dioxide; widely used in the chemical industry.
A mood or display of sullen aloofness or withdrawal.
example: Stayed home in a sulk.
etymology: Back-formation from sulky, of uncertain origin. Probably from Middle English *sulke, *solke (attested in solcenesse (“idleness; laziness”), from Old English āsolcennys (“idleness; slothfulness; sluggishness;

definition: Showing a brooding ill humor.
example: A sullen crowd.
etymology: From Middle English soleyn, from Anglo-Norman soleyn (“alone”), from Old French sole (“single, sole, alone”), from Latin sōlus (“by oneself alone”).

definition: A salt or ester of sulphuric acid.
Be a summary of.
example: The abstract summarizes the main ideas in the paper.
etymology: From summary + -ise.

definition: Southern African herb with white bell-shaped flowers.
Belonging to or characteristic of or occurring in summer.
example: Summery weather.
etymology: From Middle English somery; equivalent to summer + -y. Compare Swedish somrig (“summery”).

definition: An oil reservoir in an internal combustion engine.
etymology: From Middle English sompe, either from Middle Dutch somp, sump or Middle Low German sump from Old Saxon *sump, from Proto-West Germanic *sump, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sumpaz. Doublet of swamp.

definition: A suction pump for removing liquid from a sump.
A ray of sunlight.
example: DOCTOR: You seem to be our best bet so far, don't you think so, Mel? Mel? Where's Mel? DEPUTY: No, no, no, sunbeam. You're coming with us.
etymology: From Middle English sonnebem, sonnebeem, from Old English sunnbēam, sunnebēam (“sunbeam”), equivalent to sun + beam.

definition: A sudden emergence of the sun from behind clouds.
etymology: From sun + burst.

definition: A cooler darker spot appearing periodically on the sun's photosphere; associated with a strong magnetic field.
etymology: From sun + spot.

definition: Compressor that forces increased oxygen into the cylinders of an internal-combustion engine.
etymology: From super- + charger.

definition: (geology) the deposition of one geological stratum on another.
etymology: From French superposition.

definition: Take the place or move into the position of.
example: Those older products have been superseded by our new range.
etymology: From Middle French superseder (“postpone, defer”), from Latin supersedēre, from super (“over”) + sedēre (“to sit”).

definition: A villain with superpowers.
etymology: From super- + villain.

definition: Take the place or move into the position of.
example: The computer has supplanted the slide rule.
etymology: From Middle English supplanten, supplaunten, from Old French supplanter, from Latin supplantō (“trip up”), from sub (“from below, under”) + planta (“sole”).

definition: A prayer asking God's help as part of a religious service.
etymology: From Middle English supplicacioun, supplication, from Old French supplication, from Latin supplicatio, supplicationem, from supplicare (“to supplicate”). By surface analysis, supplicate + -ion.

definition: A message expressing an opinion based on incomplete evidence.
etymology: From Middle English supposicioun, from Anglo-Norman supposicion, from Latin suppositiō, suppositiōnem (“supposition”), from sub- (“under”) + positiō, positiōnem (“position;

definition: One of the sections (or chapters) in the Koran.
example: The Quran is divided in 114 suras.
etymology: From Arabic سُورَة (sūra, “chapter of the Qur'an”).

definition: A chemical agent capable of reducing the surface tension of a liquid in which it is dissolved.
etymology: Blend of surface-active + agent.

definition: Infer from incomplete evidence.
example: If, as I surmise, you see the ladies this evening, you might mention my intended visit.
etymology: From Old French surmis, past participle of surmetre, surmettre (“to accuse”), from sur- (“upon”) + metre (“to put”).

definition: In a surreptitious manner.
example: He was watching her surreptitiously as she waited in the hotel lobby.
etymology: From surreptitious + -ly.

definition: Someone who tries to insure their personal survival or the survival of their group or nation.
etymology: From survival + -ist.

definition: Shrub growing in swamps throughout the eastern United States and having small white to pinkish flowers resembling honeysuckle.
Imposingly fashionable and elegant.
example: A swank apartment.

definition: Imposingly fashionable and elegant.
example: A swank apartment.
etymology: From swank + -y.

definition: Factory where workers do piecework for poor pay and are prevented from forming unions; common in the clothing industry.
etymology: From sweat (“to extract money, labour, etc.”, verb) + shop.

definition: Sweet dark amber variety.
Tropical American thorny shrub or small tree; fragrant yellow flowers used in making perfumery.
Wormwood of southeastern Europe to Iran.
Excessively hot and humid or marked by sweating and faintness.
example: A sweltering room.
etymology: From swelter + -ing.

definition: The act of turning aside suddenly.
example: The swervings of the stolen car.
etymology: From swerve + -ing.

definition: Strike heavily, especially with the fist or a bat.
example: That sailor can swig whisky with the best of 'em.
etymology: Unknown, mid 16th c. Perhaps connected with Old English swelgan (“to swallow”).

definition: The act of swindling by some fraudulent scheme.
A person who administers punishment by wielding a switch or whip.
example: Career switcher.
etymology: From switch + -er.

definition: Flesh of swordfish usually served as steaks.
etymology: From Middle English swerdfysche, from Old English *sweordfisċ. Equivalent to sword + fish.

definition: An insignificant student who is ridiculed as being affected or boringly studious.
example: All I want is — guerre fini, soldat fini; and to go home without burden of any thought save music, and hard swot for a time.
etymology: From a dialectal English word, from Middle English swot, swat, from Old English swāt (“perspiration; sweat”), from Proto-Germanic *swaitą (“sweat”). More at sweat.

definition: Study intensively, as before an exam.
The act of representing something with a symbol.
With respect to the sympathetic nervous system.
example: The stimulus acted sympathetically.
etymology: From sympathetical + -ly.

definition: Share the feelings of; understand the sentiments of.
etymology: Borrowed from French sympathiser. By surface analysis, sympathy + -ise.

definition: A system consisting of a generator and a motor so connected that the motor will assume the same relative position as the generator; the generator and the motor are synchronized.
etymology: Abbreviation of synchronization or synchronized.

definition: Operating in unison.
example: The synchronized flapping of a bird's wings.

definition: Make synchronous and adjust in time or manner.
example: Let's synchronize our efforts.
etymology: From Ancient Greek συγχρονίζω (sunkhronízō), equivalent to syn- + chrono- + -ize.

definition: Cyclotron in which the electric field is maintained at a constant frequency.
etymology: From synchro- + -tron.

definition: Used especially of drugs or muscles that work together so the total effect is greater than the sum of the two (or more).
etymology: From synergy + -istic.

definition: The science of systematic classification.
etymology: From systematic + -ics.

definition: Of or relating to a systole or happening during a systole.
example: A systolic compiler.
etymology: From systole + -ic.

definition: A murmur heard during systole.
The blood pressure (as measured by a sphygmomanometer) during the contraction of the left ventricle of the heart.
Very hot red peppers; usually long and thin; some very small.
example: Robbie adores it when Heather puts tabasco on food.
etymology: See Tabasco.

definition: Plant bearing very hot medium-sized oblong red peppers; grown principally in the Gulf Coast states for production of hot sauce.
etymology: See Tabasco.

definition: Plant bearing very hot medium-sized oblong red peppers; grown principally in the Gulf Coast states for production of hot sauce.
A covering spread over a dining table.
Articles for use at the table (dishes and silverware and glassware).
etymology: From table + -ware.

definition: Abnormally rapid heartbeat (over 100 beats per minute).
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin tachycardia, from Ancient Greek ταχύς (takhús, “swift”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”). By surface analysis, tachy- + -cardia. Compare French tachycardie.

definition: In a tacit manner; by unexpressed agreement.
example: They are tacitly expected to work 10 hours a day.
etymology: From tacit + -ly.

definition: A loose temporary sewing stitch to hold layers of fabric together.
Having or showing a sense of what is fitting and considerate in dealing with others.
example: She was tactful enough not to shatter his illusion.
etymology: From tact + -ful.

definition: A person who is skilled at planning tactics.
etymology: Borrowed from French tacticien, or from tactic + -ian.

definition: Shaped in the form of a tadpole.
An apple that is covered with a candy-like substance (usually caramelized sugar).
The act of following someone secretly.
The income or profit arising from such transactions as the sale of land or other property.
A fine grained mineral having a soft soapy feel and consisting of hydrated magnesium silicate; used in a variety of products including talcum powder.
etymology: From Middle French talc, from Arabic طَلْق (ṭalq), from Persian تلک (talk), from Middle Persian [Term?] (“medicament”).

definition: (Judaism) a shawl with a ritually knotted fringe at each corner; worn by Jews at morning prayer.
Long-lived tropical evergreen tree with a spreading crown and feathery evergreen foliage and fragrant flowers yielding hard yellowish wood and long pods with edible chocolate-colored acidic pulp.
etymology: From Late Middle English thamarynde, from Old French tamarinde, from Medieval Latin tamarindus, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ (tamr hindiyy, literally “Indian date”).

definition: Long-lived tropical evergreen tree with a spreading crown and feathery evergreen foliage and fragrant flowers yielding hard yellowish wood and long pods with edible chocolate-colored acidic pulp.
A shallow drum with a single drumhead and with metallic disks in the sides.
etymology: From French tambourin (“little drum”), from French tambour (“drum”). Ultimately from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr); see it and Persian تنبور for more.

definition: An animal trainer who tames wild animals.
etymology: From tame (verb) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).

definition: Of superficial relevance if any.
example: A tangential remark.
etymology: From tangent + -ial.

definition: Tasting sour like a lemon.
etymology: From tang + -y.

definition: Arousing desire or expectation for something unattainable or mockingly out of reach.
example: A tantalizing taste of success.

definition: Any of a fairly recent class of Hindu or Buddhist religious literature concerned with ritual acts of body and speech and mind.
etymology: From Sanskrit तन्त्र (tantra), from Proto-Indo-European *ten-tlo- /*tn̥-tlo-, from *ten- (“to stretch, extend”) with the suffix *-tlom denoting instruments. Doublet of tar (“string instrument”).

definition: Ribbonlike flatworms that are parasitic in the intestines of humans and other vertebrates.
etymology: From tape + worm.

definition: Intestinal infection by a species of parasitic tapeworm; usually the result of eating inadequately cooked meat or fish.
Granular preparation of cassava starch used to thicken especially puddings.
Sweet pudding thickened with tapioca.
A tavern keeper who taps kegs or casks.
etymology: From tap + -er.

definition: Large southern European spider once thought to be the cause of tarantism (uncontrollable bodily movement).
After the expected or usual time; delayed.
example: Tardy children are sent to the principal.
etymology: From an earlier tardive, from French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus (“slow”, “sluggish”), of obscure origin.

definition: A mountain lake (especially one formed by glaciers).
etymology: From Middle English terne, tarne (“lake;

definition: The part of the foot of a vertebrate between the metatarsus and the leg; in human beings the bones of the ankle and heel collectively.
Adornment consisting of a bunch of cords fastened at one end.
etymology: From Middle English tassel, from Old French tassel, from Latin tāxillus (“small cube”), from tālus (“ankle”).

definition: Tropical Asiatic annual cultivated for its small tassel-shaped heads of scarlet flowers.
Shaped like a tassel.
With taste; in a tasteful manner.
example: The house was tastefully decorated.
etymology: From tasteful + -ly.

definition: Someone who samples food or drink for its quality.
example: A flight of tasters was served to the people who would vote on the next soda flavor to be released.
etymology: From Middle English taster; equivalent to taste + -er.

definition: An edible tuber native to South America; a staple food of Ireland.
example: We ate them taters up real good.
etymology: Representing an aphetic pronunciation of potato. Compare patater (“potato”), 'mater (“tomato”), and 'naner (“banana”).

definition: The neutrino associated with the tau lepton.
Of something having a dusky brownish grey color.
etymology: Borrowed from French taupe, from Latin talpa (“mole”). Doublet of talpa.

definition: Reddish-brown European owl having a round head with black eyes.
Having a tawny color.
A car driven by a person whose job is to take passengers where they want to go in exchange for money.
etymology: Shortened from taximeter cab, equivalent to taxi + cab.

definition: The art of mounting the skins of animals so that they have lifelike appearance.
etymology: Borrowed from French taxidermie, from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”, “order”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Analysable as taxi- + derm- + -y.

definition: Animal or plant group having natural relations.
etymology: Back-formation from taxonomy. By surface analysis, taxo- + -on.

definition: A device to keep back tea leaves when pouring a cup of tea.
Ready and willing to be taught.
example: Teachable youngsters.
etymology: From Middle English techeable, techeabyll, techeabylle, equivalent to teach + -able.

definition: As much as a teacup will hold.
etymology: From tea + cup.

definition: Anything shaped like a falling drop (as a pendant gem on an earring).
example: Devin's teardrop landed on Cody's head.
etymology: From tear + drop.

definition: The small projection of a mammary gland.
etymology: From Middle English tete, from Old French tete (“teat”) (compare French tette), from Frankish *tittā, *tittō, from Proto-Germanic *tittaz (“teat; nipple; breast”), ultimately of expressive origin.

definition: A technician who is highly proficient and enthusiastic about some technical field (especially computing).
etymology: From tech + -ie (q.v.). Compare techy and yuppie.

definition: A trademarked method of making color motion pictures.
etymology: From Technicolor.

definition: The science of architecture.
etymology: Ancient Greek τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”).

definition: The feeling of being bored by something tedious.
etymology: From Latin taedium, from taedēre (“to weary”).

definition: Being of the age 13 through 19.
example: Teenage mothers.
etymology: From teen + aged.

definition: A public utility that provides telephone service.
etymology: Diachronically, from tel + Co., from the collocation of Tel. Co. as seen, for example, in Bell Tel. Co. or the names of countless local telephone exchange companies (e.g., Savannah Valley Tel. Co., Mutual Tel.

definition: A building that houses telecommunications equipment.
A photograph made with a telephoto lens.
etymology: From tele- + photo.

definition: A camera lens that magnifies the image.
Someone who reports news stories via television.
Any binary compound of tellurium with other more electropositive elements.
etymology: From tellurium + -ide.

definition: Moderating by making more temperate.
Any of the convolutions of the outer surface of the temporal lobe of the cerebrum.
One part in ten thousand equal parts.
etymology: From ten thousand + [Term?] (ordinal suffix).

definition: A city district known for its vice and high crime rate.
etymology: From tender + loin.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of nine and one; the base of the decimal system.
etymology: From ten + -er.

definition: A racket used to play tennis.
A musician who plays the tenor saxophone.
etymology: From tenor saxophone + -ist.

definition: Having inflections to indicate tense.
Something that acts like a tentacle in its ability to grasp and hold.
example: Caught in the tentacles of organized crime.
etymology: From New Latin tentāculum, from tentō. Doublet of tentaculum.

definition: Moderately warm.
example: Tepid bath water.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin tepidus. Cognate with Sanskrit तप् (tap), Proto-Slavic *teplъ.

definition: Beef or chicken or seafood marinated in spicy soy sauce and grilled or broiled.
example: Put some teriyaki on it.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 照(て)り焼(や)き (teriyaki).

definition: Small slender gull having narrow wings and a forked tail.
etymology: Via an East Anglian dialect, from some Scandinavian (North Germanic) language, related to Danish terne, Norwegian terne, and Swedish tärna, all from Old Norse þerna (“tern;

definition: Having three units or components or elements.
example: A ternary operation.
etymology: From Late Latin ternārius (“consisting of three things”), from ternī (“three each”).

definition: Brief and to the point; effectively cut short.
example: Short and terse and easy to understand.
etymology: From Latin tersus (“clean, cleansed, rubbed or wiped off; neat, spruce; terse”), perfect passive participle of Latin tergeō, tergō (“to clean, cleanse, rub, wipe, wipe off”).

definition: Protective outer layer of seeds of flowering plants.
example: The testa develops from the tissue, the integument, originally surrounding the ovule.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin testa.

definition: Easily irritated or annoyed.
example: He made testy remarks.
etymology: Middle English testif (“headstrong”), from Old French testu, from teste (“head”) + -u. Compare modern French tête (“head”), têtu (“stubborn”).

definition: Brightly colored tropical freshwater fishes.
etymology: From translingual Tetragonopterus, an obsolete genus that included these fish, ultimately from Ancient Greek τετράγωνος (tetrágōnos, “square, quadrilateral”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing, fin”).

definition: Not feeling or showing gratitude.
example: How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is / To have a thankless child!
etymology: From Middle English thankles, equivalent to thank + -less.

definition: Hair resembling thatched roofing material.
etymology: From Middle English thacchen, from Old English þeċċan, þeċċean (“to cover”), from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną (“to cover”), from Proto-Germanic *þaką (“cover, covering”, noun) (see above).

definition: Small palm of southern Florida and West Indies closely resembling the silvertop palmetto.
Small palm of southern Florida and West Indies closely resembling the silvertop palmetto.
No longer frozen solid.
example: The thawed ice was treacherous.

definition: The process whereby heat changes something from a solid to a liquid.
example: The thawing of a frozen turkey takes several hours.
etymology: From thaw + -ing.

definition: The doctrine or belief in the existence of a God or gods.
example: The term stands in contradistinction to theism which, in its widest sense, means belief in a personal god, goddess, gods and/or goddesses.
etymology: Coined, theo- + -ism. ultimately from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”). Attested in English from 1678, theist being attested 16 years earlier in 1662.

definition: Of or relating to theism.
etymology: From Ancient Greek.

definition: With regard to thematic content.
example: Thematically related.
etymology: From thematic + -ally.

definition: A political unit governed by a deity (or by officials thought to be divinely guided).
example: Tibet was a Buddhist theocracy ruled by the Dalai Lama prior to Chinese annexation.

definition: As regards theology.
example: The candidate was found theologically sound.
etymology: From theological + -ly.

definition: Concerned primarily with theories or hypotheses rather than practical considerations.
example: Theoretical science.
etymology: English theory + -etic, from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

definition: To believe especially on uncertain or tentative grounds.
etymology: From theory + -ize. First use appears c. 1599 in the text A pil to purge melancholie.

definition: Near that time or date.
example: Come at noon or thereabouts.
etymology: The adverb is derived from Middle English there-aboutes, þare aboutes (“of a place or an object: around there, in its vicinity;

definition: With that or this or it.
example: I have learned that whatever state I am, therewith to be content.
etymology: c. 1200, from Middle English therwith, from Old English þǣrwiþ (“therewith, in return, in exchange, against”), equivalent to there + with. Cognate with Danish derved (“therewith”), Swedish därvid (“therewith, thereby”).

definition: By means of heat or with respect to thermal properties.
etymology: From thermal + -ly.

definition: A nuclear fusion reaction taking place at very high temperatures (as in the sun).
A nuclear reactor that uses controlled nuclear fusion to generate energy.
The warhead of a missile designed to deliver an atom bomb.
Having the property of softening or fusing when heated and of hardening and becoming rigid again when cooled.
example: Thermoplastic materials can be remelted and cooled time after time without undergoing any appreciable chemical change.
etymology: From thermo- + plastic.

definition: A material that softens when heated and hardens again when cooled.
Vacuum flask that preserves temperature of hot or cold drinks.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θέρμος (thérmos).

definition: Vacuum flask that preserves temperature of hot or cold drinks.
Vacuum flask that preserves temperature of hot or cold drinks.
Make thick or thicker.
example: Thicken the sauce.
etymology: From Middle English thickenen, thikkenen, perhaps from Old Norse þykkna (“to thicken”); equivalent to thick + -en. Cognate with Swedish tjockna (“to thicken”), Icelandic þykkna (“to thicken”).

definition: A dense growth of bushes.
example: He had to complete a thicket of paperwork before he was allowed to join the company.
etymology: Compare typologically Bulgarian гъстак (găstak), Macedonian густеж (gustež), Czech houští, Polish gęstwina (< *gǫstъ); Latin dūmus (akin to Latin dense).

definition: Tending to form dense thickets.
Spoken with poor articulation as if with a thick tongue.
example: After a few drinks he was beginning to speak thickly.
etymology: From Middle English thikly; equivalent to thick + -ly.

definition: Densely populated.
The act of taking something from someone unlawfully.
example: The thieving is awful at Kennedy International.
etymology: From thieve + -ery. Compare Old Frisian deverie ("thievery; theft"; > West Frisian dieverij; Saterland Frisian Däiweräi), Dutch dieverij (“thievery”), German Low German Deveree (“thievery;

definition: Given to thievery.
As much as a thimble will hold.
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English thymbyll, thimel (“thimble”) [and other forms], from Old English þȳmel (“thimble, thumbstall;

definition: Shaped in the form of a thimble.
Mixed with water.
example: A cup of thinned soup.

definition: Shears with one serrate blade; used for thinning hair.
A narrow ventricle in the midplane below the corpus callosum; communicates with the fourth ventricle via the Sylvian aqueduct.
To or toward that place; away from the speaker.
example: The argument tended thither.
etymology: From Middle English thider, from Old English þider, an alteration (probably by analogy with hider (“hither”)) of earlier þæder (“to there”), from Proto-Germanic *þadrê.

definition: A branch of the descending aorta; divides into the iliac arteries.
One of 12 vertebrae in the human vertebral column; thoracic vertebrae extend from the seventh cervical vertebra down to the first lumbar vertebra.
Apparent communication from one mind to another without using sensory perceptions.
A calm, lengthy, intent consideration.
etymology: From thoughtful + -ness.

definition: Position 1,000 in a countable series of things.
etymology: From thousand + -th (suffix forming an ordinal number).

definition: A farm machine for separating seeds or grain from the husks and straw.
etymology: Originally a variant of thresher; equivalent to thrash + -er.

definition: (of a leaf shape) divided into three lobes.
Three times as great or many.
example: A threefold increase.
etymology: From Middle English threfold, from Old English þrīfeald. Equivalent to three + -fold.

definition: Having a throat as specified.
example: Deep-throated.
etymology: From throat + -ed.

definition: Pulsate or pound with abnormal force.
example: My head is throbbing.
etymology: From Middle English throbben; possibly of imitative origin. Cognate with Scots thrab (“to throb”). Compare also drub.

definition: The act of suffocating (someone) by constricting the windpipe.
Large nightingale of eastern Europe.
One who intrudes or pushes themself forward.
etymology: From thrust + -er. The surfboard sense was coined (but never trademarked) by Simon Anderson, who created the design in 1980. The name was almost immediately applied generically to any surfboard with that fin design.

definition: A single sharp crash of thunder.
etymology: From thunder + clap.

definition: A dull hollow sound.
example: The basketball made a thunk as it hit the rim.
etymology: By analogy with past participles ending in "-unk", such as drunk and sunk.

definition: Preventing realization or attainment of a desire.
A ductless glandular organ at the base of the neck that produces lymphocytes and aids in producing immunity; atrophies with age.
etymology: From New Latin thymus, from Ancient Greek θύμος (thúmos, “warty excrescence, (also, as used by Galen) thymus gland”).

definition: A ductless glandular organ at the base of the neck that produces lymphocytes and aids in producing immunity; atrophies with age.
Difficult to handle; requiring great tact.
example: Hesitates to be explicit on so ticklish a matter.
etymology: From tickle + -ish.

definition: A small tasty bit of food.
etymology: From Old English tid (“fond, tender, nice”) + English bit (“morsel”).

definition: Low-lying coastal land drained by tidal streams.
etymology: From tide + water.

definition: A stream in which the effects of the tide extend far upstream.
A stream in which the effects of the tide extend far upstream.
A midday meal.
example: He took his tiffin from home and ate the food two hours later in school.
etymology: Apparently from English tiffing, present participle of tiff (“to take a small drink, to sip”) (slang).

definition: Tightly stretched rope or wire on which acrobats perform high above the ground.
etymology: From tight + rope.

definition: An acrobat who performs on a tightrope or slack rope.
Walking on a tightrope or slack rope.
Land that is covered with trees and shrubs.
etymology: From Middle English *tymbre-lond, from Old English timberland, tymberlond, equivalent to timber + land.

definition: (music) the distinctive property of a complex sound (a voice or noise or musical sound).
example: The timbre of her soprano was rich and lovely.
etymology: From French timbre, ultimately from Ancient Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon, “drum”). Doublet of tympanum, timpani, timbal, and tymbal.

definition: The distant past beyond memory.
example: From time immemorial.

definition: Being at the right time.
etymology: From timely + -ness.

definition: A measuring instrument or device for keeping time.
example: The only timepiece she allowed in the house was a sundial. She usually kept the curtains pulled.
etymology: From time + piece.

definition: A substance that colors or dyes.
example: A tincture of orange peel.
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English tincture (“a dye, pigment; a colour, hue, tint; process of colouring or dyeing; medicinal ointment or salve (perhaps one discolouring the skin); use of a medicinal tincture;

definition: Prong on a fork or pitchfork or antler.
etymology: From Middle English tine, alteration of Middle English tinde, tind, from Old English tind, from Proto-West Germanic *tind, Proto-Germanic *tindaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts (“tooth, peg”).

definition: A harrow used to refine seed-bed condition before planting, to remove small weeds in growing crops and to loosen the inter-row soils to allow for water to soak into the subsoil.
example: Tine and chain harrows are often only supported by a rigid towing-bar at the front of the set.

definition: A tuberculin test in which a disk with several tines bearing tuberculin antigen is used to puncture the skin; development of a hard red area indicates past or present exposure to tubercle bacilli and the need for further testing.
Foil made of tin or an alloy of tin and lead.
etymology: From tin + foil.

definition: Sealed in a can or jar.
Food preserved by canning.
Meat preserved in a can or tin.
Impart a cheap brightness to.
example: His tinseled image of Hollywood.
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English tinsel (“destruction, loss; damnation, spiritual loss;

definition: A person who leaves a tip.
example: A generous tipper.
etymology: So called from the first brewer of it, one Thomas Tipper.

definition: Truck whose contents can be emptied without handling; the front end of the platform can be pneumatically raised so that the load is discharged by gravity.
Truck whose contents can be emptied without handling; the front end of the platform can be pneumatically raised so that the load is discharged by gravity.
The tip of a toe.
etymology: From Middle English tipto, typto; equivalent to tip + toe. Compare fingertip.

definition: A white powder used as a pigment for its high covering power and durability.
A tiny or scarcely detectable amount.
example: The foure pricks or tittles are these. The first is a full prick or period. The second is a comma or crooked tittle.
etymology: From Middle English tytle, titel, titele, from Anglo-Norman titil, titule and Medieval Latin titulus (“small stroke, diacritical mark, accent”), from Latin titulus (“title”).

definition: The side sheltered from the wind.
Cooking to a brown crispiness over a fire or on a grill.
example: Proper toasting should brown both sides of a piece of bread.

definition: Long-handled fork for cooking or toasting frankfurters or bread etc. (especially over an open fire).
A mixed drink made of liquor and water with sugar and spices and served hot.
Fishtail palm of India to Malay Peninsula; sap yields a brown sugar (jaggery) and trunk pith yields sago.
The nail at the end of a toe.
example: Toenail clippings.
etymology: From toe + nail.

definition: Snobbish; pretentiously superior.
etymology: Probably from toff or from toffee-nose + -ed.

definition: A one-piece cloak worn by men in ancient Rome.
etymology: Borrowed directly from Latin toga, from tegō (“to clothe”). Doublet of toge.

definition: Doing arduous or unpleasant work.
example: Toiling coal miners in the black deeps.

definition: A disposition to tolerate or accept people or situations.
example: All people should practice toleration and live together in peace.
etymology: From Middle French toleration, from Latin tolerātiōnem, accusative singular of tolerātiō, from the verb tolerō (“to tolerate”). Compare tolerance.

definition: Male cat.
etymology: From Tom + cat, popularised by The Life and Adventures of a Cat (1760), by an anonymous author, in which the male cat was called Tom.

definition: Provided with or resembling a tongue; often used in combination.
example: Tongued shoes.
etymology: From Middle English tonged, tunged, equivalent to tongue + -ed. Compare Old English ġetynġe (“skilled with speech, talkative, eloquent”).

definition: Loss of sensation confined to the skin or mucous surfaces (as when benzocaine or Lidocaine is applied to the surface).
The layer of soil on the surface.
example: Little grew on the farm, after the floods from the hurricane washed away the topsoil.
etymology: From top + soil.

definition: Resinous or aromatic chiefly tropical shrubs or trees.
Characterized by intense emotion.
example: A torrid love affair.
etymology: From Latin torridus, from torreō (“parch, scorch”).

definition: Highly complex or intricate and occasionally devious.
example: Tortuous legal procedures.
etymology: From Middle English tortuous, tortuose, from Anglo-Norman and Old French tortuos, from Latin tortuōsus, from tortus (“a twisting, winding”).

definition: Extremely painful.
etymology: From Middle English torterous, from Anglo-Norman torturous, from Old French tortureus, from Latin tortūra. By surface analysis, torture + -ous.

definition: A ring-shaped surface generated by rotating a circle around an axis that does not intersect the circle.
example: A 4-variable Karnaugh map can be thought of, topologically, as being a torus.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin torus (“a round, swelling, elevation, protuberance”).

definition: Loss of all ability to communicate.
A skilled typist who can type a document without looking at the keyboard.
example: It's easier to make data entries if you're a touch-typist.
etymology: From touch + typist.

definition: Make tough or tougher.
example: This experience will toughen her.
etymology: From tough + -en.

definition: A mineral that is a complex borosilicate and hydroxide of aluminum containing iron and magnesium and calcium and lithium and sodium; it is usually black but occurs in transparent colored forms that are used as gemstones.
etymology: From French tourmaline, ultimately from Sinhalese තෝරමල්ලී (tōramallī, “carnelian”)

definition: Bandage that stops the flow of blood from an artery by applying pressure.
etymology: From French tourniquet, from tourner (“to turn”).

definition: The people living in a municipality smaller than a city.
etymology: From town + -s- + folk.

definition: Membranous tube with cartilaginous rings that conveys inhaled air from the larynx to the bronchi.
etymology: From late Middle English, from Medieval Latin trāchēa (“the windpipe”) (also borrowed as Late Latin trāchīa), from Ancient Greek τρᾱχεῖᾰ ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (trākheîă ărtērĭ́ā, “windpipe, trachea”).

definition: The system or principles and theory of labor unions.
(of goods and merchandise) labeled with proprietary (and legally registered) identification guaranteeing exclusive use.
example: Trademarked goods.

definition: An exchange that occurs as a compromise.
example: I faced a tradeoff between eating and buying my medicine.
etymology: Deverbal from trade off.

definition: A male merchant who owns or manages a shop.
etymology: From trade + -s- + -man.

definition: Someone who marks a trail by leaving blazes on trees.
etymology: From trail (noun) + blazer (noun).

definition: The beginning of a trail.
etymology: From trail + head.

definition: Having the character of, or characteristic of, a traitor.
example: A lying traitorous insurrectionist.
etymology: From Middle English trayterous, traytrous, (also Middle English traytours, treytours), from Anglo-Norman traiterous, traitourous and Old French traitros.

definition: The sound of heavy treading or stomping.
example: He heard the trample of many feet.

definition: Conduct business.
example: Transact with foreign governments.
etymology: Back-formation from transaction, or else from Latin trānsāctus, past participle of trānsigere.

definition: Write out from speech, notes, etc.
example: Transcribe the oral history of this tribe.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin trānscrībere (“to write again in another place, transcribe, copy”).

definition: (genetics) the process of transferring genetic material from one cell to another by a plasmid or bacteriophage.
etymology: 1650s, Latin transductionem, form of Latin trānsdūcō (“lead across”). By surface analysis, transduce + -tion.

definition: (psychoanalysis) the process whereby emotions are passed on or displaced from one person to another; during psychoanalysis the displacement of feelings toward others (usually the parents) is onto the analyst.
A striking change in appearance or character or circumstances.
etymology: From Middle English transfiguracioun, from Old French transfiguracion, Anglo-Norman transfiguraciun, and Latin transfigūrātio.

definition: Having your attention fixated as though by a spell.
A verb (or verb construction) that requires an object in order to be grammatical.
etymology: Coined between 1580 and 1590.

definition: Lasting a very short time.
example: Youth's transient beauty.
etymology: From Middle French transitoire, from Old French, from Latin trānsitōrius.

definition: The transport of dissolved material within a plant.
etymology: From trans- + location.

definition: An act that changes the form or character or substance of something.
etymology: Late 14th century, from Old French transmutacion (“transformation, metamorphosis”), from Late Latin transmutationem, from Latin transmutare (“to change”).

definition: So as to be easily understood or seen through.
example: His transparently lucid prose.
etymology: From transparent + -ly.

definition: Prejudiced against transgender people.
etymology: From trans- + -phobic.

definition: Turned about in order or relation.
example: Transposed letters.

definition: Any abnormal position of the organs of the body.
etymology: From Middle French transposition, from Medieval Latin transpositio.

definition: A swing used by circus acrobats.
etymology: From French trapèze, from Latin trapezium. Doublet of trapezium.

definition: Concluding state of pregnancy; from the onset of contractions to the birth of a child.
etymology: From Middle English travailen, from Old French travailler, from the noun (see above). Doublet of travel. Displaced native Middle English swinken (“to work”) (from Old English swincan (“to labour, to toil, to work at”)).

definition: A long fishing line with many shorter lines and hooks attached to it (usually suspended between buoys).
A long fishing line with many shorter lines and hooks attached to it (usually suspended between buoys).
A conical fishnet dragged through the water at great depths.
A fisherman who use a trawl net.
etymology: From trawl + -er.

definition: Having the character of, or characteristic of, a traitor.
example: His treasonous actions earned Benedict Arnold eternal scorn.
etymology: From treason + -ous.

definition: Erect deciduous shrub or tree to 10 feet with maroon flowers; New Zealand.
Arboreal wallabies of New Guinea and northern Australia having hind and forelegs of similar length.
Latticework used to support climbing plants.
etymology: From Middle English trelis, from Anglo-Norman treslis, from Old French treille (“arbor”), from Latin trichila (“arbor", "summer house”).

definition: Forecasting technique which uses statistical methods (such as exponential smoothing or moving averages) to project the future pattern of a time series data.
example: Accurate trend extrapolation is the most important part of future planning.

definition: A feeling of alarm or dread.
example: I decided, with considerable trepidation, to let him drive my car without me.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin trepidātiō, from trepidō (“be agitated”).

definition: A supporting tower used to support a bridge.
etymology: From Middle English trestel, from Old French trestel (“crossbeam”) (French tréteau), from Latin trānstellum, diminutive of trānstrum.

definition: A bridge supported by trestlework.
A table supported on trestles.
A trigonometric method of determining the position of a fixed point from the angles to it from two fixed points of a known distance apart; useful in navigation.
etymology: From Medieval Latin triangulātiō (“triangulation”), from triangulō (“to triangulate”) + -tiō (noun-forming suffix). Triangulō is derived from triangulus (“triangular; triangle”), from trēs (“three”) + angulus (“angle;

definition: An annoying or frustrating or catastrophic event.
example: Life is full of tribulations.

definition: Any skeletal muscle having three origins (but especially the triceps brachii).
etymology: From Latin triceps (“triple-headed”), from trēs (“three”) + caput (“head”). See there for more details.

definition: Not worth considering.
example: A trifling matter.
etymology: By surface analysis, trifle + -ing.

definition: Neat and smart in appearance.
example: The trig corporal in his jaunty cap.
etymology: From Middle English trig, tryg, from Old Norse tryggr (“loyal, faithful, true”), from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz (“loyal, faithful, true”). Cognate with Old English trīewe (“faithful, loyal, true”). More at true.

definition: A note that alternates rapidly with another note a semitone above it.
etymology: From Middle English trillen, from Italian trillo, trillare. Compare German trillern, Norwegian trille, Swedish trilla.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of one and one and one.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes From triple + -et.

definition: The normal version of the genetic code in which a sequence of three nucleotides codes for the synthesis of a specific amino acid.
Art consisting of a painting or carving (especially an altarpiece) on three panels (usually hinged together).
etymology: From Ancient Greek τρίπτυχος (tríptukhos, “consisting of three layers, threefold”), from τρι- (tri-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “a fold”).

definition: A radioactive isotope of hydrogen; atoms of tritium have three times the mass of ordinary hydrogen atoms.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin tritium, from Ancient Greek τρίτος (trítos, “third”) + New Latin -ium. By surface analysis, trit- + -ium.

definition: Relating to or celebrating a triumph.
example: A triumphal procession.
etymology: From Middle English triumphal, triumphall, tryumphal, from Latin triumphālis and Old French trionfal, triumphal.

definition: A monumental archway; usually they are built to commemorate some notable victory.
In a triumphant manner.
example: She shouted triumphantly.
etymology: From triumphant + -ly.

definition: A group of three men responsible for public administration or civil authority.
A Russian carriage pulled by three horses abreast.
etymology: From Russian тро́йка (trójka, “a group of three”).

definition: Of or relating to nutrition.
example: A trophic level on the food chain.
etymology: From Ancient Greek τροφικός (trophikós, “pertaining to food or nourishment”), from τροφή (trophḗ, “food”).

definition: A singer of folk songs.
etymology: From Old Occitan trobar (“to find”) via Old French troubadour. Piecewise doublet of trouveur.

definition: Someone who deliberately stirs up trouble.
example: Local troublemaker.
etymology: From trouble + make + -er.

definition: Solve problems.
example: He is known to be good at trouble-shooting.
etymology: Back-formation from troubleshooter; by surface analysis, trouble + shoot.

definition: Small tropical American shrubby tree; widely cultivated in warm regions for its sweet globular yellow fruit.
Parasitic tree of Indonesia and Malaysia having fragrant close-grained yellowish heartwood with insect repelling properties and used, e.g., for making chests.
Evergreen North American honeysuckle vine having coral-red or orange flowers.
A musician who plays the trumpet or cornet.
etymology: From trumpet + -er (occupational suffix) or + -er (agent noun suffix).

definition: Large pure white wild swan of western North America having a sonorous cry.
A low bed to be slid under a higher bed.
etymology: From Middle English trondlin, trondelen, a variation of Middle English trendlen, from Old English trendlian. More at trendle, trindle.

definition: A low bed to be slid under a higher bed.
etymology: From trundle + bed.

definition: The trait of deserving trust and confidence.
etymology: From trustworthy + -ness.

definition: The quality of being truthful.
An amino acid that occurs in proteins; is essential for growth and normal metabolism; a precursor of niacin.
etymology: From German Tryptophan, from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “to appear”).

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of a czar.
etymology: From tsar + -ist. Piecewise doublet of Caesarist.

definition: Of or relating to occurring in a tube such as e.g. the Fallopian tube or Eustachian tube.
example: Tubal ligation.
etymology: From tube + -al.

definition: Ectopic pregnancy in a Fallopian tube.
A fleshy underground stem or root serving for reproductive and food storage.
etymology: From Latin tūber (“bump, hump, swelling”).

definition: Erect perennial of eastern and southern United States having showy orange flowers.
