A bunch of hair or feathers or growing grass.
(of plants) growing in small dense clumps or tufts.
A powerful small boat designed to pull or push larger ships.
etymology: From tug + boat. Sense 2 from monthly tugboat, a reference to the saying "our ship has come in," here referring to a small, "reliable" "tugboat" instead of a large windfall.

definition: A fine (often starched) net used for veils or tutus or gowns.
etymology: Borrowed from French tulle, named after French Tulle (a town), named after Latin Tūtēla (a Roman deity), from Latin tūtēla (whence English tutelary), from Latin tueor (whence tutor, tutorial).

definition: Any plant that breaks away from its roots in autumn and is driven by the wind as a light rolling mass.
etymology: From tumble + weed.

definition: Pale soft wood of a tupelo tree especially the water gum.
etymology: From Creek topilwa < íto 'tree' + opílwa 'swamp'.

definition: Any of several gum trees of swampy areas of North America.
Someone who guards prisoners.
etymology: From turn + key. (jailer): Compare typologically Russian вертуха́й (vertuxáj) (akin to верте́ть (vertétʹ)).

definition: Something causing antagonism or loss of interest.
etymology: Deverbal from turn off.

definition: An oleoresin obtained from conifers (especially pines).
Low-growing sticky subshrub of southwestern United States having narrow linear leaves on many slender branches and hundreds of tiny yellow flower heads.
A sweater or jersey with a high close-fitting collar.
etymology: From turtle + neck.

definition: A high close-fitting turnover collar.
Fight or struggle in a confused way at close quarters.
etymology: Related to tousle.

definition: Utter ‘tsk,’ ‘tut,’ or ‘tut-tut,’ as in disapproval.
A loudspeaker that reproduces higher audio frequency sounds.
example: The sound system had both tweeters and woofers.
etymology: From to tweet + -er.

definition: To dance with thrusting hip movements and a low squatting stance.
etymology: Blend of twitch + jerk. The "sexually-provocative dance" sense was particularly popularized since c. 2000 by hip-hop from the United States of America, and again in 2013 by singer Miley Cyrus.

definition: A weave used to produce the effect of parallel diagonal ribs.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English twyll, twylle, from Old English twilīċ (“two-threaded”), a partial calque of Latin bilix, bilic-, from bis (“twice”) + licium (“thread”).

definition: A weave used to produce the effect of parallel diagonal ribs.
Having twin beds.
Cause a stinging pain.
example: My side twinges if I sit too long.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English twengen (“to nip, pinch, tweak;

definition: Producing two offspring at a time.
etymology: From twin + -ing.

definition: A sharp bend in a line produced when a line having a loop is pulled tight.
example: The conductor gave his baton a twirl, and the orchestra began to play.
etymology: Of Scandinavian origin, akin to Norwegian Nynorsk tvirla, Old High German dweran (German zwirlen, quirlen), Dutch dwarrelen and Icelandic þyrill;

definition: Marked by repeated turns and bends.
example: Had to steer the car down a twisty track.
etymology: From twist + -y.

definition: Consisting of two chambers.
Having two leaves.
Having two lobes.
Typewritten matter especially a typewritten copy of a manuscript.
etymology: From type + script.

definition: A printer that sets textual material in type.
A form of salmonella that causes typhoid fever.
Someone paid to operate a typewriter.
etymology: From type + -ist.

definition: Classification according to general type.
etymology: From type + -ology.

definition: Large carnivorous bipedal dinosaur having enormous teeth with knifelike serrations; may have been a scavenger rather than an active predator; later Cretaceous period in North America.
etymology: From translingual Tyrannosaurus, from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “tyrant”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”). Doublet of tyrannosaur.

definition: An ugly or unpromising child who grows into a beautiful or worthy person.
etymology: Calque of Danish grim ælling. From the fairy tale of a duckling, considered ugly, that matures into a magnificent swan.

definition: A small guitar having four strings.
etymology: From Japanese 受け (uke), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 受(う)ける (ukeru, “to receive, to get”).

definition: Of or relating to or characterized by ulceration.
example: Ulcerative colitis.
etymology: From ulcerate + -ive.

definition: In or of the month preceding the present one.
etymology: First attested in 1582; from Latin ultimō (elliptically for ultimō diē or ultimō mēnse), masculine ablative singular form of ultimus (“last”); cognate with Dutch ultimo, the German ultimo, the Swedish ultimo, etc.

definition: Protrusion of the intestine and omentum through a hernia in the abdominal wall near the navel; usually self correcting after birth.
Not embarrassed.
example: A tinseled charm and unabashed sentimentality.
etymology: From un- + abashed.

definition: In an unabashed manner.
example: Unabashedly, he asked for more.
etymology: From unabashed + -ly or un- + abashedly.

definition: Continuing at full strength or intensity.
example: The winds are unabated.
etymology: From un- + abated.

definition: (used of texts) not shortened.
example: An unabridged novel.
etymology: From un- + abridged.

definition: A dictionary that has not been shortened by the omitting terms or definitions; a comprehensive dictionary.
Not to be accounted for or explained.
example: Perceptible only as unaccountable influences that hinder progress.
etymology: From un- + accountable.

definition: Not mixed with impurities.
example: Unadulterated maple syrup.
etymology: From un- + adulterated.

definition: Oblivious of dangers or perils or calmly resolute in facing them.
etymology: From un- + afraid.

definition: Carried out without aid or assistance.
example: His first unaided walk through the park.
etymology: From un- + aided.

definition: In an unambiguous manner.
example: She told him unambiguously to leave, yet he failed to leave.
etymology: From unambiguous + -ly, or from un- + ambiguously.

definition: Everyone being of one mind.
etymology: From unanim(ous) + -ity, from Middle French unanimité, from Late Latin ūnanimitās. Displaced native Old English ānmōdnes (literally “one-mindedness”).

definition: Not anticipated.
example: Unanticipated and disconcerting lines of development.
etymology: From un- + anticipated.

definition: (of characters in literature or drama) tending to evoke antipathetic feelings.
etymology: From un- + appealing.

definition: Not likely to be rewarded.
etymology: From un- + appreciated.

definition: Immune to attack; incapable of being tampered with.
example: She won the debate with her unassailable logic.
etymology: From un- + assailable.

definition: Unsupported by other people.
etymology: From un- + assisted.

definition: Not fastened together.
example: Take the unattached end of the rope in one hand.
etymology: From un- + attached.

definition: The quality of not being available when needed.
etymology: From un- + availability.

definition: To an unbearable degree.
example: It was unbearably hot in the room.
etymology: From unbearable + -ly or un- + bearably.

definition: Not in keeping with accepted standards of what is right or proper in polite society.
example: Language unbecoming to a lady.
etymology: From un- + becoming. Compare Middle English unbicomelich (“unbecoming”). Equal to unbecome + -ing

definition: A rejection of belief.
etymology: From Middle English unbilefe, unbileve, equivalent to un- + belief.

definition: Clear or remove an obstruction from.
example: The procedure unblocked his arteries.
etymology: From un- + block.

definition: Seemingly boundless in amount, number, degree, or especially extent.
example: Unbounded enthusiasm.
etymology: From un- + bounded.

definition: An interval that does not include its endpoints.
Not buttoned.
example: The wind picked up the hem of her unbuttoned coat.
etymology: From un- + buttoned. In some instances possibly from unbutton.

definition: Lacking affection or warm feeling.
example: An uncaring person.
etymology: From un- + caring.

definition: In an unceremonious manner.
example: He was dismissed unceremoniously.
etymology: From unceremonious + -ly or un- + ceremoniously.

definition: Conforming to the same principles or course of action over time.
etymology: From un- + changing.

definition: Distinctive and not typical.
example: A book uncharacteristic of its author.
etymology: From un- + characteristic.

definition: In uncharacteristic manner.
example: He was uncharacteristically cool.
etymology: From uncharacteristic + -ally.

definition: Without civilizing influences.
example: Fighting is crude and uncivilized especially if the weapons are efficient.
etymology: From un- + civilized.

definition: Exceptionally.
example: A common remedy is uncommonly difficult to find.
etymology: From uncommon + -ly.

definition: Lacking in interest or care or feeling.
example: Blithely unconcerned about his friend's plight.
etymology: From un- + concerned or unconcern + -ed.

definition: A state lacking normal awareness of the self or environment.
example: I was roused from unconsciousness by the alarm clock.
etymology: From unconscious + -ness or un- + consciousness.

definition: Lacking conviction.
example: I remain unconvinced.
etymology: From un- + convinced.

definition: Not convincing.
example: As unconvincing as a forced smile.
etymology: From un- + convincing.

definition: Not cooked.
etymology: From un- + cooked.

definition: Unwilling to cooperate.
example: An uncooperative witness.
etymology: From un- + cooperative.

definition: Lacking in cooperative planning and organization.
example: Uncoordinated scheduling often resulted in conflicting games.
etymology: From un- + coordinated.

definition: Lacking refinement or cultivation or taste.
example: An untutored and uncouth human being.
etymology: From Middle English uncouth, from Old English uncūþ (“unknown; unfamiliar; strange”), from Proto-West Germanic *unkunþ, from Proto-Germanic *unkunþaz (“unknown”), equivalent to un- + couth.

definition: Unshaken in purpose.
etymology: From Middle English ondauntit, undauntdid; equivalent to un- + daunted.

definition: Not announced or openly acknowledged.
example: Fighting an undeclared war.
etymology: From un- + declared.

definition: Lower side.
example: The underbellies of clouds.
etymology: From under- + belly.

definition: Framework that serves as a support for the body of a vehicle.
etymology: From under- + carriage.

definition: Belonging to the lowest and least privileged social stratum.
example: Underclass mothers and children.
etymology: From under- + class.

definition: A subdued emotional quality underlying an utterance; implicit meaning.
example: The meeting was pervaded with an undercurrent of dread, as the managers tried not to admit that firings were looming.
etymology: From under- + current.

definition: Under the feet.
example: Trampled the beans underfoot.
etymology: From Middle English underfoote, underfote, equivalent to under- + foot. Cognate with Middle Dutch ondervoet (“underfoot”). Compare also Middle Low German undervôt (“pedestal, base”).

definition: The brush (small trees and bushes and ferns etc.) growing beneath taller trees in a wood or forest.
example: Tangled undergrowth.
etymology: From under- + growth. Cognate with West Frisian ûndergroei (“undergrowth”).

definition: Be or form the base for.
example: A stratum of clay underlies the surface gravel.
etymology: From Middle English underlien, underliggen, from Old English underliċġan (“to underlie, to be subject to, give way to”), equivalent to under- + lie.

definition: An underground tunnel or passage enabling pedestrians to cross a road or railway.
etymology: From under- + pass.

definition: Support from beneath.
example: You should underpin the mine roof to prevent further collapse.
etymology: From under- + pin.

definition: Smaller than normal for its kind.
etymology: From under- + sized.

definition: Inadequate in number of workers or assistants etc.
example: Overcrowded and understaffed hospitals.
etymology: From under- + staffed.

definition: A quiet or hushed tone of voice.
example: Spoke in undertones.
etymology: From under- + tone.

definition: The archeology of underwater sites.
Guarantee financial support of.
etymology: From Middle English underwriten, from Old English underwrītan (“to write at the foot of, write under, subscribe”). Compare Dutch onderschrijven (“to endorse”), German unterschreiben (“to sign;

definition: A banker who deals chiefly in underwriting new securities.
example: They were the underwriters of the company's shares, but only on a "best efforts" basis.
etymology: From underwrite + -er.

definition: Not deserved or earned.
example: Has an undeserved reputation as a coward.
etymology: From un- + deserved.

definition: Not deserving.
example: The undeserving poor.
etymology: From un- + deserving.

definition: Not desired.
example: An undesired result.
etymology: From Middle English undesired; equivalent to un- + desired.

definition: Not deterred.
example: Pursued his own path … undeterred by lack of popular appreciation and understanding.
etymology: From un- + deterred.

definition: Not subjected to discipline.
example: Undisciplined talent.
etymology: From un- + disciplined.

definition: Not gained by merit or labor or service.
example: Accepted the unearned rewards that came his ways as well as the unearned criticism.
etymology: From un- + earned.

definition: Personal income that you did not earn (e.g., dividends or interest or rent income).
An unearned rise in the market value of property resulting from general market factors.
Personal income that you did not earn (e.g., dividends or interest or rent income).
A run that was scored as a result of an error by the other team.
Discover by investigation.
example: The CIA unearthed a plot to kill the President.
etymology: From un- + earth.

definition: Feelings of anxiety that make you tense and irritable.
etymology: From uneasy + -ness.

definition: Free of encumbrance.
example: Inherited an unencumbered estate.
etymology: From un- + encumbered.

definition: Not enforceable; not capable of being brought about by compulsion.
example: An unenforceable law.
etymology: From un- + enforceable.

definition: In an uneven and irregular way.
etymology: From uneven + -ly or un- + evenly.

definition: Not to be accounted for or explained.
example: An unexplainable fear.
etymology: From un- + explainable. from explain + -able. from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”).

definition: Still capable of exploding or being fired.
example: An unexploded bomb.
etymology: From un- + exploded.

definition: Not liable to failure.
example: The unfailing sign of an amateur.
etymology: From un- + failing.

definition: Of purchase orders that have not been filled.
etymology: From un- + filled.

definition: Not shrinking from danger.
etymology: From un- + flinching.

definition: (of an image) not being in or brought into focus.
example: At their edges, things were pretty much unfocused.
etymology: From un- + focused.

definition: Not furnished with funds.
example: An unfunded project.
etymology: From un- + funded.

definition: Not funny; especially failing to achieve the intended humor.
example: A very unfunny joke.
etymology: From un- + funny.

definition: In an unpleasant way.
example: They were unhappily married.
etymology: From Middle English onhappily, unhappili, unhappily, unhappyly; equivalent to un- + happily or unhappy + -ly.

definition: Not slowed or blocked or interfered with.
Not injured or harmed.
etymology: From Middle English unhert, un-hurt, unhurt, unhurte, equivalent to un- + hurt.

definition: Deficient in originality or creativity; lacking powers of invention.
example: Unimaginative development of a musical theme.
etymology: From un- + imaginative.

definition: Not slowed or prevented.
example: A time of unimpeded growth.
etymology: From un- + impeded.

definition: Not capable of impressing.
etymology: From un- + impressive.

definition: Not fit for habitation.
example: The earthquake left many homes in the area uninhabitable.
etymology: From un- + inhabitable.

definition: Not inhibited or restrained.
example: Uninhibited exuberance.
etymology: From un- + inhibited.

definition: Not initiated; deficient in relevant experience.
example: It seemed a bizarre ceremony to uninitiated western eyes.
etymology: From un- + initiated.

definition: Not injured physically or mentally.
example: Of the three, two were hurt and went to hospital, but the uninjured one made her way home.
etymology: From un- + injured.

definition: Having no intellectual or emotional or spiritual excitement.
example: The production was professional but uninspired.
etymology: From un- + inspired.

definition: Depressing to the spirit.
example: A villa of uninspiring design.
etymology: From un- + inspiring.

definition: The system or principles and theory of labor unions.
etymology: From union + -ism.

definition: Act of forming labor unions.
example: The issue underlying the strike was unionization.
etymology: From union + -ization.

definition: Of or relating to or tending toward universalism.
etymology: From universal + -ist.

definition: The quality of being universal; existing everywhere.
etymology: From Middle English universalite, from Middle French universalité, from Old French, from Late Latin universalitas. By surface analysis, universal + -ity.

definition: Incapable of being justified or explained.
etymology: From un- + justifiable.

definition: Not neatly combed.
example: Wild unkempt hair.
etymology: From earlier unkembed, unkemmed, from Middle English unkempt (“uncombed”), equivalent to un- + kempt. Compare Old Norse úkembdr (uncombed; unkempt";

definition: Not knowable.
example: The unknowable mysteries of life.
etymology: From un- + knowable.

definition: Unaware because of a lack of relevant information or knowledge.
example: An unknowledgeable assistant.
etymology: From un- + knowing.

definition: Not treated with lead.
example: Unleaded gasoline.
etymology: From un- + leaded. The US standard of identity comes from 40 CFR §79.32.

definition: Gasoline that has not been treated with a lead compound.
Not on a list.
example: An unlisted telephone number.

definition: A security traded in the over-the-counter market.
Stock that is not listed and traded on an organized exchange.
Difficult to use or handle or manage because of size or weight or shape.
etymology: From un- + manageable.

definition: Without possibility of mistake.
example: This watercolor is unmistakably a synthesis of nature.
etymology: From unmistakable + -ly.

definition: Not diminished or moderated in intensity or severity; sometimes used as an intensifier.
example: Unmitigated suffering.
etymology: From un- + mitigated.

definition: Not changed in form or character.
etymology: From un- + modified.

definition: Without motivation.
example: An unmotivated student.
etymology: From un- + motivated.

definition: Emotionally unmoved.
example: Always appeared completely unmoved and imperturbable.
etymology: From un- + moved.

definition: In an unnatural way.
example: His other arm lay across his chest, unnaturally, as if placed there deliberately, for a purpose.
etymology: From Middle English unnaturelly, equivalent to unnatural + -ly and/or un- + naturally.

definition: Not necessary.
etymology: From un- + needed.

definition: Deprived of courage and strength.
example: The steeplejack, exhausted and unnerved, couldn't hold on to his dangerous perch much longer.

definition: Free from impediment or obstruction or hindrance.
example: An unobstructed view.
etymology: From un- + obstructed.

definition: Not obtrusive or undesirably noticeable.
example: A quiet, unobtrusive life of self-denial.
etymology: From un- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + obtrusive.

definition: Not original; not being or productive of something fresh and unusual.
example: The manuscript contained unoriginal emendations.
etymology: From un- + original.

definition: Not pleasant or acceptable to the taste or mind.
example: An unpalatable meal.
etymology: From un- + palatable.

definition: Showing lack of love for your country.
etymology: From un- + patriotic.

definition: Not capable of or suitable for being played or played on.
example: The golf ball was in an unplayable lie.
etymology: From un- + playable.

definition: The feeling caused by disagreeable stimuli; one pole of a continuum of states of feeling.
etymology: From unpleasant + -ness.

definition: The quality of lacking general approval or acceptance.
etymology: From un- + popularity or unpopular + -ity.

definition: The quality of being guided by sudden unpredictable impulses.
etymology: From un- + predictability.

definition: Lacking pretension or affectation.
example: An unpretentious country church.
etymology: From un- + pretentious.

definition: Not refined or processed.
etymology: From un- + processed.

definition: Incapable of being questioned.
example: Unquestionable authority.
etymology: From un- + question + -able, compare questionable.

definition: Generally agreed upon; not subject to dispute.
etymology: From un- + questioned.

definition: Not arranged in order hierarchically.
etymology: From un- + ranked.

definition: Inaccessibly located or situated.
example: An unreachable canyon.
etymology: From un- + reach + -able.

definition: Not informed through reading.
example: He seems to have been wholly unread in political theory.
etymology: From un- + read.

definition: Not easily deciphered.
example: Unreadable handwriting.
etymology: From un- + readable.

definition: Of persons; marked by failure to realize full potentialities.
example: Unrealized dreams and ambitions.
etymology: From un- + realized.

definition: Not penitent or remorseful.
etymology: From un- + repentant.

definition: Not reserved.
example: An unreserved forest.
etymology: From un- + reserved.

definition: Not subject to restraint.
example: Unrestrained laughter.

definition: Eminent beyond or above comparison.
example: Unrivaled mastery of her art.
etymology: From un- + rivaled.

definition: Not made explicit.
example: Things left unsaid.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Without salt or seasoning.
etymology: From un- + salted.

definition: Not sanitary or healthful.
example: Unsanitary open sewers.
etymology: From un- + sanitary.

definition: Not up to expectations.
etymology: From un- + satisfying.

definition: Not saturated; capable of dissolving more of a substance at a given temperature.
example: An unsaturated salt solution.
etymology: From un- + saturated.

definition: A chemical compound that contains carbon-carbon double bonds or triple bonds, such as those found in alkenes or alkynes, respectively.
example: Saturated and unsaturated compounds need not consist only of a carbon atom chain.

definition: Not furnished with or using a script.
example: Unrehearsed and unscript spot interviews.
etymology: From un- + scripted.

definition: Not established or confirmed.
example: His doom is as yet unsealed.

definition: Remove from political office.
example: The Republicans are trying to unseat the liberal Democrat.
etymology: From un- (suffix meaning ‘not’) + seat (“to provide with a place to sit”).

definition: To forget an image.
example: I have only seen the performance once; and I would not unsee it again if I could; but none the less I am a broken man after it.
etymology: From un- + see. Compare Middle English unseen, unsen (“to fail to see, be unable to see”).

definition: Not in keeping with accepted standards of what is right or proper in polite society.
example: Unseemly to use profanity.
etymology: From Middle English unsemli, probably a partial calque of Old Norse úsǽmiligr (“unseemly”); equivalent to un- + seemly.

definition: Disregarding your own advantages and welfare over those of others.
example: The man was in an unselfish mood that day, so decided to give a £20 note to the next charity he came across.
etymology: From un- + selfish.

definition: Not wise in the ways of the world.
example: Either too unsophisticated or too honest to promise more than he could deliver.
etymology: From un- + sophisticated.

definition: Not in good condition; damaged or decayed.
example: An unsound foundation.
etymology: From un- + sound.

definition: Not left to spoil.
example: Tourists descending on unspoiled areas.
etymology: From un- + spoiled.

definition: Subject to change or variation.
example: Her unsteady walk.
etymology: From un- + steady. Like steady, the word first appeared in English around 1530. The word is comparable to Old Frisian onstedich, Low German unstadig, etc.

definition: Free.
example: A man with a mule got my car unstuck.
etymology: From un- + stuck.

definition: Not easy to combine harmoniously.
example: An unsuited astronaut.
etymology: From un- + suited.

definition: Spotlessly clean and fresh.
example: The unsullied snow of mountains.
etymology: From un- + sullied.

definition: Not capable of being improved on.
etymology: From un- + surpassed.

definition: Not causing surprise.
etymology: From un- + surprising.

definition: Not made sweet.
etymology: From un- + sweetened.

definition: Not sympathetic or disposed toward.
example: Unsympathetic officialdom.
etymology: From un- + sympathetic.

definition: Release from entanglement of difficulty.
example: With gentle combing, untangle your hair.
etymology: From un- + tangle.

definition: Not neat and tidy.
example: Careless and untidy in her personal habits.
etymology: From un- + tidy.

definition: Undo the ties of.
example: They untied the prisoner.
etymology: From Middle English untien, unteyen, untyȝen, untiȝen, from Old English untīġan (“to untie”), equivalent to un- + tie.

definition: Not tied.
etymology: From un- + tied.

definition: Not in keeping with accepted standards of what is right or proper in polite society.
example: Moved to curb their untoward ribaldry.
etymology: From un- + toward (“to + -ward”).

definition: Not turned.
example: Left no stone unturned.
etymology: From un- + turned.

definition: Lacking proof or substantiation.
etymology: From un- + verified.

definition: Of or associated with the great masses of people.
example: The unwashed masses.
etymology: From Middle English unwasched, unwasschyd, unwessched, a weak verb conjugation of earlier Middle English unwaschen (“unwashen”), equivalent to un- + washed.

definition: Of someone who has not been married.
example: Unwed mother.
etymology: From un- (not) + wed.

definition: In an unwilling manner.
example: He had sinned against her unwillingly.
etymology: From unwilling + -ly or un- + willingly.

definition: Not done with purpose or intent.
example: An unwitting mistake may be overlooked.
etymology: From Middle English unwittinge, unwitand, from Old English unwitende (“unwitting; not knowing; unaware; unconscious”), from Proto-Germanic *unwitandz (“not knowing”), equivalent to un- + witting.

definition: Not capable of being carried out or put into practice.
example: These plans seem unworkable; moreover, a budget for their implementation remains a fantasy.
etymology: From un- + workable.

definition: Remove the outer cover or wrapping of.
example: Let's unwrap the gifts!
etymology: From Middle English unwrappen, equivalent to un- + wrap.

definition: Not yet wrapped or having the wrapping removed.
example: She faced a mountainous pile of presents still unwrapped.

definition: Stubbornly unyielding.
example: Unyielding pressure.
etymology: From un- + yielding.

definition: Open the zipper of.
example: Unzip the bag.
etymology: From un- + zip.

definition: Exalted emotionally especially with pride.
A transmission from Earth to a spacecraft or the path of such a transmission.
etymology: From up + link.

definition: Designed for consumers with high incomes.
example: He turned up in well-cut clothes … and upmarket felt hats.
etymology: From up- + market.

definition: The jaw in vertebrates that is fused to the cranium.
A swinging blow directed upward (especially at an opponent's chin).
etymology: From upper + cut.

definition: In or into the most prominent position, as in the mind.
example: Say what comes uppermost.
etymology: From Middle English upper-moste; equivalent to upper + -most.

definition: Toward the source or against the current.
etymology: From up- + river.

definition: Move (people) forcibly from their homeland into a new and foreign environment.
example: The war uprooted many people.
etymology: PIE word *wréh₂ds From up- (prefix indicating a higher direction or position) + root (“to tear up by the roots; (figuratively) to remove forcibly from a place; to eradicate, exterminate”, verb).

definition: A phenomenon that follows and is caused by some previous phenomenon.
example: I'm not interested in hearing all the details. Just give me the upshot.
etymology: Presumed from up- + shot, referring to the last shot in a match of archery.

definition: A sudden forceful flow.
etymology: From up- + surge.

definition: Having been turned so that the bottom is no longer the bottom.
example: Sat on an upturned bucket.
etymology: From up- + turned.

definition: Spatially or metaphorically from a lower to a higher position.
example: The fragments flew upwards.
etymology: From upward + -ly.

definition: The condition of being urbanized.
Made urban in nature; taking on urban characteristics.
example: The urbanized Eastern states.

definition: A specialist in urology.
etymology: From urolog(y) + -ist or uro- + -logist.

definition: Fit or ready for use or service.
In a useful manner.
example: Extra money could be usefully spent on this project.
etymology: From useful + -ly.

definition: The introduction of something new.
example: It signalled the ushering in of a new era.

definition: Seize and take control without authority and possibly with force; take as one's right or possession.
example: He usurped my rights.
etymology: From Middle English usurpen, from Old French usurper, from Latin ūsūrpō.

definition: One who wrongfully or illegally seizes and holds the place of another.
etymology: From Middle English usurper, usurpour, usurpur, from Middle French usurpeur; equivalent to usurp + -er.

definition: An exorbitant or unlawful rate of interest.
example: In medieval Europe, Jews were often linked to usury and therefore persecuted by authorities.
etymology: From Middle English usurie, from Latin ūsūria, from ūsūra (“lending at interest, usury”) from ūsus (“use”), from stem of ūtī (“to use”). Compare usurp and use.

definition: An implement for practical use (especially in a household).
example: We have convenient storage for all the kitchen/eating utensils.
etymology: From Middle English utensyl, from Old French utensile, from Latin ūtēnsilis (“useful, usable”).

definition: Necklike opening to the uterus.
Doctrine that the useful is the good; especially as elaborated by Jeremy Bentham and James Mill; the aim was said to be the greatest happiness for the greatest number.
etymology: From utilitarian + -ism.

definition: The use of uttered sounds for auditory communication.
example: He has a good utterance.
etymology: From Middle English utteraunce, outeraunce; equivalent to utter + -ance.

definition: Perform vaccinations or produce immunity in by inoculation.
example: We vaccinate against scarlet fever.
etymology: From vaccine + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Devoid of intelligence or thought.
example: A vacuous mind.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vacuus (“empty, vacant”) + -ous.

definition: Unclearness by virtue of being poorly expressed or not coherent in meaning.
example: The Conservative manifesto is a model of vagueness.
etymology: From vague + -ness.

definition: The student with the best grades who usually delivers the valedictory address at commencement.
etymology: Formed 1759, from valedictory (“of a speech made when leaving”) + -an.

definition: A plant of the genus Valeriana having lobed or dissected leaves and cymose white or pink flowers.
With valor; in a valiant manner.
example: He fought valiantly until the end.

example: Choking exasperation and wordless shame.

definition: Using or containing too many words.
example: Newspapers of the day printed long wordy editorials.
etymology: From Middle English wordy, woordi, from Old English wordiġ (“wordy, verbose”), equivalent to word + -y. Cognate with Icelandic orðigur (“wordy”).

definition: Person with a compulsive need to work.
example: All workaholics should move to Hong Kong, where working hours average over 50 per week.
etymology: From work + -aholic.

definition: A strong worktable for a carpenter or mechanic.
etymology: From work + bench.

definition: Machine that performs dependably under heavy use.
example: The IBM main frame computers have been the workhorse of the business world.
etymology: From Middle English werkehorse, equivalent to work + horse.

definition: Work consisting of a piece of metal being machined.
example: Make sure the workpiece is properly secured in the chuck before turning on the lathe.
etymology: From work (noun) + piece (noun), a calque of German Werkstück (“piece of work; object being worked on”).

definition: Hours or days of work in a calendar week.
etymology: From work + week.

definition: Sadness on thinking about the evils of the world.
etymology: From world-weary + -ness.

definition: Any of several small slim salamanders of the Pacific coast of the United States.
Any of several low composite herbs of the genera Artemisia or Seriphidium.
etymology: From Middle English wormwode, a folk etymology (as if worm + wood) of wermode (“wormwood”), from Old English wermōd (“wormwood, absinthe”), from Proto-West Germanic *warjamōdā (“wormwood”).

definition: A dark bitter oil obtained from wormwood leaves; flavors absinthe liqueurs.
Silky-leaved aromatic perennial of dry northern parts of the Northern Hemisphere; has tawny florets.
Showing adoration.
etymology: From Middle English worshipful; equivalent to worship + -ful.

definition: The quality or state of having merit or value.
etymology: From Middle English worthynesse, equivalent to worthy + -ness.

definition: Writing paper having a very faint mesh pattern.
An angry dispute.
example: Wrangle and bloodshed followed thence.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English wranglen, wrangle (“to contend with (someone) in a test of strength; (figuratively) to make misleading arguments to entrap”);

definition: An instance of intense argument (as in bargaining).
etymology: From Middle English wranglyng, wranglinge, equivalent to wrangle + -ing.

definition: A garment (as a dress or coat) with a full length opening; adjusts to the body by wrapping around.
example: The addition of integers is unchecked, so wraparound occurs if the resulting value is beyond the representable range.
etymology: From wrap + around.

definition: Someone who demolishes or dismantles buildings as a job.
example: Home wrecker / marriage wrecker / party wrecker.
etymology: From wreck + -er.

definition: Small Asiatic and African bird; constructs nests like those of tailorbirds.
Obtain by seizing forcibly or violently, also metaphorically.
example: Wrest the knife from his hands.
etymology: From Middle English wresten, wrasten, wræsten, from Old English wrǣstan (“to twist forcibly, wrench”), from Proto-Germanic *wraistijaną, (compare Proto-Germanic *wrīhaną (“to turn, wind;

definition: The act of wiggling.
etymology: From wrig + -le (frequentative suffix). Compare Dutch wriggelen (“to wriggle, squirm”), Low German wriggeln (“to wriggle”).

definition: Marked by wrinkles.
example: Tired travelers in wrinkled clothes.
etymology: From wrinkle + -y.

definition: A watch that is worn strapped to the wrist.
etymology: From wrist + watch.

definition: Being two more than twenty.
Being four more than twenty.
Water travel for pleasure.
A cap with a flat circular top and a visor.
A measure or standard used for comparison.
example: On what kind of yardstick is he basing his judgment?
etymology: From yard + stick.

definition: Ubiquitous strong-scented mat-forming Eurasian herb of wasteland, hedgerow or pasture having narrow serrate leaves and small usually white florets; widely naturalized in North America.
etymology: Origin unknown. Perhaps imitative of the bird's cry; compare yaffle, hewhole.

definition: A young child who is just beginning to walk.
example: A yearling lamb.
etymology: From Middle English yerling, yerlyng, equivalent to year + -ling. Cognate with Dutch jaarling (“yearling”), German Jährling (“yearling”).

definition: Greatly desired.
Eurasian perennial herb with hairy divided leaves and yellow flowers; naturalized in North America.
Climbing deciduous shrub with fragrant yellow (later orange) flowers in terminal whorls; southeastern United States.
Pigment consisting of a limonite mixed with clay and silica.
Easily frightened.
etymology: From yellow + bellied; see yellowbelly.

definition: Officer in the (ceremonial) bodyguard of the British monarch.
An academy for the advanced study of Jewish texts (primarily the Talmud).
etymology: From Yiddish ישיבה (yeshive), from Hebrew יְשִׁיבָה (y'shivá, “sitting”).

definition: The time that has elapsed.
etymology: From yester- + year.

definition: Time long past.
example: This word comes from the days of yore.

definition: The young of certain carnivorous mammals such as the bear or wolf or lion.
Any of several evergreen plants of the genus Yucca having usually tall stout stems and a terminal cluster of white flowers; warmer regions of North America.
etymology: Variant of yuca, sometimes said to be from Kari'na yuca (“cassava (Manihot esculenta)”), but this latter appears to be a ghost word.

definition: Large ornamental tropical American tree with bipinnate leaves and globose clusters of flowers with crimson stamens and seed pods that are eaten by cattle.
etymology: From Cariban.

definition: Ludicrous, foolish.
etymology: From Middle French zani, zanni, from Italian zanni (“a kind of masked clown character”), from Zanni, a Venetian form of Giovanni. Doublet of Zanni, John, and Giovanni.

definition: A fervent and even militant proponent of something.
etymology: Initially only found as Middle English zelote, an epithet of Simon the Zealot, acquiring its current senses in the 16th and 17th centuries.

definition: Inch long mollusk imported accidentally from Europe; clogs utility inlet pipes and feeds on edible freshwater mussels.
example: Zebra mussels are causing significant problems as an invasive species in North America.

definition: Having short sharp turns or angles.
Very large indeterminate number.
example: A zillion people were there.

definition: A colorless water-soluble powder; used as a mordant or to preserve wood or for the electrodeposition of zinc.
A fastener for locking together two toothed edges by means of a sliding tab.
Quick and energetic.
etymology: From zip (“to move in haste; to make (something) move quickly”) + -y (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘having the quality of’).

definition: A common mineral occurring in small crystals; chief source of zirconium; used as a refractory when opaque and as a gem when transparent.
etymology: From German Zirkon, possibly via French zircon, formed in the 1780s from Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn), borrowed from Middle Persian zlgwn' (/⁠zargōn⁠/). Doublet of jargoon.

definition: A white crystalline oxide; used in refractories and in insulation and abrasives and enamels and glazes.
(anatomy) any encircling or beltlike structure.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin zōna. Doublet of zone.

definition: Relating to or of the nature of a zone.
example: The zonal frontier.
etymology: First attested 1865–70, from zone + -al.

definition: A specialist in the branch of biology dealing with animals.
etymology: From zoology + -ist.
